Festive Reception in Honour of Leib Jaffe.

Yesterday at 3,50 in the afternoon the director of „Keren Hayesod“, the Hebrew poet Leib Jaffe, arrived in Będzin by train. At the railway station and around the square hundreds of people from all strata of the Jewish population gathered. But because the reception committee had not taken care of order, chaos reigned and the reception was not as it should have been.
At the station Mr. Jaffe was greeted by the „Agudat ha-Tsiyonim“, „Mizrachi“, „Hitachdut“, „Hakoach“, the Right Poale Zion, „Chiza“[?], the Artisans' Association, and by delegations from the surrounding towns.
The orchestra played the Polish and the Jewish anthems and, accompanied by hundreds of people, the guest was escorted in a great crush, to the sounds of the orchestra, to the Hotel „Bristol“.
In front of the hotel a crowd of a thousand had gathered. Among them all the youth organisations — among them „Hakoach“, „Brit Trumpeldor“, „Ha-Shomer ha-Tahor“[?] — in their uniforms and with blue-and-white flags.
Mr. Jaffe comes out on the balcony of the hotel and, after the playing of the Polish and Jewish anthems, Mr. Jaffe delivers the following short greeting:
My sisters and brothers! To this cold, snow-covered town I bring you a greeting from our Land. From your sisters and brothers who are building our future. During my stay in Będzin I shall have occasion to tell you of the great light that shines in our Land — be greeted!
Then a march-past (défilade) of the youth takes place and the demonstration disperses.
In the evening a festive academy took place in the „Nowości“[?], in which representatives of the municipal authorities also took part.
A more detailed report in the next issue.
First Session of the Będzin City Council. / Mr. Fürstenberg — Vice-Chairman of the City Council.

Yesterday evening the first session of the Będzin City Council took place. On the agenda was the election of 1) the chairman of the City Council. 3) [sic, for 2)] the vice-chairman and 3) a secretary.
The session naturally aroused great interest. Although admission was by entry ticket[?], a large number nevertheless gathered in the „gallery“.
At 4,15 the vice-president, Mr. Rubinlicht, opens the session, explains the agenda and proceeds to the election procedure.
Before the elections are begun, Mr. Fajgier[?] (Left Poale Zion) makes a statement that his group will not take part in the elections.
The oldest councillor, Mr. M. Sztajer, and the youngest, Mr. M. B. Rotenberg, are invited onto the scrutiny (vote-counting) commission.
The elections give the following result: as chairman (with 23 votes) the hitherto chairman of the City Council, Mr. Żebrowski, is elected; as vice-chairman (23 votes) Director Mr. Sz. Fürstenberg; and as secretary Mr. Szkutnik (N.D.), 20 votes.

Jubilee Concert of Joseph Winogradow in Będzin.

Extraordinary interest has been aroused by the great jubilee concert of the famous Jewish singer Joseph Winogradow, which takes place on Thursday the 10th of this month in the „Korso“[?]. Winogradow, who began his artistic career as a poor boy without residence rights in Moscow and rose to the rank of an Imperial singer, is today one of the most popular people in the world. For almost a quarter of a century Winogradow stood at the top of the greatest Western European and Russian opera stages and, also [lit. „also in“] with his colossal dramatic baritone and fiery temperament, was everywhere crowned as a first-class operatic force. But at the very height of his career he leaves the Russian stage and devotes himself to the idea of creating a Jewish opera. He travels to London and stages there a whole series of operas in Yiddish, which attract everyone's attention. From then on he devotes himself mainly to Jewish music, and his concerts all over the world are a triumph for the artist. Winogradow captivates the audience with his singing; every song of his calls forth a storm of applause.

Grünbaum's "Squeal"

[Article — Jewish politics in Poland, the Sejm; followed by: radio; Katowice — aviation.] Dep. Grünbaum "squeals" — that is the knock-down argument of his old and new opponents.
Dep. Grünbaum has been "squealing" for a good many years now, and he himself has not yet grown hoarse. The Jewish street has not grown tired of hearing the "squeals", as the last Sejm elections proved. We have become a bit of Jewish politicians and a bit of Jewish journalists.
Are their ears so delicate that they cannot bear any loud tone? — No, they are afraid that the others, the deciding factors, have such delicate ears, and therefore one must speak to them quietly, pianissimo, with a little smile on the lips and with "przepraszam" ["I beg your pardon"] in front and behind.
Actually I am only trying to guess what the anti-Grünbaum side means, because after all the articles and speeches of the anti-squealers it is in no way clear to me what concretely they want. I therefore think that the truth is not being spoken out. We must therefore guess that they propose not to wage any struggle, but to "get by". I do not even know what "getting by" means when the other side does not want to go to any arbitration at all. The "anti-squeal" side could have had a case with its arguments if the deciding factors had, at the very least, sat down with them at the table and at least talked with them, discussed taxes, Jewish rights, the admission of Jews to state posts, recognition of the Jewish school system, etc., etc. Then it would have meant: with "squealers" the government does not want to talk, but with us — by all means. But the fact is that Dep. Reich has exactly the same "shraga" [?] as Dep. Grünbaum. So one must, it is said, try f i r s t with non-squealing tones. But such a thing has already been tried a hundred times, and better than Reich and even Kirszbraun want it. Jewish public emissaries have already danced on all fours, bowed themselves in three and begged — did they achieve anything more by it than the title of "Mah Yafit"?
And however hard the situation of the Jewish community is today, are we any better off than before merely because we do not dance "Mah Yafit"?
Certainly [printed "ourai"] today is a different time. New people stand at the helm of power. But everyone knows that at the helm of power today stand people of character. Marshal Piłsudski in particular hates servility from the depths of his soul. Even Premier Bartel, for all his elasticity as premier, has shown himself to be a man of character. These are people of struggle and not of servility. I see the ironic little smile that appeared on the Marshal's lips when one of the Jewish deputies, the president of the Warsaw kehilla, delivered at the Belweder, in the presence of thousands of Jewish children, the famous "Mi sheberakh" speech...
I do not intend to defend Grünbaum's camp. The "anti-squealers" do not direct their attack against Grünbaum's camp, in which are found Rabbi Rubinstein of Vilna, Sz. Budzyner of Łódź and R' Heszel Farbstein of Warsaw. The arrows are aimed directly at Dep. Grünbaum, and it is precisely the p e r s o n of Dep. Grünbaum that interests me here. It is a matter of the t o n e in which Dep. Grünbaum speaks — a tone that is truly foreign to the ear of some Jewish bourgeois representatives. Where does this tone come from?
I want to give my answer to that.
The Jewish minority in Poland suffers, in some respects, even more than other minorities. There are great masses who, because of their situation, are tremendously embittered. There are other strata which are less embittered; there are those who feel only wronged; and there is also a smaller stratum that does not feel badly off. With the others, all these tones find expression on the Sejm rostrum. It is quite different with the Jewish representation. There is not in the Sejm the Jewish demos that would give expression to the protest. And if you knew [?] the anger and fury felt in the poorest Jewish street — we have so many suffering and oppressed that they cannot even [?] speak, but a cry tears itself out of them, a s q u e a l. This squeal from the depths of the soul, "from the depths", cannot be given expression by the greater part of the Jewish deputies, because they personally feel differently.
Grünbaum is the only one who has an ear for what is happening in the Jewish street. And from time to time the s q u e a l breaks out of him. A squeal which ought to be made ten times sharper and more ruthless than Dep. Grünbaum does it. And if this Jewish "squealer" were in the Sejm, Dep. Grünbaum would not be "the worst", his head would not be demanded; the authoritative factors would argue that Grünbaum — by all means, but that other "squealer" — is impossible. And I am all the more convinced that Grünbaum's position would be different if the "real squealers" were also in the Sejm.
A. Szwarcer.

New Year's Eve and 'Our Brethren the Children of Israel'...

[Sosnowiec and Katowice — social life; humorous sketch on New Year's Eve.]
This year's New Year's Eve (Sylvester) was celebrated by "our brethren the children of Israel", especially those of Sosnowiec, according to all the rules. Though not as lavishly as in the former "years of plenty", people still rejoiced at the new year: they sang, danced, drank a glass of liquor and wished one another:
— "God willing, in a year's time — Sylvester in good health."
All that was missing were the words:
— "May you be inscribed for a good year"!
* *
On Monday evening, i.e. New Year's Eve, the preparations to welcome the new year were in full swing. At the "rezures" [?, apparently barbershops] people stood in the "queue"; many of those who shave only "in honour of Shabbat" had gone about with their "little beards" until Monday evening, in order to welcome the guest — 1929 — with a nicely shaven face.
The same was true at the ladies' hairdressers; our "palekhshkes" [?] too waited until the last minute and got ready as is proper, cleaned a bit of dirt out of their nails — one must show the new year that we have "clean hands"...
———
In all the restaurants and confectioneries "tables" were lacking. A "table" cost 50 gulden [złoty], apart from "little extras"...
Besides the restaurants and confectioneries there were also many New Year's Eve parties in private homes: people bought a bit of liquor, set up a gramophone and "conducted the Seder" until broad daylight.
The greatest celebration took place in Katowice, where all the tables, the reserved "places" [?], were snapped up already before Shabbat — all, naturally, by our brethren the children of Israel; only at the "Monopol" were there also a few "goyim". But as it later turned out, these were employees of the confectionery...
———
On Tuesday morning one saw couples wandering back, sleepy, exhausted, barely keeping on their feet...
They greeted the first morning of the year 1929 without signs of life and —
— masked...
L—cz.
"At Night in the Old Marketplace"

[Będzin — theatre; performance review.]
Dramatic poem in 3 acts by I. L. Peretz.
Staging and direction: Nukhimov [?].
Sets and costumes designed by Sadzki [?].
Music paraphrased by M. Kager.
The Jewish dramatic society "Muze" (Muse) in Będzin has undertaken to stage a very serious and sincere thing. Peretz's "At Night in the Old Marketplace" is one of the hardest problems in our life. Years ago, while the author was still among us, attempts were made to stage the dramatic work, but they did not last. The actors could not enter into and live with this hidden world, and the thing could not be carried out on the boards of the Yiddish theatre.
Now people have begun to understand Peretz better; they have begun to draw closer to the great artistic soul that eternalised Yiddish literature with so many pearls. Peretz wanted to save, at least for the museum, the Jews of Sabbaths and holidays. With all the delicacy of his artistic soul Peretz eternalised for us the old generation, which remains for our children a deep riddle of the past.
"At Night in the Old Marketplace" is thus for the masses an almost incomprehensible problem, which in any case demands much explanation and illumination. "At Night in the Old Marketplace" therefore cannot be played the way it came from Peretz's artistic pen, and so we see here only fragments, transformations, short scenically chopped-up little pictures, which nevertheless say so much and carry you over into another world. You watch the conversations, the rebuking speeches, and then you listen, bewitched, to what is mirrored before your eyes. The thing somehow pulls you along into the deep abyss, and at the same time you become absorbed in these souls and would like to find a solution to this difficult problem.
And just such a thing was undertaken by the "Muze", which actually consists merely of amateurs, who could have been forgiven had they not performed it as well as professional actors — for we hold to the principle that for amateurs it is enough that they want to play good literary things; for dilettantes the mere good will to stage pure artistic things suffices us.
How did the "Muze" stage "At Night in the Old Marketplace"? How did the sets, costumes, direction and music look? On the whole, good. We see that the people approached the thing with full sanctity and reverence; the whole ensemble strove to embody Peretz's great work, and they performed the dramatic poem without a prompter.
In places the voices were too weak, and the same was true of the music. We also think the costumes consist of too many garish colours, which does not harmonise when we imagine the dead crawling out of their graves. Likewise the searching for the nails was too weak. That fragment should have come out considerably stronger; it should have carried the auditorium along.
On the other hand one must welcome the fact that we hear a beautiful Yiddish; one sees that everyone understands the task of his role and the responsibility for an artistic production, which we value so highly. At times we saw excellent mimicry from Messrs. Abramczyk and Kleiner. The children, too, were good in their roles and also understood them [?].
On the whole, however, the thing succeeded all round, and some defects can be corrected. The main thing is that the serious problem was approached with understanding and with sanctity.
It goes without saying that first and foremost a "yasher koach" is due to the leaders, comrades Nukhimov, Sadzki, Kager and Fidrikh, who invested so much effort so that the thing should come out as it should.
Also to be welcomed is the order that reigned in the hall (especially in Będzin). Thanks to it, it became possible to carry out such a serious thing, which demands enormous calm and order.
And therefore, if we always approach the Yiddish stage seriously and with love, we will also be able to hope that the audience will meet us halfway.
R. Let.
The Tasks at the Present Moment

[Trade — taxes; editorial.]
(A timely word for every citizen.)
When a tax assessment comes round and people learn afterwards how much they have been assessed, for instance in the turnover tax [„abrotowe“ — podatek obrotowy], a man is beside himself when he finds out that he has been wronged. People start writing appeals [„rekursn“] and storming the „Ferayn“ [the association, i.e. the merchants' union], and all this lasts until a fresh tax comes along, by which one again feels wronged, and one writes — too late [?] — more appeals, and so it goes on in order from one tax assessment to the next.
And as practice has shown us, the assessments grow larger from year to year, regardless of whether this or that firm did more or less business during the year; and many a firm, when it draws up its balance sheet, when it looks around to see where it stands in the world, how much expenditure and income it had in the course of the year — its owner feels anything but easy at heart. He loses courage at such a moment, he is beside himself, and the question arises: what aim do I have in life, what am I working for and for whom am I working, if the expenses are greater than the income?
We do not know what things look like elsewhere; possibly in Galicia, Poznań and Upper Silesia, where the population was brought up in the „constitutional countries“, whose citizens enjoyed cultural education and political maturity, it is different; there, as we know, every business is set up in the European manner, and such a merchant can certainly [?] find his way better: he buys better, he is versed in making the calculation, he knows how to work out what percentage administration and other expenses cost him on every article, and on top of that he does not forget to add his profit.
It is quite different with us in Congress Poland: we here were brought up under the Russian regime, where we paid almost no taxes, or at best the tax was so small, so minimal, that nobody reckoned with it and it occupied no position at all as an expense for the merchant. Moreover, under Russian rule people were so backward that there was no need to modernise the business — let alone when it would have cost money. And in exactly the same conditions almost all middling merchants and even small industrialists find themselves to this very day, not to speak of petty traders and artisans.
Nowadays we are citizens of the free Polish Republic, and as such the government must tax its citizens with higher taxes, for one must not forget that Poland rose from the dead [„tkhiyes hameysim“] before our very eyes, and precisely because of that she has needed greater expenditure, which must be taken from the citizens.
It would still be quite bearable, though, if the tax system were adapted to all inhabitants of the Republic. It would be bearable if village and town, the landowner [„porets“] and the peasant, the industrialist and the merchant were measured with one. and the same yardstick [?], if the tax system were thus rationally distributed among all citizens of the Republic — but this is far from so. Much has already been said about the town having to maintain the village, and since the Jews live exclusively in the towns, it necessarily follows that we pay the largest share of taxes; in addition, at every tax assessment one has in view first of all the open shop, that is the shopkeeper and the artisan, and therefore it is no wonder that precisely the small and middling ones are regularly under the yoke of taxes.
One is not finished with one tax and a fresh tax is already on its way.
In the past, when one was wronged with too large a tax assessment, the wronged party was sure that it would be reduced — it must surely have been a mistake; after all it is not possible that because of paying a tax they would let him go under. But now one already sees that nothing came of the hope, everything has remained as before, and now one knows at least [„akhol-poním“] that one must weep and pay.
And therefore, since there is no hope that the taxes will be reduced, the question arises: how can one exist and at the same time pay the burdensome taxes?
As we have already pointed out above, we are not accustomed to conducting trade in a modern way. We know that an article or a metre of goods costs so-and-so much, we add so-and-so many percent as profit and are content with that. But one forgets that on this very „profit“ one loses when one adds in the taxes and other expenses which the firm must bear on its shoulders.
Actually, when the government found the merchant public [„oylem hamiskher“] in such a state, it was its duty to teach its citizens to trade and produce, so that they would understand how to calculate the goods and stay on their feet [?]. But it did not do so, and therefore there is no other way than to become conscious ourselves, to become mature ourselves, to know how to calculate ourselves, and for that the first important thing is to hold the pen in hand: write everything down, calculate everything, note everything, reckon every expense.
We must pay taxes and we also want to pay them, but we also want to live and not be torn up by the roots. The time has therefore come when one must start keeping books — official books for the authorities, which will prove our entire situation: how we stand, how much expenditure and income we have.
We know perfectly well that this is no easy thing for average people, who are constantly harried and plagued, who cannot keep the books themselves and also cannot afford to pay a bookkeeper to take over the keeping of these books. But there is no other way. We see that the government wants it, and only this system can ease our situation, for we do want to pay taxes according to a correct assessment, so that we do not lose the ground from under our feet.
One must think it over seriously, and not only think it over but really set about energetically carrying out the urgent proposal. True, we are not used to it; perhaps the devil is not as terrible as we paint him; moreover one must not forget that „all beginnings are hard“. Let us take it up, let us consider the matter with full seriousness — and then we will see [—] that there is no other way [—] and that the [proposal ?] can become a reality.
For this purpose the members and the sections must gather in their associations and demand that the managing boards come to their aid on this point.
Now is the right time: after the New Year one can begin to put book-keeping into practice, so one should not neglect this right moment. And in this case one should remember that mere words [„dibúrim“] will not help at all here; the time has therefore come when our situation can be improved only if we show the will and the deeds.
L. Sz.
A Greeting from Eretz Israel

[Będzin — Leib Jaffe's visit.] The darling of the Jewry of Eretz Israel and of Poland, the great Jew and leader, the poet Leib Jaffe, who for 40 years has carried in his heart the sorrows of the Jewish people, from his very earliest childhood years to this day, is coming to us and will bring us a greeting from the present-day reality of Eretz Israel.
His visit is the most pleasant surprise for our town, for he has left his permanent place of residence, Jerusalem, only for a short time, and he cannot possibly satisfy the requests of all his admirers throughout Poland to visit their towns; and we are proud that Będzin is one of the few towns that have had the great honour of seeing and honouring the stubbornly devoted [?] people's activist of extraordinary self-sacrifice, Leib Jaffe. For him nothing in life exists except people and land, land and people. From his childhood years to this day he has been spreading this lofty ideal in the world. — He cannot rest when he sees that the people does too little for the upbuilding of Eretz Israel. He forgets himself entirely, his health, which has been weakened by 40 years of strenuous, tireless work; he forgets the high position he holds in the movement as director of the Keren Hayesod head office in Jerusalem, and even his wife and children — he is wholly swallowed up by his life's aim: "Et achai anokhi mevakesh" ("I seek my brothers"), and with his eternal youthful enthusiasm he awakens the people, wandering across the whole world, seeking his brothers everywhere.
And with this "I seek my brothers" Leib Jaffe comes to us, and we Jews of Zagłębie welcome the distinguished guest, from whom we receive a greeting from the reality of Eretz Israel.
How the New Year Is Greeted Among Various Peoples

New Year is a universal holiday among all the nations of the world. That is self-evident: every people divides time into years, and the beginning of the year is naturally a holiday everywhere.
But not all peoples celebrate the day in the same way. Every nation and tongue celebrates its new year in its own peculiar, characteristic manner. At the beginning of the year every people reflects on what it has accomplished in the past year in the fields it considers important, and it holds ceremonies that mirror the soul of the people concerned.
It will be interesting to tell how various peoples greet their New Year.
Well, how Jews celebrate Rosh Hashanah one need not tell Jews; among no people is religion so deeply rooted in life as among the Jews, and the result is that the Jewish Rosh Hashanah is a thoroughly religious festival.
The ancient Romans used to begin their year in winter. In the very oldest times their year began on 21 December, but the famous ruler Julius Caesar changed their calendar and fixed New Year on the first of January. That is why the civil year begins to this day on 1 January, as a legacy of Rome.
How did the Romans celebrate their New Year? Mainly with dissoluteness. People would put on masks, hold masked balls and get drunk, until they could no longer tell "cursed be Haman" from "blessed be Mordecai". Their New Year was a kind of Purim, except that all sorts of carousals ("hulyankes") also took place; they also used to send each other gifts, though there is no mention of any gifts to the poor. The officials of the land used to take up their offices on that day, and it was the custom to send fine presents to the new magistrates. On New Year the emperors used to receive a pound of gold from their subjects.
Some days before New Year, as a preparation for the real holiday, the Romans used to spend merry days dedicated to the god Saturn. The chief characteristic of the Saturnalia (as those days were called) was harlotry. Since the Romans were steeped in lewdness, in their month of Elul (a thousand distinctions apart) and their Rosh Hashanah, too, were holidays for harlotry.
The ancient Babylonians used to celebrate their New Year at the beginning of spring, at the time when the night is exactly as long as the day. That is approximately 22 March. The Babylonians were the first to notice that on that date, 22 March, the sun crosses the equator (a kind of circle in the sky). The Babylonian New Year festival used to last eleven days. The Babylonians used to gather in their temples at New Year and read a heroic poem which told how their idol Marduk (printed "Madurkh") killed a devil and then introduced laws and order into the world. This Marduk was the Babylonian sun-god and he ruled especially over spring. Today's critics interpret the heroic poem, which used to be sung in Marduk's honour, as meaning that in spring the sun kills the winter, which is represented as a devil. Many monuments and vessels have been found in Babylon that show pictures of Marduk slaying the devil with a weapon.
In ancient Egypt New Year used to fall at different times of the year — sometimes in summer, sometimes in winter. To us that looks strange; we are used to a holiday always being at roughly the same time. But the ancient Egyptians did not have a good calendar. Their year consisted of twelve months, each month had exactly thirty days, and every year they added another five days. That means every year consisted of 365 days. They knew nothing of intercalation; since the solar year is a little longer than exactly 365 days, they fell behind by one day every four years; in 121 years their New Year fell a month too early, and in 1461 years they lost an entire year. The Egyptians used to celebrate New Year by bringing sacrifices to the gods.
The Persians, as is well known, worship fire. To this day there are still members of this ancient Persian religion in India and in Persia. This faith recognises two chief gods: Hormiz, the god of light, and Ahormiz (as printed; i.e. Ahriman), the god of darkness.
The Persians spend the last days of the old year giving charity and praying. On New Year they rise early, say special prayers at home and immerse themselves ritually. Then they put on new clothes and go off to the fire-temples, where they revere the holy fire that burns perpetually on their altar. The Persians believe that if a person does not perform this ceremony for the new year, his soul after death will not be able to cross the bridge that leads from the earth to heaven. After the service they go to wish a happy holiday to all their relatives and good friends, and during these visits they hold a ceremony of giving one another "shalom aleichem". Afterwards they devote the day to merrymaking. The new garments they put on for New Year they do not wear the whole year; right after the holiday they give the clothes away to servants and poor people.
Among the Chinese, New Year is the most important holiday of the year. All debts must be paid before the New Year begins. For New Year they buy themselves new clothes. They make merry with thousands of Chinese paper lanterns covered with coloured pictures of landscapes.
In Japan New Year is celebrated with great feasts. People decorate doors and gates with symbolic objects.
The "Higrusn"[?] celebrate New Year with song. They play balalaikas and give dramatic performances in which Hungarian[?] women take part. Afterwards girls dance with bottles of water around a fire and sing merrily.
On the Threshold of the New Year

It is not one who complains, but a second and a third as well, that the situation is a hard one and that it is moreover becoming ever harder and worse.
Here we are now entering a new year, and of course one enters the new year, as usual, with fine hopes and bright prospects — and who else knows how to embellish life for himself as we do? Who else lives with so many hopes and with such strong faith in a better and finer future as we Jews do? And it is no longer news that faith and hope are what refresh the Jew; yes, the faith and the hope that someday it will get better give us strength and courage to live on in further hopes and to bear on our exhausted shoulders all manner of heavy suffering and torments that come against us on our hard path of life, which grows ever harder and worse, while the fine prospects and bright horizons grow paler and paler before our eyes.
We have only just stepped across the threshold of the European new year — and with what worries and pain, hardship and responsibility we take over the new year 1929, into which we would so much like to enter with many good hopes, as human beings and as citizens!
We want to be good citizens in Poland, and we strive to be such; we bear, and want to bear, on our shoulders all the burdens of citizenship, however heavy they may be for us. We also strive by every possible means to adapt ourselves to the proper regulations, and in return we demand only one thing: that we be treated as citizens, that we be given the proper civic rights not only on paper but in reality, in life. We know very well that in free, independent Poland there officially exist no restrictions whatsoever concerning us Jews — and yet how they do exist in life, what restrictions we meet at every step!
We have in Zagłębie several hundred Jewish families who live by carrying various goods around Upper Silesia from house to house, content[?] with a smaller profit, so that the worker and the clerk buy the goods more cheaply and more conveniently. Is that then a sin? Are there any regulations whatsoever saying that Jews may not carry goods around for sale? And yet they are hunted and harassed, and even spied upon[?], as if they were the dregs of society and first-class parasites. One would think these people work hard, and dragging the bundles on their shoulders from one village to the next is no light matter either, so that before they live to see the piece of bread they have earned they first suffer through fears and sweat. One would think a government should be glad to know it has such hard-working citizens, who shrink from nothing but toil hard and bitterly just to be able to make an honest living — and besides, they do hold the proper licences (patents) and also pay the taxes imposed on them. Why then are these people hounded, who seek a livelihood in an honest way? Why is a clique of riff-raff allowed to set itself up and incite, openly and freely, by every sort of legal and illegal means, against people who want to work, fulfil their civic duties and at the same time lead a modest and honest life? What does anyone have against these people, a category that brings every country so much benefit?
That is what the situation looks like for our brethren who seek their piece of bread in Upper Silesia — for whom it would be a blessing if not so many prickly thorns were laid on their path.
If the Upper Silesian authorities really and sincerely wished to concern themselves with this category of common people, their only task in that case would be to check whether the pedlars observe the proper regulations with regard to the government, whether they buy the proper licences the law demands of them, whether they pay their taxes as citizens; and besides that, the authorities there would have one more responsible mission, namely to check that undesirable elements do not sometimes slip in among them who, under the shield of peddling, could swindle and cheat naive people. That is a matter one really ought to be concerned with. But since one is dealing with honest people, with people whose only task is to work, pay taxes and thereby make an honest living — why then should irresponsible individuals be allowed to disrupt legal trade, which is permitted in all countries and places?
And if all this is in order, if the peddling is conducted honestly and permissibly, it is the duty of the authorities in Upper Silesia not to allow incitement and the spreading of illegal antisemitic propaganda among the masses, for whom the antisemites take pains to invent incredible "facts" full of poison and hatred between Christians and Jews.
It is understood that in a free constitutional state the interests of every single citizen must be protected without distinction of faith and religion, and if this is disturbed by undesirable elements, the authorities must in that case show themselves and not allow the first instances of incitement, which can lead to the worst conflicts.
Until now the authorities have not reacted properly to these undesirable phenomena and have thus given the antisemites the opportunity to continue their dangerous games in all their size and splendour.
There is nothing more to say. No one here needs to be convinced of the danger of the situation; if the authorities look on at all this with indifference, every possible means must be taken to convince them that the continuation of their hatred and enmity leads to very sad results for us.
We have taken just one single grain to illustrate the sad state of our life; we have delved into just one little corner here — and that is already enough for one to hear the deep groan that bursts from the heart of the Jewish soul.
Yes, we have only just stepped over the threshold of the new year, and we would certainly, certainly not want to lay heavy stones upon the Jewish organism — for that is just why we are Jews: we go firmly and surely with strong faith and with hope for a finer and better tomorrow, even though the prospects are so hidden from us.
Selekt.
The Year 1928 — in General and Polish Politics

[World and Polish politics — review of the year 1928.]
The year just ended stood under the sign of peace, disarmament and arbitration. All year long people talked about peace, held conferences, negotiated and concluded agreements meant to guarantee eternal peace, which is so longed and thirsted for. To preserve peace, efforts were made to settle all the difficulties and obstacles that hold up the "And it shall come to pass in the end of days" and that could call up the spectre of a new, cruel world war.
One obstacle was posed by Germany, demanding the liberation of the Rhineland from the French occupation, which had been fixed for 15 years in the Treaty of Versailles as the guarantee securing peace on the part of the German state. This evacuation question was dealt with by the League of Nations, and yet to this day the matter has not been positively settled, and the question does not leave the agenda of the League of Nations.
The second obstacle is the disarmament question. It was demanded that states should not maintain any standing army, ready to throw itself onto the battlefield at the slightest political conflict. As long as — it was argued, rightly — the army is not abolished, the danger of war always threatens. In this respect the League of Nations began to do something, but all the same cruel preparations for a new war are being made in secret. Still fresh in memory is the terrible explosion at the gas factories in Hamburg, which produce chemical agents capable of destroying all of mankind. We still remember the crisis that broke out in the German government over the building of the German armoured ship, which is to cost up to 10 million German marks.
France too has begun to build huge fortresses and fortifications on its borders against Germany and Italy.
On 17 August 1928 the American Secretary of State Kellogg proposed concluding a pact on peace, to which 15 states acceded. On the above-mentioned day the representatives of the greatest nations gathered in Paris and with great ceremony signed Kellogg's anti-war pact, which is to be a blessing for tormented and exhausted mankind.
Poland, which has great merits in the field of peace, suffers many troubles from its eastern and western neighbours. Lithuania, in the person of its Foreign Minister Voldemaras, has had the urge to sharpen the sword and intrigues against and provokes Poland at every step, demanding Wilno, which has been recognised [as] Poland's. Soviet Russia, which is interested in the Polish-Lithuanian conflict, has several times spread provocative press alarms about a war with Lithuania and about Marshal Piłsudski's marching on Kowno. All negotiations between the two states in Königsberg and the interventions of the League of Nations have so far not succeeded because of the obstinate attitude of the war-minded Voldemaras.
Germany too has had the urge for a new conflict with Poland. The German President Hindenburg, while in German Upper Silesia, said at a large public meeting that Germany will never consent to the partition of Upper Silesia and will never recognise the decision of the League of Nations Council of 20 October 1921 on giving Poland a large part of Upper Silesia. Hindenburg's stand against Poland caused an uproar in the political world. The German nationalist "Volksbund" in Upper Silesia, under the impression of Hindenburg's provocative speech, began to conduct an anti-Polish campaign.
At the last session of the League of Nations Council in Lugano the Polish Foreign Minister Zaleski strongly protested and reacted to the inflammatory speech of the German President and to the anti-Polish actions of the German "Volksbund". Minister Zaleski's speech at the Council led to a sharp exchange of words between him and the German Minister Stresemann. Because of this conflict the last session in Lugano broke up without having dealt with the points of the agenda.
———
All pacifist attempts have no real value, and the air is full of explosive material.
The new war will be a horrible one, by means of air and gas. Supposedly in the name of science one wants to master stern nature, but in essence this is done under the cloak of militarism.
Nobile's unsuccessful flight expedition to the North Pole, the fluttering of the Italian Fascist flag in the snows of the North, the tragic death of the well-known explorer Amundsen, the death of the French Minister of Air Communications, the Jew Bokanowski, Kubala's and Idzikowski's flight across the Atlantic — they aim at accustoming nature to the purposes of war.
———
The year 1928 was celebrated all over the world with great joy, because in this year 10 years had passed since the peace was concluded which put an end to the last cruel world war. Many nations, Poland among them, celebrated the 10th jubilee of their revival, independence and sovereignty. On the threshold of the new year we must wish that in the coming year peace should not remain merely a beautiful illusion and a sweet dream, but should be realised in life.
Themis, the Goddess of Justice

A Greek legend.
Yiddish by Y. Deutscher.
The goddess of justice is represented with bound eyes.
On the castle hill in Athens there was a commotion. They were celebrating there the festival of the goddess of justice.
It was in those heroic times when the gods of Greece had not yet abandoned men and used to come down to them in order to take part not only in their celebrations but also in their work.
The men of Athens sat down in a half-circle under the immortal olive tree. Below them stood children and old men, women and charmingly beautiful girls.
The other part of the circle was occupied by the gods themselves, wrapped in robes[?] and lit by the rays of the sun.
Not a single one of the gods was missing from the festive assembly, and over all the gods reigned Zeus, the one who rules with his gaze, whose eyes shone with a reflection of wisdom and might.
But it was not at the highest god that everyone was looking. In the middle, between gods and men, stood upon a rock Themis, the goddess of justice. Beside her stood her three daughters, gazing with love into their mother's eyes.
The figure of the goddess of justice shone with beauty and majesty. A heavenly stillness reigned on her brow, and her wide-open eyes gazed into infinity.
In one hand she held a sword, in the other — a scale with two pans. On these pans the thoughts of all the gods and men present were concentrated, and at these pans, which hung in the air, everyone was looking, for on this scale-pan depended the fate of the living and of the dead. One saw how human wickedness fell with a heavy groan onto the pan of evil deeds. That pan filled more and more and sank ever deeper. The second pan, however, the one meant for good deeds, rose higher and higher, light as a swallow's wing. The pan of evil deeds grew ever heavier and sank and sank.
Suddenly the hand of the goddess trembled.
Among the serpents of human wickedness, among the gall, blood and misery on the pan of evil deeds, there appeared the pale, crumpled[?] face of human misfortune, aching and full of troubles.
With great terror the face looked at the goddess. It became so quiet that not even a fly moved its wings, not a leaf fell from any tree, and everyone held their breath.
Themis saw the human misfortune on the pan of evil deeds. A shadow of sorrow covered her brow, she lowered her head and two large tears fell from her eyes onto the pan of good deeds. That pan wavered and began to sink so deep that it outweighed the pan of evil deeds. Everyone was silent — "What has happened there?" — called out Zeus, the lord of the gods.
The goddess was silent, but her daughters began to explain!
— Lord and Father! At the root of human wickedness lies human misfortune. This misfortune is even greater than the wickedness itself, but the tears of our mother, the tears of compassion, weigh more than evil and misfortune together.
Zeus gave a sign, and one of the gods, whose task it was to watch over the conscience of gods and men, went up to the goddess Themis and bound her eyes.
From that time on the goddess of justice does not see what happens on the scale-pan. Only when the sighs of human misfortune reach her does she tremble like a young tree in a storm, and the scale in her hand trembles too,
The Rebbe's Son — A Jewish historical novel by Yaakov Zimmerman. 15.

— Give us your blessing! — both princes now asked, rising from the ground.

Rabbi Shimon granted their wish and blessed them.

An almost heavenly rapture now rested on the face of the old R' Shimon the Tzaddik. When he raised his half-extinguished eyes to heaven, his lips quietly murmuring a prayer, he said aloud to the two princes, who stood before him with bowed heads:

— May the Master of the Universe, who gave a great victory to our forefather Abraham over the four kings, help you too to defeat your enemies. May your sword be just like lightning, and may your foes be blinded by it; may your word be thunder, by which they shall be hurled down to the earth; may your spirit always be right and clear, and may your foot always be on the road to victory. May triumph accompany you in every battle, until you have entirely overcome your enemies. May the greatest blessings and successes and a long peace be the reward for your heroic deeds. May the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob always be with you, amen!

After such a spiritual exertion a deep weariness came over the old and feeble R' Shimon the Tzaddik, and he fell back powerless into his armchair. For a few minutes everything in the room was so still that one could hear the heavy breathing of his chest.

But suddenly the young lad Yosef broke the silence. His face was now red, for every drop of blood in him was seething and boiling, and from great agitation he could hardly bring his words out. But at last, more blurting them out of himself than saying them, he uttered the words:

— Grandfather! Let me go with these men of war into battle! Allow me to accompany the noble princes in the fight for my people and fatherland! Let me too help defend my defenceless and unfortunate brothers and take revenge for their blood, shed in vain. Have no fear at all, I am no longer a child. I feel within me that my arm is strong enough, my eye sharp and my foot sure! I want to be an example to my young Jewish brothers, that in us too flows warm blood that scorns death. Grandfather! Do not hold me back, I can no longer stay sitting quietly at home. Allow me to go!

With hopeful suspense Yosef now gazed at the figure of his blind grandfather. But he also noticed the shining eyes of his sister Tzipora, as if she had already consented to his request and thereby expressed her approval. He also saw how his relative, Yona the physician, stood beaming with pride at his words. He also felt upon himself the friendly glances of both princes, who looked at him with admiration. But he also saw the figure of his dear old grandmother, who sat waiting with bated breath for the decisive words of her beloved husband.

All present were all ears when the old R' Shimon the Tzaddik now made himself heard:

— Your wish will be fulfilled, my dear child! You have a right to follow the voice of your heart, which calls you to such noble resolutions. I know, I know, I feel it, that our people Israel will attain great honour and help through you. Right after Shavuot you will be able to go, together with Yona, wherever you desire. I myself will also be with you. But first I still want to call upon and inspire our Jewish brothers not to spare their goods and chattels, their fortune and also their blood for the holy work of the defence of us all.

Great joy now seized all present. Young Yosef did not know what to do with himself for joy; he kept on kissing and hugging his old blind grandfather. Only the old grandmother wept quietly to herself, for she did not want to disturb anyone with her weeping.

— Many thanks to you, noble and holy man! — said the old prince[?] Wiśniowiecki. — You need not worry at all about your grandson. I will keep him close to me and will not take my eyes off him. And now farewell! Pray to your God and at the same time do everything that must be done for the welfare and good of us all. Be Jews and also steadfast men! If I am not at all mistaken, and all Jews are such as those I see here now, I may be sure that the days of the robber-hetman Chmielnicki and his band are already numbered... Farewell, all of you!

Both princes now took a warm leave and went off; almost everyone in the house went out to accompany them to the carriage. Meanwhile the coachman Kaminski had quite a bit of work holding the fiery, well-rested horses in place. Luckily for him, however, Chaim the wagoner soon caught sight of him; he had come here to thank his Christian friend once more for all the kindnesses he had shown him in the last bad days.

Ayzik Yekeles was also here now; something had driven him here so that he might send with the prince, who was now leaving for Kraków, a warm greeting to his wife and daughter.

As if thunderstruck he now stood still when, to his great surprise, he recognised in the young prince the young officer whom he had met on the Vistula bridge and who had told him his dream, that in Kraków, at his, Ayzik Yekeles's, home, a treasure was hidden in the baking oven...

He wanted to open his mouth and say something to the young prince, but at that moment the coachman Kaminski gave a shake and a tug at the reins, and the horses with the carriage began to run and disappeared.

But before this happened, the young prince still managed to catch a friendly glance with the beautiful Tzipora. Now she no longer lowered her eyes before him. In a soft[?] voice she took leave of him and of the old prince and wished them a good journey.

———

The German, Paul Herger, was now sitting by the sickbed of our acquaintance R' Eliyahu. For quite a while a deep silence reigned in the room. Each of them was lost in his own thoughts. The wounded R' Eliyahu was now — in his thoughts — at home, which lay not far from the places where the most dangerous battles were being fought between the Polish soldiers and the Ukrainian bandits under Chmiel's leadership. His heart kept telling him that his dear and beloved ones were surely in great danger.

Paul Herger, too, grew more and more pensive and felt greatly embarrassed. Instinctively he felt how R' Eliyahu wanted to creep into his soul and tear out from there such things as he now wished to hide from him.

The silence was now broken.

— Paul Herger! — R' Eliyahu now began to say to him. — I feel, and my heart tells me, that you are hiding something from me. A great misfortune has befallen me, you know about it, but you do not want to tell me.

What Is the Yiddish Scientific Institute (YIVO)?

[Culture — Jewish scholarship.] (Sent in to the "Zaglembier Tsaytung").
Lately so much has been written among us about the Yiddish Scientific Institute (YIVO), so much is said about the publications it has issued and is issuing, but not everyone knows what YIVO actually is and what it represents. We therefore consider it necessary to acquaint our readers with the enormously important activity of this institution, still quite new among us, all the more so as not long ago, in December of last year [p. y. = "last year", i.e. December 1928], it was 3 years since YIVO began its actual activity.
The organising committee of YIVO, which was formed back in August 1925 and consisted of Dr. M. Weinreich [printed "Weigreich"], E. Tcherikower, Z. Reisen and N. Shtif, set itself the goal:
The Yiddish Scientific Institute must be: a) the centre of scholarly work in Yiddish and, first and foremost, the central authority for the research and development of the Yiddish language and literature; b) the place where new workers in the field of Jewish scholarship and culture are trained; c) the central registration point for Jewish cultural life in every corner of the world.
According to the plans of its founders and organisers, YIVO is soon to be transformed into an institution of higher learning. Up to this moment, however, a colossal work is meanwhile being carried on there, which among [other] peoples is done by the state, or at least with the help of large state subsidies.
We have had, and we have, various societies, each of which works in this or that field of Jewish scholarship and culture. But a society that would concentrate almost all branches of Jewish scholarship and culture — that we have not had until now!
One of the richest collections of Jewish folklore, a museum unique of its kind, an archive with the rarest documents, a bibliographical centre that registers the printed Jewish word of the whole world, philological, economic-statistical, historical and a whole series of other publications with the participation of the greatest Jewish scholars and researchers in every corner of the world — this and much more is, in brief, the fruit of 3 years of work of the Yiddish Scientific Institute.
Let us not forget that all this has been done without any secure sources of money, solely thanks to the devoted work of individuals [printed "yikhudim"].
The great work of the Institute has literally been done with paltry pennies. From summer 1925 to the end of 1928 the Institute spent about 30,000 zł., and even this sum was made up of small and irregular contributions.
It is clear that the Institute's work could have been incomparably greater, were it not for the constant shortage of money. The municipal bodies and the kehillot must subsidise the Yiddish Scientific Institute. Lately some steps forward can be seen in this respect. The city administrations of Łódź, Białystok, Grodno, Płock, Słonim, Łuck, Kowel, Lida, Grajewo, Wołkowysk, Międzyrzec [?], Terespol and Hrubieszów have granted YIVO larger or smaller subsidies. The kehilla in Vienna has been subsidising the Institute for several years already. At the end of 1928 a subsidy resolution was also adopted in Zwickau (Germany). Some kehillot in Poland have also granted subsidies to the Yiddish Scientific Institute (Warsaw, Kutno, Stanisławów).
This support from the kehillot must become systematic and general, because the Yiddish Scientific Institute is not a matter for individual scholars, but a concern of organised Jewish society. The growth and development of the Yiddish Scientific Institute lies in the interest of the entire Jewish community.

An Important Project Concerning Bills of Exchange.
Almost every merchant knows the taste of searching for a bill which he has to pay. Sometimes the issuer of such a bill has to run around all the banks, telegraph to the person who handed the bill over for collection, and track down all the endorsers.
Lately such cases occur very often, especially in the larger towns. To blame for this are the banks, which neglect the collection notices. As a result many bills are sent on to the notary (rejent), and this forces even the most reliable bill-payers to bear unnecessary expenses.
In this connection a regulation is being planned which will provide for the following matters:
Every notice about a bill sent for collection must be sent with a confirmation. If the bill-payer does not receive any advice (awizo) of where the bill is, he will have the right to deposit the amount of the bill with a notary, or at the post office in the collection department, or at the P.K.O.
In such a case, if he does so, he will not have to pay the unnecessary notary's costs, and the costs will be charged to the collector of the bill.

The Eretz Israel Week in Będzin

(The visit of Mr. L. Jaffe).
As was to be foreseen, the news of the coming of the guest from Eretz Israel, the director of "Keren Hayesod", Mr. Leib Jaffe, aroused great interest and an enthusiastic mood among all strata of the local population. The few days that Mr. Jaffe spent in Będzin were turned into a Jewish holiday, into a splendid Zionist manifestation. The town breathed the "air of Eretz Israel"; the Jewish population forgot its daily worries and its protested bills of exchange and stood under the impression of a victorious Zionism.
Mr. Jaffe's arrival was announced by hanging out the Polish and Jewish flags, which flutter on the balcony of the "Bristol" hotel, where the guest is staying. On Thursday, 3 January, at 4 o'clock in the afternoon, Mr. Jaffe arrived, accompanied by a special delegation of the reception committee, which had waited for him in Ząbkowice. Despite the great snowstorm, a large crowd gathered on the platform and welcomed the dear guest with fervour. After the greetings a procession formed, and to the sounds of music the huge crowd marches to the hotel, where the orchestra plays the Jewish and the Polish anthem. Mr. Jaffe appears on the hotel balcony and thanks them warmly for the warm reception.
The organisations "Hitachdut", "Gordonia", Hashomer, the Revisionists and "Hakoach" march through the main streets, and on Sobieski Square the procession disperses with a dance[?] under the open sky.
In the evening a festive academy took place in the "Nowości" theatre. Będzin had not seen so brilliant an event for a long time. Hundreds of Jews had to leave the theatre because it could not hold the great crowds. At 9 o'clock the curtain rises, and before the audience of a thousand a magnificent picture appears. The stage is splendidly decorated by the young, talented decorator M. Friedler. The stage is bathed in a sea of flags and greenery; around the tables the 30 members of the reception committee take their seats. The guard of honour is formed by "Hashofar". In honour of the guest a march-past of "Hakoach", "Gordonia", "Hashofar" and "Brit Trumpeldor" takes place in the hall.
The academy is opened by the member of the Keren Hayesod council in Poland, Mr. Chaim Szejn. The chair is taken by the former Sejm deputy Dr. Weinzieher, who greets the guest and the representatives of the authorities and the police. Dr. Weinzieher reads a letter of greeting from the starosta, who because of a cold could not take part in the celebration. Speeches of greeting were made by: Vice-President Mr. Rubinlicht on behalf of the town; Mr. Winodzki[?] on behalf of the kehilla; the Zionists, "Mizrachi", "Hitachdut", Poalei Zion, WIZO, Tzeirei Mizrachi, the League for Labour Eretz Israel, the Revisionists, "Hakoach", the "Yavne" gymnasium, Tarbut, Hashachar, Gordonia, "Freiheit", the artisans, the small traders, Herzliya, Brit Trumpeldor, Hashomer Haleumi, the JNF (KKL), "Dobroczynność", Linat Cholim, etc. Mr. Jaffe delivers a splendid hour-long lecture, which was a masterpiece of a God-blessed, talented poet. With his luminous descriptions the speaker leads the audience into a world of infinities, of dreams — which today, however, are a piece of reality. With a powerful resolution, "Hatikvah" and "Techezakna"[?] the imposing academy closes in a very elevated mood.
On Friday evening a youth meeting took place in the large hall of "Hitachdut", attended by a huge crowd of young people who besieged the whole entrance. The police as well as the stewards could not control the ever more storming crowd. Mr. Jaffe is received with much fervour and enthusiasm; because of the great heat and the crush Mr. Jaffe says only a few words in the hall and in the courtyard. His warm words and his call for self-sacrifice and deeds are received with great ovations in Jaffe's honour.
On Saturday morning the guest prayed in the town synagogue, which was packed full; the women's gallery, too, was heavily occupied. Before the Torah reading the parnas G. Rechnitz greets Mr. Jaffe on behalf of the kehilla. Mr. Jaffe gives a short speech about Eretz Israel and urges the Jews to contribute to the Jewish reconstruction fund. The guest is also honoured with an aliyah (call-up to the Torah).
On Saturday afternoon a women's meeting of over a thousand women took place in the largest cinema hall. Mr. Jaffe and the well-known Zionist activist, councillor[?] Mrs. Rosner, call on the Jewish woman to join the ranks of Zionism. The meeting closes with chalutz songs.
On Saturday at 10 in the evening a festive reception was held in the halls of the "Yavne" gymnasium, with 250 invited guests. At the banquet a family of well-known wealthy men and communal workers contributed 3,000 dollars for the Keren Hayesod. The fine sum for the Keren Hayesod was received with resounding applause. Short speeches were given by Dr. A. Lubrani (head of the Chamber of Commerce in Haifa), Mr. Zeiren[?] and Garzałka (delegates of the central Keren Hayesod bureau). The young violinist Mr. Berenblat and the young pianist Miss Goldsobel perform some Jewish and Oriental motifs; the poet Leib Jaffe recites some of his works, "The Chalutza" and "In the Orchard"[?], which are received with great applause. With a "hora" dance the brilliant banquet ends at 4 o'clock in the morning.
On Sunday and the following days they set about the practical work. The town was visited by Będzin collectors, who were received cordially by the Jewish population. The results will far exceed all contributions so far for the whole time of Będzin Jewry[?].
On Monday at 10 in the evening a festive banquet in honour of the poet L. Jaffe took place in the home of Mr. Chaim Szejn. The banquet, held under the chairmanship of Dr. Weinzieher, was attended by up to 60 people of the Będzin "notables"; the mood was festive. Speeches were made by Messrs. Żmudzki[?], Dr. Rechtman, Buchweitz, Rosner, Szejn and Jaffe. With music, song and Eretz Israel dances the banquet went on until grey dawn.
M. Hampel.

The Start Must Be Made

(A letter to the editors.)
The Jewish school system in Poland can record great achievements over the last few years. In dozens of towns and shtetls there are today model Jewish secular schools; thousands of Jewish children are brought up in these schools as free and healthy people, who will be able to fight for a better life on their own.
After all, these schools supply reserves of fresh, modern public activists; after all, intellectual forces stream out of them, of which we have so few to this day. It is therefore no wonder that the Jewish secular school system is so deeply rooted in the heart of every Jewish worker and intellectual, who are ready to make the greatest sacrifices for its existence.
In dozens of towns and shtetls we already have such schools and educational institutions. Only Będzin has not a single Jewish secular educational institution. True, many attempts have already been made by the local branch of the TsIShO [Central Yiddish School Organization], but the efforts have so far remained without a positive result because of material reasons.
Much has been done by philanthropic institutions for the Jewish orphans, but for the children of the Jewish workers and the popular masses nothing has been done so far. After all, Jewish poverty lives in the most terrible suffering and need; after all, our children live in damp, cold and dark cellars and cramped attic rooms, where illnesses are a very frequent phenomenon — it is therefore a social duty to take into our own hands the care for our children and to create educational institutions that will bring up a developed and healthy generation.
The board of the „[—] Evening Courses for Workers“, after long deliberation, has resolved to open in the coming[?] weeks a children's home for the children of the Jewish workers and popular masses, who have no possibility of placing their children in private children's institutions, which involve larger money payments. We want to create the best possibilities for the children of the poorest strata to receive a proper upbringing: to take the children at least for a few hours a day out of the dark and cold dwellings, to bring them into warm rooms, to surround them with a warm-hearted and loving environment, to procure various toys for them, for which the child's soul yearns and longs. Let the little Moyshes and little Khanes enjoy their youth and life; let them forget, at least for a while, the misery and need of their home.
It is hard, however, to realise this plan. But the start must be made. The health and upbringing of the Jewish worker's child are too dear to us for us to be frightened off by various obstacles. Będzin must not remain without such an institution.
For this, however, the help of all friends of the Jewish worker's child is needed. The initiators of the children's home must be surrounded by a warm-hearted and warm atmosphere from the public; we need both moral and material help in order to continue the work that has been begun, with support, and to create the children's home that our town needs so badly.
Y. Ka.
An Outrage Has Been Committed in Israel

Most esteemed editors!
We ask you to print the following statement in your esteemed paper:
This Sunday a filthy pamphlet entitled „HaEmet nitan likhtov“ („The truth may be written“) was distributed in our town against the „Keren Hayesod“ campaign, against the halutzim and the new Yishuv in Eretz Israel, which, according to the words of the pamphlet, desecrates the Sabbath and defiles the holy things of the Jewish religion and people.
We looked into the source of the pamphlet and turned to the printing house in Sosnowiec where the pamphlet was printed. The owner of the printing house declared to us that on Friday the 4th of this month at 2 in the afternoon Messrs. Erlich (Małachowska 26) and Zysze Suszek[?] (Plac 3 Maja) of Będzin, both well-known members of „Tseirei Emunei Yisrael“, came to him and ordered the printing of the pamphlet for Saturday night (motzaei Shabbat) at 5 in the evening.
To our question why he had agreed to print such a vile pamphlet, which other Jewish printing houses had not wanted to do, he answered that the other Jewish printers had not accepted it because they do not work on the Sabbath, but at his place they work on the Sabbath; he had therefore stated clearly that the work would have to be carried out on the Sabbath, to which the customers agreed. The printing-house owner told us that he is ready to testify to the same before a beit din if he is called upon to do so. We must also point out that in Będzin there are several Jewish printing houses, among them also a printing house belonging to an outspoken Agudist, yet the customers sought out a small printing house in Sosnowiec that works on the Sabbath. We bring this outrage to the attention of the Jewish public.
Respectfully,
Avraham Hampel,
Levi Yitzchak Jungster.
Będzin, 7 January.

Begrudgers (from the Polish press).
When the director of „Keren Hayesod“, the poet L. Jaffe, arrived in Będzin, he was given — as in other towns — a festive reception with music at the railway station. As is customary, before „Hatikvah“ was played the Polish national anthem was played. The „Kurier Zachodni“ immediately seized on this, claiming that the honour of the Polish anthem is desecrated when it is played for private persons. In a note the above-mentioned paper (No. 3) writes, among other things, the following:
„Last Thursday a certain (!) Jewish activist from Palestine arrived in Będzin and was received with the Polish anthem and with „Hatikvah“. In general the custom is accepted that with the national anthem [printed: „custom“] only representatives of the state are greeted; yet it turns out that the Jews greet quite private persons with the Polish anthem, which in our opinion is highly improper.“
„It may[?] be that the arriving activist is a quite respected public figure among the Jews, but in any case he is a private person, and greeting him with the Polish anthem was a great tactlessness on the part of the organisers, which — we hope — will not be repeated.“
It would be interesting to know in which Shulchan Aruch the people of the „K. Z.“ found the rule that the national anthem is played specifically in honour of statesmen. We know that out of respect for the state in which we live the state anthem is always played before the Jewish one, but never for persons. Until now our internal „good friends“ begrudged us the playing of the national anthem [Hatikvah]; from today on we know that our external enemies do not like it either. Incidentally, „be wise and know what these people are after[?]“...
Sh. Sh—r[?].
What's new in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The city administration is 'thrifty' and schoolchildren shiver with cold

[Będzin — education and municipality.] A group of Jewish parents has turned to us with the following complaint against the local city administration.
In the premises of 'Piast' is housed Public School No. 4. The premises are not fitted with double windows, etc. Because of this the children shiver with cold and cannot properly benefit from their lessons.
New rulers — new decrees...

[Będzin — electricity.] For long years we bore the heavy burden of the Sosnowiec power station, and we always consoled ourselves that in the end Będzin would free itself of that power station and conclude an agreement with another company.
The matter has been realised. Będzin supposedly has its own power station, but with... new troubles; such things as happen today did not occur then. It did not happen that, for no reason whatever, the electricity was cut off at subscribers who are blameless.
— Let the management take care that the population should not suffer from unjust [?] reprisals.
The brothers litigate and the grandchildren hit...

[Będzin — family feud.] For a long time now there has been no peace between the Altman brothers because of an inheritance dispute. The matter has already reached the highest instances, which, however, recognised the claim of Hershel Altman.
Now that the opposing party no longer has the possibility of litigating, he finds protection with his grandchildren, who take revenge and almost every evening attack Mr H. Altman and his family, whom they 'honour' with blows.
'He has no one to live for'...

[Łazy — suicide.] Behind [?] Łazy the dead body of a 25-year-old Christian from Ksawera was found.
The Christian committed suicide by shooting himself, having declared beforehand that, having no parents any more, he had no one to live for.

[Zagłębie — unemployment.] In the course of 6 days, i.e. from 30 [?] December to 5 January, the number of unemployed grew by 503 persons.
The number of unemployed in the districts (powiats) of Będzin, Zawiercie and Olkusz amounts to 11,161 persons.
Of this number, about 4,000 unemployed receive benefits from the P.F.B. [?] (probably the State Unemployment Fund).
Register your patents, provide yourselves with price lists and pay the advance instalments.

The first Jewish ławnik in Sosnowiec.

[Sosnowiec — city council.] (Sh—kh) On Monday the second session of the city council took place, at which a president, a vice-president and ławniks [members of the municipal executive] were elected. With a delay of a good hour, the chairman, advocate Pawełek, opened the session with a funeral address devoted to the recently deceased councillor and first chairman of the Sosnowiec city council, Dr. Zieleniewski. Before proceeding to the agenda, Dr. Budziński submits a motion that, in order properly to honour the memory of the deceased councillor, the magistrate should pay out 5000 zł. for poor pupils who are finishing elementary school and wish to continue their studies. The motion is accepted in principle. Councillor Dr. Budziński (N.D.) makes a statement that, since his club does not know who will be elected to the presidium, they will take no part in the elections. A statement before the elections is also made by councillor Hamburger (P.Z.), who says that because of the reactionary majority of the present city council they will abstain from voting. Then the elections are held, with the following result: Dr. J. Marczyński (Sanacja) is elected president with 29 votes, and as vice-president, with the same number of votes, Jaża[?] (P.P.S.). In the election of the ławniks a tangle[?] arises between the Endeks and the P.P.S. The point is that the P.P.S. together with the Sanacja want to push through 2 ławnik-referents (a ławnik-referent receives almost as high a salary as the vice-president). The Endeks, however, who are in the minority on the city council, are against it. A discussion develops around the matter. After the discussion the motion of [?] [?] is accepted, i.e. that 2 referents are elected. Elected as ławniks were: Hugo[?] (Sanacja), Dr. H. Fruks[?] (Jewish club), Dr. Dobrowolski (P.P.S.) and T. Kicewicz[?] (N.D.); as referents: Dr. Dobrowolski and Olsztes[?].

Sławków.
The rabbinate question — almost settled.
[Sławków — rabbinate.] Since the passing of the local rabbi of blessed memory, the question has arisen of who will occupy the rabbinical seat in our shtetl. Many rabbinical candidates applied, but it could not be decided which of them was the most suitable.
Because of this a meeting was held last week, at which it was decided to elect a commission of town notables, of such people as would be able to settle so difficult a question.
The commission, numbering 6 persons, consisting of scholars and town notables, began to look into the rabbinate question.
Last Tuesday the 6 persons paid a visit in Sosnowiec to the candidate, the great Rabbi R' Dovidl Halberstam, brother-in-law of the Radomsko Rebbe, may he live long, with whom they spent several hours.
Rabbi Halberstam made, with his acuity and erudition, such a great impression on the delegation that they immediately offered him the rabbinical contract.
Rabbi Halberstam answered that he accepts the proposal to take over the rabbinical seat in Sławków, but first all matters there must be settled in the best way.
The delegation's answer aroused great satisfaction among the local Jewish population, so that the surest candidate for the local rabbinate is the great Rabbi R' Dovidl Halberstam, may he live long.

Why did Dr. Meladysta withdraw from the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec?

[Sosnowiec — Jewish hospital; followed by: Dąbrowa — Zionism, Keren Hayesod.] In connection with the report that Dr. Meladysta has officially resigned as permanent physician of the Sosnowiec Jewish hospital, we turned to him with the question whether the report is confirmed, for we did not believe that Dr. Meladysta, for whom the Jewish hospital was a part of his soul, would take such a step.
To our regret, however, Dr. Meladysta explained to us that the resignation is a firm decision on his part, and the reasons are as follows:
"For 8 years already," Dr. M. explains, "I have been working in the Jewish hospital. The work was for me a sacred task with regard to the Jewish sick. I suffered great material losses because of it, since for several years I worked entirely for free and later for a paltry remuneration; and even recently I received 240 zł. a month, i.e. 8 zł. for spending several hours in the hospital... Obviously such a sum is ridiculous, but the harmony that reigned between me and Dr. Perlman, of blessed memory, and the love for the institution bound me to the Jewish hospital.
When Dr. Perlman died, the gentlemen of 'Dobroczynność' [the charity society] — who with their former management had brought it about that the hospital was closed for months — held, on the very day of the funeral, a meeting at which they were already devising plans to bring the hospital back under their rule...
Since then the assimilationist rulers have been waging a campaign against the present hospital committee and also against my person, because besides being a doctor I am also a Zionist..
The struggle is a harmful one; the hospital, which with much effort and sweat of the hospital committee and devoted doctors was raised to its present level, is already beginning to decline. The signs of the decline are already showing, and foreseeing the situation in the future, I have decided to withdraw from the hospital."
—o—
A festive Eretz-Israel academy.
On Tuesday a large academy took place in the "Venus" hall in Dąbrowa with the participation of the poet Mr. Leib Jaffe. The chairman of the Zionist Organization and of the Keren Hayesod committee, Mr. Nachm.[?] Gutman, opens the academy. The Polish and the Jewish anthems are played and the greetings begin. Greetings are given by: the kehilla administration, the kehilla council, "Mizrachi", "Poalei Zion", "Hashomer", "Freiheit", "Gordonia", the city councillors' club, "W.I.Z.O.", "Pa'p."[?], the "Artisans' Association", the "Women's Association", the K.K.L. [Jewish National Fund], "Tze'irei Mizrachi", the "Merchants' Association" and "Tarbut".
Then the guest Leib Jaffe takes the floor for his lecture "The Legend of Eretz Israel" and appeals to those present to take part in great numbers in the Keren Hayesod campaign.
At the end a resolution proclaiming the Keren Hayesod campaign in the town was adopted unanimously, and to the strains of "Hatikvah" the gathering dispersed.
Later a banquet took place at "Ham Loraki"[?] with the participation of a large number of invited guests.
