The Eretz Israel Week in Zagłębie.

(The visit of Mr. L. Jaffe).
II.
In connection with Mr. Jaffe's stay in Zagłębie, a festive Eretz-Israel mood reigns on the Jewish street, growing more and more. After the last hard years full of despair and apathy, Mr. Jaffe has succeeded in breathing into our grey, everyday, heavy[?] reality a new soul and a stream of fresh life. Zagłębie Jewry has awakened from its lethargic sleep and has felt the inner urge towards national awakening and revival. All the "Keren Hayesod" events, Jaffe's public appearances at academies, meetings and gatherings were transformed into splendid demonstrations, and his appeal to Zagłębie Jewry finds a broad echo, and the campaign for the K.H. [Keren Hayesod] is being crowned with due success.
The results already known so far in Będzin exceed by 50 percent the income of the K.H. for the whole period of the last 7 years. Day by day new prominent people, who until now had not been seen at all in day-to-day Zionist work, place themselves in the service of the Construction Fund [Aufbau-Fonds, i.e. Keren Hayesod]. Among the new activists taking part in the practical fund-raising, mention must be made of Mrs. and Mr. Fürstenberg and Mr. Izaak Szpigelman.
On Tuesday evening Mr. Jaffe appeared at a large meeting in Dąbrowa. The local reception committee arranged a banquet in his honour, attended by the best people of the town; 10 pairs went out there to work [canvassing], assisted by the delegate of the head office, A.[?] Zajden.
On Wednesday at midday a delegation from Sosnowiec numbering 9 persons came to Będzin in 3 automobiles decorated with Polish and Jewish national flags, in order to take the guest to Sosnowiec. The chairman of the reception committee, Mr. Izydor[?] Fürstenberg, gives a short welcome. The Będzin notables (pnei ha-ir) also accompany Mr. Jaffe to Sosnowiec. Before the academy a short consultation about the forthcoming campaign took place over a glass of tea in the home of Mr. M. Rajcher.
In the evening a festive public meeting took place in the large Municipal Theatre. Speeches were given by the English consul from Katowice, whose speech was translated by Mr. Dr. Lubrani,) Dr. T. Melodista[?], J. S. Wejgryb[?], Kwiatek, Dr. Lubrani (director of the Chamber of Commerce in Haifa) and L. Jaffe.
On Thursday a banquet with the participation of 160 people took place at the "Merchants' Association" (Sochrim-Ferein). On the spot several persons pledged considerable sums for the K.H. On Sabbath Dr. Eliezer Lubrani, who is successfully leading the work in Sosnowiec, spoke in the town synagogue (Stadt-Schul).
On Sabbath afternoon a large youth meeting took place in Będzin at the "Namaszczi"[?] cinema; it was opened by Mr. S. Oppenheim (in Hebrew). Mrs. Ratner set out in her speech the tasks of the youth towards the people and the land. Mr. Jaffe speaks about the young Jewish community in Palestine that is building itself, about the halutzim [pioneers] and their heroic deeds.
"Go, youth," the speaker concludes, "into the Jewish home and carry the tidings of the awakening Jewish people, and may your heart kindle a fire, and make exile[?] life finer, brighter and more festive."
The young audience is enthused by Mr. Jaffe's speech, rich in images, and as a unanimous answer that the youth will remain forever faithful to the Zionist ideal, the mighty singing of "Hatikvah" resounds through the hall.
In the evening Mr. Jaffe visited the youth organisations "Ha-Shahar" and "Herzliya". Everywhere he is received with great enthusiasm and cries of "Baruch haba!" [Welcome!]. Imposing was the meeting of the school youth "Herzliya", which had just celebrated its 2nd anniversary. The guest is welcomed by Mr. Inhald[?]. Mr. Grundman gives a report on the 2 years of activity of "Herzliya". Further speakers are Messrs. Gärtner, Spitzberg, Miss Tinspolwer[?], Mrs. Ratner and Mr. Jaffe, who connects and analyses the symbolic name "Herzliya" with the name of the unforgettable leader Dr. T. Herzl.
The youth rejoices with the guest by singing various songs and dancing the "hora".
On Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) and Sunday large consultations of responsible Zionists and respected K.H. activists took place at the "Mizrachi", at which a report on the work done was given.
On Monday morning Mr. Jaffe visited the local "Mizrachi" school. The head of the school, Mr. Pilk, welcomes the guest on behalf of the teaching staff. Rubin, a pupil of the 7th class, delivers a lecture in Hebrew and pledges on behalf of all his fellow pupils that they will always remain faithful to the Jewish people, the Land of Israel and the Hebrew language. The pupil Majtlis recites "Al em ha-derech" [At the Crossroads]; the little boys of the "Gan Yeladim" [kindergarten] sing "Shalom aleichem Yehudi" and ask the poet "Ma nishma sham be-Eretz Yisrael?" [What's new there in the Land of Israel?]. Mr. Jaffe speaks to the children in Hebrew and conveys to them greetings from their lively little brothers who study in the schools of the Land of Israel.
The children, deeply moved by the poet's heartfelt words, sing "Techezaknah" and "Hatikvah" and accompany him with cheers of "Long live the poet Leib Jaffe!"
In the evening the first general meeting of the "Keren Hayesod" pledgers took place at the "Merchants' Association". Over 100 contributors take part. Mr. Goldfeld presides. The delegate of the head office, Mr. Nożałka[?], reports on the progress of the campaign. The report is a satisfactory one. Mr. Jaffe lectures on Palestine in figures and facts. From his lecture it is plain to see how a people of brokers and "Luftmenschen" was transformed into a creative, lively working people, and how the Land of Israel, which not long ago was a strange, wild, desolate land, has grown into a Jewish Yishuv.
Mr. Jaffe's speech, rich in content, with which he leads the listener into a world of infinities and eternities, is received with well-deserved ovations.
A "Keren Hayesod" committee is elected "en bloc". Honorary chairman: Mr. Chaim Szajn; chairman of the council: Mr. Szymon Fürstenberg; on the council: Chawa Baruszykowska[?], Juta Buchowicz, Baruch Brama[?], Szlama Gutman, Jakób Gelbard, Dawid Erlich, Jakób Erlich, Mosze Kalman Erlich, Chawa Hutner, Herszlewicz, Icchak Wygodzki, Dr. S. Weinzieher, Mrs. Dr. S. Weinzieher, Hersz Jakubowicz, Meszulem Lizer[?], Tobiasz Merin, Nachman Tenenberg, Jakób Najberg, Mrs. S. Fürstenberg, Szmul Pelk, Hirsz Pfefer, Mosze Preger, Majer Cymberknop, Chaja Kurland, Icchak Majer Kurland, Necha Ratner, Dr. Ruben Rechtman, Eliezer Rubinlicht, Ch. W. Sztajnhart, Chana Szajn, Icchak Szajn.
Members of the executive: Lajbisz Buchowicz, Natan Goldsobel, Abraham Hampel, Dawid Hofer, Cukierkandel, Mosze Rozenker, Dawid Elimelech Ratner, Mordek Szajn, Cesia Szajn.
On the audit commission: Jakób Gutman, Józef Goldfeld, Michał Lewin, Szaja Ratner, Icchak Szpigelman.
The closing word is given by Mr. Jaffe, who thanks all contributors and activists for the cordial reception and hospitality, wishes all Jews better times and calls for constant readiness to sacrifice for Palestine. With "Hatikvah" and in an elevated mood the general meeting is closed.
On Tuesday the guest, accompanied by director Mr. S. Fürstenberg, visited the local social and philanthropic institutions such as "Linat ha-Cholim", the Bank Spółdzielczy [co-operative bank], the new "Yavneh" gymnasium which Mr. Fürstenberg built, and others.
The same day at 8 in the evening a very imposing and festive farewell evening took place at the "Yavneh" school under the chairmanship of Mr. Fürstenberg, to which 100 invited guests came. Speeches were made by Messrs. Żmucki, S. Szajn, Dr. Lubrani, Mrs. Ratner, Mrs. Cesia Szajn, Wygodzki, Preger[?], Nożałka and the master of the banquet, Mr. Fürstenberg, who expresses his sympathy for the idea of Jewish renaissance and his ardent love for the Land of Israel. Mr. Fürstenberg, who at the banquet pledged a handsome sum for the "Keren Hayesod", declares that he officially joins the Zionist ranks that stand at the head of the national work, and that the "Yavneh" school and its new building will be run in a national spirit. His declaration is rewarded with loud applause.
With "Hatikvah" and cries of "Long live the poet Jaffe" the chairman closes the successful, intimate farewell banquet.
On Tuesday at 1 at night Mr. Jaffe left Zagłębie. At the Będzin station, from which Mr. Jaffe departed, a large crowd came to see off the dear guest. Hearty farewells are exchanged, the train moves, the crowd sings "Hatikvah" and calls out "Tzetcha le-shalom!" [Go in peace!]; from the carriage window Mr. Jaffe bids farewell to his friends.
Mr. Jaffe's visit to Zagłębie will long, long remain in memory.
Mordechai Hampel.
A farewell letter from L. Jaffe

[Będzin, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa — Keren Hayesod; letter to the editor.]
Most esteemed Editors!
I ask you to print the following lines in your esteemed paper:
I express my deepest thanks to the entire Jewish population of Będzin for the extraordinary hospitality and warmth that were shown to me.
I thank all the comrades-collectors („zamler“) for their energetic and devoted work. Special thanks to the distinguished women, who helped so much towards the success of the campaign. I also thank the youth of all the organisations and groups for their work.
I express my thanks to the Jewish population and to all the comrades of Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa for the warm reception and for the loyal and energetic cooperation.
I hope that the work for Eretz Israel will be carried on with deep and constant enthusiasm and devotion.
I wish the Jews of Zagłębie that their life may become finer and brighter, and that the light of Eretz Israel may shine upon them.
L. Jaffe [Leib Jaffe].

Sosnowiec is becoming Jewish...

[Sosnowiec — Zionism; Keren Hayesod; Leib Jaffe's visit.]
(From the banquet in honour of the poet Leib Jaffe.)
Sosnowiec, as is well known, has been a „frozen“ town ever since the pre-war years. Jewish nationalism here, among the so-called better classes, is a kind of lethargic sleep, from which it is hard to wake. And yet today Sosnowiec is becoming Jewish, and even there one sees that the Jewish renaissance is still far from dead: seeing how the Jewish public receives the guests from Eretz Israel, the features of the renaissance sound even more prominently, and it echoes. The ingathering of exiles [the mixed public] applauds the personalities who bring with them the warmth of the Eretz Israel sun, with which they warm the hearts of the Jews who stand even quite close[?] to assimilation, but in whom the Jewish spark is not yet entirely extinguished.
And so even in Jewishly „assimilated“ Sosnowiec there is a Jewish stirring, thanks to the guests who are staying here. It is truly to be marvelled at what enthusiasm and statesmanlike respect the guests — the poet Leib Jaffe and Dr. Eliezer Lubrani — call forth. Eretz Israel has won! Won not only in the practical sense of building towns, creation and industry, but it has also won in the spiritual and political sense. [It has] learned to value and honour its spiritual leaders, its poets and creators, who were always ours, only we never knew them. It shows them to us in a light in which we could never see them. It teaches not only us how to value them, but it also teaches other nations how to honour them. This is a great gain not only for them, the poets and artists, but also for us Jews in general, because it teaches us respect for our own creative forces.
The banquet in honour of Leib Jaffe took on a festive mood from the minute the guests appeared in the hall. The warmth of the Eretz Israel sun, poured out over the tanned face of Dr. Lubrani, warmed even the hearts that had never had any sentiment for Eretz Israel. In his speech, with its clipped expressionist sentences: „Jews, what do you want of us? Why do you hold us here?“ — [these words] were cried out with the heartfelt bitterness of a true son of the people, who feels hurt by the dullness of the exile Jew, who does not sufficiently understand the important work being done for him in Eretz Israel. Dr. Lubrani is the proud expression of the modern Jew, who does not beg. Dr. Lubrani does not come cadging with the begging[?] tune of the Rabbi Meir Baal ha-Nes collectors. He comes with the boldness of a proud tax-collector, driven by duties of state. He feels that the Jewish state must exist, because its society builds, because its society creates.
He, the Eretz Israel Jew, knows that with every blow of a pioneer's hammer on the roads of Eretz Israel a new miracle is born for the future Jewish home.
He knows that for every dollar he demands of us and receives, a spiritual seed is planted there, in the schools, in a child — one that no thousand cannons will be able to destroy.
He knows that every farmer in Eretz Israel tills not only the soil there, but also tills the exile here among us.
He knows that Jewish productivity in Eretz Israel strengthens not only the community there, but also the ingathering of exiles here among us.
And we know it too: the stronger the proletarianisation and productivisation there become, in the physical and in the spiritual sense, the stronger we too become here.
And because he knows this, he comes to us with the conviction of his strong spirit and demands what is due to him: without poetry, without flowery phrases, because he himself is the most modern thing and[?] Eretz Israel poetry itself. He is the expression of the spirit of upbuilding from there, where labour sings its way into our future. And therefore he does not sing about the land and does not beg for the land, but demands the necessary material nourishment that makes possible the labour which sings out the Jewish future.
Moshe Apelboim.
Jewish Financial Institutions

[Dąbrowa — economy; Jewish banks.]
(Subheading:) Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] has 300 registered Jewish merchants and — four banks.
Antisemitism, the bad economic conditions, the restriction and the outright refusal to give any credit to Jewish firms taught us to create our own financial institutions, independent banks, which over the course of a number of years developed splendidly.
As to how and why the banks developed among us, one can say that the process came about by a miracle, and this happened because people did not know how such an enterprise is run. It was thought that we had no strength or capacity at all to run a bank, and thanks to that the matter was approached with caution and with full seriousness. A bank, people knew, must be guarded both from within and from without; that is why [?] the experiment succeeded, and victory and triumph were strengthened everywhere the institutions were regarded as a cautious enterprise that must be respected.
Now, however, our banks find themselves in entirely different circumstances. Our brethren the Children of Israel have realised that the devil is not as terrible as he is painted. Respect and caution are no longer needed; people approach a bank like any other enterprise — without deliberation and without special caution. Wherever a party, wherever a faction "makes Shabbat for itself" [i.e. goes its own way], it founds its own bank.
Some years ago, when we saw that the forces were beginning to be crumbled and that people were setting about creating too many banks, we warned from this very place and pleaded: do not exchange our flourishing [?] financial institutions — which can rise to a very high level — for little shops; do not allow — we said then — fine institutions to be split up into little banklets. We argued then that it is better to have a counted few strong institutions than many well [?] existing party banklets.
True, the newly created financial institutions exist and even develop, and here people will surely come and ask us: what do you care that the institutions multiply, as long as they exist? Every enterprise, we are told [?] — people will say — that exists has a full right of existence, to live side by side with the others, with the bigger ones.
And precisely because they exist, it is worth casting an attentive glance. We knew quite well that the appetites among us would not stop. Once the front was broken, nobody would say: there are so-and-so many banks, and here one must stop and say "dayenu" [enough]; and that is exactly what we feared — we feared that every society would found its own bank, just as every few people go about founding their own societies.
Unfortunately, unfortunately, the bank system has risen to just that level. It has already come to the point that a society without a bank is like a craftsman without a workshop.
Here we have in our Dąbrowa, thank God, no fewer than four Jewish banks; Dąbrowa, which has three hundred registered Jewish merchants, possesses four banks — can one even grasp how far we make ourselves ridiculous with such crumbling and splitting of Jewish forces? How does it look to the outside world, and what use can such a splinter bring to the inner Jewish camp?
Financial institutions have been turned into party societies, so that every faction has its own bank; and that is not all — Dąbrowa still has the option of making the portions [?] smaller too, for how does it follow [?] that these four banks should supply all of Dąbrowa with money? Are they really able to give as much money as the Jews of Dąbrowa need? And therefore, probably a little later, a fresh proposal will be born that every minyan should have its own bank, and since every shtibl is independent, then [?] why should not every section have its own bank? And then — where are the various Zionist currents, and where are the Mizrachi and the Tze'irim and the Po'alim of every party? There are, after all, now some groups and associations that are not in the minority — so why should all of these not be separate too? What, are their souls different? Do they not need to have any money?
That is how we look, that is how we fall apart. Out of large and strong enterprises we make miniature toys, and the end is that the slightest breeze blows them apart, and they leave the stage.
Let us pass on to Będzin and Sosnowiec, where there are larger banks, prospering well, operating with large capital; nevertheless none of them has any immovable property or buildings of its own. We, however, hold that it would have been considerably better if we had fewer banks with more secure assets and their own buildings, so that the first rainstorm could not wash them away, as has happened more than once both in Będzin and in Sosnowiec.
Just as we did not know [?] how to touch banking matters, and when people did touch them they proceeded with caution — thanks to which the development came about — so exactly has it now become fashionable [?], so that every young man wants to open a bank for his party; and therein lies the tragicomedy of our communal activity.
Let the question of communal financial institutions be considered more seriously and more sincerely; let it be borne in mind that our financial system [?] must not be allowed to suffer.
If we do not want to allow things to come to a catastrophe, if we want to take precautionary measures in good time, we must already set about removing what is undesirable, what can stifle the foundation of the Jewish banks, which has cost so much Jewish money, strength and energy.
R. Let.

Extinguished Hope

(A story) — by B. Tapuach.
Apparently the worry had been gnawing at Shlomo for a long time already. Somewhere deep inside him sat a dissatisfaction with his life. And there a faint [?] shadow [?] grew, but he had no time to think about it. Meanwhile [?] he was a Jew, a learned man; the clever head, the arbiter and the rich Jew was busy with town affairs, with communal matters and with the big shop — Reb Shlomo, they called him. He himself did not know what grief was growing inside him.
But now —
Now Shlomo had ceased to be a merchant. He had grown older. The shop began to wither, the shelves grew sparser, the young merchants were fiery as flame, nimble, and he came down in the world. He lost his zest for the shop and had already left the whole business in his wife's hands. It looked as if, in the middle of running, in the middle of the bustle, he had stopped on the spot and come to his senses from the noise. What is all the noise for?
So he became a quiet man, a silent one, and in town they already began to call him "Shlomo of Chana Sara". People stopped coming to him to ask for advice, to call him to arbitrations, and —
The worry came out of its hiding place. The grief spread [?] over his face, looked out of his eyes, and the sorrow bent him over:
— What is his purpose now?
A whole life has passed. Always toiling [?], chased about. And now what? What is left to him of all the toil [?]? All that is left is a Jew, a poor man [?], an aging man with a grey beard and stooped shoulders.
What remains to every person?
Another is left a child, a son, a daughter... one waits for a grandchild. A generation grows. But he?
Another year will run by, and another year. It will not help; his time will come to go to the next world, to give an account. With what will he come there? Whom will he leave behind him? Who will remember him? And who will say kaddish after him?
Darkness began to grow in Shlomo. He began to feel like the tree that stands dry in the courtyard. All the trees grow, turn green, rustle with leaves and branches; that tree stands dry, with hard branches sticking out, without a leaf, without moisture. So what does it stand for?
And remorse began to grow. Why had he kept silent until now? What had he been waiting for? He has known for years that it is not his fault. A doctor told him so explicitly. But what then? He waited, meanwhile he traded, served as arbiter, gave advice... Because of that he even quietly laughed at the doctor. As if I know what a doctor says! There is a great God in the world! But now he understands that he deceived himself.
After all, it is an explicit law: one who has lived with a wife ten years and had no child must divorce...
So why had he kept silent until now?
To go now to the rabbi, to have a get written — now, in his old age? Why, people will laugh up their sleeves...
The thought no longer left Shlomo. It looked as if he were constantly walking about with some mad [?] secret. He began to keep away from people, and at home he stopped talking. He did not even look at his wife, and when he sometimes sat studying in the evening — his voice wept [?] with a childish weeping, and it would wring Chana Sara's heart, and fear wound itself around her body like wet sheets.
Chana Sara asked him nothing. She was afraid to hear his answer. And anyway, why ask? Does she not know what is the matter with him? She only began to be afraid of him. She trembled at remaining alone with him at home. She would sit on in the shop till late at night. She sat and spun sad thoughts, had a foreboding that a great disgrace was drawing near her... Tears often choked her throat, and she would whisper:
— Better death than such a disgrace!
At night she often wept in her sleep, but Shlomo did not hear it, or pretended not to hear.
And so they became strangers to each other. And each one thought their sad thoughts to themselves and was afraid to speak.
So it dragged on a summer and a winter and another summer. And by itself the spring of speech dried up — husband and wife stopped talking to each other altogether.
Shlomo kept silent; Chana Sara did not close an eye through the nights, swallowed her tears and prayed:
— Master of the Universe! Better take my soul than such a disgrace in old age!
Until — God heard her prayer.
[She] caught a bad chill last winter, did not take care of herself at all — perhaps caught the chill on purpose — lay a couple of weeks with a high fever, said the confession in time, and died.
Hope lit up in Shlomo. He kept it under seven locks, did not betray it even with a glance. Only his face did become brighter... His conscience, however, was clean. She was already around sixty. She had had a doctor. What more could he have done? Probably it is destined that he should not leave the world a lonely man [?]... and — praised be God.
* * *
But now he was afraid to wait.
And indeed he did not wait long. A few weeks later he put on his Sabbath kapote on an ordinary weekday, combed his beard and went off with a matchmaker to a village. There he saw a woman, still young, healthy, and above all: she had three children by her first husband, who had been a simple village man. So Reb Shlomo was a great match in lineage for her. And shortly they were married.
The woman and her children came to town and settled in Shlomo's house, and Shlomo — old age fell away from him. He became nimble, straightened up. His head lifted and — he threw himself back into business.
He refreshed the shop. New goods arrived, the woman had brought a little money, a little he borrowed on the house, and he started bustling again, calling in customers, pulling peasants by the sleeve, and the takings grew stronger.
There is hope, there is something to work for. Any moment now — and the dry tree will feel sap, and the branches and little leaves will begin to sprout and turn green...
The little boy he will name Mendele... after the old Kotzker [Rebbe Menachem Mendel of Kotzk]... A pale little boy he will be, with black sidelocks, and —
— How are you, Mendele? What are you going over [?]?
And the smile in him grew, poured through all his limbs like strong wine, laughed out of his eyes, and outside it is bright, delightful. It simply smells good in the shop.
But —
Time does not stand still. Half a year has already passed... and — the little boy who is to be called Mendele is getting farther away [?]. The little face more blurred, and who knows? Perhaps Mendele will not be born at all? Eh?
But what is the hurry? There is still time.
And so a year passed and another half year. The hope began to go out. Sorrow began to rise in Shlomo again. He did not yet give in; he held on to the hope with both hands: he constantly said Psalms, made vows, and —
One day, when he was in the big city for goods, he went to the doctor, just as he had done once, for Chana Sara. It was the same doctor, a short, oldish man with a clever face and thoughtful eyes. He examined Shlomo, examined him closely. Shlomo waited with a faint heart, as one waits for a verdict.
— My dear Jew... back then, years ago, there was still time... but now... too late.
— Late?
— Quite simply: you are too old...
Shlomo turned pale; the hope went out.
———
He came home a quiet man, an extinguished man. In his heart remorse wept: what did he need this strange village Jewess for? It would have been better for him if Chana Sara were with him... she had been so close to him... so homely...
His eyes began to go dim again, his shoulders began to bend again, and old age began to creep over him again.
The air must be cleared — On the frictions in the Sosnowiec Jewish Hospital

(On the frictions occurring in the Sosnowiec Jewish hospital.)
With what respect, with what reverence, with what pride and dignity we always look upon and speak of the beautiful and useful building that is called "the Jewish Hospital".
And is it any wonder that we boast and simply preen ourselves at every opportunity whenever the talk turns to this useful building, whose destiny is to save the sick and suffering? After all, we are so poor in public buildings of our own, intended to heal and save people without distinction of class or tendency, profession or outlook.
A hospital, we hold, is in the fortunate position that it can, and has the means to, save all those who are in need of rescue. A hospital in general, and a Jewish one in particular, must have the necessary strength and the firm will to absorb into itself the great amount of suffering and pain of its patients, in order thereby to ease the heavy groan and the deep wound [?] that bursts out of unfortunate hearts.
And so things went on in the Sosnowiec Jewish hospital, quietly and modestly; without noise or tumult the work was done there by specialists who understood the responsibility they were taking upon themselves, and with full accountability carried their idealistic work on their shoulders.
And so we were sure that the holy, responsible work would go on, but suddenly a different wind began to blow there, until the atmosphere was filled with the smell of "politics", owing to the fact that the harmonious activity gradually turned into frictions, caused by the resignation of a man as devoted to the hospital as Dr. Meladysta [?], who has great merits for his idealistic work.
It is interesting: in the last issue of the "Z. Ts." [Zaglembier Tsaytung] Dr. Meladysta tells us that since the death of Dr. Perlman the assimilationists have been thinking about how to get control over the hospital back into their hands, so that from then on frictions began, which led to Dr. Meladysta having to throw up his work at an institution that was dear and precious to him, and with which over the last years he had become so bound up that the resignation surely weighs on his heart.
Actually, we learn a secret here: that the "Dobroczynność" [charity society] assimilationists have pushed their way in there, who have been busy seizing power in the hospital. After all, we did not know at all that all sorts of undesirable elements had pushed their way in there, who to a national Jew must be like a thorn [lit. a spider] in the eye. We are aware that the hospital has a committee which conducts its management; so how do Dobroczynność assimilationists as such get in there? They already once had the hospital at their disposal, and who does not remember in what state they left it? There was then a complete liquidation; they went bankrupt, handing over the hospital with padlocks hanging on it. Can one grasp what it means to bring such an institution to a state of padlocks? We understand that in order to hang padlocks on a hospital one must first get rid of the sick people who come to be healed; can one grasp what situation one is in when forced to liquidate a fully equipped hospital?
And do we no longer remember what energies Dr. Perlman applied then so that the padlocks would be taken off and the gates opened wide to the poor sick people? He knocked on every door then, he stormed our editorial office — write, he begged — rouse, encourage the public, so that they give us the possibility to tear off the locks that had already rusted; and as soon as a kehilla administration arose that began to show signs of life, he received protection and help there too. The great Jewish heart did not rest until he succeeded in tearing off the locks and opening the hospital gates wide to all strata of the Jewish population, and the end was that the hospital acquired such a good reputation that not only well-to-do Jews but also Christians come there.
And now? Now the wheel is starting to turn over, and who knows whether, God forbid, it may not lead to the same state as in the times when the Dobroczynność ran the institution.
Where, then, is the committee to which the institution was entrusted and in which the town places so much trust? Where are those devoted people to whom the institution is so dear and precious? Why did they allow things to be brought to the present state? If something or other undesirable occurred among the leading persons, it was the committee's duty not to let it come to frictions. Within the walls [printed "וועגט"] of the hospital everything should have been stifled, so that nothing would be carried out into the street that could disgrace the honour of the one important institution we possess in Zagłębie, and for which we must have respect and regard both for the walls of the hospital with its patients and for the people who have been sacrificing themselves for years. One must not forget that this is not some little society existing on paper, such as we have lately grown used to. The Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec is, after all, a large enterprise. It is a whole factory.
So are they dragging politics in there too? Have they found "dangerous elements" there too, of which one must rid oneself? Incidentally, it is also interesting what the danger consists of and to whom they are dangerous, for as far as we know, nobody in the hospital knew anything more than healing the sick and seeking means to cover the expenses, over which there was always a struggle to wage. Of other "fighters" we have never heard.
It must not be allowed that the dangerous microbe of playing politics should creep into the hospital too — the microbe that everywhere eats away at the health of an institution and leads to its real ruin.
It is therefore important to stifle this dangerous situation. An end must be made to the unfavourable state of affairs, which may lead to the suppression and degradation of the prestige of this useful people's institution.
One must now set about radically cleansing the poisoned air that has just arisen there.
A trial must be held; an all-round, honest investigation must be arranged that will shed light on the state of the institution. We must hear clear and open words, so as not to let the smallest stain fall either on the institution or on the people who sacrifice themselves for the institution, which they have set before themselves as an ideal on their life's path.
It must be established once and for all who are the disturbers and who — the builders, so that those whom we need should not have to leave their positions, and on the other hand those who come to play politics and poison the air should not be admitted.
— The air must therefore be cleansed in public!
Selekt.
Supplementary Budgets and the Growth of the High Cost of Living

[Poland — finance and taxes.]
On the 10th of this month the Finance Committee of the Sejm [the Polish lower house] met to consider a series of government proposals on taxes. The projects are as follows: raising the land tax by one hundred percent; raising the "local tax" [podatek lokalowy, a tax on dwellings and premises] by fifty percent; introducing a permanent property tax amounting to 4—5 per mille of the assessed value of the property, or 5—10 percent of income; and reducing, under certain conditions, the turnover tax on certain articles of industry and trade at the discretion of the Finance Minister.
The government hopes to obtain from these sources some 600 million złoty of new revenue, which will be earmarked for budget purposes, first of all for paying the housing[?] allowance for state officials.
Earlier still, in August of last year, the passenger railway fare was raised by twenty percent. At the end of the year the postal tariff was raised, and now an increase of the freight tariffs by twenty percent is also being announced.
From the government's operations and projects one may conclude that, despite the optimism of official spheres, the budget has not been brought into any equilibrium.
The opposition groupings in the Sejm, too, assure that if the implementation of the government's tax programme secured a stable financial equilibrium, at least for several years, a majority for this programme would be found in the legislative bodies. But Minister Czechowicz's [Gabriel Czechowicz, Finance Minister] programme is a vicious circle in which the state budget has been turning for a number of years already.
The vicious circle consists in this: with the increase of the tax burden for budget purposes — which automatically brings about a growth of the high cost of living and once again calls forth an increase of budget expenditure, personnel and all[?] other — the budget worked out by the government for the raising of taxes and levies becomes unreal because of the rise in prices. The consequence is that the government must overstep the budget and draw up supplementary budgets, for which new sources of cover must be sought.
The state official, for whom means are being sought to cover his allowances, will not gain from them; for what benefit will it be to him if, simultaneously with the few-złoty housing[?] allowance, the housing[?] tax is raised by fifty percent — not to speak of the masses of workers, employees and the middle class, for whom no special gratuities are foreseen and who are merely exposed to all the consequences of the rising cost of living.
Stabilisation of the budget is possible through stabilisation of prices, and the latter stabilisation will certainly not be attained by raising taxes and charges. If a reform of taxation is necessary, it lies in the direction of spreading them out, so that not one part of the population pays the price of the privileging of the other part. The road now chosen by the Finance Ministry forces the state economy to go on turning in the same vicious circle.
G. T.
Państwo Kugelszarben at a Jewish Concert

(Humoresque)
By Yosef Dov.
When Pan Kugelszarben [roughly "Mr Kugel-scraper"], on his way home at midday, caught sight from afar of the big blue poster with its "Kiddush-Levanah" [huge] letters: Koncet Winogradowa [sic, for Koncert — "Winogradow's concert"], his face lit up like the sun in Tammuz.
In his great joy he did not read the whole text of the poster. What interested him now above all was the bottom line: where one gets tickets.
And indeed, without much delay, he went off in a flash ["hegdum pegdum"] and bought up the front seats.
— "No—no—no! To się moja Aldona ucieszy" [Polish: "Well, well, well! Won't my Aldona be pleased!"] — he kept humming under his nose, and, pressing his briefcase tightly under his arm, he hurried home with quick steps.
At lunch Pan Kugelszarben did not say a single word about the tickets he had bought. Being in general a man of principles, he held especially to the principle that one must give a wife "niespodzianki" [surprises], and so this time too he buried the secret in his heart until supper (kolacja).
In the evening Pan Kugelszarben and Pani Kugelszarbenowa celebrated supper lavishly; even the special little smile that used to dance between Pan Kugelszarben's moustaches at lunch was not missing.
The little bell hanging from the chandelier (żyrandol) above the table worked wonders.. The clatter of forks, knives and spoons was interrupted from time to time by some humming under the nose, which came now from Pan Kugelszarben himself and now from Pani Kugelszarbenowa...
Suddenly Pan Wacław took his wallet out of his inside pocket, drew out of it, with relish, the two tickets and presented them to Pani Kugelszarbenowa, exclaiming with pathos:
— "Matuś! Bileciki na koncert Winogradowa!" ["Darling! Tickets for Winogradow's concert!"]
— "Co mówisz!" ["You don't say!"] — cried Pani Kugelszarbenowa with such vehemence that she nearly fell out of her armchair, and in her great surprise she ran to her "kochany mężulek" [beloved hubby] and gave him kisses.
Soon the whole household staff of Państwo [Mr and Mrs] Kugelszarben was on its feet. The preparations for the concert were in full swing.
The feverish work on the toilette of Pani Kugelszarbenowa, which as if out of spite would not come together this time, was finally crowned with due success, and at exactly half past eight in the evening Państwo Kugelszarben, decked out in honey and milk, appeared at the "Corso" [?] theatre.
In the waiting hall of the theatre stood young people chatting and even allowing themselves to "szwargotać" [jabber] out loud — in real "kugel-language" [Yiddish].
Państwo Kugelszarben exchanged astonished glances: how on earth had they landed here among this "chałata" [derogatory: caftan-wearing Jews]! It could only be some "nieporozumienie" [misunderstanding]...
They looked cautiously around on all sides, lest, God forbid, some gentile acquaintance should notice them, and then they went into the hall as quickly as possible, where they both sat down comfortably in the first row and began to study the concert programme.
Suddenly Pani Kugelszarbenowa's nose turned white as chalk, her heart began to pound, and everything began to swim before her eyes...
— "Wacuś! — she almost cried out loud — patrz go! Co za kompromitacja! Winogradow, carski śpiewak, będzie śpiewać żargonowe piosenki... Nie wytrzymam!..." ["Wacuś! Look at that! What a disgrace! Winogradow, the tsar's singer, is going to sing jargon (Yiddish) songs... I can't bear it!..."]
Pan Kugelszarben opened his eyes wide. Now everything had become clear to him; now he understood why the "chałata" had gathered here. How gladly he would have run off to where the pepper grows, but alas it was already too late. The hall was as bright as day, and it seemed to him that everyone's eyes were turned on him. He was afraid to turn his head.
In his mind a thought was brewing [?]: how to "uspokoić" [calm down] his wife, Pani Kugelszarbenowa, to find some excuse, some consolation. At last he hit upon a ruse.
— "Matuś! Dajże spokój... — he began to soothe and persuade her — pan jegomość z tego Winogradowa... nabiera Żydków, a potem ich wystawia na dudka... Rozumiesz?"... ["Darling! Do stop it... this gentleman Winogradow... is taking the little Jews in, and then he'll make fools of them... Understand?"]
Pani Kugelszarben laughed so hard at her Matuś's cleverness that she shook all over as if in a fever. But Pan Wacław himself did not believe his own words, and in his heart he felt that a terrible, unavoidable catastrophe was bearing down on him...
Meanwhile the hall went dark. The first part of the concert began. Winogradow appeared as Pagliacci ["Payats"], sang, and the audience kept applauding.
Państwo Kugelszarben, gradually swept along by the current, finally went into a trance and completely forgot their impending misfortune, just as one forgets a bad dream... They enjoyed themselves together with the whole audience.
But no happiness in the world lasts for ever. And the joy of the Kugelszarbens too was a very short one.
The second part of the programme began, and it turned out that the bad dream had become [?] a "sad", oh! a very sad reality...
Winogradow sang with gusto one Yiddish song after another, and the Jewish audience was in seventh heaven ["in the feathers"]... The hall stormed and shouted "bis!" for all it was worth.
To Pani Kugelszarbenowa it seemed she was riding a carousel... She felt all her blood rushing to her face... She sat on hot coals. At last she could hold out no longer and burst out in anger:
— "To jest okropnie, przecież!... Czysta manifestacja syjonistyczna!... Mały Tel-Awiw!.." ["But this is dreadful!... A pure Zionist demonstration!... A little Tel Aviv!.."]
On the nearby benches a little commotion arose. People began to shout: "Cicho! Sza! Nie przeszkadzać!..." ["Quiet! Shh! Don't disturb!..."]
But Pani Kugelszarbenowa could not calm down by any means. She was all thrown about with agitation and kept grumbling: "Taki skandal!... Takie świństwo!..." ["Such a scandal!... Such a swinish trick!..."]
Pan Kugelszarben himself sat quietly with his head lowered like a mourner, and only God in heaven knows what was going on in his heart... He found it terribly stuffy ("duszno"), and from time to time he passed his hand over his face exactly like someone driving away a swarm of pesky [? "zludne"] flies...
The folk-song concert was rich in Jewish and Hasidic songs, among them also the well-known song "Kaddish" by Reb Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev.
That was already too much...
Pan Kugelszarben's patience finally burst and he flew into a rage.
— "Co za prowokacja — he shouted — na Starym Rynku!... To nie bóżnica..." ["What a provocation — on the Old Market Square!... This isn't a synagogue..."]
He got up from his seat and wanted to leave the hall, but at that very moment all the electric lamps went on and the curtain came down.
Helplessly [? "afhendig"] he sank back into his seat and, turning towards Pani Kugelszarbenowa, he hunched himself up so much that he could hardly be seen.
During the last part of the concert the Kugelszarbens were so crushed that it was simply pitiful and frightening to look at them. Even the merriest number did not amuse them. In their ears rang constantly the "terrible" words: "Kaddish", "Kaddish"... and before their eyes stood like ghosts the "cheder", the "bóżnica" [synagogue] and the "Sądny Dzień" [Day of Judgment, Yom Kippur]. — — — — —
When the concert ended, Państwo Kugelszarben stole out of the hall through a back door and fled as if from a plague.
On the way home they did not exchange half a word. Pan Kugelszarben walked like a condemned man. He felt that he was to blame for everything: why hadn't he read the poster before buying the tickets — then he would not have come to this misfortune. He also knew that his wife's present silence was no good sign at all...
And indeed his foreboding did not deceive him. They arrived home safely, but only here did the epilogue of the concert begin to play out...
As soon as Pani Kugelszarbenowa had opened the door, she let out a great shriek like a "tekiah gedolah" [the long shofar blast], collapsed like a bomb onto the floor and began to convulse as if in mortal danger.
The servants, who had already been asleep, came running together in great alarm. They brought ether, valerian drops, laid on cold compresses...
Pan Kugelszarben paced nervously up and down, his hands clasped behind his back, never ceasing to argue with and justify himself to himself:
— "Istna kara boska!... Któż by się spodziewał, że ten carski Winogradow z niebieskiego ptaka [?] jest zwyczajnym syjonistą?!..." ["A real punishment from God!... Who would have expected that this tsarist Winogradow, the rogue ("blue bird") [?], is an ordinary Zionist?!..."]
— — — — — — — — — —
Only at about two in the morning was order restored in the apartment of Państwo Kugelszarben, and the normal rest and quiet set in again... Only from their bedroom there still came from time to time single, unclear sounds, as if spoken in sleep: "Ta—ki... skan—dal.. Ta—ki skan—dal..." ["Such... a scan—dal..."]
The Rebbe's Son (17)

[Serialized historical novel — the 1648 massacres, Chmielnicki's camp; installment 17, ending with the opening of Chapter Eight.]
A historical Jewish novel by Yakov Tsimerman.

Her blue arms, which showed from under the thin cloth with which she was covered, were clear as marble, but they were weak and almost motionless.

Beside the sick woman her daughters sat on the ground, and with bated breath they listened to the slightest rustle made by the gravely ill woman's body.

It was such a sad and pitiful picture that it could have moved the heart of even a Chmielnicki...

"Well, how are you, Miriam?" Chmielnicki asked with a feigned calm expression. "How do you like life here in the camp? After all, you wanted to stay together with your daughters, and I granted your request, because I remembered the kindnesses you once did me. But now you must surely see that your body is already too weak for you [printed "di" for "du"] to be able to bear the hard strains of camp life."

"I shall soon be released from it, Bogdan Chmielnicki," the sick woman answered in a weak voice. "But I have one more, single request of you, which I hope you will fulfil for me. Why, you yourself have just spoken of the kindnesses I used to do you. And now, in memory of those good old times, I want to ask you to allow my daughters to bury my dead body here at the edge of the forest under the tree in whose shade I have spent the last few days of my life. Miriam took your part at a time when you were not as powerful as today, and now, in my dying hour, I beg you not to refuse my last wish..."

"Your wish shall be fulfilled!" Chmielnicki answered, and he was already about to leave.

"Stay!" the sick woman cried out with her last strength. "I have one more wish on my heart, and because I can see in you that you are now in a milder mood, I hope you will fulfil my last request as well... I once saved your life, and in your great need I had pity on you; so now you too have pity on my children..."

The sick woman had overexerted herself. Her feeble strength left her and she fell back powerless onto the bundle of straw.

A little later, when she opened her eyes again, she saw that Chmielnicki was no longer there.

A sad smile now played on her tired and withered lips.

"Why did I humble myself so before him?" she thought to herself. "Do I not know all too well that his heart is as if of stone and incapable of any feeling of pity? Nevertheless he did promise me my first request... and I know that he is used to keeping his word, in good as well as in bad..."

"Children!" she now turned to her daughters. "If after my death they make any difficulties for you over my burial, you should turn about this [printed "wenen dem"] to Chmielnicki and see that he keeps his promise. I want to lie buried here under the tree. Only yesterday I had a sweet dream that I met there with your father and my own father, and it seemed to me that all three of us were united there..."

"Mother!" the elder daughter cried out with great warmth. "Don't be so worried and despairing, don't talk so much about death. We have a great and good God. He can work great wonders, and He will surely help us, bring us all back together and unite us again. Don't be so sad and worried — you are frightening us, dear, only and beloved mother!.."

"Of course I am sad, dear children," the sick woman answered in a weak voice, "and how could I not be, when I feel that my last hour has now come. But worried I am not, because I never was in all my life. Don't you remember, dear children, the beautiful verse in Psalms: 'Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no [evil], for now [sic; the verse reads "Thou"] art with me; Thy rod and Thy staff, they comfort me' — even when I walk in the valley of the shadow of death I am not afraid of any evil, for You are with me, Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me!

"The earth on which we sinful people wander about is for us a valley of the shadow of death. Nevertheless I do not lose heart, and I beg you, my dear children, that you too should not lose heart, even when the hardest thing befalls you...

"Do you hear me, dear children! May I take this assurance with me into the grave? And I also want you to dig my grave with your own hands, and that no strange, unclean hands should help you [printed "me"] in it..."

The children wept bitterly, and to calm the sick woman a little they promised to fulfil her last wish, however hard it might be for them...

"Thank you, my dear children," the sick woman said with her last strength. "I know you and I know that you will keep your word, but the cruelty of our enemies and the weakness of your bodies may perhaps, God forbid, yet bring it about that you cease to be pure, chaste Jewish daughters; so I beg you that each of you lay her right hand on my heart and swear to me that you will rather choose death, by your own hand or at the hands of the enemy, than lead a life of disgrace and shame. Swear, dear children, lay your hands on the heart of your mother, who still lives and breathes only for your sake!..."

"We swear!" both girls cried out, and laid their trembling hands on the heart of their dying mother.

"I thank you, dear children! Now I can die in peace."

For a good while longer the sick woman talked, but incoherently. Her last words that could still be understood were a greeting to her husband — if he is still alive and the children are granted to see him again, then when [printed "men"] the land one day grows calmer, they should take her out from under the tree again and bring her to burial in the cemetery in Niemirów.

"Hear, O Israel... the Lord our God... the Lord is One!..."

With these very words she gave up her pure soul to God, blessed be He, who sits on high and looks on at the terrible cruelties that people commit against one another in His name and in the name of the true religion...

— — — — — — — — — —

Bogdan Chmielnicki sat in his tent and, in the presence of his two chief men, Gebaba and Moradenko, listened to the report that the runaway Cossack Piatrov had brought about Prince Wiśniowiecki, who is now in Warsaw.

He listened to it all with great attention, and when Petrov had finished telling, Chmielnicki jumped up from his chair and with great satisfaction laid his hand on Petrov's shoulder and said to him:

"Bazyl Pietrov! You have now shown that you are a true Cossack! For that you shall stay close to me and fight at my side. You will want for nothing, and from the most beautiful Jewish girls you will be able to pick as many as your heart desires. You will surely be content and richly rewarded for all the dangers you endured on your flight here to us, and for the rifle bullet that the scoundrelly young prince sent after you. Only be patient! You will yet meet that young fellow, just as I hope to meet his father once more; then we will pay these lords back in our Cossack way..."

Bazyl Pietrov's face shone with happiness, and on his lame and wounded leg he tried to limp over to Chmielnicki to kiss his hand.

"Gebaba and Moradenko, come!" Chmielnicki now called out. "I want to hand over to you the two Jewish girls whose mother is surely dead by now. The blonde one, who is called Hadassah, shall be for you, Gebaba, and the other, the dark-eyed and beautiful Judith, shall be yours, Moradenko! You, Pietrov, come along with us too; for you I have other girls — they are not to be brushed aside either, and they will surely be to your taste.

"But there is one thing I want all three of you to know. You must leave the girls alone for the time being. I promised the mother that the daughters may bury her under a tree at the edge of the forest, and I want my given word to be kept. Come, and meanwhile have a look at their pretty little faces!..."

— — — — — — — — — —

Beside the dead body of the late Miriam sat the younger daughter, Judith. The elder, Hadassah, dug the grave under the tree with her delicate hands, and when she grew so tired that she could no longer move a limb, the second sister took over the spade and went on [printed "meyter" for "vayter"] with the work.

So the girls took turns again and again until evening, when the sun was already about to set, and then at last they were done. They kept their promise, and the mother already rested deep in the earth under the tree, as she herself had asked.

Now the four "dear" personages appeared in the distance: Chmielnicki, Gebaba, Moradenko and Pietrov. They soon came up to the girls. Without much ado Gebaba and Moradenko each seized a different girl and led them away in different directions.

The girls were badly frightened; they felt instinctively that after this parting they would not soon see each other again. Unable to find any words, they merely took leave of each other with a shake of the head, and at that each of them clutched the parchment amulet that hung around her neck.

That same eve of Shavuot, which in the camp of Bogdan Chmielnicki had looked so terrible, wore a quite different face in Kraków — a merry and a festive one besides.

The Rothschilds' „Ancestral House“

(Impressions from a visit to Frankfurt).
By Moshe Zinowitz.

One of the last sights still to be seen in the former „Judengasse“ [Jews' Lane] in Frankfurt is the „ancestral house“ of the famous Jewish family, the Rothschilds, in Frankfurt am Main. The house where the founder of the Rothschild banking house, Mayer Amschel Rothschild, lived — and there, in this modest house, the foundation stone was laid of the greatest world firm of its time — that of the „Rothschild Brothers“.
Over the last 100 years, since the Jews of Frankfurt moved out of the narrow ghetto, being permitted to live throughout the city, the „Judengasse“, today's „Börnestraße“, has been very sparsely inhabited by Jews. In the course of time this street has been rebuilt and has changed its old appearance. Apart from the old Jewish cemetery, which lies next to the „Börnestraße“, there is no other historic monument here except the old house of Mayer Amschel Rothschild. His family has seen to it that this „ancestral house“, so cherished by them, should not be pulled down, and it is carefully preserved.
From outside, the 3-storey house makes quite a handsome impression with its old building style. Everything has remained as of old. The small window-panes, the painted pictures and drawings and the various carvings on the house doors and windows show the great efforts of the house administrators employed there to keep the „Rothschild house“ true to its old pattern.
I examine the interior of the house: first of all I see the first „family room“, which lies by the street. The room belonged to the old lady Gerela [sic; Gutle] Rothschild, who lived much longer than her husband Mayer Amschel and was still privileged to see with her own eyes the great world wealth of her sons.
The children themselves no longer lived in Frankfurt. Their great businesses took them to London, Vienna, Naples, etc. Only one son remained in Frankfurt, who managed the Frankfurt bank branch — Baron Amschel — Mayer Rothschild.
Although the emigration from the „Judengasse“ to the other parts of Frankfurt was large, the old lady Gerela Rothschild did not want to part with her old dwelling in the „Judengasse“, there, where she and her husband had had the great luck and success of becoming so rich. „There, where I became rich, there I also want to die“ — she answered her children, who begged her to move to the city centre. By a corner window there still stands the armchair in which this modest woman sat watching the passers-by of the ghetto. Behind the armchair hangs her portrait. In the traditional lace bonnet, in an old-fashioned shawl, she gives the impression of a typical small-town Jewish woman of the ghetto era.
„When this picture was made — my „guide“ tells me — she is said to have already been an old woman, one of the oldest women among the Frankfurt Jews.“
On the wall opposite one sees the portraits of her 5 sons, handsome Jewish faces with the genuine Jewish smile and charm.
The wallpaper on the walls is of the same „original pattern“ as 100 years ago, and so everything breathes the character of the old times.
The sofa also catches the eye. A quite ordinary piece of furniture in any petty-bourgeois home, but in those days it was reportedly regarded as a luxury article... Among the Frankfurt Jews it is still told to this day that when Mayer Amschel Rothschild bought the sofa, the ghetto Jews ran to look at it as at a wonder...
Next to the door of the room one notices a wall cupboard built into the wall, which reportedly served Amschel Mayer as a sideboard, and there Mrs. Rothschild kept the cake and tart that she gave her children to taste from time to time...
I also see a quite plain room with an old safe — there was the counting-house, or rather, the „exchange room“ of Mayer Amschel Rothschild. I look at another storey, where the real „living room“ is said to have been, the apartment of Mayer Amschel, which in recent years, however, has been turned into a private house of study (beit midrash).
At the front, next to the kitchen, one can notice traces of a well, which Mayer Amschel had made in his house for convenience. The walls there are still intact and, as before, painted in blue and white stripes.
For all her modesty, the old lady Rothschild, who did not want to stir from her ghetto house, knew the power and influence of her sons. Thus, for example, it is told that in the year 1848, the year of war and revolution, a neighbour ran in to Gerela to ask her whether she knew that war had already been declared, about which the whole „Judengasse“ was talking so much. In a calm tone the old Gerela answered her that she could go home in peace. „I shall tell my sons not to lend the princes any money — and then they will not wage any war anyway“...
Of all the 18 children she bore, only 10 remained to her, 5 sons and 5 daughters, and only[?] the eldest of the sons, Baron Amschel, remained living in Frankfurt as head of the Frankfurt branch of the world firm „Banking House Rothschild“.
He himself no longer lived in the „Judengasse“. In his former residence „on the Zeil“ there is now a „care home“ for old Jewish women. He did not let a single day pass without visiting his old mother in the Judengasse. Every time he used to drive up, dressed in his original garments, with his equipage, it was always a sensation. All the inhabitants of the „Judengasse“ came running to look at and gaze upon the Jewish millionaire... The house was besieged by curious people and by plain poor folk, who stretched out their hands for alms, and he indeed used to give each of them money with a full hand.
Baron Amschel Rothschild was a great wit, and very many anecdotes about him have remained among the people of Frankfurt. Thus, for instance, the following story is told: once he went for a walk and heard two workers saying to each other that it would be only fair for Rothschild to divide his fortune among the people, and that he ought to be forced to do it. The baron listened, and laughing he went up to them and said:
— Why do you need to force me to divide my fortune? I give it away voluntarily, and I'll start with you. Here, each of you gets one gulden; more than that won't come to your share anyway...
The „ancestral house“ of the Rothschilds, which has stood for over 200 years, is a fine monument to old historic Jewish Frankfurt and to the children of the „Judengasse“ who, by their energy and initiative, made a name for themselves throughout the world.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: A Bloody Fight between a Policeman and Bandits

[Head of the local page; Będzin — crime.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 7 / 7 Shevat 5689 — Piątek 18 stycznia 1929 [Friday, 18 January 1929].)
Będzin
A bloody fight between a policeman and bandits.
1 bandit killed — the policeman seriously wounded.
On the Warpie, the quarter where the underworld has its home, a bloody fight between a policeman and bandits took place on the night from Saturday to Sunday.
Policeman Tarba[?], standing at his post, saw several persons carrying filled sacks. Wanting[?] to stop the thieves, the policeman fired several times into the air.
The bandits answered with a volley of shots, and a bloody fight broke out between the two sides. The result is that 1 bandit was killed and the policeman was seriously wounded by 7 bullets.
The policeman is in the municipal hospital.
Killed a Man with a Slap. The Slapper Acquitted of Any Punishment.

[Będzin — crime; court.] In the month of lipiec [July] the caretaker (house-watchman) of Altman's house in the Old Market was killed by a slap. These days the slapper stood before the district court in Sosnowiec, and after hearing a series of witnesses the court issued an acquittal.
In the Old Market the Trams Will Run More Slowly.

[Będzin — transport; trams.] As we are informed, the tram management has adopted a decision that, in order to prevent accidents, the trams on the new Będzin—Czeladź line will run slowly, especially in the Old Market, where it will travel at a speed of 9 kilometres per hour. (On the Będzin—Sosnowiec — Dąbrowa line it runs 40 kilometres an hour.)
Stops („przystanki“) will be on Potocka[?] street next to Strapflich's[?] house, on Jana street and just after the bridge.
Before Going to Jail She Drank „L'chaim“...

[Będzin — attempted suicide.] A certain young Christian woman of Zawodzie[?] 14 had been sentenced to 1 day's arrest. When a policeman came to her flat to take her away to jail, the sentenced woman asked the policeman to allow her to go into the other room to get herself ready.
When the policeman saw that his „client“ was not coming out, he went into the other room, where he found her lying on the floor without signs of life.
In this condition she was taken to hospital, where it was established that she had drunk a small bottle of vinegar essence.
Suicide Because of Unemployment.

[Będzin — unemployment; attempted suicide.] The 33-year-old Minacz[?] came here from Czeladź to look for work so as to be able to save his family from hunger.
For a whole day he found no work and had no money to buy something to eat. Coming to the restaurant „Kryształ“, he got a real appetite, but, not having the means to enjoy this pleasure, he bought himself a small bottle of vinegar with his last groszy and drank it.
In a serious condition the would-be suicide was taken to hospital.
18 Wagons of Coal Distributed, but Reb Winter Laughs at It.

[Będzin — relief; coal for the poor.] The „notables“ of the town of Będzin remember every winter to donate coal for poor families. In this respect our town distinguishes itself, for in no town in Zagłębie is a coal campaign carried out in winter.
As we are informed, 18 wagons of coal have been distributed so far, at 2—4 and 9 korzec of coal per family. But the winter is growing stronger and the poor people are freezing.
Those who have not yet given for this purpose must settle it at once with Mr. M. Rozenzaft or at the office of „Dobroczynność“.
Sosnowiec — General Meeting of the „Merchants' Union“.

[Sosnowiec — trade; merchants' union.]
Sosnowiec
General meeting of the „Merchants' Union“ („Sokhrim-Fareyn“).
In its own premises (Piłsudskiego 12) the annual general meeting of the „Merchants' Union“ took place last[?] Sunday.
The merchants showed a „great interest“ in the meeting. At the appointed hour, 4 in the afternoon, for the second term, out of more than 300 members no fewer than 12 came (exactly[?] twelve, like the number of the twelve tribes); only when the clock already showed past six did the number of interested parties rise to 25...
With such a number of members the meeting is opened by the president, Mr. Zylberszlag, who hands over the chair — at the request of those assembled — to Mr. Zendel, with Messrs. Motel Merin and Israel Moshe Wajgryb[?] as assessors, secretary Mr. Berkowicz. The report on the activity so far is delivered by Mr. Zylberszlag. From the report we learn little of any substantive activity; but Mr. Z. delivers an accusatory speech against the headquarters in Warsaw, especially against deputy Wiślicki, for their disregard of the „Merchants' Union“, owing to which[?] the union has received no representation in the Chamber of Commerce that is to be opened[?] in Sosnowiec.
After the report a discussion developed, in the course of which a dispute arose between ex-president Mr. Warman and some board members, whom Mr. Warman proposes to expel for causing damage to the union.
The proposal took on a stormy character, and the upshot is that no concrete proposals at all were adopted; only a temporary commission was elected, which is to bring about a second meeting.
A New Network of Tram Lines in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — transport.]
As our readers already know, the Będzin—Czeladź tram will begin running in the next few days.
A ticket from Będzin to Czeladź (from the bridge onward) will cost 35 gr., from Małachowska Street 50 gr.
Besides this, preparations are being made to lay out a new network of tram lines. The plan provides for linking Czeladź with Siemianowice, Sosnowiec with Sielec and Środula, Sosnowiec—Mysłowice, Sosnowiec—Czeladź—Saturn and Dąbrowa—Strzemieszyce.
Work on the new projected lines will begin in the spring.
114 Reports against Those Who Rode “na gapę”

[Zagłębie — transport.]
The tram management asks us to draw attention to the tactless behaviour of passengers who ride the trams “na gapę” [free-riding, without paying].
The statistics have shown that in the month of grudzień [December] 114 reports were drawn up for cheating the conductors with nearer stations or for buying no tickets at all.
The management complains that many passengers, when the conductors ask them for tickets, answer with tactless words that lead to conflicts, so that the conductors cannot carry out their duties properly.
The “City Fathers” Have Divided Things Up...

[Sosnowiec — municipality.]
The new city administration held its first meeting under the chairmanship of President Marczyński.
At the meeting the work in the magistrate was divided up.
President Marczyński took over the department of finance and construction, Vice-President Jarosz[?] — sewerage and municipal workshops, alderman (ławnik) Dobrowolski — schooling, and alderman Sztet[?] — social welfare.
Merchants “na grandę”...

[Rybnik — fraud.]
Three months ago 3 local Jewish young men founded a “spółka” [partnership] in Rybnik, where they opened a big business.
The little “merchants” soon obtained credit from a number of local merchants, but when the bills of exchange became “ripe” the “merchants” packed up the “shop” and vanished...
This Tuesday the Rybnik police found a large quantity of goods lying in a cellar.
A True “Woman of Valour”...

[Court — crime.]
In the 120-year-old [combined ages] Chełmiński couple, “domestic peace” had vanished, and the 62-year-old little wife decided to poison her husband...
To this end she went to a merchant she knew and confided to him a “secret”: that she needed a strong poison to poison the rats (szczury) in her flat.
The merchant, suspecting that the “woman of valour” wanted to use it to poison her “two-legged rat”, sold her drinking soda and assured her that “the powder (proszek) will drive away the rats”.
The “secret” was discovered and the old woman stood trial for it before the local court. Because there was no clear evidence of her guilt, she was acquitted.
Railway Employee Crushed

[Zagłębie — accident.]
A freight train going from Ząbkowice to Grojca[?] (perhaps Grodziec) ran over the 19-year-old railway employee Dziadosz and cut off his head and hands.
—o—
Excise Inspector in Court.
Before the local district court stood the excise inspector Skrzeczyński[?], who was accused of having extorted, by means of threats, 4,500 zł. as bribe money from the distillery belonging to Messrs. Paszmikiewicz[?] and Grunwald.
The accused was acquitted.
—o—
A Faithful Dog.
Three weeks ago Dr. Zieleniewski died here. Since then his dog runs every day to the grave of its former master.
—o—
Despite What You Say, “Panie jabie”[?]...
Jan Paszkowski, general inspector of the firm A. Brzeziński in Königshütte [Chorzów], took up residence at the “Grand Hotel” in Łódź and placed several advertisements in the newspapers saying he was looking for employees.
Naturally, there is no shortage of unemployed, and dozens applied to him. Paszkowski engaged them all and would demand from each of them a deposit (kaucja) of several hundred zł.
Meanwhile several of the employees were not satisfied with Paszkowski's negotiations and turned directly to the firm Brzeziński in Königshütte.
How surprised they were when they received an answer from the firm that Paszkowski had indeed worked for the firm some time ago, but had been removed from there for swindles, and consequently had no right whatever to engage anyone for the firm.
This was reported to the investigation office, which ordered the “bird” arrested.
The further investigation established that Paszkowski had not only engaged employees for the firm Brzeziński, but had also sought to make a match, and he conducted this campaign “en gros”: he answered all the matchmaking advertisements in the newspapers, and since many of the girls looking for a match took a liking to him, he managed to swindle larger sums out of them for “setting up a flat”, and so on.
Dąbrowa — Last Session of the City Council

[Dąbrowa — municipality.]
This coming Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) the last, liquidation session of the old city council will take place.
The first session of the new city council will probably take place next Wednesday.
—o—
A Jewish Young Woman Sentenced to 2 Years in Prison.
On Monday the local young woman Golda Dymant sat on the defendants' bench in Sosnowiec for conducting communist activity.
D. was sentenced to 2 years in prison and loss of rights.
Labour Courts — Already in Operation / Olkusz: From the Court / Three Peasants Poisoned by Denatured Spirit / Theatre Repertoire of the Polish and German Theatre in Katowice

[Labour — the labour court in Będzin; followed by four short items: Olkusz (two), Katowice — theatre, Będzin — cinema.]
Since Tuesday the labour court has already been operating here; it has been introduced throughout Poland by the decree of the Ministries of Justice and of Labour.
The local labour court covers the courts of Groyitse [?] [probably Grodziec], Dąbrowa and Będzin.
There are 90 lay judges, i.e. 45 from the employers and 45 from the employees.
The office of the labour court is at 3 Maja [Street] 14.
—o—
Olkusz.
From the Court.
A trial took place in the local magistrate's court, brought by the professional (trade) union “Garl” [?] against Mrs. Grosman, owner of the union's premises, for evicting the union without the court's consent.
The defendant argued in her defence that for a long time she had not been paid any rent and that the premises had always been left unlocked. The police commandant, Mr. Sawicki, appeared as a witness; he confirmed this and added that illegal lectures had been held on the premises by Miss Warszawska of Sosnowiec, among others, that the union was generally suspect in the eyes of the police, and that the union had been evicted with their knowledge. The court acquitted the defendant.
—o—
Three Peasants Poisoned by Denatured Spirit.
In the village of Pshutnin [?] near Olkusz a group of peasants got drunk on denatured spirit. The result was terrible: three peasants died the next day and several are still ill.
A. G.
