From the Public to the Public

[Letters to the editor — free tribune.]
(A free tribune for our readers).
I.
Esteemed Mr. Editor!
We ask you to print the following letter in your newspaper:
Of the former literary-musical society "Hazamir", which years ago was well known to the public in our town, there has unfortunately remained no more than a mere library, which is in a moribund state.
After a period of 15 years we have not had the privilege of hearing from the so-called management any report whatsoever on the state of the library, which cost so much effort and work.
We, a group of readers of the "Hazamir" library, have decided to turn publicly to the management with the "demand" to give a clear account of its 15 years of activity.
At the same time we turn to the public, to whom the remaining cultural institution is dear, to express its opinion on this matter.
Respectfully,
A group of readers.
(10 signatures follow).
II.
Honoured Editor!
Allow me space in your newspaper to print the following letter, for which I thank you in advance.
In "Zaglembier Tsaytung" No. 2 a note was printed under the title "Why did Dr. Melodysta step out of the Jewish hospital?!"
Quite apart from the fact that the published [?] conversation in many details does not agree with my position, the whole note came to me as a great surprise, because I could not at all believe that your correspondent, with whom I happened to have a private conversation, would permit himself to publish in my name, as it were an official statement on the hospital question, since in general I have not reacted officially up to today, nor will I in future, to what is now happening in the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec.
Dr. T. Melodysta.
III.
In the history of mankind and in the history of nations there are names so great that they fill an entire epoch by themselves; there are names so exalted that at their sound one is filled with reverence; there are names with so much content that it seems every letter composing them says much more than thick learned folios; names that sound like the call of the shofar and shine like a torch through the centuries.
Such a name — a symbol, such a name — a watchword, such a name — an incantation full of wondrous power, is for many Jews and Poles the name of Berek Joselewicz, the colonel of the Polish forces in the days of Tadeusz Kościuszko and participant in the desperate struggles of the period of the Napoleonic wars.
To popularise this great name, to make it known to the masses — that is [printed "in"] the task of the Wilno Committee for Honouring the Memory of Berek Joselewicz.
The Wilno Committee, which has the honour of standing under the patronage of Marshal Piłsudski, and which also counts among its ranks many prominent citizens of Jewish and Polish society — this committee already made itself known on the day of 6 May of this year by the solemn prayer service in the Wilno Great Synagogue (Kahal-shul) and by the academy (commemorative assembly), which deeply moved all of Wilno and found a sympathetic echo in the Wilno press and in the press of other Polish cities.
Shortly there will appear from the press a jubilee album in honour of Berek Joselewicz — a splendid book with 150 illustrations, with a text prepared by outstanding literary forces and with valuable illustrative and iconographic material drawn from the museum and archival collections of all Poland, as well as from Vienna and Paris. This memorial book — the album will be the first cornerstone of the monument that will be erected through the cooperation of Jews and Poles in honour of Berek Joselewicz.
We turn with an appeal to all Polish citizens, without distinction of nationality and faith, to support our undertaking according to their strength and means. Let there be no house in Poland where the jubilee album of Berek Joselewicz is not found in a place of honour. Let there be in the whole Republic not a single Polish or Jewish firm, industrial, commercial or financial, that does not place its advertisement in this album. By acquiring copies and giving paid advertisements, each of us pays barely a small part of the unpayable debt that both societies, the Polish and the Jewish, owe to the shining memory of the hero who, with the most painful [?] sacrifice of blood and life, threw across a bridge of peace, unity and brotherhood between the peoples who, by the will of Divine Providence, have lived for many centuries on one land and nourish themselves with its fruits [printed "frudtn"] thanks to their common creative forces.
Honour to the memory of Berek Joselewicz and praise to those who are ready to honour this memory in a fitting manner!
Honorary members:
Marshal of the Senate Prof. J. Szymański, Senator Rabbi J. Rubinstein, Wilno Voivode Wł. Tatshkevitsh [sic; presumably Raczkiewicz], Army Inspector Gen. St. Burhardt-Bukacki, Curator of the Wilno School District Stefan Pogorzelski, President of the City of Wilno Józef Folejewski.
The Committee.
IV.
The "Koło" (caucus) of the Jewish councillors of the Sosnowiec City Council asks to print in your esteemed newspaper the following statement:
In response to some notes in the press about the Jewish ławnik (alderman), obtained with effort and exertion, in the person of Mr. Dr. Pruks [?], we have the honour to inform you that our esteemed ławnik Mr. Pruks never had any intention of renouncing the mandate in favour of another person, and that the notes on the question published up to now are invented.
Respectfully,
Chairman Dr. S. Melarysta [sic; presumably Melodysta],
Secretary Dr. J. Rotsztejn.
“The Jews Are Still Dissatisfied.”

[Press review — the Polish press and the Jews.] (From the Polish press.)
A new danger is threatening Poland. The Polish Jews, who live in Poland not at all badly, are seizing more and more of Polish trade, in which they do very well, and they have the chutzpah to demand of the Polish state that it improve their situation. That really is chutzpah. Most frightened of this danger is our local “Kurier Zachodni”. The organ of the Endeks [National Democrats] takes a very keen interest in the Jewish question in Poland. In issue no. 11 of the paper we find a fairly large article under the heading “The Jews Are Still Not Satisfied”, in which the author operates with statistical figures and shows how well off the Jews are in Poland.
“There has not yet been — the article begins — a single Sejm session at which the Jews did not complain that they are persecuted and wronged. They are always talking about their ‘krzywdy’ [grievances], at the plenum of the Sejm as well as in the committees, especially in the budget committee.
In spite of all this they push their way into ‘antisemitic’ Poland, and even when they leave it, they come back after all.”
There follows a series of statistical figures with which the writer of the article shows how many Jews have gone to Palestine in recent years and how many have come back to Poland, and he arrives at the conclusion that:
“In Palestine there are about 150 thousand Jews, in Poland over 3 million. It is no wonder that here they feel safest and come forward with ever more impudent demands. The Jews also complain about the ‘numerus clausus’ applied in the institutions of higher learning. A wondrous restriction, amounting to 20–30 per cent (where are the universities and higher schools in which the Jews make up barely 2 or at most 3 per cent? — Ed.) of the total number of students. That is, twice as much as the Jewish population’s share in Poland. So the Jews are in no danger of being left without an intelligentsia. On the contrary, Polish society must fear a Jewish flood.”
—o—
[Będzin — city council.] The Thursday “Tragicomedy” of the Będzin City Fathers.
On Thursday evening a meeting of the city council took place for the purpose of electing a city administration [magistrate]. Because of the great interest the meeting was held in the “Ochronka” hall on “Góra Zamkowa”[?]. The hall was packed full.
The meeting is opened, the agenda is adopted and the chairman announces that they are proceeding to the elections. The floor is taken by Hetmańczyk (P.P.S.), who declares in the name of his “club” that, because the majority of the city council consists of the Polish-Jewish reaction, they will not take part in the elections.
The same declaration is made by Mr. Fajner (Left Poale Zion), Ehrlich (Right Poale Zion), Dr. Rechtman (“Hitachdut”). Then the Left leave the hall.
After a break of 15 minutes they proceed to the elections. 22 councillors took part; Mr. Michał received 14 votes and 8 ballots were blank. Then the chairman declares that, since the president [mayor] must receive an absolute majority (17 votes), the elections are held for the 2nd time — and give the same result. Then the chairman unexpectedly closes the meeting.
Mr. Fürstenberg committed a moral wrong by his absence from such an important meeting.

Councillor of the Left Poale Zion reads a declaration in Yiddish

Session of the Sosnowiec City Council.
The Saturday session of the City Council, at which the "clubs" [factions] read declarations and the president delivered his programme speech, aroused great interest. The session, chaired by Dr. Pawełek, was conducted in a calm tone.
As soon as the session is opened, Dr. Pawełek greets the new municipal administration, wishing it success in its work for the good of the city.
Before proceeding to the agenda, declarations are delivered by all the clubs. The first declaration is read by the representative of "Eynsl"[?], Mr. Górecki; on behalf of the P.P.S. — Mr. Pal; of the Jewish Koło — Dr. Melodysta[?]; Left Poale Zion — Mr. Hamburger, who reads the original in Polish and then translated into Yiddish.
The chairman points out that he tolerated it this time, but in future he will not allow declarations to be read in other languages.
Declaration of the Poale Zion faction.
The Poale Zion faction, which at the last City Council elections received the confidence of the broad working masses, will fight for the City Council to fulfil the aims and demands of the working masses and to satisfy their needs.
In particular, true to its electoral platform, the Poale Zion faction will demand:
In fiscal policy.
To free the working population from taxes and shift the entire tax burden onto the propertied classes by:
1) Abolishing consumption taxes.
2) Exempting small dwellings from the housing tax.
3) Introducing a progressive tax on larger dwellings and building plots.
4) Increasing the tax on real estate.
5) Introducing a tax on the increase in the value of real estate.
6) Imposing a tax on luxury articles.
7) Imposing a special building tax on the wealthier strata.
On the housing question we shall demand:
1) A just distribution of dwellings.
2) Launching a broad and planned building campaign of cheap, hygienic flats for the poor population.
3) Supporting housing cooperatives.
4) Proper protection of the homeless and the evicted.
5) A struggle for tenant protection and against evictions.
In the fight against unemployment we shall demand that the city carry out public works on a broad scale, which would provide the unemployed with work — especially in the building campaign, the water supply, sewerage works and the paving of streets.
In hiring for public works we shall demand that no distinction be made on national or party grounds.
The "Poale Zion" faction will fight: for free medical aid, proper sanitary supervision and protection for indigent sick people;
for free secular schools for all children of school age, and building an adequate number of schools with Yiddish as the language of instruction.
For full equal rights of the Jewish population, wiping out the anti-Semitic policy pursued until now. For equal rights for Yiddish in all institutions and offices, conducting cultural enlightenment work also in the Yiddish language, and proper care of the quarters inhabited by the poor Jewish population.
Declaration of the Jewish Koło.
On behalf of the Koło of Jewish councillors I have the honour to submit the following declaration:
The Jewish population considers it its duty to cooperate in solidarity with other groups of the population for the good of the city and its all-round development.
In this respect we shall support all efforts made with the aim of building up the city, raising its basic condition[?] to an aesthetic level, and developing general municipal institutions, so that the population which bears the tax burden may possibly receive full satisfaction of equal value.
We consider it our duty to stress that all municipal authorities must, in their activity, stand guard over justice and care for the good of all groups of the population without distinction of faith, nation and social rights.
Our aim will be that the municipal economy rest on sound foundations of taking into account the economic strength of the population and a just distribution of taxes.
As representatives of the Jewish population we demand first of all a just treatment of the population in municipal matters, and recognition of our national, religious, economic and cultural postulates.
We declare that we shall give confidence and support only to a city administration that will carry out the above-mentioned programme.
At the end of the session the following commissions were elected: finance, building, "Ulpen"[?] [probably "ulgi" — tax relief], audit commission, general affairs, public health, and social welfare.
On the commissions the Jews are represented as follows: finance commission — dentist Rotsztajn; building — Hamburger and Tobiasz; "Ulpen"[?] and[?] audit commission — S. Ziskind; general affairs — Rotsztajn and Hamburger; health — Dr. Melodysta and Hamburger; social welfare — Dr. Melodysta and Dr. Liberman; school council — Dr. Melodysta; People's University — Dr. Rotsztajn; municipal library — Dr. Liberman.

The statistics are for the month of Listopad [November] of last year. The Jewish Unemployed Man

(A few words addressed to the left-wing and democratic representatives.)
Unemployment — as we read here not long ago — is growing in Zagłębie, and this is no blessing for the Jewish population either, which is bound up with the working strata both in this district and in the surrounding towns of Zagłębie.
After all, it is well known that Zagłębie is a great industrial centre, so that even the smallest percentage of unemployment at the same time causes harm to the Jewish shopkeeper and craftsman as well, and thus[?] reaches all the other strata of the population too. But first of all, of course, the small man suffers — the shopkeeper and the craftsman, who reduces the number of workers in his workshop. Thus we know that among the shoemakers there is a great crisis and many of them are suffering hunger, not to mention that the people [the workers] have been dismissed.
The situation among commercial and office employees is no better, and more than once the question comes to mind: who cares for the welfare of this element? Or, better said: who sees to it that these people are supported with the barest necessities in a time of crisis? Who gives a thought to it that these people should not have to perish of hunger at so grave a moment, when one does not earn even enough for a piece of dry bread?
True, our magistrates [municipalities] receive foodstuffs and money which are meant to be distributed among unemployed people, but unfortunately our unemployed do not benefit from any of it.
Recently several Jewish unemployed came into the editorial office and complained that the magistrate distributes foodstuffs, and earlier money was given to the unemployed, but they do not benefit from any of it, only because they were not registered as unemployed, and so from a legal standpoint they cannot receive any support.
Such is the low state in which our working element finds itself. Such is the indifference and apathy with which it treats even a matter that costs no money — one need only go and register. There is in Sosnowiec a labour office („Urząd[?] Pracy“) which one must notify of one's unemployment, and then it may happen at times that through its mediation one can obtain work; if not, one then benefits, together with all the other unemployed, from the moneys and foodstuffs designated for them.
But such ignorance reigns among our working elements that a man knows nothing at all of such an office, and he who does know sometimes does not remember that he must register there; and be that as it may, when things are bitter, at the time when people are hungry, there is no one to help them, either with money or with advice, or[?] with any information whatsoever, which people, as helpless ones, need so badly in such dangerous moments of hunger.
Now, and all year round, these people are abandoned; it makes no difference which party or tendency one may belong to.
It is quite different, however, when elections come round. Then they show off with them, then everyone wants to snatch them for himself, and they are promised literally the „plate from the sky“ — to say nothing of such human things as free flats, bread, coal, potatoes, candles and who knows what else!
But on the morrow of the elections, that is, when his vote is no longer needed, one forgets that such a person exists and wants to live.
We know very well that all these various parties and associations, whatever they may be called and whoever they may be, cannot take upon themselves the maintenance of the persons who voted for them; we know too that they are not even able to give them money; and yet they commit a great error in distancing themselves completely from the people who are left without means of livelihood.
True, they cannot give them all the things listed above, and yet the unfortunate could be helped a great deal at the moment one does not distance oneself from them. In a moment of despair, at a time of neglect, one must draw close to the members, and even a piece of advice then plays an enormous role.
Parties and associations, thank God, are not lacking among us, and these are not just parties for form's sake; we have them in various editions: left ones and ones still more left than the left, to say nothing of „Poale Zion“ Left and Right, the „Bund“, the „Hitachdut“. Now, where are the purely professional and the craftsmen's associations? Why should these associations not see to it that the unemployed are registered when people have no work, so that they may benefit from government support together with their Christian fellows? What do the parties gain by abandoning their members in the gravest moments of their lives? In this at least they can surely help them.
A sacred duty lies upon these associations to take an interest in their members not only at election time but also at the time when they find themselves in the bitterest moments of their lives. By the way, let us not deceive ourselves: the parties that have representatives in the self-government bodies or other local institutions can certainly do a great deal for their members when the situation is at its worst. Their representatives should not think that they are represented in the institutions only in order to dance to the tune of the left wing. One may, after all, sometimes demand something for oneself too, and not take anyone into account.
But the first thing that matters is that the workers' associations, regardless of tendency, should gather their members around them and enlighten them about everyday matters, which play a great role nowadays. Above all they must stand on guard and protect the interests of the poorest strata of the population, in whose name they are always so fond of speaking.
They should organise weekly „popular talks“ for the people, in which it would be explained to them how to carry on their livelihood. The workers must not lag behind the times; if they do, they go backwards, which means decline.
The first and most important thing, above all, is that the associations should make clear to their members that in time of unemployment they must not be lazy but must register as unemployed, so that they have the possibility of benefiting, through the magistrates, from the government moneys and foodstuffs together with their Christian fellows.
Let no one regard this matter as a trifle; rather, let it be seen to and carried out at once.
R. Let.
Nikolai Sells His Grain to the Germans.

The entire Polish and foreign press is full of articles, character sketches and episodes about Nikolai Nikolayevich [Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolayevich Romanov], who died last week.
These pieces expose in full sharpness the sorry role that the Romanovs played in the history of Russia.
We shall bring here one of the many[?] episodes, because it is very characteristic of Nikolai Nikolayevich, who has hundreds of Jewish lives on his conscience; more than one Jew went to the gallows merely because he was suspected of having sold a German a little flour, a loaf of bread or a pound of sugar.
This episode shows how strong Nikolai Nikolayevich's patriotism and love of the fatherland were — the fatherland in whose name he destroyed millions of young lives, sending them in droves[?] under the hail of the enemy's shells and bullets.
It was in the autumn of the sad year 1914. The war had just flared up; Nikolai Nikolayevich, as commander-in-chief, had gone off to the front, and he had left his estates in Ukraine in the hands of his stewards. That very year there was an exceptional harvest. In other years Nikolai Nikolayevich used to sell his grain to Greece and Italy. He used to ship the grain via Odessa and Constantinople. Because of the war, however, the route to Italy and Greece was cut off, and the great quantity of grain lay without a buyer.
The stewards then turned to their master, asking him to advise them what to do with the millions of poods of wheat and rye.
The greatest enemy of the Germans and Austrians, who was waging a bitter war against them on all fronts, told his stewards to sell the grain to the Austrians or the Germans.
His instruction was enough for the stewards. They first turned to the Austrians, but the "sheymtsulnikes"[?] rejected the proposal. The Germans, on the other hand, snapped it up like a roast [i.e. a bargain] and bought from Nikolai Nikolayevich 18 thousand wagons of wheat. The grain transports went via Romania and Austria to Germany. Thus the commander-in-chief of the Russian army supplied food to the hated Germans with whom he was waging war. This fact proves once again why this bloody tyrant Nikolai Nikolayevich slaughtered so many Jews — supposedly for showing good friendship to the Germans.
The King and the People

[Essay — England; the King's illness and the unemployed.]
By A. S. Zaks.
In the Middle Ages people imagined society in the form of a pyramid, of a rounded, pointed mountain that grows narrower and narrower the higher it rises. The very summit of the mountain consists of a single grain of sand, which is the highest point.
The medieval social edifice did in fact look like that.
The lowest layer was the broadest and the largest. It consisted of the common people, of the peasants, artisans and workers, who with their labour sustained all the other layers and groups of the population. Above this toiling mass lay the landowners, the squires (pritsim), who themselves did no hard work at all and merely ordered others, their enserfed peasants, to carry out all the important work.
Above the landowners stood the titled aristocrats, who did not even come into contact with the common people. They confined themselves merely to the intrigues that went on in their own and in foreign courts. Above the ordinary aristocrats stood the barons, above the barons — the princes, above the princes — the grand princes, and above the grand princes stood out the highest point of society — the king.
Between king and people there was a whole series of higher and lower officials (chinovniks), with higher and lower ranks, which indicated their pedigree and their power in the state apparatus.
Although it was clear to every single person who had any notion of the appearance of society that all the upper lords and under-lords are carried on the shoulders of the toiling people lying below, on the lowest rung, people nevertheless tried to persuade others and themselves that the lower layers live by the grace of those above, that the mass of workers and peasants draws its livelihood from those whom it drags on its back and who oppress and choke it.
The king with his princes and other lieutenants was everything, the people — nothing. The king was regarded as the soul that had breathed life into the skeleton of the people, which by itself could not stir or move.
When the people suffered — nobody knew of it. In general, no fuss was made about it. If a hair got bent up there on some prince — let alone on the king — a whole wail went up. The whole country was wrapped in mourning. Things happened: no trifle, the king is ill! The king is in bed! The king has a headache, suffers from a stomach ailment and cannot eat. When the people wants to and can, but has nothing to eat, it is nothing. When the king has and wants to, but cannot eat — that becomes a tragedy, a disaster, and all the church bells are made to announce it.
This self-persuasion, that the king is everything and the people is nothing, was so deeply rooted in people's brains that even now, when the rule of the lords has drowned in the sea of the past, it floats up to the surface at certain times.
For weeks and weeks public opinion, not only in England but in the whole official world, was occupied — and is still occupied now — with the reports about the King's illness. Over the telegraph wires of the entire world the news from the bulletins that the doctors had printed was transmitted several times a day; the radios announced every sleepless night, every crooked grimace; the newspapers counted the minutes the King had dozed. They drummed out every expression the patient made.
At the very same time and in the very same England a million unemployed are literally dying of hunger. They have nothing to eat, they have nothing to put on, they go about black and gloomy, torn and tattered [?], with lips swollen from hunger. Their bodies are covered with rags, they have no money to buy a candle to light their cold and empty homes — and nobody said a word about it. Were it not for the Crown Prince of the English throne, who is here in England because of his father's illness and who appealed for help for them, one would not even have known of the great ruin and the great suffering that the English unemployed are going through.
"One can gain some notion of the great disaster — writes a correspondent in Thursday's 'Times' — only when one looks closely at how a million Englishmen live. A family of five persons must get by on seven dollars a week. A day and a half a week each one must fast. And on the days when one is supposedly allowed to eat, one must make do with a piece of bread, margarine and tea. Only once a week can one see meat in the homes of the 'unemployed'.
"All social institutions are closed. Almost all clothing shops and other shops are closed; many shopkeepers have gone bankrupt because they had no customers for their goods, abandoned their 'businesses' and left.
"At every fire there are souls who warm their hands in the flames. In England too there were 'people' who licked a bone from the disaster.
"Some 'business people' exploited the poverty of the unemployed and bought up their belongings. The unemployed had to sell every item in their house so as to be able to get a piece of bread for it.
The indescribable misery into which people are sinking undermines not only their body but also their spirit. They are turned into beggars without strength to live and without courage to die."
Who until now knew of this misery and of the suffering of a million people?
Yes, even now there is still a great difference between man and man, between king and people.
Shall the Building Be Completed?

[Sosnowiec — charity and institutions.] Sosnowiec has put up a building for an “old-age home” — it only needs to be completed.
Poor are we, the Jews of Sosnowiec, in public work; poor are we in philanthropic activity; everything among us is done without calculation, without any plan. Public activity among us is good by chance, just as very often it is bad by chance, clumsy. That public work among us should be planned in advance — of that nobody knows.
We have, for instance, a hospital with which other cities would pride themselves and show off, yet here the average Jew does not even know that such an institution exists, because it costs him nothing; for very, very few Jews in town pay the very minimal monthly fee, and therefore the hospital very often finds itself in a very depressed state, so that one is forced to rattle the charity boxes (pushkes) and to cry out: Jews, do not let the only institution for the sick collapse, do not bring it about that the Jewish hospital should find itself in a dangerous state.
That is how people relate to an institution that exists and is active — never mind how apathetic they are towards institutions that still have to be created, built and realised.
Now 2—3 householders were found in town who set about building an old-age home in the European manner. The initiators collected 50 thousand zł. among 60 donors, and with this sum the building was put up. It would seem that this is a very fine gesture, since they managed to obtain from a handful of people a sum that made it possible to raise such a building up to the roof. But one must not forget that with this the institution still cannot begin its activity. To complete the building another approximately 40 thousand zł. is required, and precisely for that reason things have come to a standstill and cannot move from the spot.
So the question arises: is it really hard to raise these 40 thousand zł. in town, when only 60 householders by themselves gave 50 thousand zł.? We understand very well that it was the richest who gave, so that now only the middling ones remain, who cannot give any large sums of money; but one must not forget the proportion: once all who possibly can do give, it will come to a minimal sum for each citizen, which everyone will certainly be able to afford. For what does it mean to raise 40 thousand zł. in total from the whole city? We know very well that this amount can be put together quite easily.
But one must not forget this: Sosnowiec is a city of merchants; everyone understands only that he must trade, do business and earn; and when that is not the case, when there is hardly any takings — then why talk at all about “nonsense”, about useless matters, about things that nothing comes of? That is the opinion of the average Sosnowiec Jew. This, however, by no means proves that he refuses to support what needs to be supported, what needs to be maintained and built up. And precisely for this reason one must know how to “work on” these people, who are far from public-mindedness and do not realise that, just like all others, they too must care for the welfare of the community.
We know that the initiators of the old-age home will say: do we even have anyone to “work on”? And why should we do it? Because we ourselves are the givers and have sacrificed so much time and effort? And who — they will say — “worked on” us so that we would get to build this building? It is possible that the claim is right, and possible that it is not justified either, because the people must be accustomed to giving: they have to see that the big ones give according to their means, and then one must implant in them the will and the understanding that the smaller ones should give according to their strength. The average Jew, however, never had the opportunity to witness the big ones creating and building grandiose public buildings, and so people naturally became distant and cold towards realising this public idea.
If one wants the average Jew and the relatively well-to-do firm to understand the duty of creating public institutions, one must educate them to it; and since among us this has not been done by anyone, giving larger sums of money to public institutions seems incomprehensible; and therefore we say that the only ones to blame for this are the big ones, the “carp heads”, those who always could and should have given, and did not; and therefore a duty lies on these very people, who are giving now, to see to it that the middling man also gives.
So one must come and educate the people; one must tell those who can give that it is a duty not to remain indifferent to public obligations. Just as a young person gradually gets accustomed to work, so must people be educated one by one to understand their responsibility towards society.
And now, let the Jews of Sosnowiec not wait to be begged; let us remember that since 60 Jews raised 50 thousand zł. and put up the building for “an old-age home”, and another 40 thousand zł. is still missing to complete the building, at this moment the whole city — everyone who can possibly give — must pull together and see to it that the necessary sum is created, so that the completion of the “old-age home” is realised.
The prospects, one must not forget, are indeed brilliant, for the building is already built and the city has as yet given almost no money for this purpose; and when a building stands and pleads, “let me finish it, and I shall bring so much benefit to the poor old Jew” — when one considers this situation and reckons how much work, effort and expense have already been put in here, one must come to the realisation that all means must be applied to complete this so useful institution, which can bring the city so much honour by creating a quiet and cosy home for old people who have nowhere to go.
Let the initiators set to work, let them begin their activity, and the city will — and must — come to their aid unconditionally in their sacred work.
Dr. Papuri.
Short Feuilleton: The Severed Tongue

[Feuilleton — current affairs, Poland.]
The Severed Tongue.

Three sensational acts of revenge were carried out in the course of the past week here in our country.

In Piotrków one municipal (magistrate) official shot dead another merely because the latter did not want to belong to the same party as he.

In Warsaw a French girl committed an ugly act upon a young Jewish man...

And in Kraków a female apostate cut off the tongue of a well-known local lawyer over some love caprice.

Well, never mind. The first act of revenge did not surprise the public that much — after all, thousands of years ago, as soon as the world was created, one brother killed the other.

The second act of revenge was no great surprise either — if the Jewish "Ruszke the fine one" [?] was allowed, then surely a French girl may...

But the third act of revenge — the severed tongue — shook us all, exactly as though we had felt the pain ourselves..

A trifle, a tongue — "Death and life are in the power of the tongue"...

Had it at least been a woman's tongue, it would not have been such a calamity — fewer nine measures of talk, less slander and gossip...

But the tongue of a man, and a lawyer's at that, who out of "life and death" chose only the first — he makes a living from it himself and saves other people's lives — that such a tongue should fall victim to the love caprice of a married woman, and an apostate besides — where, then, is the justice, morality, righteousness and all the fine principles our society preaches?

Only, I think the answer lies in the question itself.

The matter is not as simple as we imagine — every death has its excuse and every punishment has its crime.

I do not mean by this that the Kraków lawyer is a criminal — we are not speaking here of the individual, only of the general.

That same general, or better said — that same society, which keeps on preaching justice, morality, righteousness and all the other fine principles, itself sticks out its tongue at these very principles at every opportunity; and so the stuck-out tongue has brought its verdict..

The Kraków lawyer merely symbolised here the "sin-offering of the congregation," the sacrifice for society — for a sacrifice one chooses the best, and what tongue could be sharper than a lawyer's?...

And the woman who carried out the punishment was also very well suited to her role — she took here the place not of a judge but of an executioner, and an executioner is never a righteous man — always the worst of society...

In any case, what matters here is not who carried out the punishment but the punishment itself, which was directed against all of us — we all felt the pain, and that is why it shook us...

J. G. Steinsapir.
Remedies for a Cold

[Feuilleton — humour.]
By Y. Marshelis.
So I caught a cold. And what do I get for it? Is merely having a cold, so to speak, too little for a person?
On top of that my friends have to meddle too: one of them gives me advice — take castor oil. So I take castor oil. Along comes a second one and laughs at me.
— What do you mean, — he says — you took castor oil? For a cold you took castor oil?
— So what, — I ask — does one take for a cold?
— For a cold, — he says — if you take anything at all, you take rhubarb.
In short, I took rhubarb as well.
That was not the end of it that evening. Two other friends of mine declared that they would not leave the house until I took a gogl-mogl. Then my aunt Zlate came up with a new refrain:
— Put on him, — she shouted — this very minute a bag of hot salt on the throat.
I, of course, had to [?] both drink a gogl-mogl and let them put a bag of hot salt on my throat.
Late in the evening a cousin turned up with a brand-new "patent": cupping glasses. If, he said, they did not give me cupping at once, let no one come to him later with any complaints. And so that nobody, God forbid, should mistake what he meant by the word "later", he called out so that everyone would hear:
— Remember, then! If he happens to die, let everyone know that I told you to apply cupping glasses...
In short, I had cupping glasses put on too, and wet ("cut") ones at that. Right after the cupping I fell asleep, luckily.
When I woke up I heard a debate going on in the house about whether to give me something to eat or not. My cousin Beile not only ordered that I be given food, but to be fed so much that afterwards, she said, I would not be able to move from the spot for three days running.
— And why, — my aunt Zlate wanted to know — don't you also tell them, while they're at it, to take his measurements for a shroud?...
Aunt Zlate was sure that giving a person with a cold food is exactly like giving him poison. Cousin Beile, on the other hand, held that "a sick man must be fattened up". Uncle Shimon had no opinion of his own on the matter, but he was inclined to agree with cousin Beile.
— I don't see, — he said — what harm it can do to give him food; either way: if he is fated to die, let him at least not die hungry...
Their words, however, were wasted. The question, as I understood it that morning, was not whether to give me food or not, but whether to call the doctor at once or wait a little longer. Firstly, from a terrible headache I could not open my eyes; secondly, I could not breathe; thirdly, I kept being thrown from heat to cold.
— Send — I begged — for a doctor.
Four people burst out laughing, and the fifth, my uncle Czale, said:
— Look at this, a new millionaire. For an ordinary flu they should call him a doctor...
To crown it all, it was a Sunday morning as well, and relatives started coming from every side. The first was my step-aunt, Chantshe Perl.
— Put a hot mustard plaster on him!
— she ordered.
Her order was carried out at once. Not an hour had passed and my shoulder, from the mustard plaster, was blazing like a lime-kiln. I tossed about, groaned, screamed, threatened, begged — but nothing helped. The compress stayed on until my step-aunt ordered it taken off.
— And now, — she said, allowing the compress to be removed — give him five grams of quinine, and let him go to sleep.
From the quinine my ears began to ring and my temples to pound as if with hammers; and put me to sleep — the quinine did not do that either.
A little while later two of my cousins came by, and on hearing that I had been given quinine they were horrified.
— Why, — one of them asked — didn't you rather give him a dose of carbolic and be done with it; at least he wouldn't have to suffer.
The second cousin went even further. He declared that if they gave me quinine once more, he would immediately notify the police that his cousin had fallen into the hands of poisoners.
Both cousins demanded — no, insisted — that I be given this very minute at least ten grams of phenacetin. This, of course, was done at once.
What effect the phenacetin had on me I don't remember; I was by then in such a state that nothing mattered to me any more.
Only two things do I remember: nausea and a quarrel. The nausea overcame me after, in the course of some 15 minutes, I was given one after another:
a) bicarbonate of soda;
b) hot milk with Vichy water;
c) emetic wine;
d) raspberries.
So much for the nausea. As for the quarrel, it broke out because as soon as one relative ordered that I be given some remedy, another relative jumped up and declared that he would not allow it.
Bad as I felt then, I nevertheless understood that my weakness had stirred up a great feud in the family, and that if, God forbid, I died now, I would not have even a minyan of people at my funeral. That, I believe, is what strengthened me and gave me the strength to survive not only the cold, but also the terrible devastation that all those remedies had wrought in my insides; for were it not for that, mind you, there is no understanding how I lived through it. Unless, mind you, I am made of iron...
The Rebbe's Son (18)

[Serialized novel — a Jewish historical novel; Kraków on the eve of Shavuot; installment 18.]
A Jewish historical novel by Yankev Tsimerman [Jakub Zimmerman].

Life is — as is well known — a mirror image of nature, and just as in nature nothing can be uniform, the same everywhere — in one place a wilderness and elsewhere again blooming and fruit-bearing fields — so life cannot be the same everywhere; but if in one place there are desolations [?], laments and suffering without measure, there are on the other hand other people who have the good fortune to avoid everything bad, or at least to push it away [?] from themselves for a while, and therefore they have every reason to be cheerful and merry.

It was in Kraków, on the eve of Shavuot.

Shavuot has always been, among Jews, one of the most esteemed holidays, and people have always taken more pleasure in it than in the other holidays.

Besides the lovely, fine weather that usually prevails in this season, neither too hot nor too cold, Shavuot is the kind of holiday about which there is a saying: "that then one can eat what one wants, where one wants and when one wants" — which is certainly not the case with the other holidays, Passover, Sukkot and Rosh Hashanah.

In Kraków, in the Jewish quarter, people were preparing for Shavuot; green branches and all sorts of flowers adorned the doors and windows of all the Jewish houses. It looked as if these children of living nature had come to refresh the hearts of the ever-sad people of Israel and to share with it a little of their joy and zest for life...

In the poor house of our friend Chaim the carter, too, they were working hard in honour of Shavuot [printed "Shvies"]. The elder girl, Sarah, under her mother's supervision, polished, cleaned and scrubbed the house, and also directed her younger sisters to help her with the holiday-eve chores.

Everything was burning in their hands, and a good while before sunset everything was already finished and ready for the holiday. In the house everything gleamed and sparkled. The food was ready, and the children washed, their hair washed, and dressed in clean little clothes. Chaim's wife and her elder girl were already so far done that they could allow themselves to sit down a little and rest from the hard day's work.

"What do you think, Sarah," the mother now began, wiping her forehead, wet with sweat, "will Father still come home for the holiday? I would be so glad if he arrived now..."

"Is Father coming?" the smaller children began to shout merrily, crowding round [printed "arumtsuriglen"] their mother and their elder sister.

"Be quiet, children, be good and quiet children and pray to God, blessed be He, and Father will surely [?] soon come home in peace," the mother said, lovingly pushing them away from her. "But even if he cannot come today," she turned again to her elder daughter, "a letter from him will surely arrive soon; he will surely want to know what the children are doing and what the boys have learned while he was not at home. All day long my heart keeps telling me that we will get a letter from him. I myself don't even know where this thought came to me from. But it won't let go of me. And if people have a saying that the heart senses the bad that is to come, why shouldn't one also sense the good in advance?..."

"Sarah!" exclaimed the eight-year-old boy. "When Father comes home, I'll tell him the beautiful story of Ruth and Boaz that I learned this week in cheder. The story is so beautiful that I've never heard one like it. Father will beam with delight and listen open-mouthed, all ears [the sentence runs on without punctuation:] I even know what Rashi says..."

The mother smiled happily as she now glanced at her children — at her eight-year-old, so "learned" son, and at her elder daughter, who in her eyes looked the cleverest and prettiest girl in the world.

Sarah now drew her little brother to her with great love.

"I'll test you a little now. Let me see whether you really know everything you're boasting about... You tell it, and you, children, keep quiet and listen."

With sparkling little eyes and reddening little cheeks, the eight-year-old lad now stood up and, in a thin [?] but clear little voice, began to tell the old-new and ever so beautiful and moving story of Ruth.

He did not content himself, however, with the bare narrative as it is found in the Bible, but also related, just as his rebbe in cheder had studied it with him, all the stories and legends told about it in the Midrashim and other Aggadah books.

But not everything was so smooth and clear to the clever boy. His young little mind, which was already used to thinking and pondering a little on its own, did not want to accept everything just as it is, but liked to ask questions and objections.

He was now annoyed with Orpah, Naomi's second daughter-in-law: why had she not followed the fine example of her sister-in-law Ruth and, like her, stayed with her mother-in-law [printed "shvinger" for "shviger"], but had left her...

The elder sister, who had also once studied in cheder and had listened there to all these stories, tried, as far as she knew how, to calm her little brother and to justify Orpah.

But the boy was a bit of a stubborn one and did not want to give in so quickly. The sister kept on answering and he kept on asking. Mother and the smaller children stood and gaped; they could not understand the whole debate and grasp clearly what it was actually [printed "eyngtlikh"] about.

In the midst of this the door suddenly swung open and in came Blumele, Eizik the baker's girl. In her hands she held two large tin baking pans, full of all kinds of sweet pastries and honey cakes.

"Children!" she exclaimed as soon as she entered the house, "I've brought you some good things here, which I myself baked for your sake in honour of Shavuot [printed "Shvies"]."

Great was the joy among the children when Blumele began to share out among them the good, sweet things from one pan. She did not stint, and kept on giving to the children until she had soon emptied the whole pan.

Chaim's wife thanked Blumele nicely for the unexpected gift and wished her that soon, God willing, [they would celebrate] her engagement (tno'im) with the right match. The girl blushed and gave thanks with a nod of her head.

The children now went out into the street; Chaim's wife went off with the second pan of pastries to put it away for the holiday, and the two girls were left alone.

Both girls were the same age; they had gone together to the same cheder and were friends. But ever since Chaim the carter had travelled with Eizik the baker to Warsaw, the girls had grown even more intimately attached, and their friendship had become even stronger. They both felt instinctively that their fathers' joint journey would bring them all luck and blessing. But as long as the fathers had not yet come back home, the girls were constantly frightened and longing. Wartime... such a long journey... no good news is heard... Jews are hunted and tormented everywhere... all such sad things, which can throw the hearts of young girls into unrest...

At first the girls sat quietly beside each other. They had nothing to talk about. Everything that lay on their hearts had already been gone over a good many times...

"I'm so happy today, dear Sarah," Blumele nevertheless began to speak, "that I would give away and hand over everything I possibly could, so that others too might feel, as I do, the taste of happiness. I'm in such a mood today that I can't put it into words for you. I myself don't know what is the matter with me."

The Fig.
(Leading article by little Amotz).
The most important fruit, for me, has always been — the fig.
A fruit that is not stretched out proudly like the carob, not coarse like the orange and not hard like nuts, but humbly small of growth, round as the moon, and one can use it in everyday life more than other fruits.
Thus, for example, when some Będzin "Tseirei Emunei"-[?] youngsters tried to harm the "Keren Hayesod" campaign, they were shown — a fig [Yiddish "a feyg": also the contemptuous thumb-between-fingers gesture, i.e. "nothing at all"]...
The chairman asks the kehilla board in Będzin to come to a meeting to consider the appeals against the budget — they show him — a fig.
Representatives of institutions come into the gmina [the Jewish community office], where they ask for the allotted subsidies — they are shown — — — a fig...
The initiators of building an "old-age home" (moshav zekenim) in Sosnowiec appeal to the rich men there for support — they get — — a fig..
The board of the Sosnowiec "Merchants' Association" took a fancy to having a representative in the Chamber of Commerce — they were given — a fig.
When a group of readers demand that a general meeting of the Będzin "HaZamir" be held, the board shows them — — a fig.
Jewish traders run to the Treasury office in Katowice, where they ask to be sold trading licences (patents) for Upper Silesia — they are honoured with — — — — — — — — — — — a fig.
A merchant hands over a parcel of goods and takes a bill of exchange for it without any fear, but when the due date comes the buyer vanishes somewhere and shows the merchant — — — — — — — — — a fig.

A Reception for the Flu.
At last the doctors' union in Zagłębie has prevailed on the announced guest to visit our industrial district too.
Where has it not been already — starting with America, then across the ocean to England, France, Belgium, Germany and who knows where; everywhere it filled the doctors' spirits with joy, everywhere it foretold them a good future and a sure livelihood, and finally our doctors too begged for it — and the guest is here.
The flu has visited Zagłębie. The young doctorlings rub their hands with joy and exult: Be greeted, oh thou fulfiller of our dreams!
The Health Insurance Fund (Kasa Chorych) has appointed a special reception committee, which adopted the following resolutions:
To prepare a hundred barrels of "vaserati" [water, with a mock-Polish ending] from the "Pshemshati" [the Przemsza river]; to engage several yard-keepers ("dozortses", Polish dozorcy) who are to pour this beverage into small bottles and distribute it among those who will be privileged to be visited by the great guest — the flu.
For the convenience of the public it was resolved that the flu-holder shall simply send in his photograph. This photograph will within a week be forwarded to the doctors so that they may give their opinion; to heat the stoves in the outpatient clinics so that the visitors are not bored when they have to wait twenty-four hours.
To buy telescopes for the doctors, so that they can look, for example, from Modrzejowska 42 all the way to a patient in Old Sosnowiec...
Besides this an amnesty has been issued for the insured: they need not report before they have a 40-degree fever.
Lemekh,

The Foreigners Question in France

[France — immigration and minorities; letter from France.] (A letter from France).
People keep talking about the foreigners — in the press, in parliament, at public meetings. The "wanted" [?] foreigners — agricultural and other workers — are discussed when the budget is debated.
Protests against the "unwanted" ones arise when a bloody settling of accounts takes place between political émigrés, when crimes are committed of which foreigners are guilty. Only recently the press was full of such accusations concerning Modugia [?; apparently Sergio De Modugno], who murdered the Italian vice-consul Nardini.
But when the figures of births and deaths are published, the newspapers note melancholically that the stagnation of the population in France continues. And if it does not decline, that is only thanks to the influx of foreigners and the high number of births among them.
Some 60–70 years ago foreigners used to be absorbed in France among the local population. Lately their number keeps growing. Before the war there were over a million of them, in 1921 one and a half million; since then they have been increasing by 300,000 persons a year, and their number is already approaching three million, so that there is now one foreigner to every 12 Frenchmen. It is therefore no wonder that these guests, who bring along the necessary working hands but also a foreign language, customs and sympathies, cause the masters of the house a great deal of worry.
For the great works of rebuilding the devastated departments hundreds of thousands of workers were needed, and the government itself recruited them in Poland, Italy, Czechoslovakia and Belgium; a large part of them stayed in France. When America introduced restrictions on immigrants in 1924, the influx to France grew at the expense of those who had previously gone to America. And France suddenly took second place in the world by the number of emigrants it used to receive. France put no obstacles in the way of the emigrants and created no "Island of Tears". Above all, France became a place of refuge for the political émigrés from Russia, Spain and Italy, and the opponents of Stalin, Mussolini and Primo de Rivera set up their headquarters here. Actually this is nothing new: the history of Poland's liberation, Czechoslovak independence, the activity of the Russian socialist parties — all are bound up with Paris.
Three million foreigners — that is a whole state. These are several "national minorities". True, they cannot come with any demands of "human rights" — everyone in France has those. But the very existence of whole "foreigner colonies" must create and raise a series of practical questions and tasks. Fortunately for the foreigners living in France, the French are the least intolerant towards strangers. But the government and the politicians, who look a little beyond the near tomorrow, have pondered over the material with which France must be charged with new forces to cultivate the land, to fill the factories and to keep the state a great one. And the government's most immediate task has become to assimilate — if not the parents, then at least the children, the second generation. Deputy Charles Lambert, who has specialised in questions concerning the "foreigners", has listed a whole catalogue of dangers threatening from unrestricted immigration. He pointed to the overpopulation of the cities, to which the emigrants mostly strive, and the emergence of conspirators' centres there, where large masses of foreigners are found. In northern France there are whole villages of Polish miners who came there with their wives and children. They have their own churches and schools where the children are taught in Polish; in the south-western departments the Italian "flood" is even stronger. There was a case in which a priest in a village baptised 20 children, of whom only 4 were French and the rest Italian. Lambert is especially afraid of the peaceful conquest of the border departments by Germany and Italy.
"What shall we do with the foreigners in case of war?" he asks. "We shall have to hand over all our trains to them for several weeks to deliver them to the borders, and if we lock them up in concentration camps, half an army will be needed to guard the millions of 'prisoners'. And at the same time the mines and factories, where foreigners form a considerable part of the workers, will have to reduce their productivity."
Lambert draws no conclusions at all. He understands that France needs the influx of "strangers". But the newcomers must be "Frenchified".
The new naturalisation law has made it easier to acquire citizenship. Lambert proposes to accept as citizens [persons] of thirty years [?], to introduce compulsory military service and to give them the right to change their family names into French ones.
The new naturalisation law raised the number of new citizens to 86 thousand (in 1916 [sic; perhaps 1926] — 45 thousand). Half of them are Italians, followed by Belgians, Spaniards (about 10 thousand each), Germans (8,500), then Russians, Poles, etc.
The strongest assimilators are the Italians, Spaniards and Belgians; Black people assimilate poorly, and their marriages with French people produce a high percentage of degenerate children [the author's wording]. It is therefore interesting that over 40 percent of those who opted [for French citizenship] are married to French women.
The Italians, Belgians and Spaniards assimilate quickly and settle in southern France as farm labourers, tenant farmers, etc. The Fascist government wants to halt the assimilation process and supports them so that they can preserve their distinctiveness. The assimilation process goes on very strongly, and the Frenchification of the new colonists, who are already here in the tens of thousands, is advancing with giant strides.
P. S—w.
What's new in Zagłębie? — Będzin — Another tragic death of a Jewish woman

[Będzin — tram accident.] Since Saturday the Będzin–Sosnowiec tram service has been increased. From that day on the tram runs there and back every 10 minutes. The change, however, has already claimed a victim — the Jewish woman Sobotka, who on Monday at 10 in the morning, while crossing Małachowskiego (Palachowska) street, was struck on the head by the tram arriving from Sosnowiec.
From the strong blow the woman fell down and went under the tram wheels. The motorman still managed to stop the tram instantly, so that the woman's body was saved from being horribly crushed.
Unconscious and covered in blood, the woman was taken to the hospital, where she received first medical aid.
Who the woman was could not be established, because no documents at all were found on her. Various guesses therefore arose, among them that the woman was from Dąbrowa.
Only at 3 in the afternoon, when the teacher Mr. S. Sobotka came home for lunch and heard the maid explain that the lady had gone out in the morning and had not yet come back, did Mr. S., in great alarm, go to the hospital, where he recognised that it was indeed his wife.
It is remarkable that Mr. Winer's house, where Mr. Sobotka lives, is right next to the hospital, and no one in that house knew until 3 o'clock that a misfortune had befallen their neighbour.
Despite all rescue measures the unfortunate woman did not regain consciousness, and the next day, Tuesday, she died.

Sosnowiec — How a factory "director" swindled the unemployed

[Sosnowiec — crime.]
In the hall of the "Zagłoba" cinema, where the unemployed are paid their benefits, a young Christian turned up and introduced himself to a group of unemployed men as the director of a large enterprise who had come to Zagłębie, where he expected to find 60—70 skilled workers.
The unemployed, hearing such good news, swarmed round the "director" like bees, and every one of them wanted to find favour with Mr. (pan) "Director", if only to be taken on for the work.
The "Pan Director" listened to everyone's request and then declared to them that he could enrol only those who would pay in a few złoty each towards travel expenses.
This condition the unemployed carried out with joy: they signed up for the work and paid in a few złoty each.
In their great joy the workers invited the "Pan Director" for a glass of drink and spent several hours together.
When several days had gone by and the "director" had sent no word at all, the unemployed only then understood that they had fallen victim to a cunning swindler, and they reported the matter to the police.
The "director" has been arrested.

With 13 Jewish votes Mr. Rubinlicht was elected vice-president in Będzin

[Będzin — City Council.] On Wednesday evening the 4th session of the Będzin City Council took place in the hall of the "Ochronka", to elect a vice-president and 4 ławnicy (aldermen, members of the municipal executive).
The session, which naturally aroused wide interest, was interesting enough.
At the session the great Jewish public and also the political leaders once again became convinced that when a Jewish question is at stake, the "best good friends" turn into enemies of the Jews. The base role was played here by the Endecja (National Democrats), who, numbering no more than 3 councillors in the present City Council, obtained the president with purely Jewish votes, and at the election of the vice-president they, by way of "gratitude", handed in blank ballots...
Altogether, such a situation arose during the election procedure that Mr. Rubinlicht's candidacy was in danger, but at the critical moment the "pintele yid" (the Jewish spark) awoke in councillor Jakub Erlich (Poalei Zion Right), and he saved the situation.
———
The session is opened; the chairman reads out [?]: 1) that secretary Skumnik is leaving the Endek club, and 2) a rescript from the voivode stating that in electing the presidium of the city administration there must be a majority of the number of councillors present; on that account Mr. Michel [מיכעל; Michał?], who received 14 votes, is confirmed as president.
Before proceeding to the election of the vice-president, Dr. Jarzębowski declares, in the name of the B.B. club [BB — the Non-Party Bloc for Cooperation with the Government], that owing to the prevailing Jewish hegemony(?) in the present City Council the club will not take part in the elections.
In the name of the PPS and Poalei Zion (Right and Left), Hetmańczyk declares that they will not take part in the elections. The Left and the B.B.B. [sic], 15 persons in number, leave the session hall.
Then the presiding chairman, Mr. Żebrowski, tries to bring the "tragic" act to an end, and he pleasantly declares that because 16 councillors, i.e. half of the total number, are not taking part in the elections, the session cannot be continued.
Mr. Rubinlicht reacts to this move, points out that there is a quorum in the hall, and demands that the session be carried on.
The chairman does not change his standpoint, even when Dr. Rechtman declares that, for the good of the interests of the local Jewish population, he withdraws the first declaration he made at the previous session and will indeed take part in the elections.
The declaration did not find favour with the chairman, and having no way out he handed over the chair to the vice-chairman, Mr. Sz. Fürstenberg, followed the example of his comrades and walked out of the hall.
But the gentlemen of the B.B. did not rest, and by force simply dragged the secretary of the City Council, Mr. Szkumnik [so spelled here; above: Skumnik], out of the hall, in order at all costs to leave the City Council incomplete (without a quorum),
The situation was truly critical, there is no quorum, but unexpectedly councillor Erlich came into the hall and courageously and proudly declared that, because the Sanacja aims to create chaos, to bring things to the point where a commissioner is installed and the whole [municipal] economy is paralysed, he is remaining in the hall so that the session can be held.
Mr. Erlich's declaration is received with loud applause.
In a tense atmosphere the elections then take place, giving the following result: with 13 Jewish votes Mr. Eleazar Rubinlicht is elected vice-president. The 3 Endeks handed in blank ballots.
The conduct of the Endeks aroused bitterness among the Jewish population.
The election of the ławnicy is, on the proposal of Mr. Jakubowicz, postponed to the next session.
With that the "historic" session is closed.

Lawlessness

[Sosnowiec — press polemic.] I recall the time when "Ha-Tsefira" appeared under the editorship of Nahum Sokolow; in those days a feuilleton was printed every Friday under the name "Mi-Shabbat le-Shabbat" ("From Sabbath to Sabbath").
Every reader of "Ha-Tsefira" looked forward to the Friday issue with "Mi-Shabbat le-Shabbat" quite literally with longing eyes, for it was a masterpiece, about which there was something to talk and argue not only on the Sabbath but the whole week afterwards. It was a true spiritual pleasure, especially for the "additional soul" — a "Sabbath fruit" with which our great Nahum Sokolow, the "Sabbath guest" (Oreach le-Shabbat), delighted us from "Sabbath to Sabbath".
But times change. The war, too, brought an upheaval in every field; "Ha-Tsefira" meanwhile ceased to appear, and our great Sokolow too ceased to be an editor. But how does the saying go: "In nature nothing is lost." So now we have the "privilege", in Sosnowiec itself, of having an editor — begging your pardon — and a little daily sheet — may it be said to the stones [i.e. heaven preserve us] — with all the trimmings, and also with a Friday feuilleton, "From Sabbath to Sabbath", by the home-grown [samorodny] editor.
Here before me lies the little Friday sheet "Unzer Tog" ("Our Day"), number 16, with just such a "feuilleton". But what does one find there in this "feuilleton", may it be said to the stones? Some notice about the last general meeting of the "Association of Independent Merchants", Piłsudski 12, and "the brilliant proposal of Mr. Warman to begin negotiations for a union with the other merchants' associations". Quite apart from the fact that the proper place for such a notice is in the chronicle, our "editor" goes on to crack jokes at the expense of the "Merchants' and Industrialists' Association", Kowalska 2, already quite in the manner of a regular "ya tebye dam" [Russian: "I'll show you!"], and shows by the way his proficiency in florid language too: "The King of Acorns and the Ober of Red go about (why just these two figures, Mr. Editor?) with puffed-out cheeks, and the victorious queens triumph." Well, how do you like that language? Then follows a "joke" that is told as far away as Belgium, simply "finger-licking good"; meaning that the editor in his own person took the trouble to go all the way to Belgium for the sake of that joke...
And if Mr. A. G—kh has only just come from Belgium, it is no wonder that he is still little versed in local affairs, because the proposal of the president, Mr. Sh. Warman, is not new at all; the negotiations for a union with the merchants' association of Kowalska 2 have been going on for quite a long time — in fact ever since the energetic and tactful action on the part of Mr. Y. M. Weinryb, who separated the association at Piłsudski 12 from... merchants (not from the club), and thanks to that the situation there is so lamentable.
The merchants who founded the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association, Kowalska 2 — these same men were in their time the founders of the merchants' association at Piłsudski 12. Unfortunately, in the course of time they were outvoted by the small shopkeepers and a few wholesalers, who later ignored the founders entirely. Faced with such conduct they had no other way out but to join as members, and after a certain time they did indeed found the association at Kowalska 2, which today counts among its members the most respected local merchants; at its head stand qualified merchants, capable of organisation, who understand that a merchants' association is not only for writing appeals, but — as in all European cities — also a social institution, where every member should be able to come in: one to talk over commercial questions, one to read a newspaper, or indeed to pass the time at chess or even to play cards — which takes place in an entirely legal manner.
The walls of Kowalska 2 can also tell of a lively and creative organisation, not only in the commercial field but in general, of general Jewish and national activity here among us in Sosnowiec. They can tell, for instance, of the whole "Keren Hayesod" campaign, which was organised and carried out there, and also of the reception [raut] in honour of the esteemed guest, the poet L. Jaffe, which was arranged there. And after all this, some Mr. A. G—kh still has the audacity to come and besmirch and condemn such a lively and useful organisation! To this one must react as sharply as possible; such lawlessness must not be permitted. "This one came to sojourn, and he would play the judge?!" [Genesis 19:9]
W. G—r.

II.
To the Jewish public in Zagłębie.
The board of the Zionist Organization in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] has resolved to set up on its premises, within the next 4 weeks, a large Jewish-Hebrew [Yiddish-Hebrew] people's library, which is to be at the service of the broad Jewish popular circles.
Coming to the Jewish public with this proposal, we find it important to note that the planned library will not be something new, but a continuation of the old and first Jewish library in Dąbrowa, named "Ezra", which was created 13 years ago with great love and reverence by the first swallows — the heralds of the idea of national revival in our town — and where, over the course of 11 years on end, book upon book was gathered with rare devotion, and a corner of culture grew up on which the greater part of our intelligentsia and semi-intelligentsia was reared.
But 2 years have already passed since the moment when the local Jewish public was shaken by the wicked deed committed by a few lawless fellows from a certain political party, who, like common robbers, destroyed that institution. Since then the road to the Jewish book has been barred to the better part of our youth!
But the demands of life give no rest to those who feel the need to create an institution of this kind, for they know that a large part of the self-taught youth is pinning its hopes on the library, and this gives us the courage to rouse the broad circles to come to our aid and join the ranks of the builders.

Tsaytung", as well as through donations of books, which is being organized by a committee.

A Łódź Firm Imitates PePeGe Patents

[Łódź — industry and patents.] As we are informed, on the 24th of this month, by order of the public prosecutor's office, a search was carried out at the "Dżentelmen" ("Gentleman") factory in Łódź, which had been using, without having any right to do so, the manufacturing method patented by the well-known firm "PePeGe", a joint-stock company in Grudziądz.
During the search, 202 pairs of shoe-lasts ("kapites") were seized, which had been made according to the invention of the "PePeGe" firm, and because of this the popular-footwear department at the "Dżentelmen" firm has been stopped for the time being.
As it turns out, the "PePeGe" firm has already been conducting a lawsuit in this matter against the "Dżentelmen" firm for a year, and has won the case in the first two instances.
It is worth noting that the costs of the trials carried out by the "PePeGe" firm in the field of patented footwear amount, for the current year, to approximately a million zł.
An album in memory of Berek Joselewicz

[Zagłębie — public affairs; memorial album.] Every Jew is well acquainted with the heroism of the Jewish colonel (polkovnik) Berek Joselewicz during the uprising in Poland — how he fought, together with other troops, for Poland's liberation.
In order to immortalise this hero, a committee has been formed in Wilno under the patronage of Marshal Piłsudski, together with Polish and Jewish communal activists, who have undertaken to publish a memorial album with 150 illustrations and various materials from his life.
For several days now representatives of the committee have been staying with us in Zagłębie, taking subscribers for the album here. It is to be hoped that the Jewish public in Zagłębie too will support this communal undertaking, on a par with other towns in Poland.
Rudolf Mosse's Address Book

[Commerce — publisher's notice (apparently a paid puff).] In the publishing house of the International Advertising Company Rudolf Mosse in Warsaw there will appear in the coming days the third, improved edition of the Polish Address Book for trade, industry, crafts and agriculture. It is superfluous to write once again about the necessity of the said publication, which has so far won general recognition and popularity among the interested circles.
The Polish Address Book, which makes possible direct relations between producer and consumer, required long-lasting and costly preparatory work.
The necessity of the book already became evident after the appearance of the first edition, which was exhausted within a short time.
The publisher deserves recognition for his labour and expense in creating the work.
The new edition will surely be found with every merchant, so as to go on serving the spread of modern address methods among our economic circles.
