In the Chasm of the Abyss — Where the Splintering of the Economic Institutions Leads

[Sosnowiec — commercial life; article.] In the Chasm of the Abyss.
To what a level things are being brought by the splintering of the economic institutions.
Not long ago we attended here a general meeting of one of the Sosnowiec merchants' associations, at which a minyan of people gathered.
When a stranger comes to Sosnowiec and learns that we possess as many as three Jewish merchants' associations, he is filled with enthusiasm, and he is surely glad to hear on what a high level the Jewish merchant class stands, how far they are developed, that each has his own economic interests which concern him. On a stranger this makes the impression that, since there are three types of merchants and each is united in a separate association, in a special organisation, they presumably display activity and initiative and life and temperament.
We, however, when we watch a general meeting of a merchants' organisation take place with a “numerous attendance” of 10—12 men, cannot begin to understand this comedy. If an association is treated with such indifference, then why does one need so many associations, so many little shops? Why must each one “make Sabbath for himself”, when the Sabbath is not being arranged at all? Why have so many associations when it interests none of us?
And at the very same time we learn that the Polish merchant class of the whole of Zagłębie has united in one central body. It goes without saying that we cannot even dream of similar projects, which, incidentally, have been touched upon more than once in the columns of our newspaper.
How can we even speak of a union of the Zagłębie merchants' institutions, when every town in Zagłębie has its own several associations? Why make fools of ourselves, why speak hollow words from which nothing can come?
A rare phenomenon. Among ourselves we tear at one another with all our might over the slightest trifle; we can never come to any understanding, even when it concerns the most cardinal matters, the most important affairs. Among the nations of the world, by contrast, it is said that we must be reckoned with, that we are a force, if only because we hold together united, because we are organised.
It is tragic for a people when from outside it is thought to be conscious, organised, a mighty force that must be reckoned with. Thanks to this we are often treated with reverence; but hardly does one draw near to us and catch sight of our true face than one comes to the conviction that there is nothing to fear from our unity. At that very moment the whole picture is revealed in its true shape. When one comes closer to us one sees that not only are we not united into a mighty force, but we are torn apart at every step, that everything in our possession is rotten and stale, that we can never reach any unified understanding, so that the dangerous abyss of decline grows ever deeper and more terrible among us; and if one considers seriously and sincerely into what a chasm we are sinking and how far we may get under the prevailing situation, at such a moment one's eyes begin to swim and one loses heart, so that one fears this time to lose consciousness and balance.
This is not just some phrase, this is not said idly into the air; these are words that come from the heart, about which people polemicise often enough, but they no longer take fright at them. People have grown used to speaking of it as of all other everyday matters, and quite forget that what is at stake here is nothing more and nothing less than losing the ground from under our feet, existence and annihilation.
And so, precisely at such grave moments, people only ponder and split hairs over how to tear things to pieces, they try to tear one limb from another, so long as we fall apart into small bits that have no significance whatsoever.
Our merchants' associations are chopped up and broken into bits and pieces and accomplish nothing, only because they are broken shards..
But people do not stop at that. Although the danger from the broken-up institutions is so great that every merchant suffers from it, they are beginning to take the road of destruction in the field of our financial interests as well.
Thanks to our unity our banks are in a not-bad condition; but people have made it their sacred aim to break and tear these apart too. They keep thinking up how to create a separate bank for every shtibl, as though this were not an institution necessary to every merchant, but something needed for playing politics and for all kinds of election machinations and who knows what else; they keep reckoning on creating new financial institutions, which will thus further undermine the secure basis of the existing banks, and from the newly arisen ones new kinds of little shops will grow, which will bring us nothing but humiliation and shame.
Should one really not stop at such grave moments and give a thought to where this splintering leads? Do we really still not see that we are falling into the chasm of the abyss? Will this go on and on without any composure of mind and logical reflection?
Selekt.
Little Feuilleton: Complaints

[Feuilleton.] Heaven and earth and complaints. I sit for a day in the editorial office and listen to complaints — about whom not? Beginning with the rabbi and ending with the doctor, everybody has complaints, and against everybody there are complaints. Were one to try to describe them, one could not write it all out even on an ox-hide. I therefore want to describe only the complaints of the latest day.
In comes a young man and tells how his wife had a hard labour. He ran at four before dawn to the doctor, but the doctor answered that before eight o'clock he does not stir from the spot; even the intercession of the doctor's wife did not help — he does not go earlier than eight o'clock! Having no choice, they had to go to a second doctor, and he at once [thus in print; a word such as “came” seems to have dropped out] and with good luck delivered the child. And the young man asks: how can it be? How is it that a doctor will not go to a woman in childbirth before eight in the morning?
Such a complaint I passed on to the doctor, who happens to be an acquaintance, and he answered, as is the custom, with a story:
Once a doctor was called to a woman in childbirth in the middle of the night. The doctor came, sat down in the next room and smoked a cigarette. The woman in labour groaned, sighed and screamed, and the doctor pretends not to hear. When an hour had gone by, the woman began to scream in Polish “Boże mój” [“My God”]; the doctor still does not stir from the spot. Another hour passed and the woman took to screaming in plain Yiddish “Gevalt, mame” — only now did the doctor go in to her.
“Do you understand me,” says the doctor, “when a Jew comes at four o'clock to call a doctor to a woman in childbirth, you may be sure that at eight in the morning it will still, God forbid, not be too late. That I know from experience.”
So answers the doctor. Which of the two is right I do not know. I am no doctor, and not the happy father either. I only wanted to pass on a complaint that I heard out today in the editorial office; let the reader judge for himself.
A Heymisher [“one of our own”].
From Times Past (Memoirs)

[Literature — memoir; a shtetl figure.] By B. Apelboim [ב. עפעלבוים].
It comes to my mind now:
If the legend is true that in every generation there are thirty-six hidden righteous men by whose merit the world endures — then I knew one of them.
A long time has passed since then. The road from my childhood to this day lies across lands and seas; the figures I met on my wanderings have been erased — only this one figure still stands before my eyes.
* * *
Short of stature, frozen in silence and humility, the lips pressed tight and the head bowed; the small white beard beckoned [printed "געווינקן"] with a concealed sadness. The eyebrows were thick and overgrown; only the eyes shone with a goodness that wells up from the heart. His name was Yaakov, and people called him Yantshe the cobbler [יאנטשע שוסטער].
He was a simple village cobbler; on his pointed shoulders dark worry sat the whole week long. The yoke of earning a living had bent his back, and so he went from village to village, carrying on his shoulder the little sack of tools. He patched peasants' boots, mended peasants' "tshizmes" [high boots], slept in peasants' houses; he got through his days on bread and salt. In summer — with a bite of radish or onion on the side, a few roasted potatoes, sometimes a roasted egg as well.
So he strode the whole week from village to village. On summer mornings he strode very [?] unhurriedly over the sandy roads and quietly sang the verses of the Psalms. The breeze caressed, the sun rose, and Yantshe, with great pleasure and love, praised the One Above for the world that is beautiful, for the fields that smell sweet, for the sun that warms. With light steps, with joy on his face, he strode along and hummed the verses to himself.
This is how he looked then: a man in disguise, a king's son who had dressed himself in the garments of a servant.
Sometimes, though, he would happen to strike upon a verse that expressed the sorrow of the heart; then he lifted his pure eyes to heaven and let out a sigh:
Help, Father in heaven.
For Yantshe had a wife, a sickly woman. For years she had been ailing, lay paralysed, could not move a single limb — neither living nor dying.
Just one sigh, and he goes on saying Psalms; presumably it was so ordained by His beloved Name.
And at once he remembered his only daughter: Dvoyrele is already a grown girl; she is God-fearing, quiet, gentle. She has large dreamy eyes and looks exactly like his wife when she became his bride. And he grows more cheerful: with one hand He punishes and with the other He heals.
And again he arrived in a village and again patched peasants' boots. He kept silent, was humble and bowed.
And so until Friday at dusk.
When the dear holy Sabbath arrived he became quite a different man; the weekday worry fell away from him, he peeled himself out of the dejection of a servant, and once more a king's son began to shine.
The market grew quiet, the shops closed, the weekday was driven off into the gentile street; in the windows of Jewish houses the Sabbath candles twinkled, and Yantshe the cobbler came out of his lane — not at all the same man as during the whole week.
He was dressed in a greenish, shiny "serge" [printed "סערזשענער" (?)] kapote and a tall velvet cap; the camel-hair gartel clasped his loins firmly, the white beard was like pure silver, the eyes clear and bright, and the whole face shone with Sabbath radiance. He strode step by step and looked taller, his back straightened; the worry of livelihood did not sit on his neck, no care lay on his shoulders.
It is the Sabbath! And the Sabbath is rest.
And so it was the whole Sabbath: he had such great strength in him that he could strip himself entirely of the weekday; he thought of nothing, spoke no weekday words, was with God and with his additional Sabbath soul.
He was among the first in the synagogue at Sabbath daybreak; he recited the entire Book of Psalms, and took great pleasure in the Psalms, as a hungry man takes pleasure in food. Then he went home, drank a glass of something warm that had stood in the oven since the day before, then sat at the spread table and went through the weekly Torah portion aloud, in a singing voice, then went to pray. After prayers they made kiddush, ate, sang zemirot; the girl helped along, the sick wife smiled, and —
What power the Sabbath has — even the sick feel well on the Sabbath!
He rested a little, then the beit midrash again; they are saying Pirkei Avot...
Yantshe the cobbler felt himself redeemed from servitude, freed from all troubles.
Sabbath!
* * *
And the main thing:
The Minchah prayer of Sabbath at dusk.
Yantshe had held the established right for a number of years: Minchah he prayed before the lectern.
To this day I can feel the fragrance of Yantshe's Sabbath-dusk Minchah.
Shadows filled the beit midrash. Jews already sense the weekday worry, which is already standing behind the shtetl, ready to enter every house after Maariv; but the Jews brace themselves, do not want to remember it — one does not want the week...
The beit midrash is packed; children nestle in fear against their fathers, the faces pale, the eyes glistening with sadness. And Yantshe wrapped himself in the dusk, took his place before the lectern, felt the Sabbath packing itself up for the road, and with deep sadness and longing his voice began to tremble:
— Atah e-chad ve-shim-kha e-chad, u-mi ke-amkha Yisrael goy echad ba-aretz ["You are One and Your Name is One, and who is like Your people Israel, one nation on earth"]...
What a sweet, pent-up sadness there was in his voice — the sadness of an orphan... the sadness of a longing lover... It began to press upon the heart; the loneliness that comes with the week was frightening. Yantshe the cobbler's voice was so clear and slightly hoarse. And a hidden groan was in the voice — the groan of a king's son who does not want to put on the clothes of a servant, and yet has not the slightest will to disobey.
It is so good to obey the Father in heaven — but the week is so bad...
It was no cobbler who stood before the lectern! There stood a prophet, mourning in secret over the weekday-ness of human beings... He longed for redemption, for an eternal Sabbath.
In the beit midrash it had already grown dark. Yantshe began the "Tzidkatkha", and his voice trembled still more. It seemed: Moses our Teacher had only just passed away, and we were left lonely, forsaken.
* * *
And once, when Yantshe was standing before the lectern, his girl ran into the beit midrash weeping loudly:
— Mother is dying.
Everyone looked round in sorrow and fright. But Yantshe did not interrupt; he did not even turn his head; he stood as before, only his voice was thicker, more choked.
The girl choked on her weeping and went back out of the beit midrash, but Yantshe did not interrupt; his voice trembled:
— Atah e-ch-ad ve-shimkha e-ch-ad!
I remember:
Down my boyish cheeks hot tears ran.
* * *
To this day, when I recall Yantshe the cobbler's Sabbath Minchah, my heart tightens and I feel again the fragrance of those Sabbath dusks.
If the legend is true that there are thirty-six hidden righteous men in every generation, then I am certain that Yantshe the cobbler was one of them.
The Tram and Society

(How can catastrophes be avoided and eliminated?)

Zagłębie is among the foremost cities [sic] in Poland; life in Zagłębie is big-city life. The work, the rushing and the toiling, the earnings and the sources of livelihood — everything proceeds in the European manner. Now that Upper Silesia too has been added, life has become bound together even more in the European manner, so that in our present day man is being turned into a machine, designed to drive and chase the coal [?]. Possibly we do not notice this, because the gaze of our eye is too short-sighted and we see only what is happening today, and our memory has already forgotten what yesterday looked like.

But when we cast a glance at the recent past we see that the man-machine is progressing — and with rapid steps at that.

Let us leaf back a few pages: a few years ago, when a Sosnowiec man needed to travel to Będzin or the reverse, when a Będzin or Dąbrowa man needed to be in Sosnowiec, one went to a train. Later people were no longer content with the trains and the autobuses were added; but that too became too little, and we got the tramway service — only this traffic, too, does not suffice. One cannot wait 15 minutes for a tram when life is racing and every minute plays a significant part, so the service must be a more frequent one, and already now we have a tram every 10 minutes. It goes without saying that the traffic, too, will be speeded up, for in the end people will realise that to wait 10 minutes for a tram one needs patience nowadays, above all when man is becoming a machine that has to be a kind of motive power, producing ever more and ever faster — just as machines of ever newer types are continually demanded so that they may turn out the product faster...

It is forgotten, however, that being swept along by the rapid tempo does not happen systematically here; the population is not prepared for this process, and because of that it is bound up with so much suffering and so many human victims. How many human victims has the tram already taken among us? The wounds from those killed not long ago are still fresh, and here we find ourselves under the impression of a new victim, by which we have been shaken.

We have already pointed several times to the lack of caution of the citizens. One must remember that trams run in the streets. We have remarked that people are not careful, and that one must remember not to treat it as a trifle when one finds oneself in a street along which a tram line has been laid.

It is a fact, however, that for the most part those killed are precisely careful people. Thus we know that Mrs. Lewkowicz was a very careful woman; but she could not imagine that in the dark she would stumble on a log right beside the tram, thanks to which she met her death.

The same is true of Mrs. Sobotka [printed: Sabatka], who has just perished and who was also careful. She saw the tram going and waited for it to pass, so that she crossed the street after the tram had gone through; and at that moment another tram came towards her on the second line, from another direction — which she had not expected, because she was sure that there was no more than one tram on the line. A victim, then, of not being versed in the progress of the tramway service, which had come into effect two days earlier.

After all, one must not forget that a human being is no more than a human being, and that it cannot occur to him to ponder something he takes no interest in. The unfortunate dead woman, Mrs. Sobotka, could not have known that for two days the trams had been running simultaneously in two directions. And just as such a log, on which Mrs. Lewkowicz met her death, must be removed, in exactly the same way it is a duty of the tram company to make known to the population beforehand that at such-and-such places the trams pass one another, and that people should take note of it. Perhaps such announcements would have drawn the citizens' attention, and a human victim would thereby have been avoided?

In general the value of human lives is held cheap; otherwise things would be altogether different. Our self-governing bodies do not react and take no interest in so important a question, one that is claiming human victims.

Thus, for example, we do not see in any city at all a tram running through the busiest streets at such a rapid pace as it does here. And why do the city fathers not react to this? How many times has this already been spoken and written about? And what of it? It interests no one. Why, it is unheard of! We also often hear very little ringing, which is inadmissible. Just last week the writer of these lines was a witness to how the tram driver moved off from a stop without even ringing beforehand. Can a catastrophe not happen in such a case? We know that the tram company cannot know about everything, just as the citizens are not obliged to know about everything; and for that very reason a duty lies on the tram company to make known to the citizens what they need to know, so that responsibility shall indeed rest both on the citizens, when they do not observe the regulations, and on the tram employees, when they do not observe what is incumbent on them.

And something more: in Będzin people are frightened of the new Czeladź line, which has been laid through narrow lanes and the Old Market, where the traffic is heavy and the crowding heavier still. Moreover, one must not forget that the people there are not accustomed to tram traffic, and at best one sometimes forgets oneself. It is therefore absolutely necessary that the tram company take this into account and order the motormen to be very, very careful. The citizens of that district, too, must accustom themselves to remembering that trams run past their doors, so that they must watch out for themselves and for the children.

The city councils in Zagłębie do almost nothing in this field, and we hold that they can and must be in contact with the company. One must, after all, not forget that what is at stake here is, all in all, no more and no less than human lives — and who is obliged to react to this if not our city fathers?

It is already high time to stop remaining indifferent to what ought to be treated with the greatest care and seriousness. A mutual responsibility must arise. The tram employees must be responsible for all their faults, just as the population must observe the regulations that are binding on it.

Our self-governing bodies should remember well that they can and should play an important part in this matter.

Y. Sh.
The Co-operative Movement of the Jewish Middle Class

[Economy — Jewish co-operatives in Poland.] The co-operative movement began to develop among the Jews not long ago. Before the war the type of credit co-operative was widespread among the Jews — banks for mutual aid and savings-and-loan funds; the war destroyed them all. During the war consumer co-operatives sprang up en masse[?]. Their emergence, and even their development in the early period, was helped by the circumstance that in wartime these co-operatives used to receive for their members the rationed articles (bread, kerosene, sugar and so on); and as soon as the war ended and the business of rationed articles ceased, these co-operatives began to go under, and of the many hundreds there now remain a few dozen, which are kept up more for reasons of principle than because of their practical necessity. Instead, the type of credit co-operative, the co-operative bank, developed strongly among the Jewish middle class.

The greater part of the Jewish middle class — artisans, petty traders, merchants — was impoverished during the war and lost its workshops, machines, working capital and so on. These groups had been quite weak before the war as well and had needed support from outside. That support they used to receive from various outside organisations. During the war the workshops of a large part of the artisans were ruined; with others the workshops and machines became obsolete and new ones were needed. The small merchants, who lost their fortunes in the war, the medium merchants — all of them needed credits. The state's credit policy strove first of all to satisfy agriculture and industry. Commerce, even large-scale commerce, was not supported by the government with credits, and this policy is in part being continued even now. From this general credit policy alone it followed that the Jews, by and large, did not benefit from the state credits, although it was precisely they who needed the credits most. Poland possesses very little liquid capital and therefore the discount rate is a very high one. It reaches 2½–3 per cent a month, although officially it is altogether 12 a year. It is worth comparing the circulation of money in a number of countries in order to understand how great our shortage of money is. In England, for example, there was in 1927 a circulation of 47.6 dollars per head; in Belgium 36.7 dollars; in Denmark 27.9; in France 55.7; in Spain 32.3; in Germany 20.9; Norway 32.7; Romania 8.1; Switzerland 46.6; Sweden 23.7; Italy 24.5 dollars, and in Poland it comes to barely 3.9 dollars per head. That is so enormously little that all the money in circulation must turn over several times in the course of a year merely to cover the taxes. If one also takes into account that the terms of bills of exchange were, until the very latest time, quite short here, and the turnover in cheques small, only then can one understand how great the hunger for liquid money is and how strongly this lack of money has been felt precisely by the Jewish middle class.

Characteristic of the lack of money among the Jewish middle class is the fact that interest and fines for taxes not paid punctually were collected from the merchants to the amount of 20 million zł., i.e. double what the peasant population paid in income tax.

The population in general has been impoverished, and the total sum of savings, which before the war reached over 3 million gold francs, now reaches barely something over one million. Moreover, according to the estimate of "Bank Polski", the difference is this: whereas formerly these were savings that could be disposed of for longer terms, they are now "reserves of the economic enterprises", which can only partly be used for short-term credits. It is no wonder that, with such a lack of money, it became a truly urgent necessity to make the savings of the Jewish middle class as liquid and as mobile as possible.

This could be done only through the Jewish co-operative banks, and that is indeed why they grew so quickly; thanks to the support of the "Foundation" and other Jewish public institutions, these co-operative banks have in the course of a few years developed and grown into an important factor in Jewish economic life. The government and the official circles that set the tone in the state's credit policy continue to pursue towards Jews the same policy as before, with the difference that formerly one did not even promise, whereas now one promises credits, one even fixes their amount precisely, but — one does not give them, under various pretexts.

In this situation it is understandable that the Auditing Union of the Jewish co-operatives, which embraces up to 450 such institutions, occupies an important place in our public life.
We Cabmen! (A Droshky Driver's Monologue)

[Feuilleton — humorous monologue.] (Monologue of a droshky driver.) By K. Davidzon.
A cholera and a choking fit on that clever "sugar-scabhead" who thought up today's machineries with today's "inventions", with today's 'tomobiles and 'tobuses! May the falling sickness grab hold of his guts! And may he never again be able to think up more such things, more such calamities in the world.
Listen to a story: I myself, as you see me alive, am a Jew, a cabman, who knows how long, since back in peacetime. My father was a cabman, my grandfather, my great-grandfather, may he rest in peace, were cabmen — and who ever saw or heard of such calamities as nowadays? You had a pair of horses, fine chestnuts, real lions! And a coach fit to stand in the Kaiser's own house, and — nothing more to it! You'd snatch a nice few fares in a day and live like God in France! Folks knew you've got to let a Jew earn something, and that really was living! Whose head did it ever get into, devil take it, such a notion — that a time would come and such a filthy world would plant itself here? Who ever worried, what's this, that such calamities would come, such troubles pouring down [?], eh? You've got to understand, I'm not one of those who don't know what's going on behind their backs; I'm no Hotsmakh or Grunam, not to see that they've sat down on top of us and are tearing the reins out of our hands and telling you: Brother, stój — halt! Today's times aren't the old days! You'll yet have to lead your stallion out to sell at the fair! You'll yet stand a whole day on the Czeladź bridge, freezing in the cold, and not lay eyes on a first fare [początek]! And the horse, a cholera, will be swallowing its spit, and the feed-basket will be empty, and you'll croak for want of a bite — you might as well go and rob a church!
Who can figure how people have gotten so frisky; it doesn't suit them any more to ride in a droshky — only on the autobus, if you please! Since when has everybody become such a squire, such a count? When all's said and done, you're simply staking your life!
What do you do when it, the autobus, throws a fit and lets loose in a wild gallop, turns over head-down — go call it "knak-nisl" then [idiom: go complain to somebody], go summon it to Unesaneh Toykef then! And on the other hand, what's a Jew like me to do, who can't buy such a machinery? Am I really supposed to croak for a piece of bread?
There was one, a second came, so there are already two — enough, you'd think! No! Welcome, a third has come, and by what they're saying, the tramways are yet to come. Well, I ask you, what are we poor folks to do? It'll come to putting your teeth up on the shelf, and sit yourself down to write mezuzahs!
Look, as you see me, a Jew, today I haven't, a cholera, even once taken the whip in my hand, haven't even once clucked to my poor hungry nag: "Wio, giddy-up, there'll be enough for a bite of breakfast!" And here they're shortening our days and years: don't stand here, don't drive there, polish this, wash round that, wipe the lantern a hundred times a day, go about dressed up as for parade, and after all that — prrr... only then sit in a heap of troubles and wait for a fare!
I'm hungry, the horse is hungry, the wife and children are hungry, and you wait for a miracle — maybe some lunatic will turn up who'll ask to be driven somewhere.
Well, is that a thing a man can stand? Is it possible that the days and nights should pass like this and no remedy be found for such a calamity, a cholera take it; the 'tobuses and tramways ought to be cleared off the face of the earth, and that'll be the end of it and good riddance!
You surely think I'm going to become an idler and stroll about the market with a little walking stick? Feh, forget it! A fire take all those machineries along with the tramways! We won't sell off [?] our nags, our bays, our stallions for any money! Let the world be torn up by the roots first, before we should have to do that! Let the world even go under, and we won't throw away our livelihood, won't lose our bit of bread! We were cabmen and we'll stay cabmen! We don't want to look for bread in anything else! We're stronger than anybody and will outlast everything! Nobody toys with us; we weren't born yesterday!
But all those 'tomobiles and tramways are dead matter, while we cabmen are living people; and as long as we're living people we'll outlive every one of them! Even if the world should go under — we cabmen will not give in!...
The Rabbi's Son — a Jewish historical novel by Yaakov Zimmerman (instalment 19)

— What is the matter with you today? — Sarah answered lovingly, stroking Blumele's hand as she spoke. — I myself am also convinced that your father's wish will surely be fulfilled, even if he finds nothing at all on the Vistula bridge in Warsaw and comes back home with empty hands. My heart, which loves you so dearly, tells me so, and you know, after all, that a loving heart feels, and you know, after all, dear friend, that a loving heart feels and knows more than the greatest prophet...
— But for that I want to have my reward too. You must show him to me, that so handsome and dear young man, when he goes to prayers this evening with his famous father, the rabbi. You know well, dear Blumele, that it is not mere curiosity alone that drives me to it; rather, I feel in my heart that your father's journey will surely not be in vain, and that it will bring it about that his strongest wish, for the happiness of his only daughter, will be fulfilled...
— You will see him — Blumele answered with a bashful look, and tears now began, as always, to roll down her lovely cheeks.
— You know, Blumele — Sarah now answered — my heart, too, is no longer entirely free... Yes, that is how it is... For the last eight days I have felt within me such a strange but happy feeling as never before. It has taken hold of me so that I can hardly master myself... It keeps seeming to me that the man with the handsome black beard, who has been hanging about our little house here for the last eight days, is somehow a near relation of ours... He looks so much like my father that my mother has already noticed it too and told me so... He looks so sad, and he must surely be carrying a great sorrow about with him. Ah, if only I could help him, with anything at all...
At these words the door opened. Chaim's wife came in from the street, where she had been taking a look at her children. But right behind her there appeared on the threshold that very man of whom the girls had just been speaking.
He begged pardon for having the boldness to come in here on his own.
— Only a short time ago I was a rich man, the rich father of two beautiful daughters, who looked very much like you, my dear girls. But the villain Chmielnicki, may his name and memory be blotted out, destroyed my whole fortune, carried off my wife and my children and perhaps even murdered them. And I myself wander about the world here as if in the world of chaos. My only aim is to seek out my father and the heroic Prince Wiśniowiecki; perhaps they will still be able to help me with something... Be so good as to allow me to stay here with you in the house until after Shavuot. It will keep seeming to me that I see before my eyes my two beautiful and beloved children...
The stranger fell silent. But his words bore the seal of truth, and so they made a deep impression on all who heard them. This was especially the case with Sarah. It kept seeming to her that she was now hearing the beautiful, clear and firm voice of her father...
The two girls were silent too. They looked with pleading eyes at the mistress of the house, and Chaim's wife, after a very brief reflection, said:
— Children, take the man and lead him to your house, Blumele. I will follow soon; there we shall all take counsel as to what we should do, whether we should eat the holiday meal together. Take him there.
The girls went off with the stranger to the nearby little house of Esther, the wife of Ayzik the baker. The wife of Chaim the wagoner still saw to something in the house and at the oven, and after she had told her children not to go far from the house, she too went off to Esther.
The latter was now standing at the open window. She was thoroughly tired from such a hard day's work — the eve of a holiday, and, no evil eye, so many challahs and pastries to bake... But her thoughts were not on that now. She had on her mind her dear Ayzik, who was now so far away, all the way in Warsaw...
The two girls arrived with the stranger. Some two minutes later Chaim's wife came in as well. Esther stood there as if a little confused. She kept on looking at the strange man with the black beard, who seemed so familiar to her, but for the life of her she could not recall who he was and when she had seen him.
The same was the case with the man. He too kept on looking at Esther, but who she was he still could not remember.
But suddenly a thought ran like lightning through Esther's mind, and she cried out:
— Shimon?! Is it you?!
— Esther?! Is it you?! — burst at the same instant from the stranger's breast. He had heard Esther's voice and suddenly remembered who and what she was...
But before the two, who had now so suddenly found each other in such a peculiar way, had time to exchange a few words, or perhaps even to fall on each other's necks, at that very minute a splendid carriage, drawn by four costly horses, drove up and stopped before the door of Ayzik's little house.
Two finely dressed men now stepped out of the closed carriage, and each of them held a letter in his hands.
When the stranger with the black beard, whom Esther had only a minute earlier called Shimon, caught sight of the elder of the two men, he exclaimed with great surprise and in a trembling voice:
— My lord Prince!
Indescribable astonishment and surprises now reigned in Ayzik the baker's small house. Hardly had Esther recognised her cousin Shimon, the son of her uncle Eliyahu, whom she had not seen for over twenty years, since she had stayed at their house as a girl, when the other great surprise was added: before her now stood the great and famous Polish lord, the magnate Wiśniowiecki, of whom she had already heard so much told, and that he would yet even become King of Poland... What does he want in her house? And what sort of paper is that he is holding in his hand?
Not much smaller was the surprise of the Prince when he suddenly saw before him here Shimon, the son of "his" Jew and friend Eliyahu, about whom the German Paul Werner had only a few days ago delivered a report that he had perished at the hands of Chmielnicki's bands — and here he sees him alive and well.
The Prince was even more delighted when he saw here, together with Shimon, the two girls Blumele and Sarah; he thought that these were Shimon's two daughters, Hadassah and Yehudit, and it pleased him greatly that they too had been saved from Chmielnicki's bands.
The two girls were utterly surprised. They could not understand at all what was going on here. They did not know Shimon, and they had not the slightest idea for what purpose such a distinguished and mighty Polish lord had come here. And, while they were at it, who indeed was that other, younger Polish lord, who kept on looking at them with such friendly glances?...
The wife of Chaim the wagoner, a good but quite simple woman, certainly could not grasp at all who and what these persons were and for what purpose they had gathered here at the baker's. She stood agape, with open mouth and wide eyes, and understood nothing of what was happening around her.
The first who quickly came to himself was the Prince. He spoke to Shimon and put several questions to him, and soon he learned in what manner Shimon had been saved alone, without his wife and daughters, and that they had remained as captives with Chmielnicki's bands.
The Prince sighed deeply. He understood only too well what a terrible fate awaited all three, especially the girls, in Chmielnicki's camp. But he kept his feelings to himself, and to the despairing and dejected Shimon he first of all conveyed greetings from his father, who was at present still in Warsaw, and he gave him great hope that everything would end well and that he would soon be reunited with his wife and daughters.
(To be continued).
What Was Heard, What Was Seen

[Będzin and district — weekly feuilleton.] Retold by Ben Amotz.

A.
If not for the receipt...
— Have you heard about the libel, which did not come off, of several Ger Hasidim against the Radomsker Rebbe [R. Shlomo Chanoch Rabinowicz, who lived in Sosnowiec]?
— A libel, no less? And against the Radomsker Rebbe at that? Well, to think up libels against rabbis who do not belong to the "Aguda" camp [Agudat Yisrael] — of that they are capable; but against a rebbe who is far from party politics and does not show the slightest opposition to the "Aguda"?
— Yes, yes, precisely against our rebbe — one of the intimates of the Radomsker Rebbe, may he live long, confirms to me. And he relates:
At the time of the occupation [the German occupation in the World War], certain in-laws, Ger Hasidim, deposited a dowry with the above-mentioned rebbe. And it came to pass — the rebbe was then in Marienbad — that the bridegroom's father, who lives in Germany, came to the rebbe and, because of the money inflation, demanded the deposited dowry.
The rebbe, although he was at that time taking a cure, gave orders to an intimate of his in Berlin, who at once, in accordance with the agreement[?] of the interested party, sent off the requested sum through the Berlin post office.
In the course of time great changes took place in world history, kingdoms went under and new ones floated up, and in the heads of several Ger Hasidim too the idea was born that one ought to "wash one's hands[?] at the Radomsker Rebbe's" [i.e. sit down to a meal at his expense]:
— After all, we shall not come away with nothing...
And so it was. For the "job" the chief hero came here, the bridegroom's father, with whom it was rehearsed that he should plead "it never happened" [lo hayu dvarim me-olam], just like the idiot in "The Seven Who Were Hanged" [Leonid Andreyev's story], who knows nothing more than to shout: — "Me not killed"...
And the remaining roles were distributed among several Będzin "fine Jews", who are such "God-blessed talents" that, sitting in the "shtibl", they nevertheless "saw everything that goes on in Berlin" at the time...
The "play" was performed in Będzin, at Reb Dawid Szpringwald's. All the "actors" assembled, and they carried out their roles brilliantly. At weak moments, for instance when the rebbe's side demanded proofs, the "eyewitnesses" played dramatically, threatened with their fists, swore all the oaths in the world that "the rebbe must give for the debt no less than 3 thousand dollars"...
The "play" was a success, but when they had already reached the last act, and the artistes were already about to take their "fee" [gaża], along came the "Yekke fool" and turned the whole tragedy into a... comedy...
Oh, "Yekke fool", over your orderliness many people are now weeping, who had dreamed such a sweet dream of a whole three thousand dollars...
— In the archive of the Berlin post office it was found, written and signed, that on such-and-such a day of such-and-such a year there was sent through the post to So-and-so son of So-and-so 5 thousand zł. [so printed]...
— I tell you — the narrator speaks with joy — when I showed them the receipt from the Berlin post office, the claimants stood petrified; each one looked for a nearby door to escape through...
— Well, is such a thing not worth making known to the whole world? Why, it is no less than the Beilis trial [Kiev, 1913], the Steiger affair [Lwów, 1924–25] — eh?..

B.
A symbol of the time.
The expanse of Potocka Street is taken up with people. A huge crowd, a mixture of all classes and of various ages, the majority — of the female sex; among them very young things with milk on their lips, who stand impatiently [waiting] for the gates of the "Nowości" to open for them...
A large number of policemen work hard to disperse the huge crowd, but the mass does not budge; their eyes are turned there, to the entrance, where several policemen stand guard.
I think: surely an interesting theatre performance, or a great scholar has come here and will give an instructive lecture; yes, the thirst for culture is still great enough.
With great effort I fought my way through to a policeman, whom I asked:
— What extraordinary thing is taking place here in the "Nowości"?
— Instead of an answer, he hands me a leaflet, from which I learn that a film is being shown under the title "The Diary of a Doctor", which shows the modern tragedies...
— Hm.., I understand already; it became clear to me that the crowd and the young misses are thirsting to see "the secret tragedies".
— A symbol of the time...

C.
She wept...
When Panna [Miss] Genia came in to the dressmaker to try on the dress which she "absolutely" [koniecznie] must have in honour of the masquerade ball taking place in Katowice, it struck her, like a hammer-blow over her little "garçon"-cut head, — the news that the "pani majstrowa" [the mistress dressmaker] is ill with the grippe and is actually lying in bed.
— So what will become of the dress? — a furious cry burst from Genia in plain Yiddish; in her great agitation she even forgot that at the dressmaker's an "inteligentna panna" [a cultured young lady] ought to speak Polish...
From the other room the dressmaker's husband appeared, who took pains to calm his customer and said to her:
— Well, you see for yourself that nobody here is to blame; do understand that if my wife had been asked whether she wants to fall ill with the grippe, she would certainly not have agreed. The thing is, however, that nobody asks us, and for several days now she has been lying ill.
But Miss Genia did not want to hear the excuses and did not stop being angry:
— But one does not do such a thing!... It is "bezczelne" [impudent], it is "niesłychane" [unheard of], it is...
More she could not say. She choked up and, like an offended child, burst out crying aloud.
Tears like brilliants fell from her kosher Jewish eyes, fell on the faithfully powdered little face and ruined an hour's work at the mirror...
— She wept.

D.
They are right...
They, the representatives of the "Women's Association" [Froyen-Fareyn] in Dąbrowa [Górnicza], have a complaint against me, and to tell the truth a justified complaint.
A few weeks ago I gave a "tickle" in this column to the Dąbrowa philanthropic institutions, asking why they do not support the fallen, unfortunate Krems[?] family.
Among the institutions the local "Women's Association" was also, by mistake, "hooked in".
Well, they argue: all right, other institutions "deserved the stone", but we, who conduct a broad relief activity, and what is more we do not cease supporting the above-mentioned family — why then do we deserve such a verdict?
A justified complaint, upon my life; we did indeed look into it and came to the conviction that the "Women's Association" is the opposite of other institutions. Only according to its means does the association stand on guard and support with whatever is at all possible.
— On the contrary — they argue — rouse the "pnei" [the town notables] to support us, and then we shall really be active.
— Dąbrowa "pnei"! When the "Women's Association" comes for money — support them; do not start up with any women, and especially ones from Dąbrowa...
The Decline of the Youth (A Young Man's Voice)

[Opinion — youth and education.] Lately the alarm has been rung without cease: a decline among the youth! The youth is spiritually impoverished! It has no interest in, and no understanding of, material and spiritual values. Given the importance of the question, it is therefore worth examining which causes brought about this decline.
In the youth of every era one can distinguish a better part and a worse part. For there never has been, and never will be, an absolutely ideal youth. One can speak only of a preponderance of this part or that, and on this depends the "rise" or the "decline". Today we have — no one will deny it — a decline. It must be stressed, however, that the positive group too is a quite considerable one, and it stands on a very high cultural level.
Who is to blame for the decline of the youth?
An important role has been played here by the upheaval of the present era. In the perspective of history the present era will surely grow into one of the richest in content and most exalted: an era of embittered struggle of ideas, of the realization of ideals dreamed of and suffered for over long years. On the one hand, the wrestling of ideas and the revaluation of values brought revival and a zest for struggle; on the other — chaos and confusion. This affected that part of the youth which wants to follow the line of least resistance, and of such there are a great many. It has withdrawn entirely from political and social life, it has ceased to take an interest in the various questions and problems, has turned aside — and on the side-roads of life lurk the agents of Mephistopheles, and only the rare chosen few can withstand the trial...
So this part of the youth wanders about as in a desert, has no aim and consequently no interest in life. This leads to pessimism, which leads in two directions: to deep melancholy, and to Epicureanism. The first leads to suicide; the second into the whirl[?] of life, into the abyss of degeneration. The youth chooses, with few exceptions, the second. It has harnessed itself to Bacchus's chariot and lets itself gallop on the merry-go-round of life...
You see them, these young people, in the spacious dancing halls, where they amuse themselves, dance themselves into oblivion, deafened by the wildest sounds of music; they fill the theatres, of the worse kind, where they want to make themselves artificially merry with empty operettas and tasteless trash (shund); they devote themselves with all their ardour to football, with which they want to drive away the emptiness. Their gaiety is only a mask — an external, an artificial one. Inwardly they are eaten up by the worm of boredom, which they want to drive away with the help of feigned jollity.
The second important cause is — the faulty education. The school system as a whole is badly set up; it has become ossified. People are afraid of any change whatsoever, whereas a great deal ought to be reformed. It is a painful question, and no little has already been said and written about it. The school, which should educate and prepare the young person for life, is regarded nowadays merely as a road to university studies, and the latter as a means to a career. Whoever still enters the "temples of learning" with honest intentions and seeks there a little more than a "scrap of paper" is quickly disappointed and laughed at as an impractical idler. In short: the pupil leaves school raw, without any guidance for life, without any orientation in life's tangled affairs. Is it any wonder that he goes astray? The few who do carry out of school a maturity — not merely a "paper" one — owe it to quite different factors.
Still worse is the situation in our "Polish-Jewish" school system. I believe the "Jewish-Polish" pupil is lost both to humanity and to the Jewish people. The schools are in fact nests of assimilation. Does that bit of Hebrew study — which, by the way, the pupils treat with disdain — amount to national education? Can that bit of "History of the Hebrews", the trifles served in the "national" schools, awaken and develop national consciousness?
And indeed these pupils are far from the Jewish word and thought; the bloody, sad and grandiose history of the Jews is foreign to them; they do not know themselves. It is tragicomic: they learn fragments of Jewish history, crumbs of Jewish life, as these are reflected in the crooked, dirty mirror of foreign "experts". Among the others they see only the exalted, the grandiose, the splendid; among us, by contrast, only the petty and the ugly. Is it a wonder that later they hate their own stock? The few nationally conscious pupils owe it to other circumstances.
This explains the sad phenomenon that the worse, negative part of the youth is recruited for the most part from the "graduates", from young people with secondary and higher education, who ought rather to enlarge and strengthen the cadres of the Jewish intelligentsia...
Where, then, is the way out of the situation? It is not enough merely to lament. One must and one can accomplish something substantial. What has Jewish society — or better said, those who cry day and night about the decline — done for the youth? What means have they adopted against assimilation, about which they raise the alarm so much?
One should and one must develop among the youth an educational work of enlightenment. Much attention must be devoted to the older school youth, chiefly from the Jewish-Polish schools. The youth must be given initiative, preparation for Jewish and general life. Let the genuine and valuable be set against cheap sensation, let the metallic ring of values resound against the empty drum-beating — then we shall see what the youth will choose. With good will and intensive work a great deal can be achieved.
Let courses and lectures be arranged, let literary-scientific circles be organized, which will acquaint the young person with various problems of life, with Jewish history, and so on.
If only a few can be found who truly want to do something for the cause, who truly give thought to the future of the Jewish youth — then the question will find at least a temporary solution.
G. Katz.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Emigration Matters at the Kehilla Office

Friday, 21 Shevat 5689 — Piątek 1 lutego 1929 [Friday, 1 February 1929].

Będzin

Emigration matters at the office of the kehilla.

The board of the local Jewish kehilla has received a permit to open a department devoted to the emigration question.
In the department various information and advice concerning emigration matters will be given.
Meeting of the Unemployed

In connection with the government's having temporarily stopped the benefits for the seasonally unemployed, a meeting took place on Wednesday at the “Corso”, at which the question was [—] [discussed?].
After the [—] [speeches?] a delegation was elected, which is to travel to Warsaw to intervene.
The expenses of the delegation are being allocated by the magistrate [city hall].
In Sosnowiec and Zawiercie, too, such protest meetings were held.
From the Merchants' Association

[From the Merchants' Association] the following is communicated: 1) Because it happens that some members refuse to appear before the arbitration courts at the association, the board has resolved that in such cases Article 14 of the statute will be applied, and those concerned will be expelled as members and their names will be published in the newspaper.
2) By the cemetery on the Czeladź road a tram stop “na żądanie” [request stop] has been set up, by virtue of which passengers have the right to have the tram stop at that spot.
Tram Service Będzin–Czeladź

Since Sunday the tram has been running on the new Będzin–Czeladź line. According to the earlier plan the tram is supposed to go slowly in the narrow, cramped lanes, but the incident that occurred the next day, Monday, shows that the motormen are not particular about this.
On that day a tram passed through the stretch of the narrow lane at such speed that the front part of the car lifted up.
The Creator and Founder of “Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin” Is Coming to Będzin

Shortly there will come to Będzin the creator and founder of the world yeshiva “Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin”, the Rabbi of Piotrków, Rabbi Meir Shapiro, shlita.
Every Jew already knows the great ideal of the Piotrków Rabbi in founding the world yeshiva and his extraordinary achievements in erecting in Lublin the gigantic yeshiva building, which is being built according to the newest installations and conveniences and constitutes the only gigantic and magnificent yeshiva building in the world.
On Lag BaOmer the ceremonial opening of the yeshiva will take place. In connection with the opening of this world yeshiva the Piotrków Rabbi, shlita, is coming to Będzin, where he will conduct a large propaganda campaign for YChL [Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin].
The Będzin branch of “Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin” has therefore created a provisional organizing committee of the following persons: Rabbi Tzvi Chanoch Levin, shlita (honorary chairman), Shmuel Piekarski (chairman), the parnasim [kehilla board members] Abraham and Kalman Liwer (vice-chairmen), Henech Kornfeld, L. Szczekacz, J. Szpigler, Z. Suszek [?], J. Erlich (secretary), Dawid Skórnik, M. Ch. Kaminer, J. M. Szenberg, Mordechai Dafner, Dawid Skoczylas, G. Alter, Shimshon Majmon, J. L. Klajner, J. Justman, Shmelke Shapiro, M. L. Altman, Jakub Shimon [printed: “Shmen”] Urbach, Judl Kaminer, L. Berkowicz, J. Gryngras, J. Kupferwasser, D. J. Wajcman and others.
The committee also has the task of convening a larger consultation of all the organizations and communal institutions in order to form a reception committee that would represent the entire local Jewish population.
Did anyone forget something in the tram?

[Będzin — transport.] The tramway management asks us to announce that anyone who forgot walking sticks, umbrellas, gloves and the like in the tram during the year 1928 may collect them at the tram depot (remiza) until the 15th of this month.
Vice-Starosta Mr. Bielawka leaves Będzin

[Będzin — administration.] The rumours circulating until now, that the vice-starosta [deputy district head] Mr. Bielawka[?] is leaving Będzin, are being confirmed. Mr. Bielawka leaves our town today and departs for Częstochowa, where he will take up the same office.
From "Tzeirei Mizrachi"

[Będzin — movements and parties.] In connection with the resolution of the "Tzeirei Mizrachi" district conference in Zawiercie concerning the collection for the benefit of the "Torah va-Avodah" fund in the Zagłębie region, Mr. Eng. Shimon Wasserman of Jerusalem is coming to Będzin today; under his leadership the proclamation of the collection will take place in Będzin as well as in the surrounding area. For this purpose a large meeting for members and sympathisers is being held today, Friday evening, at which the esteemed guest will lecture on our tasks with regard to the religious labouring Land of Israel at the present moment.

On Saturday night a banquet is being arranged with the participation of many delegates from Katowice, Königshütte [Królewska Huta] and Zawiercie.
A "means" of settling disputes...

[Będzin — crime.] On Saturday morning, when Mr. Aharon Feldman[?] was on Małachowskiego Street, he was suddenly attacked by an unknown person, who beat Mr. F. murderously.

As it turned out, the attack was carried out on the instructions of a worshipper at the Rozprza Hasidic shtibl, who had had a dispute with Mr. F. over a protested promissory note for 50 złoty!

This kind of revenge gave great satisfaction to the antisemitic press in Zagłębie, which did not spare any "delicacies" addressed to the Jewish population.

———

A second and even sadder incident occurred a day earlier at Modrzejowska 11.

In that house lives a certain tenant, Gutnicka, from whom the landlord and the other tenants get no joy. Not a week passes without a brawl taking place in that house; above all the G. family is angry at the landlord, Mr. Kokotek, and his children, because they unmasked the tenant before the board of "Dobroczynność" [the charity society], which, believing the woman to be a "widow", had been paying her rent for her.

When the "secret" was discovered, Mrs. G.'s son attacked Mr. K., beating him murderously; from then on the matter found its place with the police and in court, and the incriminating material against the family grew larger with every week.

The epilogue of the story was played out last Friday, when several toughs attacked the landlord Mr. Kokotek and his 3 sons, throwing themselves on them with knives and other implements and inflicting severe wounds to their heads.

The police arrested several of the murderers, and fresh material has been added in court.

— Perhaps the merchants' organisations would react to this, so that the rule of the toughs should not repeat itself in our town as in the "good" old days?...
Sosnowiec — the birth pangs of the kehilla budget

[Sosnowiec — community.] Last Sunday the kehilla board again held a session, which dealt with the budget for 1929.

On almost all items of the budget there are no differences of opinion; only on the item of schooling is the work paralysed.

The crux is the demand of the Talmud Torah representatives, who require that the Talmud Torah be an exception to the rule and be subsidised with 10 thousand złoty, i.e. 5 thousand złoty more than what the girls' gymnasium and the Mizrachi school receive.
The gabbaim of the "Talmud Torah" tremble before the caretaker, and Jewish children get beaten

[Sosnowiec — education.] On Saturday Mr. Mordechai Katz raised a commotion in the synagogue during prayers, shouting: "Why is there no reaction to the fact that the caretaker (stróż) of the Talmud Torah beats the children murderously?"

Mr. Katz related in this connection that the caretaker had badly beaten his little boy, and when Mr. K. tried to interfere, the caretaker grabbed an axe against him.

The fact reported by Mr. K. aroused bitterness among the worshippers, and some of them turned to the Talmud Torah gabbai who was present, Mr. Szczekacz, with the question why it is permitted that Jewish children who study in the Talmud Torah should be left defenceless?

To this Mr. Szczekacz replied that "the gabbaim themselves are afraid of the caretaker"...
The general secretary of the PPS-Left arrested

[Sosnowiec — politics and police.] On the order of the local investigative office, the general secretary of the PPS-Left [PPS-Lewica], Mr. Dzhuma [as printed; probably Czuma], was arrested in Kraków by the police there.
The arrested man has been brought here and is in the custody of the investigating judge.
A “wedding guest” sentenced to a year in prison

[Sosnowiec — court.] To the wedding of a Christian resident of Gołonóg there came a “mechutan” [in-law/wedding guest] who, “out of necessity”, brought along a long knife, a bayonet and several other implements as a “wedding present”.
When the wedding guests had become tipsy, a quarrel arose, as usual, over a “kumoszka” [a gossip / female crony]; from words they went over to deeds, and the result was that a young Christian man aged 27 was killed by his “przyjaciel” [friend]...
The murderer stood these days before the district court, which sentenced him to a year in prison.
Lost the inheritance and will sit a month in prison

[Sosnowiec — court.] In the local district court the trial took place of a Christian from Strzemieszyce who had abused and beaten his own mother, forcing her to sign her property over to him.
The court sentenced the “faithful son” to a month in prison and to the loss of his rights as an heir.

The Keren HaYesod Campaign in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Zionism, Keren HaYesod.] Sosnowiec, which had lagged behind the neighbouring town in its national activity, has now passed the test in the Keren HaYesod campaign. Sosnowiec has shown that it possesses national consciousness, and has helped in the great work of building the national home for the Jewish people.

Rosman, delivered a report on the campaign, which is a satisfactory one. After a lengthy discussion an executive was elected, consisting of the following persons: Tencer, Rosman, Lancman, Mrs. Langer, Mrs. Rosman, Feldman, Buksbaum, Klarman and Liberman.
The following gentlemen entered the committee: M. Reicher, Dr. Melodysta, Dr. Fruks, J. Kabak, S. Reznik, J. M. Wajnryb, G. Abramczyk, A. Firstenberg, Fiszel, Grandapel[?], M. Szpigelman, Sz. Elected to the audit commission were Messrs. Lejzerowicz, Dizenhaus, Chmielnicki, Kromołowski and Wieliczker.

One Cries Out Because It Hurts

[Article — Poland: the state budget in the Sejm.] The budget has passed over to the Sejm. The general debates have begun; the decisive general battle is drawing near. Although the parliamentary representation knows from the outset that it goes into the fight with the thought of capitulating, it nevertheless rushes with vehemence to the Sejm rostrum. It wants once again, for the thousandth time, to rehearse its complaints against the government; it wants to try its luck once more, to speak to the common sense of the leading statesmen and summon them to judgment. And there is, after all, a great deal to "get off" one's chest; complaints are not lacking.
The government is not satisfied with parliament. In its eyes the Sejm is merely a place where every demagogic party seeks "a place in which to distinguish itself", where people haggle and traffic with the most vital interests of the state. All complaints are, in its eyes, masked political calculations, merely means of fighting for power. That is why it treats them so lightly.
But the government generalises too much; it leaps too easily from the particular to the general. Many complaints do indeed have a purely political-demagogic background, but many complaints are just — life itself has brought them forth.
Poland is a young state, which only recently was torn into three parts. Economically it still is so to this day. It suffered much in the time of war; the citizens are poor, earnings are small, possibilities limited. It is therefore understandable that the population is not able to bear the burden of too high a budget, and "leys tokef" [?] — if budgets of billions are fought through, and the government spends further hundreds of millions — outside the budget — can society then pass over this to the order of the day?
Likewise the consumer cannot look on indifferently as prices rise in every field, as in Poland, which always counted as a cheap country, things grow dearer with every day. Every reform, every achievement meant to make life better and finer, makes life dearer and harder. And this not only where private businessmen have the say, but also, and precisely, where the government decides. Should this not cause the ordinary citizen worry?!
The urban population is choking under the burden of taxes; there are no free funds in circulation; society's reserves are exhausted; there is nothing with which to do business. And what does the government do? Besides setting up budgets of billions, besides spending more than the budget permits, it lays out heavy hundreds of millions on investments, out of moneys which in fairness ought to have served to relieve the population of taxes and to ease the shortage of money.
The same with the state enterprises. The state's property is enormous: to the state belong the railways, whose value amounts to 4—5 billion. The state is the owner of 31 per cent of the forests, of coal mines and oil wells. And where are the revenues? How is the economy conducted there? Is the sum of 180 million zł. that they are to bring in next year (in fact the revenues decreased in the first 9 months of last year by 40 per cent) sufficient in comparison with their enormous value of billions?
And then — can the citizen look on calmly as the unjust and harmful tax system spreads with such tremendous speed? It, the government, brings in bills to ease the injustice of taxation, and when it comes to practice it does not know what to do with them? At one moment the government sits down with the representatives of the economic world and discusses all these questions with them seriously and with dignity, and at the next one sits down at the green table with other, political representatives and makes of the most vital questions of life a political Purim play.
No, the government must not reproach the citizen. It hurts him; that is why he cries out.
Mag. Sh. Bunin.
Jewish Life in Katowice

[Katowice — Zionists and communal life.] Session of the Zionist Local Committee.
The main purpose of the session was to elect a delegate to the political commission meeting at the Kraków Central Committee, which consists of 7 delegates from the largest West Galician and Silesian towns. The task of the Kraków commission is to decide the further political stance of West Galicia and Silesia on the "Koło" question [the Jewish parliamentary Club in the Sejm].
The discussion turned on whether the delegate should be given the possibility of acting according to his own views, or be given special directives.
Mr[?] Riger [Rieger] proposes Dr Tartan [?] as delegate, and also that he be given full freedom to act as he sees fit.
Because certain committee members know Dr Tartan as a "Grünbaum-eater" [a fierce opponent of Yitzhak Grünbaum], Comrade Weinberg moved an amendment to the above-mentioned proposal. The amendment is that Dr Tartan, as delegate, should submit to the political line of the Silesian Jewish masses.
Mr Weinberg's proposal was rejected, thanks to the Galician comrades, and Dr Tartan received full freedom.

A "Jewish Home" ("Yidishe Heym").
At last Katowice Jewry has risen to the level of other, larger Jewish communities and has rented premises for a "Jewish Home", where the whole of Jewish life will be concentrated. The premises are at Mielęckiego 8, and on 1 April they will be opened. For this purpose a "Golden Book" has been made for the donors. The book has been given to the artist Moshe Apelbaum to illuminate, and every donor will have an illuminated leaf with his name and the sum, artistically executed, which will remain as an everlasting historical record for those who began to conduct the new Jewish life in Katowice. The well-known philanthropist and communal worker Mr Alfred Miller [Müller], who is always the first when a Jewish cause is concerned, was the first here too, with his donation of 500 zł.

A lecture.
The well-known man of letters and dramatist Dr J. B. Cypor [Tsipor?] has been invited by the newly founded "Muze" ("Muse") to give a lecture. The subject is Peretz's "At Night in the Old Marketplace" ("Baynakht oyfn altn mark"). The lecture takes place at the "Merchants' Association" ("Soykhrim-Fareyn"), Jana 11, next Monday, the 11th inst., at 8 o'clock in the evening.

[The district — news from the localities.]
Czeladź.
Merchants and artisans go together to the city-council elections.
On Sunday the 24th of this month, city-council elections take place here. The Jewish voters, who already at the first [sic] elections were taught a lesson, not obtaining a single Jewish councilman, are now striving to strengthen the Jewish front in order to attain what the local Jews had in the first city councils.
Regrettably, Czeladź too is not short of "seat-grabbers" who push themselves forward by force, just so as to be elected; but the "seat-grabbers" have to this day achieved nothing, because the local Jewish voters know only this: that those who should be elected are the ones who have merits in communal work.
To this end a committee of small traders and artisans has been created, which is putting forward a united list headed by the councilman of many years, Mr. Rechnic.

This week a Christian landlord, with the aim of committing suicide, drank a small bottle of vinegar essence.
The reason for the suicide is that the landlord had a mind to evict a tenant, and the latter came out victorious in all the court instances and on top of that obtained a judgment that the landlord is obliged to pay the tenant 500 zł. court costs.

Strzemieszyce.
A woman — an accomplice of bandits.
In the night from Saturday to Sunday a woman knocked, at night, at the dwelling of the local rich peasant Kmiecik and begged that they take pity on her and let her stay the night.
The peasant took pity on the guest and let her into his dwelling to stay overnight.
When the woman came into the house, the Kmiecik family saw how the woman was packing up various bundles; this aroused suspicion in the family and they thought of reporting it to the police.
Suddenly the woman snatched a little whistle out of her pocket and began to whistle. At this signal 2 bandits with revolvers in their hands came into the dwelling.
A commotion arose among the M. [sic; should be K.] family, and at their cries of alarm the neighbours ran for the police, who came at once and arrested the assailants.

On Sunday a murder and suicide were carried out here at Jungster's brickyard.
The murderer was the 21-year-old Winter, who shot at his friend Szplak [?] with a revolver and mortally wounded him.
Winter, seeing his friend lying in a pool of blood, fired the remaining bullets into himself and fell dead on the spot.

The State of Affairs in the Jewish Kehillot

[Zagłębie — kehillot; opinion article.] (What responsibility do the parnasim [board members] of the Jewish kehillot in Zagłębie bear?)
The news items about the activity of the Jewish kehillot in Zagłębie are characteristic. Even when we merely read these items in the press, they are all characteristic — in their content, in the "activity", and in that modern conception [?] of theirs.
Not long ago we read an item here from which we learned that the president of the Będzin Jewish kehilla cannot get the parnasim to a session in order to consider the appeals of the payers of the "etat" [the community tax].
A second item we read in the last issue, where we learned that the parnasim in Sosnowiec cannot settle among themselves the division of the subsidies; and a third item we find in the same issue — that after a four-month interval the board of the Dąbrowa Jewish kehilla called a session, to which two parnasim consented to come.
If one reads these lines attentively, if one dwells on this "activity", one must come to the conclusion that in all the kehillot there reigns a terrible apathy and boundless indifference, reaching the point of a bizarre sickness. For how can one call it, for example, "activity" when a Będzin representative body wrongs a whole town of people, several hundred objections [reklamacje] pour in, and they do not find it necessary even to consider them? What sickly apathy must one possess to laugh at a whole town of people, by whom one was elected and to whom the voters gave so much trust? How low must one have fallen for all this no longer to interest anyone? What does it mean — one burdens a whole town of people with taxes and has not the courage to reduce them, nor even to say that it must remain as we made the assessment. We know — at the very least these representatives of ours ought to come and say: you have not been wronged, we know that you are able to pay the tax imposed, and that is the end of it. Had the people come and said one thing or the other, we would still understand it somehow; but when one says neither no nor yes, when one hides in a mouse-hole, there is simply nothing to understand; here one sees no activity and no will, no honesty and no diligence; here one sees absolutely nothing, and about nothing there is, self-evidently, nothing to say: "zero is no more than zero.
But one must not forget that money is at stake here, and the Jewish situation among us is not at all so splendid that one could say Jewish money is ownerless and one need not reckon with those from whom one wants to get the funds. However much our kehilla representatives may laugh at this taxed "etat" public, however little the whole matter may interest them, they must nevertheless remember that one may not in such a way make light of Jewish money, especially such as comes from the broad masses of the people, from one who still toils hard and bitterly before he sees the grosz before his eyes. Willing or not, one must at least reckon with groszy so hard-earned.
In no better state is the Sosnowiec Jewish kehilla. Now they are haggling over the subsidies, each wanting more, and it reaches the point that: if that faction gets 2 thousand zł., then 4 thousand zł. is due to me; and if I have 4 thousand zł., then my opponent deserves twice as much again, because he argues that he is not the sort one can brush off with a puff as though it were nothing at all; he is certain that he must be and will be reckoned with — if not, he is capable of tripping one up at every step, and then go call him "knak-nisl" [idiom: and try doing something about it]. When everything is ownerless, it goes without saying: if you will not give way to me, I will not let you through.
That, roughly, is what the system of subsidising this or that institution, this or that society looks like. One does not subsidise because the institution deserves such or such a subsidy; rather one reckons with who is demanding the subsidy and how far one must reckon with the consequences he will draw from it. The giving of subsidies has taken on the character of handing out the Sabbath fruit, where everyone strives to get a nicer portion... and the end of this handing out of Sabbath fruit is that the budget grows into a gigantic one, and the assessment, of course, must be a large one.
The question arises whether it pays, whether for the sake of the subsidies one needs to make such large budgets, especially when one must bear in mind that the greater part of the subsidies are not paid out and the institutions get nothing from them.
It is another matter — possibly, were it not for the subsidies, one could not make a budget at all, for if each did not have to guard and defend his own little shop, they would not come together at all and the budget could not be drawn up. That is indeed a plausible argument; and if it is so, it is the best proof — for as long as they are busy voting the budget they still just barely assemble, but once they have carried it through they no longer touch the door-handles of the kehilla office.
All the same, one might well reflect more seriously on the matter; the kehilla representatives might well dwell on the serious question and consider it from all sides, so that such chaos should not reign, especially where the taking of money is concerned. Let money not be taken from the population merely because one knows one has the power to do so. As it is, so little is accomplished with the money that it does not pay to burden a town so heavily.
If one saw the fruits of our kehillot we would say that it is worth the cost so long as something is created; unfortunately, however, one can already now say with a clear conscience that nothing at all is being accomplished for the good of the population. So what are the big budgets for, what is the great burden and hullabaloo for? All in order to maintain the religious functionaries? Upon my word, it is not worth taking up so much time and effort over that. To maintain the religious functionaries and look after the cemetery it is surely enough that things be run as they were run years ago — without hullabaloo, without uproar and without quarrels; for in any case nothing more is done than putting the budget together, and afterwards one no longer sees any parnasim by the light of day.
And therefore let one remember just one thing: it is not for disputes and politicking that we need the Jewish kehillot, and Jewish money must not be ownerless there.
R. Let.
