A Winter March

[Poem — satire; the frost and the coal shortage.] By Graf Kali ["Count Kali" — a pen name].

Cold! Cold! Cold! Cold!
The frost scalds and roars and cracks,
the sky looks down, desolate and grey,
and there is no coal,
and the stove, unheated,
stands there quite cross and irritated...

And the little wife — she screams
without a stop, the whole time:
Cold! Cold! Cold! Cold!
The children are freezing, poor things — help!
Why are you silent? Murderer, quick,
bring coal, and whole shoes...

But I am deeply tormented:
where, brother, does one get money?
For since long ago now
there has long been none at my place —
there is some at Eshingon's [?]...

Cold! Cold! Cold! Cold!
Don't cry, wifey, just wait a little:
the "Dobroczynność" [the charity society] does give out coal, after all,
one only has to wait a couple of weeks,
have patience for three months,
until the month of May comes...
Our Panorama

[Feuilleton — humorous weekly review; Sławków, Myszków, Sosnowiec.] By Ben Amotz.

(A topsy-turvy world. — "Culture and spring" in Sławków. — A discussion about revolution. — A revolution in Myszków. — The gabbai dynasty fallen. — "Koniec świata" [the end of the world]. — The threefold cord.)

That it is — as they say — a topsy-turvy world goes without saying, when such wonders happen. In Poland "Siberian" frosts reign, reaching as far as 33 degrees, and in France there are — according to the newspaper reports — 6 degrees of warmth.

And why should we even wonder whether the reports are true? Let Sławków be the proof! It can only be that in Sławków warmth reigns: the sky is clear as in spring, the birds creep out of their winter nests, perch on the trees covered with green and sing spring songs...

Such a "poetic mood" took hold of me on reading "the little picture" that an esteemed reader from Sławków sent us, "that we should publish it, for God's sake, so that the world may become acquainted with the culture of the Sławków girls"...

We fulfil his request in full; we do not even change his "poetic style", but give the "creation" according to the original...

The poet has the floor:

"In Sławków's main market square, through one small lane, leads the way to the cultural institutions, which for a good while now, night after night, by a small kerosene lamp, by which the shadows of the surrounding wall-pictures give a true character of the futurist art of painting, members of both sexes come together in order to debate the arranging of a 'box evening' [question-box evening] for the institution".

Here the Sławków "poet" makes a little pause. He combs his hair, and when the bright moon creeps out from the clouds, he continues his "descriptions".

"There sat 5 girls: one on the table, the second leaning (don't be alarmed.) on the third and...

That is what a Sławków "poet" can do. And at the "most thrilling, interesting" moments he cuts off his "descriptions"; but after a short break the "muse" flares up in him again and...

On a certain evening members of both sexes were sitting in the institution and discussing the revolution in the year 1917. A girl begins in such strange language: does anybody know what a revolution actually is?

— Revolution means

The same thing yet again: with bated breath I was already expecting to learn "what revolution means?" — and the "poet" breaks off his "poetic fantasy" and tells no more than that the boys turned red with shame and left the institution in haste.

— Esteemed readers, gentlemen and ladies! Perhaps you can guess what notions the Sławków girls have in matters of revolution?

* * *

The Sławków youth discuss "what actually is a revolution?", while in Myszków the "revolution" has spread itself out lengthwise and breadthwise, branched out through the whole shtetl and also entered the beit midrash, where she, the wicked revolution, cooked up a fine mess over an aliyah [a call-up to the Torah]; and if we are to believe what the Myszków correspondent informs us — it is Egyptian darkness there. First of all the "revolution" caused an upheaval in the dentists' trade: half the Jews of Myszków had their teeth "fall out" through... butchers' hands; but the worst of it is that together with the teeth "fell" the 20-year rule of the Myszków gabbai.

Wilhelm's comrade turned to Żarki for help, only because of the great snows and frosts Żarki is not in a position to send "help"; air communication too has been suspended...

* * *

The "threefold cord" of the places enumerated is — Sosnowiec. While the Sławków girls were "fantasizing" about revolution, and the Jews of Myszków were knocking out — teeth, the Sosnowiec communal activists remembered that it is already "koniec świata" [the end of the world], and having yawned several times one communal activist said:

— "Upon my life, it really is good and cold; poor people must surely be freezing; so it really would be only right that we get together a few korzec [a measure] of coal for the poor. Eh, it is already the end of Shevat? So what of it? We are after all no worse than the newspaper 'Di Naye Nakht' [?], which brings 'special' reports that King Amanullah has already bought himself new summer gloves"...

— Really only right — said a second "communal activist" — one ought to collect a couple of korzec of coal. True, we are late; Będzin distributed 20 wagons of coal right at the start of winter, but as the saying goes: "better late than never".

— Sławków culture, Myszków "revolution" and the Sosnowiec coal campaign — a threefold cord.

Ben Amotz.
Where Is the Jewish Woman?

(The trade in "living merchandise" is progressing; a women's protection society should be created.)

In all times and in every period history has tales to tell of various swindles and schemes and deceit. There has always existed an underworld, where there was a separate life, peculiar customs, an original language, so that a person who was not at home in that sphere could have no conception of any of it; and when people once spoke of that "separate world", when they began to tell episodes and stories about these "heroes", it sounded like "tales from the Thousand and One Nights".

Just as every town has always had its own fool, so it also had its underworld, which lived apart on its own "spot"; and if one wanted to get acquainted with that "little world", if one wanted to "study" the "artists", one had to take the trouble of going to them, and one was "enriched" with a piece of singularity that was written down for eternal memory.

But other times have come; we have entered a new era. People have become refined, ennobled, European, so that the underworld has almost vanished before our eyes, or it has grown pale and one does not notice it in the wide, great world, which has been so enriched with all manner of colours and hues that shout and wink and draw attention to themselves.

Today everything has become mixed together; today there is no separate ghetto for the modernized underworld, which consists of all sorts of contrivances and all kinds of schemes.

Once, after all, one recognized these people of the underworld by their clothes, by their gait and their look; but today, when we have Europeanized ourselves so, and since no machine for looking into another person's heart has yet been invented, one cannot distinguish between good and evil, and therefore it is indeed no wonder that we so very often hear of so many disappointments and abuses.

A reflection of all this we can witness in the courts, the merchants' institutions [?] and the rabbinates. Often one is struck dumb with amazement when one watches in what manner people try to catch one another in the trap.

In the rabbinical-court rooms we see, more than once, young men brought in who have several wives apiece, and not a few times we read in the newspapers stories of how a young man arrived with signet rings on his fingers, who presented himself as an American, and at once half a town of people began to dance before him as before an idol; everyone wanted to make him happy, but as soon as he had taken the money he was not seen again. And more than once these simpletons even forgo the money — only let him give them the "principal" [?]; and in that case the girl's parents are overjoyed: let him take the daughter and go in good health.

Not a few such girls have already been made unfortunate at the hands of all kinds of scoundrels. The trade in living merchandise has begun to revive; agents have been sent out across the Jewish towns and townlets who know their craft very well and recruit for themselves, as wives, the prettiest girls of the town, who are afterwards dispatched wherever they are needed.

Once such a "bird" was quickly recognized and people kept away from him; today, however, one does not recognize such a person at all, and one does not know how to guard oneself [?] against him. Moreover, parents were once cautious and allowed a strange young man near their daughter only when they knew who and what the young man was. Now no one inquires and investigates; the parents thank God that the Master of the Universe has sent them a piece of "luck", and the girl, for her part, is after all a girl of today's world, knows that she will not be lost, and besides she seeks to strike up a friendship with every young man who merely wants to look at her.

The Częstochowa and Zagłębie districts have turned out to be very good places for recruiting living merchandise, so that agents have set to work, and in Katowice, people say, the trade is carried on in a very skilled and intensive manner, and signs of the activity are already noticeable; greetings can already be heard from time to time...

It would be only right to give some thought to the matter; surely one must not allow the "trade" to develop like this without any hindrance on the part of the population and the authorities.

We believe that Katowice must be a central point for the gang of traffickers. Therefore Jewish Zagłębie must not stand at a distance and look on indifferently at the dangerous trade.

In the larger centres of the Polish cities there exist women's protection societies, whose tasks are to protect helpless and inexperienced women so that they are not drawn into a net.

It would therefore be very necessary to found among us a branch of such a women's protection society.

Our women have lately begun to understand better the obligation of communal activity; therefore they should not remain indifferent to their sisters' [troubles?]. Men too are needed here, for it is precisely they who have an important mission to carry out here; but let the woman be the vanguard here, and the man will afterwards come to help and carry on the necessary work.

Let the matter not remain stuck at dead centre; let it not merely be used as a topic for this article; let the question be considered with full seriousness by the women of Zagłębie, who understand the duty of communal work; let them rouse all strata of the population and not allow the trade in living merchandise to be conducted openly and freely, as though we were living in the Middle Ages.

Jewish Zagłębie must see to it that a branch of the "Women's Protection" is opened among us, which shall spread its wings over the heads of the Jewish daughters of Zagłębie and Upper Silesia.

Dr. Popuri.
“Bublichki” (A Russian Incarnation of a Jewish Melody)

[Culture — the wanderings of a melody.] The sensation of the day in Poland, and in Zagłębie as well, is now the brand-new foxtrot “Bublichki”, arranged after a Soviet-Russian street song of the same name.
The dance, which has literally captivated every heart and which has no equal, nor ever had one, in modern eccentric dance music, has in fact, as is known, a different past behind it, and that interesting short history we shall tell here.
In the Mogilev [Mohylew] region two Jewish wedding artists of the old cut were renowned in their day: Elye the badkhn [wedding jester] and Mordkhe the fiddler. The first was a tall, lean Jew, without a beard and without a moustache, with a face that gave the gang of jokers the opportunity to make up about him that he was nothing less than a tumtum or an androgyne — notwithstanding that God had blessed him with a fine only son.
The second, by contrast, was a short, broad-boned Jew with a handsome little beard and a pair of small, slightly curled sidelocks that could barely be seen from under his cap. Elye was a bit of a rascal, and Mordkhe was very pious — so much so that during the girls' dances he always stood in the same pose as a cantor toward the worshippers, so as not to look much at the women.
Not a single rich man's wedding or just any wedding, not a single celebration at the homes of rabbis and rebbes could take place without Elye Kritshever [of Krichev] and Mordkhe Tshetshersker [of Chechersk] (a small town in the Mogilev region) with their band.
Twice a year new words with a new melody for the mitzvah dance were created by them, and in the course of the whole period they used it at all the weddings.
An entirely new repertoire, however, they had to prepare specially for the wedding of the Loyev rebbe's 16-year-old youngest son. It was, after all, no small matter — such rich in-laws, with the well-known timber merchant and philanthropist Reb Abba Poyzner at their head, where one would surely grab “the right mortgage” [i.e. a proper haul].
But what succeeded for them more than anything was the little mitzvah dance.
To the accompaniment of all the klezmorim the badkhn begins his grand preamble in rhymes.. in honour of the rich man, the outstanding Hasid, the wonderful notable Mr. — (reckoning up his pedigree as far back as our father Abraham), who is going to dance with the bride; Mordkhe meanwhile plays on his little fiddle a heartfelt piece that brings one literally to the expiry of the soul. The father of the bride takes, with great preparations, the silk kerchief; one edge is taken by the bashful bride, whose face is covered by the veil to above the eyes, and the other — by the one called up to the dance; and while they dance the crowd, standing in a circle, claps its hands, and the badkhn sings the refrain of the text, which the whole crowd then takes up after him:
So take then, little Jews,
all the little fiddles,
and singing little songs
we shall go:
to the little mitzvah dance,
all in a little ring!
Only be a little mensch:
go and dance a little dance!
The typically Jewish melody was so beloved and so taken to heart among the Jews of the whole region that for years it remained almost like a tradition at all the weddings, and it vanished only when the custom of the mitzvah dance ceased to exist.
Thanks to the liberation of the Jews from the Russian Pale of Settlement, our brethren the Children of Israel (?) evidently dragged it off to today's Jewish Moscow, where it was reincarnated for the first time in the above-mentioned Russian street song. But how the Soviet ditty then came to hostile London and was reincarnated in the famous European foxtrot — that one cannot understand by any means..
From London “Bublichki” migrated to Poland and to Zagłębie too. Ballet dancers dance “Bublichki” and sing the words of the Russian ditty, which are as banal as those of any street song.
Soon the street caught up “Bublichki”, and wherever one stands or goes it is all “Bublichki”.
In the coffee-house “Bublichki” is one of the most important items on the programme. At home, by the stove, the cook sings “Bublichki”; the lady — in the drawing-room; the artisan — at his workbench; the worker — at his work; the merchant — in his shop; the office girl — at the typewriter.
Only recently a Hasidic melody, “Der rebe geyt” [“The Rebbe Goes”], was reincarnated in a street song; today the same transmigration is being undergone by “Bublichki”, which has become the most popular melody in Europe.
Lately a whole series of Jewish parodies of “Bublichki” has also arisen.
People Who Give and People Who Must Give

[Będzin — article: the "Yavne" school and the Keren Hayesod donors.]
The Persian poet and philosopher Omar Khayyam sings: "Fill the cup that rinses away the regret of yesterday and the fear of tomorrow — tomorrow? Tomorrow I may already be with yesterday's seven thousand years."
Only a person who is driven by his inner creative spirit can sing like that; only such a person can have the strength to rinse away the regret of yesterday and the fear of tomorrow, and to create today.
Not so the people who are driven to their creating by the outward conventions of life. Their expansive energy, their impulse, their inner spirit forces them; they create and they build not only because they want to, but also because they must. These are the higher types of human being, who must live themselves out not only for themselves, like the people who live with regrets for yesterday or with fears of tomorrow; they also live impulsively for the society to which they feel a closeness. These are no egoistic honour-seekers; these are the altruistic creators, higher human geniuses, who must live themselves out with a broad gesture in the surroundings about them.
These are the people of fine feeling, who sense the pressing needs of their society, and they serve it with the whole breadth of their souls.
Where the poet sings with poems — they sing with deeds.
The builder of the "Yavne" school in Będzin belongs, in my opinion, to those who sing with deeds, and the splendid building is the expression of a man who must build and must create.
I shall take the liberty of comparing the so-called benefactors of a different cut with the cut of Mr. Fürstenberg.
The former are able to contribute to society only when they are driven by their conventions, as for example in the last "Keren Hayesod" campaign in Zagłębie. It is true that in that campaign they distinguished themselves very handsomely, and perhaps they deserve the due "yasher koach"; but why was it necessary first to send judges and doctors from warm Eretz Israel to be "frozen" in Zagłębie?
Had they, the donors themselves, been driven by their feeling for the Jewish upbuilding in Eretz Israel, as the builder of the Yavne school felt it in Będzin, there would have been no need at all for all the conventional forms in which the emissaries from Eretz Israel wrapped them in order to get the sums given out of them. Did the donors not know, then, where the head office of Keren Hayesod is located? What need of a poet, a doctor and an English consul?
Mr. Fürstenberg built the "Yavne" school without the enthusiasm of poets and consulates, without conventions. Even without the assistance of any communal institution whatsoever — only by his own strength, inspired by the Jewish need, by his own surroundings.
And for that he truly deserves great honour, and he ought to be immortalised for his deed, because he has the spiritual strength to raise himself by his deeds to the immortality of a man who lives himself out without the regret of yesterday and the fear of tomorrow.
Let us imagine: if Zionism did not bear its present political character, and there were no need to force its work of upbuilding at such a rapid tempo as is now necessary — would Jewish life not need such material help in order to sustain the Jewish national "I", which rests on Jewish cultural work, such as schools and so on? And who would have built the schools? Not the Keren Hayesod givers? Then why have they in fact, up to now, not built a single Jewish school in Będzin or in Sosnowiec? Why do they in fact let their children go to non-Jewish schools, without even having the courage to protest against lessons on the Sabbath? Why do they not want to see how their daughters are led on an outing with a young priest at their head?
It would do no harm if many of the "Keren Hayesod" givers were to take a lesson from Mr. Fürstenberg and see the necessity of creating more Jewish schools, above all in Będzin. Above all this should be done by those who are truly interested in our national existence — and so that their children should not receive their preparation in the Polish national school, and the priest should [not] take them on outings...
Moshe Apelboim.
The Rabbi's Son — a Jewish historical novel by Yaakov Zimmerman (instalment 20)

Shimon felt somewhat comforted, and as a sign of gratitude and devotion he took the Prince's hand and kissed it.
Esther and Blumele, Sarah and her mother, now became very happy when they recalled for what purpose the Prince had come here, and that he had brought letters for them from Ayzik and from Chaim, and that both of them were, thank God, in good health, and that soon after the holiday they would come back home in peace.
As though the hubbub, the commotion and the confusion in Chaim's little house had not yet been great enough, the door was now flung open again with force, and several men carried in, in their arms, a young man who had fainted.
After them there appeared on the threshold the tall and dignified figure of the Rabbi of Kraków, Rabbi Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller, the famous author of the "Tosafot Yom-Tov". In a somewhat agitated voice he related that, as he was walking with his son to the synagogue to pray, he had seen in the street a large gathering of people who had assembled here around the carriage and the horses. As the two of them were passing by, the horses suddenly turned wild and began to rear up on their hind legs, and he, the Rabbi, was very nearly injured by them; but his young son still had time and courage enough to push his father aside and to save him. He himself, however, caught a blow in the side from a horse's hoof, so hard that he at once fell down in a faint...
The unconscious young man was at once laid on a bed, and they began to revive him with cold water and with cloths dipped in vinegar.
Blumele — although her knees were trembling with great fright and she herself was not far from fainting — nevertheless took heart and handed over everything that was needed. Her joy, however, was all the greater for it when she saw that the handsome young man, whom she had loved so in secret, soon came to himself again and opened his eyes once more...
— It is nothing! — the young man began to speak, and as he did so he held out his hand to his father. — Forgive me, dear father, for having frightened you so for nothing. But where am I now?
But when he saw the beautiful Blumele standing close to his bed, he fell silent. His pale cheeks were suddenly suffused with a flush...
— Even the horses of Prince Wiśniowiecki know that one must do a Jew no harm, and therefore I hope, my young lad, that nothing has happened to you — the Prince spoke up with a smile. — With all my powers I shall see to it that the Jews may be able to live in peace in Poland.
The Rabbi of Kraków, Reb Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller, now found an opportunity to introduce himself to the Prince and to thank him for the many kindnesses he had so far done to the Polish Jews in protecting their lives, their goods and chattels.
The Prince asked him that he, the Rabbi, permit him to pay him a visit that very evening, together with his son.
Since it was already rather late and the Rabbi knew that they were waiting for him in the synagogue with the prayers, he quickly took leave of everyone and went off. His son he left lying on the bed for the time being, until he should come to himself completely; and when he came back from the synagogue he would stop in here and take him along home.
The noblemen, too, now left.
The old Prince did not forget to hand over to the wife of Chaim the wagoner a little packet of silver thalers which Chaim was supposed to have sent her.
Shimon went off together with the Prince, in order afterwards to conduct him on the visit to the Rabbi.
Chaim's wife and the girl also left. It was already late, and she hurried home to light the candles.
Esther now did the same and lit the holiday candles.
The Rabbi's son raised himself a little and sat up on the bed. He asked that he be handed a glass of water. Blumele went quickly into the kitchen to fulfil his wish. Her hand trembled a good deal as she handed him the water, and it went no better with him when his fingers touched hers. The faces of both were as if flooded with redness, and both, abashed, lowered their eyes to the ground.
— What is your name? — the young man asked in a quiet voice.
— My name is Blumele — was the still quieter and bashful answer.
— And my name is David; I thank you, Blumele, for your trouble here on my account.
Blumele was a great lover of flowers. In her home, on the windows and wherever there was but a bit of suitable space, flower-pots had been set out. Above all she loved roses, and when they were in full growth one could seldom see the girl without a little rose on her head, among her hair, or sometimes on her breast.
Now too Blumele had this gift of nature on her; but when she handed the young man the glass of water, the little flower fell off and remained lying in his lap.
David noticed the flower, took it in his hand and asked in a moved voice:
— Will you allow me, Blumele, to take the little flower along with me?
Blumele did not answer; she simply could not answer; she only gave a nod of her head.
But now she had to go into the kitchen, for she heard the voice of her mother, who asked her about the letter from her father, which the nobleman had brought and which, because of the great confusion that had arisen here in the house, had not yet been read.
She now handed the letter over to her mother, and both sat down to read.
The letter was a long one. Ayzik had described at length everything, how he had fared in Warsaw. He also related everything about Reb Eliyahu and Prince Wiśniowiecki. The letter ended with the following words:
— As always, so now too, you are right, my faithful and beloved wife, Esther; you are a clever woman, and it is indeed true that our treasure lies in our own oven. This I have found out here. It is not on the Vistula bridge in Warsaw that it is to be found, but right in our own oven...
Who could now compare herself, in happiness, with Esther? Her heart danced within her for joy when she read the last few lines. She was very pleased that her husband had already sobered up from his dream-drunkenness, and that he would soon come home and take up his work again, which gave them, thank God, an honourable livelihood...
In her heart she was very grateful to her uncle Reb Eliyahu, who had been here only a few weeks before, and before whom she had then poured out her bitter heart and told of her husband's dream-madness. Reb Eliyahu had told her then that he himself now also had to travel to Warsaw, and because Ayzik did not know him personally — he had never seen him — it would therefore be possible for him, Reb Eliyahu, to conduct the whole matter in such a way that Ayzik would be led back onto the right road and give up his foolish dreams.
And as she now saw, the clever uncle had kept his word, and her Ayzik was already back on the right path; and for that she was grateful to him, and in her heart she thanked God that everything had turned out for the good...
Nevertheless, Esther was not entirely at ease. She was quite a clever Jewish woman and understood how things stood... When she read her husband's letter with great attention, she was able, with her fine instinct, to read between the lines that Ayzik was still going about with the sweetest dreams — hopes, concerning the match between her girl and the Rabbi's son...
(To be continued).
Yente-Matl Goes to the Masked Ball. (A Humoresque)

[Fiction — a humoresque.] By Sara Dobrzyńska.
The first snow had barely shown itself when Yente-Matl already began thinking about a masked ball.
Her father, the silent one[?], had brought her from the village and hired her out to Madame Gold. Here, in the rich household, she heard plenty about all sorts of theatres, balls, concerts. But it was with the greatest curiosity that she would listen in on the talk about masked balls. Such a curious thing [“tshekave”, from Polish ciekawe]: rich ladies can go and dress up as chimney-sweeps, men in women's clothes, like lunatics, everything exactly upside down — and she resolved that, come what may, she must go to a masked ball.
One thing she knew: the moment Madame Gold, with that pursed little mouth of hers, got wind of it — goodbye to the job...
An excuse for where she was going for a whole night she had already thought up: to a wedding, at a girlfriend's of hers...
But what does one do about the outfit? So she borrowed the Sunday finery from Maryszka, the janitor's daughter, and a pair of yellow shoes with high bootlegs she borrowed from another girlfriend of hers. And so off went Yente-Matl to the masquerade...
In the big bright hall, flooded with electric light, orchestras are playing; couples in all sorts of masks, in trouser-costumes, dance hurriedly[?], just as if they were being carried along by the music.
Silk and velvet shimmer before the eyes, winding and winding; together with the delicate rustle of silk, ringing peals of laughter go rolling. Around the sides of the hall couples stroll again; men in black tailcoats with white waistcoats let themselves be teased and “intrigued”...
Here one of them throws bonbons, raps on a bottle of champagne and winks at a blonde little woman who was wrapped in somebody's arms.
She inclines her head and winks back. She'll be right over.
So Yente-Matl stands off to one side, decked out “po krakowsku” [Cracow-style], with the coloured ribbons, with the glittering spangles which, on account of the electric light, look like hens' eyes... She stands there all a-tremble, afraid to make a move. And looks at everything in such amazement.
— Eh? What is this? What's the celebration? People actually go about in trousers, as if into the bathhouse?
It buzzes a bit all around here, like in a beehive. But little by little Yente-Matl grows bolder and ventures into the middle of the hall; since dozens of couples are strolling round and round, she too turns round along with them, thinking as she does: presumably there's a custom here of circling about, just like a bride at the badekns [the veiling ceremony]...
In all that tangle she sees a tall figure with a checked “litsepet”[?] [apparently a peaked cap] pulled down over the eyes, under the neck a white scarf with a very thick knot reaching right up to the chin; he keeps his hands in his trouser pockets and slinks along with his whole body, just like a cat.
Yente-Matl takes fright.
— A thief... she thinks to herself, and feels at her bosom to check whether he hasn't by any chance already pulled out her couple of zlotys...
And now she sees how a lady sidles up to that very same character; she wants to put her arms round him, and he still puts on airs, won't have it at all — Yente-Matl lays her hands on her heart and marvels even more:
— Master of the Universe! she thinks — the ones girls get the hots for...
But she hardly has time to look around properly when up to her sidles a young man with a little black trimmed moustache, and pesters her; like a blot[?] he sticks to her:
— My little mask [“masetshke”, Polish maseczko], let me enjoy your nearness[?].. Ah, how lovely you are in that village costume...
Yente-Matl takes a good look and recognises him! It's Staszekl Fridman, Madame's brother.
She turns red and dead-pale and her skin trembles on her — may he not recognise her, that's all she'd need.
But he, the “gentleman” with the trimmed little moustache, won't let her be, blocks her way and wants to give her a kiss... Eh! Anything you like, only that — a good cholera! She gives a swipe with her hands and runs off as if from a fire! Already standing on the stairs, she cools herself down with wild curses:
— May a fire seek them out, the gentry!... How there's just no getting rid of them.. If you're in the kitchen — they crawl into the kitchen... If you're at the masked ball, they find their way here too... How there's just no getting rid of them!... May a fire seek them out!...
Walking home from the masked ball Yente-Matl was all in a dither; she ran through the streets as if through a blaze.
Off the pavement down onto the roadway, from the slippery roadway back onto the pavement. Here again she was afraid of the masked passers-by, making their way home sleepy and tired, some of them swaying drunk.
So Yente-Matl took to running in one breath, and all the while it seems to her that someone is running after her and blocking her way...
With a pounding heart she stops at the gate, looks round the street and marvels still more.
And maybe today is Purim? The way the dressed-up ones are running about the street like mad — maybe people really have lost count of the calendar?..
Now Yente-Matl sees that same character with the checked “litsepet” approaching. At this she starts trembling like a fish: — Who knows whether the thief doesn't really mean to sneak in here along with me to my rich master, break open his cash-box and slaughter me like a heifer, strictly kosher...
Yente-Matl sets to pounding on the gate with all her might. She barely makes it upstairs alive. In despair she stops again behind the door, thinking what sort of excuse to give Madame.
— And maybe she isn't back from the masked ball yet — oh, that would be a blessing — when she comes home she'll find me asleep, as if nothing had ever happened...
Yente-Matl calms down a little and starts ringing the bell. Soon Herr Gold opens up for her, walking about wrapped in his heavy pyjamas, slipped down on one side, and sleepy, barely able to tear his eyes open.
— A — Anuszka!.. So you did remember to come home from the masked ball? — he asks tenderly, putting his arms round Yente-Matl, and leads her straight into the bedroom.
A kind of shiver runs through Yente-Matl's body as she feels her master's warm arms on her... Now she wants to start screaming and tear herself away from him. — Against her will she stays quiet, as if paralysed...
— Why aren't you telling me anything, Anuszka, how many little bonbonnières did you wheedle out? And whom else did you make a fool of?... Why do you intrigue me so much? Why have you lost your tongue? You intrigue me on all fronts, Anuszka — you told me you'd be in a domino, dressed with a black “kaske”[?], and meanwhile you've got yourself up as a Krakowianka with a red mask[?] and so many glass beads with so many ribbons.. There, Anuszka, there, come, I'll help you undress. First pull off the bows[?]. The beads with the ribbons — Herr Gold advises — and tries to unknot the tangled ribbon — at which Yente-Matl grabs him by the hand and tries to wrench herself free by force.
Someone slowly unlocks the door; in comes Madame Gold, in a very tired[?] state; she walks with slow steps through the rooms, afraid of waking her husband. Soon she slowly opens the bedroom door.
Herr Gold takes fright at seeing yet another mask, in a black domino:
— Who's there? — he cries out, leaping away from Yente-Matl.
— So, so... my husband! Not for nothing were you such a sweet little dear, telling me to go to the masquerade on my own! — says Frau Gold, shaking her head — so that you could go to the other masquerade, so as to be able to bring a mask home for yourself?
— What did you think, that your little wife would only come home in the morning and it would all pass off so smoothly for you.,. Don't imagine I'll keep quiet about this, Moritzl!... — Madame Gold is already flying into a rage, wagging her finger right in her husband's face.
Like a plaster figure Gold stands there with his mouth open and doesn't know what to think.
— Oy vey iz mir, Madame dear! Don't be so angry — pleads Yente-Matl, taking off the mask. — Why, it's me...—
— Me, Yente-Matl!
But Madame Gold could not forgive having found Yente-Matl in the bedroom in her husband's arms. The very next morning she “sent her packing” [“otpravet”, from Polish odprawiła — dismissed her]!!!
An Open Letter to the Kehilla Board in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — kehilla and the Jewish hospital; open letter.] Most esteemed Mr. Editor!
We earnestly ask you to grant space in your esteemed newspaper to the following open letter to the Jewish kehilla in Sosnowiec, for which we thank you in advance.
For some time now the Jewish public has been alarmed by various articles and notices in the press about the catastrophic situation of the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec.
We must admit that, financially, our hospital has been no exception among all Jewish institutions; yet we never raised an outcry, but quietly — even drawing on the personal credit of the members of the hospital committee — did everything to do justice to our difficult task and to keep the hospital's management at the proper level, as far as possible without a deficit. So as not to be unjust, we must stress that for the easing of our efforts we owe much to the fact that the Jewish kehilla, in the persons of Dr. Perlman, may he rest in peace, and Messrs. Lajbisz Zendel and Secretary Lewenhof (long may they live), always took a loyal attitude toward our needs and aspirations.
It is therefore a riddle to us why, and from where, the authors of the articles and notices received precisely now the inspiration to disquiet the public with the hospital's situation, which, as said, is now neither worse nor better than before.
To us the answer is clear. But we wish to keep silent about it, for silence is sometimes better than speech, and we do not consider ourselves called upon to feed the public with sensations. It is striking, however, that the articles, notices and real or supposed interviews are so constructed that among the outside public, which is not closely acquainted with how the hospital is run, they can awaken the impression that the hospital is in a state of dissolution, and that this state is — we do not wish to analyse it precisely — a consequence, or indeed the cause, of the change that has recently taken place in the composition of the hospital's medical staff. We do, however, state that the material and moral damage at which all these pronouncements were aimed, they have indeed caused — not to mention the moral depression suffered by the hospital committee, in whose path, because of personal ambitions, stones were laid on the way to carrying out its programme for putting the hospital on a sound footing, for the hospital's benefit.
Never mind: the barbs and pinpricks which in essence struck the hospital itself, but were directed against the persons of the hospital committee because they could not, without violating their conscience, satisfy the ambitions mentioned — all this we shall bear.
But we must raise our voice against a wrong that is aimed at the hospital directly, and especially because the wrong is to be committed by the entire Jewish community through its representative body, the board of the Jewish kehilla. And let the community decide whether this accords with its will, with its public conscience!
Some time ago, guided by the idea that the hospital's accounts might be closed without a deficit, we turned to the kehilla board with the request to raise the subsidy for the hospital. We must explain here that in return for the kehilla's subsidies the hospital committee undertook to admit for treatment free of charge all patients recommended by the kehilla — which makes no bad bargain at all by this, since that category of patients swallows almost 50 percent of the hospital budget. To this request we received no direct answer; the answer was given to us, however, by the street, from which we learned that not only was the subsidy not raised, it was struck out altogether. That is to say, something was indeed raised — only not the subsidy for the hospital, but an item for treating poor patients in general. In our loyalty we again turned in writing to the kehilla board, pointing to the rumours that had reached us, and asked that it either enter a subsidy or conclude an agreement with us on what basis poor patients would be sent to the hospital at the kehilla's expense.
But the hospital has evidently ceased to exist for the kehilla, or perhaps it has even lost its address, for we received the answer indirectly, through the press... And indeed by that same route we wish to come into contact — not with the kehilla on Czysta Street, but with the real Jewish community, with all Jews in general — and to ask aloud:
1) Whom does it concern on whose initiative the subsidy for the hospital was struck out? Is it any easier for the hospital that the initiative came not from Dr. Melodysta, but from members of the kehilla board?
2) How does it come about that, even before the budget was considered, an attempt was made to frighten off a well-known doctor and communal worker, to whom we had made the proposal to take on the post of attending physician (ordynatura) in the hospital, by telling him that the hospital is not viable because it will receive no subsidy from the kehilla?
3) Why did the kehilla board hasten to issue a public statement whose purpose is to rehabilitate Dr. Melodysta, and yet did not find it necessary to perform a simple act of courtesy and reply to our letters?
4) And if the kehilla wishes to create a fund for itself so as to be able to send patients to hospitals out of town, is it entitled to ignore the local hospital and strike out its subsidy?
5) And if, again, the thing was done with a certain tendency, we ask: should the kehilla be an instrument in the fight against the hospital?
With this we exhaust our questions for the time being; but in order to establish that all this is being done to make the hospital non-viable, we ask the last question:
Where is public opinion, and does it intend to keep silent about this?
The Committee of the Jewish Hospital in Sosnowiec.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Session of the Kehilla Board

Friday, 29 [recte 28] Shevat 5689 — Piątek 8 lutego 1929 [Friday, 8 February 1929].

Będzin

Session of the kehilla board.

On Sunday, under the chairmanship of Mr. Prawer, a session of the kehilla board took place.
On the agenda a series of letters was dealt with, among which there were: 1) from the reception committee in honour of the Piotrków rabbi, Rabbi Shapira [R. Meir Shapiro], which asks that the guest be received at the kehilla [“gmina”]; and 2) from the “Yeshiva Chachmei Lublin”, that the kehilla should allot a subsidy for the yeshiva.
On the first letter Mr. J. Najmark took the floor; he is against the board's honouring the rabbi with such an honour: since — says Mr. N. — the board did not accord that honour to the poet Leib Jaffe, it need not take place now either; altogether the rabbi has not deserved that the Będzin kehilla should honour him, because at the time of the famous rabbinical elections the rabbi was among those who, in the synagogue, poured curses upon the local Jews.
Mr. Wygodzki also comes out against the proposal, and by a majority of votes the proposal of the reception committee is rejected.
The same fate also befell the second proposal, concerning subsidising the “Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin”. The motive — in the present budget no fresh subsidies can be entered.
On the other hand Mr. A. Liwer is delegated to welcome the Piotrków rabbi in the name of the kehilla.
Strict Measures in Collecting Fines from Citizens

A few weeks ago a policeman drew up a report against Mr. Jakub Montag, because he had smoked a cigarette in the “Corso” hall.
Mr. Montag was fined for this to pay 10 zł. Because Mr. M. did not pay the 10 zł. in time, a policeman took him early in the morning to the police station [komisariat], where he learned that for not paying the 10 zł. by the deadline he was being taken off to prison.
Mr. M. asked the duty przodownik [police sergeant] to take the 10 zł. from him now, because as an official at the municipal power station he must come to his post on time; but the przodownik did not want to hear the request and on top of that threatened: “If you talk a lot — you will be led off to prison in shackles.”
A few hours later, when the 10 zł. had been paid, M. was released from prison.
24 Degrees of Frost in Zagłębie

On Monday morning the frost in Zagłębie reached as much as 24 degrees Celsius. People do not remember so great a frost in our parts for long years.
Because of the frosts there were several cases of frostbitten noses and ears.
Beyond Ząbkowice a 56-year-old Christian woman froze to death.
Robbed of Their Pay and Shot Dead

Beyond Łazy [?] bandits attacked 2 railway officials from the station, and after robbing them of the several hundred zł. which the officials had received as their salaries, the bandits shot at them. One official died in the local hospital during the operation, and the second is wounded.
The Decree for the Bakers Extended

The magistrate [city hall] has sent out notices to the bakery owners that by the end of November 1929 the necessary hygiene must be introduced in the bakeries, such as machines for sifting flour, kneading and the like.
The bakeries that are not mechanised will, without any consideration, be closed at that deadline.
The “Broygez Dance” of the City Council

On Monday a session of the city council was to have taken place, which was to have elected 4 ławnicy [members of the municipal executive] and a president of the city council.
At the last hour it was announced that the session is not taking place.
A sanatorium for Jewish teachers in Zakopane

[Będzin — education and society.] The Union of Jewish Teachers in Poland has taken the initiative to build in Zakopane a sanatorium for the Jewish teacher, who, when he falls ill, is left helpless and without any means of rescue.
To realise this necessary plan, the teachers' union is organising various events, and with the proceeds a suitable plot is to be bought very soon.
The Jewish teaching staff of the local elementary schools are likewise arranging, on the 16th of this month, an entertainment evening with a varied programme.
The ball undertaking is meeting with success. All the tickets are being bought with satisfaction by the well-to-do Jewish population.
It is also to be hoped that the evening will be duly supported and will yield the desired success.
Five-year jubilee of P.A.I. [Poalei Agudat Israel]

[Będzin — religious movements.] On Sunday the local "Poalei Agudat Israel" celebrated its 5 years of existence.
The programme of the celebration consisted of a lecture at the "Corso" ["קארסא", apparently the name of a hall], given by Mr. D. Zilbersztajn (Łódź), and an academy [ceremonial gathering], which took place in the evening at the "Aguda". After the greetings of delegates from the surrounding towns and townlets, the local cantor Mr. Żupowicz and his choir sang several vocal numbers, which met with great applause.
Fainted during prayers; From the "Keren Kayemet"; A lecture; From "Gordonia"

[Będzin — incidents; JNF; culture; youth.] On Sunday the following tragic incident occurred in the local beit midrash, making a shattering impression on all the worshippers. In the middle of the prayers Mr. Yitzhak Szwajcer fainted, and it took about 30 minutes until, with the help of Dr. Teichner, he was revived.
Mr. Szwajcer has left for Kraków ["קראקע"], to hospital.
—o—
From the "Keren Kayemet".
In connection with the renewed and intensified work for the Jewish National Fund, an emptying [of the collection boxes] as well as a distribution of boxes ("pushkes") is taking place on Sunday.
On account of the latest large land purchase in "Haifa Bay" and the 5th pioneer aliyah, it is a duty to double the Keren Kayemet income obtained until now.
—o—
A lecture.
This Sabbath the well-known man of letters Dr. I. B. Cipor will give a lecture in the "Nowości" cinema under the title [?] "Geniuses-madmen, madmen-geniuses".
—o—
From "Gordonia".
Last Sabbath the local pioneer youth organisation "Gordonia" celebrated the youth festival of the Fifteenth of Shevat. A manifesto to the Jewish youth, sent by the head office of the Keren Kayemet in Jerusalem, is read out [printed "געלייגט", presumably for "געלייענט"].
Mr. Yaakov Gorzałka[?] of Warsaw gives a very successful lecture on the essence and meaning of the Fifteenth. In the National Fund campaign for "Ye'ir ha-Aretz" [sic; i.e. afforestation of the Land] "Gordonia" particularly distinguished itself, collecting 140 zł. for the benefit of the "Gordon Forest".
Visit of the rabbinate to "Centrowin"

[Będzin — kashrut; trade.] The local rabbinate, headed by the Rabbi, shlita, has in recent days visited the Będzin wine and mead factory "Centrowin" (Kołłątaja 23, in the courtyard), where they established that the grape wine is kosher for kiddush even for the most scrupulous (le-mehadrin).
An important piece of news is also that the "Centrowin" wine factory is undertaking a campaign to supply the Jews of Zagłębie with good wine for Passover at so low a price that it does not pay for anyone to set up [make at home] wine for Passover.
The "Centrowin" wine factory also sells good grape wine for every Sabbath, very cheaply.
6
Sosnowiec: the kehilla council took fright and came to a session...

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] For several months now the local kehilla council has not held a single session. Because of this the budget for 1928 had still not been approved and, as a matter of course, had not been sent on to the authorities.
The kehilla council was called upon several times by the starosta [district head], but the intervention had no effect, and the kehilla council was "broygez" [not on speaking terms] with the gmina [the community].
Last week the starosta gave notice for the last time that if the kehilla council did not approve the budget, he would fine every member of the council from 100 to 500 zł.
The warning worked, and under the chairmanship of vice-president Mr. L. Szwajcer [so printed here] a session was held on Tuesday, at which the budget was signed by the kehilla council.
The session took place in great haste, so much so that out of "haste" the chairman forgot to put away his cigar, and he opened the session with the cigar in his mouth...
When the session is opened, the late Dr. Avraham Perlman, of blessed memory, is honoured by rising.
Then parnas Baruch Sicemski[?] declares that it should be recorded in the minutes that he does not agree with the budget, and that only under compulsion from the starosta must he sign the budget.
Parnas Kupferminc likewise asks to have it recorded that the blame for the kehilla council's not having wanted to convene falls only on those parnasim who do not have a clear conscience.
Vice-president Mr. L. Zendel points out that if such minutes are submitted to the authorities, the budget will not be approved, and Mr. L. [sic] appeals to Messrs. Sicemski and Kupferminc to withdraw their words.
Mr. Zendel's appeal is met, and after the signing of the budget the session is closed.
When the Woman in Childbed Died, the Midwife Sent the Newborn Child Away Too...

[Sosnowiec — crime.] A few weeks ago the wife of a worker was brought to the hospital of the Sick Fund (Kasa Chorych) to be delivered of a child.
The birth was a hard one, and after a proper operation had been carried out in delivering the child, the woman in childbed died.
The midwife then ordered the hospital attendants to carry out the dead woman together with the living little soul.
Several hours later the child began to cry, and the hospital watchman brought the crying child back into the hospital, where it died a few hours afterwards.
The public prosecutor's office took up the matter and ordered the midwife-murderess arrested.
The prosecutor's order was carried out last Friday, and the arrested woman is in the hands of the judicial authorities.
Sosnowiec Was Left "Shamed"...

[Sosnowiec — brief news.] A national exhibition will shortly take place in Poznań, at which the largest central cities of Poland will be represented:
For this purpose a technical commission has been set up, which decides which towns are to take part in the exhibition.
On the 2nd of this month the technical commission held a session at which it was resolved that, of the towns with a population of 100 thousand souls, the city of Częstochowa shall be represented, and among the towns with a population of 50 thousand, Będzin shall be represented.
The competitors of Częstochowa were Radom and Sosnowiec. Competing with Będzin were Przemyśl, Włocławek, Piotrków and Kalisz.
—o—
Among Us and Among Others...
The Polish merchants' associations have united and created a merchants' council in which every organization is represented. The council held a session these days and resolved that all the Polish merchants' organizations in the whole Kielce voivodeship shall be united in this council.
—o—
Heavy Fine for Possessing Smuggled Goods
The local resident Sz. Grin was charged with having engaged in bringing goods from abroad in an illegal manner. The trial took place in the local district court, which sentenced the accused to pay 19,927 zł. or to 2 years' imprisonment.
—o—
The Number of Unemployed Is Growing.
In the course of the week the number of unemployed in Zagłębie increased by 354 persons.
—o—
Committee to Distribute Coal to the Poor.
In connection with the crackling frosts, the committee of "Mizrachi" has undertaken an action to procure a quantity of coal for poor people.
In the course of the week the committee obtained about 100 korzec of coal, which has already been distributed to respectable [?] Jewish families.
—o—
"Fitted to the Frame" [?]...
In the previous issue of the newspaper there was a notice that the watchman (stróż) of the local Talmud Torah beats the children murderously, and that the gabbaim claim they have no means of removing the watchman.
As it turns out, however, the gabbaim tolerate even uglier doings, for in the house where the "Talmud Torah" is located there is something that no Jewish landlord would permit...
—o—
An Explosion in a Dental Surgery.
In the dental surgery of Mr. Szatensztajn an explosion occurred on Tuesday before noon, in which the technician Miss Bugajer of Dańdówka was badly scalded.
The explosion occurred under the following circumstances: a kettle of rubber (caoutchouc) was boiling in the surgery, and when Miss Bugajer hastily opened the lid, the kettle burst.
From the explosion Miss Bugajer's face was burned and one hand was dislocated.
The window-panes of the dwelling were also smashed.
—o—
Danger of a Coal Strike in Upper Silesia.
In Upper Silesia a sharp conflict has broken out between the coal workers and the industrialists; the workers have declared that if by today, 8 February, their demands are not conceded, they will on that same day proclaim a strike, to begin next Monday, the 11th of this month.
The Festive Opening of the Zionist Premises in Będzin

[Będzin — Zionism.] The successful Keren Hayesod campaign, in which the whole Zionist world is exulting, has only just ended — and Jewish Będzin has already celebrated another small holiday, which is really only a continuation of the recent "Keren Hayesod" celebrations. Leib Jaffe's last appeal, that the enthusiasm should not be extinguished, has found a fitting answer, and one can plainly see Będzin entering a new period of intensive national work.
The Będzin Zionist Organization, which was inactive in recent years, is again showing signs of life, thanks to a few devoted Zionists, and is setting about strengthened work.
On Tuesday, over a glass of tea, the festive opening took place of the new Zionist premises, which with their rich furnishings and equipment are among the finest premises in Będzin. More than 60 people gathered for the celebration, all of them communal activists, town councillors and plain ordinary Zionist soldiers.
The festive opening was not devoted, as always in such cases, to eating and drinking; it was rather a pleasant, intimate social evening which bore a spiritual character and was turned into a discussion evening, where the most topical problems were debated. The mood was a serious one.
The opening speech is given by the chairman of the Zionist Organization, Mr. Abraham Hampel, who greets all the guests present and hopes that Będzin will soon have a people's house of its own, and only then will the true "housewarming" (chanukat ha-bayit) be celebrated. The chair is taken by Mr. Goldfeld. A very successful speech, interwoven with deep thoughts, is given by Mr. Gorzałka[?], who concludes that first of all the "National Home" must be built up in Eretz Israel and the renewal of people and land celebrated. Telegrams of greeting are read out from the chairman and the secretary of the Zionist Organization in Poland, Messrs. Lewite and Cejtlin of Warsaw. Mrs. Ratner speaks, as usual in fine Hebrew and in pithy Yiddish, about the emancipation of the Jewish woman and her role in Jewish life, and about a Hebrew children's school and elementary school. Further speakers are the comrades Żmucki[?], M. Szajn, Mrs. Ratner, M. Cymberknopf[?], Goldsztajn, Goldfeld, Manela, Lidzbarski and Fürstenberg, who once again declares his adherence to the Zionist Organization and solemnly declares that in his new "Yavne" building he is placing at its disposal a large hall for Zionist lectures, where one may meet the broad masses face to face and educate them nationally. The Shortage of "Black Diamonds"

[Zagłębie — economy, coal.] Lately there has been a shortage in coal production; at the mines the coal yards have been cleared out, coal is being snapped up, so that in private trade the sale of coal has almost come to a halt.
The causes are various. First of all, because of the terrible frosts various technical difficulties have arisen; for example the "Grodziec" coal mine, which normally produces 120 wagons of coal a day, is these days turning out no more than half.
Above all, the coal shortage has been caused by the fact that the railways are taking everything[?] — for export and for internal consumption — as are the industrial[?] owners, who want to be provided with coal reserves, because there is a fear that a strike may break out.
Meanwhile the population suffers, and getting a little "black diamonds" comes with difficulties.
The Assessment of the Turnover Tax Will Be Public

[Taxes — turnover tax.] In the present assessment of the turnover tax, a large role will be played by the material supplied by the special information bureau attached to the tax offices (urzędy). In recent days the question was dealt with whether, after the assessment, the taxpayers should be informed on what basis the tax was set for them and on what information the authorities relied in doing so.
It has been decided that the assessment of the turnover tax shall be public; that is, every taxpayer who has complaints that he has been taxed too highly will be able to come to his tax office, and he will have to be told precisely and in detail all the items on which the assessment of the turnover was based. In particular, every taxpayer will have to be told the information about the transactions that was reported by the tax information bureau, as well as what was furnished by the inspectors of the tax offices.
The Ministry of Finance has given this instruction with the aim that every merchant should have the possibility of lodging an appeal if he holds that too much has been fixed for him. If only the appeals would be successful; the opportunity to appeal one does have...

To the Judgment of the Jewish Public *)

[Będzin — city council; leading article.] Many Zagłębie Jews already know that at the last sitting of the Będzin city council, in the election of 5 ławniks [members of the municipal executive], the Jews obtained 1 mandate and the PPS [Polish Socialist Party] 2 mandates.
16 Jews — 1 representative, and 8 [?] non-Jews — 2!
The fact cries out to heaven!
Words fail to describe what happened at the sitting. We turned red with shame seeing what is going on among us. Scuffles, quarrels, hard fights over a chair. No longer merely "chair-grabbing"! Let it be said openly: a chase after a post, regardless of qualifications and moral right.
It was an unheard-of scandal and, as a consequence... a defeat. What was desecrated was the honour not only of the Jewish representation in our town but also — and this is the most important thing — the prestige of the entire Jewish population.
Two months ago today, 80 [?] per cent of the Jewish voters went, in almost closed ranks, to the ballot box and elected 16 councillors — half of the city council.
But we have gained nothing from it. Who is to blame for the defeat? Who ought to be placed outside Jewish society?
Let Jewish Będzin give an answer to that; let the conscience of the Jewish voters take the floor.
As the one whom the present political leaders did not allow to speak, I have the full right now to draw up a short balance of the causes that led to the latest defeat.
From the beginning I took the position that a democratic majority must be created in the new city council, which should take over the government of the town. For this I was fought with the same methods [?] as during the city-council elections. With terror, lies and libels I was rendered "harmless", and finally, in my absence, it was decided to go with the blood-enemies of the Jewish people — the Endeks [National Democrats] — and to give them the office of town president [mayor].
All Poland already knows how they repaid their Jewish supporters: they did not vote for the Jewish vice-president, and in the latest election they supported the PPS.
The fact will not be changed by the claims that what was wanted, after all, was to elect a... friend of the Jews (?). Elections are not a question of persons; only a healthy majority and an honest policy bring benefit to the town.
It is therefore certain that those who created a bloc with the Endeks have given up as a sacrifice, besides our positions, our honour as well.
No better was the tactic of the 3 left-wing Jews.
Why, going in a bloc with the PPS, did they not demand the second place on the list for a representative of the Jewish workers? If the first place is due to the PPS, then surely the honour of the Jewish proletarian demands that at the very least the second place be filled by a Jew. Then the Jewish worker too would have had a representative in the magistrate.
Do the Jewish workers really not have candidates as suitable as, for example, Wiewióra and others, whom one often sees... sober? With what can such conduct be justified?
How disoriented some councillors are is shown also by the following fact:
Almost at the last minute before the election, foreseeing that the second Jewish candidate might be 1 vote short, I turned to Mr. Jakub Erlich, whom I literally begged to support the artisans' list with his vote. With figures I proved that the PPS candidate was assured. Mr. E. showed understanding for the matter, but — acted otherwise. The Jewish list received 9 votes, the PPS list 10. O n e vote decided!
Unheard-of and scandalous was the tactic of the 3 "Agudah" councillors.
I am far from criticising their demand to obtain a ławnik for a group of 3 persons, at a time when it even came to personal fights over that office.
But at the last minute we all believed that they would set aside the thought of revenge, "neither mine nor yours", and act as we did in the matter of electing the vice-president, for example.
The honour of the town must stand above everything!
They could have protested in dozens of other situations and demanded satisfaction, but that they — the would-be representatives of religion — would take revenge precisely when what was at stake was a Jewish ławnik in the person of Mr. Sz. [?] Fürstenberg and of one more Jewish councillor, i.e. 2 Jewish representatives — that none of us, who stand far from the fight over chairs, believed.
The first act of the comedy that has been playing in our town for 2 months now has ended.
Now it is clear why the PPS and others left the hall during the election of the presidents.
Some of them have already received the price; what others will receive, the future will show us.
For the time being, however, it is Jewish society that has paid for the mistakes of individuals: we have lost 2 offices, we have been spat in the face and our honour has been trampled.
Our heart bleeds with pain.
Dr. R. Rechtman.
*) (With part of the opinions expressed we do not agree, and we shall yet return to the question. — Ed.)
