Jewish Zagłębie (Planned public activity, decline, projects, fusion)

[Zagłębie — article; public life and institutions.]
Jewish Zagłębie.
(Planned public activity, decline, projects, fusion.)
Over the last ten years people have begun to look differently at public interests, at public obligations. One is no longer as petty as one once was. Today one is no longer so egoistic as to need everything only for oneself and nothing for the community. The population in general, and we Jews in particular, give away time and money for the welfare of the oppressed and the poor.
People have at long last become conscious, and they understand that one cannot talk oneself into believing that if nothing is done, something will create itself, that something or other will be born of its own accord. Now one sees plainly that if one does not put one's hand into cold water, nothing useful will be born; and on the other hand one sees that as soon as people are active, as soon as they take up the work, so much is accomplished that it often surpasses even every fantasy.
Of proofs there are enough and more than enough: artisans used to drift about, lonely and helpless, without the faintest idea of how to improve their situation and help themselves; then people came from their own ranks, who woke their comrades from their lethargic sleep and showed them wonders. The people rose, stretched themselves [?], straightened their shoulders, got a gleam in their eyes and saw that they are human beings, citizens, who bring benefit to the population.
And now, if we draw a parallel between the helpless artisan of those days and the craftsman of today, one sees tangibly what a distance they have progressed; notwithstanding that they are still far, far behind, these people can after all go everywhere frankly and freely, they are after all represented everywhere, they have their representatives in all communal institutions, they are represented everywhere and fight for a better existence both as citizens and as Jews. The craftsmen have their financial, economic and professional institutions. In the association they find their home, where they can share their sorrows and joys with their comrades.
A colossal change has come about in this field, one that raises the prestige of the simple Jews who earn their living in the most primitive manner.
True, the situation of these people of the folk is still at quite a low level, both financially and culturally; and yet, if one compares the artisan of 15–20 years ago with today's, we do see a colossal change, beyond all comparison. At the very least, out of the broken potsherd of those days, out of the bent back and the sunken chests, we now have people with straightened shoulders, with a proud gait and with courageous demands, which find an echo everywhere.
The same is true of other branches of public activity. People approach communal work with a broad sweep; it has been realized that the population has no sympathy for petty things, and therefore the recent campaigns are undertaken more broadly, more handsomely, more enthusiastically.
We know with what fervour — we would say, with what holiness — people set about building the home for Jewish orphans in Będzin last summer. For the will is so strong that it breaks through walls; out of fantasies and utopias it creates living realities.
There now stands in Będzin a fine monument: the orphans' house — which, one would wish, should rather be called a children's home, because that is closer, more heartfelt, warmer — is an accomplished fact. Out of a fantasy it has become a reality; there stands a roofed three-storey building which will adorn Jewish Będzin. True, a great deal of money is still needed for the interior fittings, but who doubts the continued warm participation of the population? After all, we know that many from the middling strata of the population are waiting with outstretched hands to give their donations, so that they too may count themselves among the givers, among the fortunate ones who helped to build this fine monument.
Now people have set about reorganizing "Hakoach" in Będzin. For this purpose a board of patrons has been created from among the most respected citizens of the town, whose aim is to bring the useful gymnastics and sports institution back to its former era of glory, and thereafter to make steady progress in the field of helping to raise a healthy Jewish generation. The persons who have joined the board of patrons guarantee us that "Hakoach" will revive, which is so necessary for today's school youth, who need to do gymnastics and perform gymnastic exercises.
By summer one ought to set seriously about building a large gymnasium hall, which is a first-class necessity for the school youth.
It is interesting: at the very time when in Będzin people have taken to the work a little more intensively, in Sosnowiec everything is congealed and stagnant; and one must not forget that Sosnowiec is in no worse conditions than Będzin, and yet nothing at all is done there.
The Sosnowiec institutions are in an almost shocking state; some of them give the impression of being a legacy from the Middle Ages. In any case it is a disgrace for Jewish Sosnowiec, which considers itself modernized. New institutions are not being created, and the old ones keep growing smaller and their situation is falling into the abyss.
Who does not see what a face the "Craftsmen's Association" has acquired. And what does "Maccabi" look like, which once was in a flourishing state. The hospital, too, which is an ornament of Zagłębie Jewry, begs to be refreshed and renewed.
Zagłębie Jewry in general finds itself in a rare state of indifference. People never give one another a hand; Zagłębie is, after all, almost like one town, and yet each keeps the other at arm's length.
We hold that one sister must support the other. For example: Sosnowiec, let us say, has a hospital which is the one and only in Zagłębie — it must absolutely be subsidized by the Jewish communities of Będzin, Dąbrowa and Zawiercie. And conversely: if we have institutions of which we can be proud and from which the neighbouring towns benefit, these too ought to be supported by them.
For several years now there has been talk, both in Będzin and in Sosnowiec, of building craftsmen's schools, and it goes without saying that to this very day none has been created, neither in Będzin nor in Sosnowiec.
Perhaps it is a plan that one large craftsmen's school be created for the Jewish youth of Zagłębie?
It would be only right to give this some thought and to treat the question seriously — a question which, incidentally, is already ripe.
Let the people who are competent in this matter take the floor and dwell from every side on the needed institution, which will after all have to be created.
In any case it is necessary that the public activity of the Zagłębie towns be unified, and this would give the possibility of strengthening and fusing together Jewish Zagłębie in the creation of grand and fine Jewish institutions.
L. Sh. [?]
A Command of the Hour (Addressed to the Sosnowiec Kehilla)

[Sosnowiec — kehilla; emigration.] By Sh. V. [ש. וו.]
(Addressed to the Sosnowiec kehilla.)
Now, as the community [gmina] is working out its budget for the current year, we again consider it our duty to draw attention to the importance and necessity of opening in Sosnowiec an information bureau for Jewish emigrants.
We say "again" because we have already touched on this question several times in the columns of our newspaper, in connection with opening a branch of the Jewish emigration society "JEAS". It turns out, however, that the JEAS head office, knowing in advance that maintaining such branches in the provinces burdens its budget, is for that reason in no hurry to open these branches.
Matters would be quite different, however, if the budget for maintaining such an emigration bureau were covered from local sources; then the JEAS head office would certainly show its moral and also its material support. The budget of an emigration bureau ought to be covered only by the Jewish kehilla, within whose competence the support of Jewish emigration also falls.
Emigration is the only means in which all the victims of the present crisis see a rescue; the dozens of artisans and workers whose workshops have been closed lift their eyes to the lands on the other side of the sea and are ready to take the wanderer's staff in hand.
Dozens of candidates for emigration are to be found here among today's shopkeepers and traders, who tomorrow or the day after will, for various reasons, have to close their little shops. Many emigrants will also be supplied by etatism and other "isms" [?], from which the Jews are the first to suffer.
And all these hundreds of emigrants and emigrants-to-be it is our duty to help, first of all with information, with advice. Let us not allow that for every trifle they should have to waste time and expenses in vain on going to Warsaw.
Here, on the spot, this help must be given. One need not be frightened off by the idea that opening such a bureau, which would give Jewish emigrants advice and information, involves who knows what enormous sum, which the Jewish kehilla in Sosnowiec cannot afford. If such an information bureau for Jewish emigrants is properly set up, it can be maintained for a sum that will have no influence whatever on the relatively large budget of the local kehilla.
The emigration problem now occupies an important place in Jewish life; it concerns all strata of the Jewish population, and it is therefore the duty of the Jewish kehilla in Sosnowiec to take a proper interest in this problem.
Sh. V.
Frost, Frost, Frost... — Little Pictures of the Siberian Frosts in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — humorous reportage; the great frost and the coal shortage.] Little pictures of the Siberian frosts in Zagłębie. Caught and passed on by Chazon [חזון, pen-name].
30 degrees.
Kołłątaja Street [קאלאנטאיא גאס] is as if it had died out. The wheels of the carts creak. The shop windows, the tram panes — as if hammered shut with thick grey shutters. A few people run; from mouth and nose a thick steam shoots out as from a running locomotive; everyone and everything [?] is icing over, the frost cracks, the wind cuts, the ears prickle as if with needles, and the bitterest luck has fallen, poor thing — to the nose.
Everything runs, there is no time to stand, but the only place where some people do stop is — at the barometer [sic; a thermometer is meant]; each one marvels and shakes his head.
— How much does it show?
— 30 degrees!...
At the pumps.
In many houses the water supply is not working, the water pipes are frozen, and the landlords are waiting for the spring sun...
Because of this there is a "revival" at the water pumps on the New Market [נייער מארק, Nowy Rynek]. From the neighbouring streets the servant girls gather at the pumps to snatch a bucket of living water [?]; the pumps have become the assembly point for rendezvous ["randkes" (?), from Polish randki]; gentile lads and lasses gather at the "water spring" and hold their winter sports here.
More than one housewife has waited at home for hours before she "had the privilege" of seeing her Stasia come back with a bucket of water.
Saving a life overrides the Sabbath.
In a narrow lane stand several Jews who, walking home from prayers on the Sabbath, have caught sight of a strange thing: by a small cart of coal stands a young woman wrapped in a shawl, watching that the peasant should not give her false weight...
— You are surely surprised, my dear Jews, eh? He "whom I am not worthy to mention" knows the truth: I have never in my life, Heaven forbid, desecrated the Sabbath, I am a God-fearing woman, but what else can I do when a child of mine lies sick and there is not a scrap of coal in the house...
— Do not take it amiss; the Father in Heaven will not reckon this to me as a sin; in the holy Taytsh-Chumesh it is also written that
— saving a life overrides the Sabbath...
The sukkah — a "sacrifice".
When Yente-Tsipe took the last bit of coal out of the storeroom, her bitter situation was doubled.
— What is one to do? A shortage of coal, the room is cold, the little ones are cramped up with cold, and the frosts grow greater with every day.
Sunk in such thoughts, it seemed to her as if someone were prompting her:
— "Chop up the year-round sukkah and it will be warm"...
— Ah! How can one do that? For dozens of years the year-round sukkah has been used in honour of the festival, and suddenly...
Yente-Tsipe thinks; the frost creeps in, the water in the room has become a lump of ice. "If it pleases God, then I too am content." A little while passed and the year-round sukkah lay scattered in pieces about the courtyard.
— A sacrifice has fallen.
"Swój do swego" ["Each to his own" — the slogan of the Polish economic boycott].
On Modrzejowska Street [מאנדזשעווער גאס] a cart with "black diamonds" "went astray". People came out of all the houses to see the "great wonder" — no small matter, a cartload of coal!
The "diamonds" are held up by the crowd. The coal merchant puts up "resistance", wants to "move on" further, but he does not succeed. "Let it cost head and collar" — only hand over the coal,
The shouts reached to the end of the street; the policeman on duty, seeing such a throng, also came running, and here, on the scene of the "event", he set about making order.
— "Proszę za ogonkiem" ["Into the queue, please"] — he commanded.
Having no choice, the coal-hungry crowd lined up in a "queue" ["ogonek" (?)], exactly as in the "queue times" [the war years], and the dealer in "diamonds" doled out portions...
Having barely, with great trouble, waited [?] until my "turn" ["otshered", from Russian], I get nothing less than a "welcome" from my coal supplier.
— Eh? You are here too? Where do you buy all year round? No, "nothing doing".
— But God be with you — I plead with him — give me a portion too, even a smaller one, but do not send me away with nothing at all; after all, it is a matter of mortal danger...
— You don't understand Yiddish? Then I'll say it in Polish
— "Swój do swego"...
“The Tasks at the Present Moment” (A Reply to Mr L. Sh.)

[Trade and taxes — a reply article; reprinted from the “Radomer-Keltser Lebn”.]

(In No. 1 of the “Zagl. Tsayt.” [Zaglembier Tsaytung] the editor, Mr L. Sh., touched, in an article entitled “The Tasks at the Present Moment”, on how the merchants are being pointed to various reforms that ought to be introduced in commercial life, such as harmful competition, cheap credit, bookkeeping and the like.
The article, which was reprinted in the “Radomer Keltser Lebn” [“Radom–Kielce Life”, a Yiddish paper], called forth a discussion in merchant circles, and in No. 6 of the “R. K. L.” Mr A. P—n of Radom gives a reply to Mr L. Sh.
Because of its topical importance we find it necessary to reprint the reply.)

The questions dealt with by the author must truly interest every single citizen. As a merchant I too want to take the floor and state my opinion on one of the most painfully aching economic problems.

It goes without saying that every merchant must first of all calculate his goods exactly, in order to know where he stands in the world and to find his bearings when selling [?]. But he has to reckon with the tremendous competition that prevails in each and every branch. Then, when he must hold his ground and fight for his existence — then calculation helps very little. Unfortunately, one can observe in our trade a phenomenon that leads the most solid enterprise to complete ruin, or downfall. That is the extraordinary and unjustified risk taken by the reseller.

A great many merchants misunderstand the concept “credit”, which — simply translated — means trust; that is to say, when the reseller, let us say the merchant as such, when he has worked up for himself with the manufacturer, as a stockist respectively, a certain credit — more correctly put, has earned trust — he permits himself, in an impermissible manner, to give the goods away at the smallest profit, many a time at a loss, into such hands as would, in a more normal time, have had to consider well whether they can rise to the purchase in question. Today, when we Jewish merchants are dependent on street usury, which sucks the last out of us (some of the cooperatives are not much better in this respect), one ought first of all to have introduced a system of sound trade. I.e.: not to sell at dumping prices, not to abuse the credits from which they exist (unless somebody is going about with other motives...), but to establish that a customer must be prepared sometimes to pay something in real cash for goods, and sometimes even the whole — naturally with exceptions.

Only thanks to the false understanding of the concept “credit” there has lately developed a kind of new system of instalment payment, which involves the reseller in large but not at all secured debts. It seems to the merchant that he is making a turnover (“obrut” [Polish obrót]). But that is a false reckoning, which creates a type of merchant whom the authorities do not know, and it turns out that we merchants pay taxes for them and for such “goers” [?], to whom we so unreckoningly give away our hard-won trust, only to be sure of getting caught in the end.

Nor is it any better with the customer who buys from us directly, without a middleman. We ourselves accustom him to it — through the above-mentioned system — to get everything from us without a grosz of money. It is enough for someone to show us an identity paper, from whatever office it may be, for us to give on credit our hard-earned and entirely alien [i.e. other people’s] property. As said, we permit ourselves to abuse credit, which every single merchant ought to regard as a thing for which he is very much responsible; I do not even speak of the fact that such a manner of trade brings us great losses from mass protests [of bills], and that we maintain at our expense a kind of parasites, idlers, discount brokers, etc. So then, trade in and of itself must first be put on a sound footing.

Then, passing over to the tax system, I want to make one small remark: that the tax authority, if not perfectly, is at any rate sufficiently informed about each and every merchant. It goes without saying that while the merchant cannot produce any books, the material gathered from banks, the railway, the post, etc. is greatly magnified.

The remark of Mr L. Sh. is indeed correct, that the tax authority demands books; but one must not forget that there are also cases when even official books are not readily recognised; books cannot always help — all sorts of pretexts are already found. Besides, in many cases the trust placed in the bookkeeping ledgers by the tax organs is a doubtful one.

One thing is important: that we merchants should, as a collective, obtain the full trust of the tax authority for the merchants as a whole, and precisely for those who, for various reasons, cannot keep official books. This can be achieved with success, but through laborious work, only by the representative bodies: for merchants, on the part of the “Merchants’ Association” and the Merchants’ Bank; for artisans, on the part of the Artisans’ Club and the Artisans’ Bank.

But about that another time.

A. P—n.
A Visit to the Sosnowiec Agudah Bank

A Visit to the Sosnowiec Agudah Bank.

A "sleeping-bench" [shlof-bank; a pun — in Yiddish bank means both "bank" and "bench"]? — Nothing of the kind ever happened! — There, of all places, nobody sleeps any more. It is a bank with all the trimmings, a bank from Bank-land, with books as big as the Vilna Shas Gemaras, lehavdil [not to compare sacred and profane], books the size of, lehavdil, little Mishnah volumes, and with little Hasidic lads with sprouting little beards, with "roguishly" turned-down little collars and little black neckties, who only a couple of weeks ago were still swaying and twirling with the [— ; so printed: "mit di iber", a word seems to have dropped out, perhaps "thumb"] over the big volumes of the Shas, and are swaying [still]:
— "O rachunki weksli, ma rachunek kasy" [Talmudic sing-song over Polish ledger headings: "either 'bills-of-exchange accounts' — then what is 'cash account'?"]. Granted, a bills account is a thing plain and simple to grasp, for with a bill of exchange one has to reckon days, one has to reckon interest [?], one has to [make] a heter-iska and work out the damno [Polish banking term: the discount deducted from a loan]; but rachunek kasy — heikhi mishkakhat lah, where is such a case to be found? — How is it conceivable that a cash-box, an inanimate thing of iron standing in a corner, that such a golem should need to be reckoned up?...
That is how one lad splits hairs, and when he cannot find his way out of the difficult sugya, he goes over to a second one, who is a "Sinai and uprooter of mountains", and asks him.
The other answers:
— "Let a book be brought and we shall see" — let us just look inside, in order: what is rachunek kasy... rachunek kasy..! Fool! What don't you understand? — Surely that means the movables, the small change, which has to be converted into dollars...
Dollars he does understand, because he also demands that his dowry be paid out to him in dollars, and precisely a whole thousand pieces — after all, he is no less than an "urzędnik" [Polish: clerk, official] in a bank!
Certainly an "urzędnik"! And not only he, but perhaps two minyanim, no evil eye, of such "urzędniks", in round little Jewish caps pushed onto the tips of their shrewd [?] little heads, from under which peep tiny "gzhibelekh" [apparently forelocks, from Polish grzywka; possibly little combs, grzebyk], tiny ones, purely for appearance's sake, "gzhibelekh" not for use, God forbid, only for ornament...
But the "gzhibelekh", the little caps and even the "roguish" turned-down collars with the black neckties have nothing whatever to do with the bank. A cap is a cap and a bank is a bank.
Of course it is a bank! And here is the proof: Jews come, homely Jews, men of our own circle, and hand in bills of exchange, hand in money, sign underneath and receive money... The bank even possesses "woźnys" [Polish woźny: bank ushers/messengers]; these are a sort of fledgling-priest lads who have not yet forgotten their bar-mitzvah sermons; these lads flit from one desk to the next, bringing and carrying away little papers... and should such a slip of paper fall to the floor, the lads pick it up with love and out of habit. They bring it to their little mouths like, lehavdil, a scrap of "shemos" [sacred writings] — unbelievable.
In comes a Jew, one of those Jews who study the Daf Yomi every day. The Jew has a "packet" [a bundle of bills], and he lays it down on the desk, quite at home:
— Moshe, will you do the packet for me?...
— What sort of packet is it, a long one or a short one?
— May I know as little of a cold Melaveh Malkah [printed "meluve-malke"] as it is true that today all "packets" are short!...
— I'll put it before the director.
— So, the director is here now? — Good morning, Reb Alter, look here, I ask you, I really was wondering why one sees you so seldom in the shtibl — you've become a director here?
— What can one do, Itshe Meir [?], "in a place where there is no man..." the director excuses himself jokingly, and looks through the "packet" with awe and love — be so good as to come in tomorrow, God willing, and it will be settled for you, auspiciously [be-khi tov], without a vow!
Well, is that not a bank, a proper one, a bank like all banks [also: "like all benches"]?...
And, if you like, they even speak "Gentile" there too:
In comes a little Hasidic miss — a little raisin, one need only say the blessing "who creates the fruit of the earth" over her — and she goes up to the first lad she finds, who is sitting over a Shas-sized book:
— "Proszę pana, czy tu się płaci?" [Excuse me, sir, is this where one pays?]
The poor lad turns red and deathly pale, and without casting a glance at her he shows her.
"Proszę panią, tam na lewo." [Please, madam, over there on the left.]
My guide, who had brought me into the bank, let me in on a secret, whispering in my ear:
— You know what, you I may surely tell, you won't write about it after all: the "Agudah" is planning to open an Agudah theatre of its own and a cinematograph, where men will be admitted separately and women separately...
— How will they manage that, and who will play the women's parts?...
— Teiku [the question stands unresolved], my guide answered me — the Agudah can do anything!
Y. Sorehles [י. שרהלעס].
The Man Who Seeks Justice

[Feuilleton — social satire; London.]
By L. Geltman.
[Epigraph:] At a sitting of the London House of Commons a commotion arose, caused by a spectator in the upper gallery who threw a heavy book down into the chamber, crying out: "Justice".
A man in a grey soldier's greatcoat wandered about the streets of London and sought justice.
His face was pale and emaciated, his eyes feverish and restless, and his whole bent, gaunt body gave him the look of some distant, dark ghost.
The man was already tired and dejected from walking about on his wooden legs, but before his eyes stood the picture of want and misery in his cramped, dark home, and he dragged himself on and on through the foggy and noisy streets.
— Where is justice?
He put the question to many passers-by and waited to hear an answer from them. He asked clever and learned doctors, rich and well-fed manufacturers and merchants, pious, God-fearing priests and monks, and even strong, solidly built generals and heroes, but all of them looked at the man in the grey soldier's coat in astonishment.
— It is justice you are looking for — one of them, a learned man, answered with a smile — it lies in the books; read and study and you will find it...
— Justice lies in the pocket — the manufacturer and merchant answered him — the richer a man is, the more justice he possesses
— Only in heaven is there justice — the priest assured him — pray much to God and it will show itself.
— Justice lies in strength; these healthy muscles here, the solidly built arms, the rifle and the cannon — they are justice.
But the man in the soldier's coat could not seek justice in a book, nor in wealth, nor with God in heaven, nor even in his own strong fists; he was poor and hungry, weak and ignorant, and had no strength to seek justice in those places, nor did he believe in that justice of the fist and of the pocket; so he went on walking the streets with a heavy heart, seeking a little fairness and justice for a poor, downtrodden man.
On the chest of the man in the grey soldier's coat dangled war decorations which he had received fighting for justice; he knelt before those crosses and asked them:
— Tell me, iron crosses, the price paid for my strength and blood, do you not know where justice is to be found?
But the crosses were silent.
A policeman standing at his post noticed the strange man in the soldier's coat and stopped him.
— What are you looking for, strange man? Justice?
— Justice! For whom?
— For myself, sir; for justice I lost my health on the battlefield... there is a wife with children at home... they want to eat... so I am looking for Madame Justice, perhaps she will help me out.
— Justice is at the police station [the commissariat], I am a watchman — said the policeman — go there and you will find it.
When the man handed his request to the commissioner, the latter shouted at him:
— You charlatan, justice you are looking for; if so, why, you talk like a Bolshevik! Clear off! Or I'll thrash your bones for you this minute!...
But the man did not lose his hope and again dragged himself about in search of justice.
He went to the executioners [?] of justice, to the judges, to ministers and great people, but nowhere was he given a clear answer.
The judges even explained to him plainly that they had once had a little justice, but they make no use of it, because all the justice has been given away to the rich and the strong.
The poets, for their part, said that justice is where one is paid well and given splendid compliments.
One, a minister, expressed his great regret that he had no spare bit of justice for an invalid, but promised him that in the government's next budget he would see about putting in a few lot [a small unit of weight] of justice for him too.
One, a manufacturer, of whom the man in the soldier's coat inquired after justice, said:
— Foolish man, if I were to have justice now, I would not be a manufacturer and would own no houses. And with that he confessed to him that once, in his young years, before he married and began to think of a practical purpose in life, he had carried on a bit of a love affair with Madame Justice.
The last stage of the man in the soldier's coat in his search for justice was in Parliament; there, where there are learned and clever men, God-fearing and pious, rich and strong — there, he thought to himself, I shall ask where justice is to be found; all of them together will help me to find her.
And the man in the grey coat believed that in that house was the headquarters of justice, which goes out from there over the whole country, and he went off there.
For a long time the man sat up on high and listened to every word. He was certain that there justice receives instructions and directions where to go and what to do. But alas, he was disappointed. The clever and the learned, the strong and the pious, the rich and the God-fearing all spoke, of all things, about stifling workers' movements and drowning distant and foreign peoples in blood; they spoke about sucking out as much as possible of the people's meagre blood and about improving the lot of squire and priest.
The patience of the man in the grey soldier's garb burst. He seized the heavy book of justice, the book of laws, and hurled it down into the chamber.
— Where is justice for me, for the crippled working man? — he cried.
But his cry was drowned in the uproar and laughter of the deputies and government men, who came running together to see the madman who, in the year 1929, seeks justice in... the English Parliament.
The Rabbi's Son — a Jewish historical novel by Yaakov Zimmerman (instalment 21)

[Serial historical novel — "The Rabbi's Son" by Yaakov Zimmerman, instalment 21; set in the time of the Chmielnicki massacres (1648–49).]
How then can such a thing be? How is it possible? A rabbi, a great and famous rabbi, should suddenly agree that a son of his should marry a baker's daughter? Has such a thing ever happened before? And although she was a mother, who would surely have wished to see the greatest happiness for her only child, she nevertheless strongly doubted the possibility of it — although her foolish mother's heart kept on pounding at this thought, as though it wanted to talk her into it and give her courage to believe in it...
And is it not a thing from Heaven, that which took place here today? Are there then few houses in the Jewish street? They are here in Kraków in their hundreds... Why did it happen just so, that the young man, the Rabbi's lad, should faint precisely before the door of her house, and that he should be brought in here and laid down on Blumele's bed?... Is that not a thing from Heaven, a finger-sign from Heaven that it is after all possible that their hopes, though very distant and almost unattainable, should yet one day be fulfilled?...
Blumele, while her mother was sunk in her thoughts, went back into the second room to ask the Rabbi's lad whether he did not want something. He answered her, and the girl did not go back to her mother any more. The young people, though both bashful, nevertheless little by little found their tongues, so as to carry on a bit of a conversation between them.
Meanwhile the door opened and, accompanied by several Jews, in came the Rabbi of Kraków, Reb Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller. He had come to see how his son was faring and whether he could now go home with him.
— A good Yom-Tov! — said the Rabbi kindly to Esther. And when he saw that his lad was already prepared to go home with him, he now thanked her for the trouble she had had here through his son's fainting.
— Rabbi! — Esther answered him in a modest but firm voice — for the great fright we had to endure here on account of your child, I want to have my reward! I beg you, dear Rabbi! Bless my only child with a holy blessing of yours. I am a poor woman, and apart from the little house in which you now find yourself, and my husband, who is now far away from home, I possess only this one and only child...
Reb Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller, the Rabbi of Kraków, fulfilled Esther's wish; he laid his hands on Blumele's head, and after he had quietly said quite a long prayer, he said aloud in a firm voice:
— I give my heartfelt blessing to you, you woman of valour, and also to your husband and only daughter. "Yegia kapekha ki tokhel, ashrekha ve-tov lakh!" [Psalms 128:2] — when you eat of the labour of your hands, happy are you, and it shall also be well with you!
Who was now as happy as Esther and Blumele? It now truly seemed to Esther that in her oven there really was a treasure. She had only just now received such a precious blessing from such a holy man, and he had promised her that it would always be well with her, her husband and her child.
The Rabbi and his son took their leave and went off home.
Blumele simply shone, in seventh heaven. She — and only she alone — had noticed with her sharp eyes how "her" David (so she called him to herself, in her heart) held her little flower in his hand, and at the leave-taking he brought it to his lips...
— They are dear and honest people — the lad said to his father on the way, and the Rabbi nodded his head at this, as though agreeing with his son's words. It pleased him that he had blessed the girl and her mother, and he now strongly wished that his blessings should indeed be fulfilled.
Walking on, the Rabbi was absorbed in his thoughts. He was thinking about Prince Wiśniowiecki, whom he had met this evening for the first time in his life and who had made a very good impression on him. He is not at all like the other half-mad, wild and pampered Polish noblemen, but appears to be an honest and serious man... The Prince had told him that he would visit him this evening... Would it perhaps be more practical for him to anticipate this and pay him a visit first?... Yes, that would be very good indeed. But who knows where the Prince is to be found, somewhere in the great city of Kraków, and where one could find him quickly?..
— A good Yom-Tov, Rabbi! — a voice was now heard. It was Shimon, who had just set out to go to his kinswoman Esther, to bid her "a good Yom-Tov" and to be her guest this evening at the festive meal; but when he heard the Rabbi's wish, he was at once ready to lead him to the Prince's lodging.
— But the Rabbi, long may he live, must hurry a little, if he wants us still to find the Prince at home — said Shimon — the nobleman has a great many things to attend to here in Kraków and very little time. He told me to come to him in about an hour, so that I might bring him to the Rabbi's house.
Grave and absorbed, each in his own thoughts, all three walked through the quiet and scantily lit streets of Kraków.
Reb Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller was thinking what and how he should speak with the Prince; he wanted to thank him in the name of his son, David [?], for the first aid which he, the nobleman, had given him when he, his son, was carried in in a faint. But since Reb Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller also knew that the Prince would perhaps speak with him about political matters as well, he therefore asked his son that he had better wait in the anteroom and not go inside with him to the Prince. Shimon would remain with him. With this both were content, above all Shimon, who in any case had been intending very shortly to have a talk with the Rabbi's young son and to lay before him a plan of the Prince's, which — as Shimon hoped — would be to the young man's liking, and for his sake his father, the Rabbi of Kraków, would also agree to it.
— — —
Let us, for a short time, leave the three persons — we shall soon meet with them again — and meanwhile take a look at what is now going on in the little house of Chaim the wagoner.
There we now find Adam Kamiński, the coachman of Prince Wiśniowiecki, who had brought with him personal greetings from his friend, from Chaim. Sarah had already read out Chaim's letter to her mother, word by word.
A good many tears of love and gratitude were shed by mother and daughter when the letter was read, in which it was described in detail what troubles Chaim had had to endure on his journey, and above all in Warsaw, where the Cossack, Bazil Petrov, had all but killed him when he would not allow the Cossack to steal the fine and faithful horse, Hassan, out of the stable.
Chaim related in detail in the letter how good the Prince had been to him and how nobly and in what a truly Jewish manner Reb Eliyahu had treated him. Also, that he had been taken into the Prince's service and that he would soon come driving with a pair of precious little horses which the nobleman had given him as a gift. He would not, however, stay long at home, because he would soon be going off with the Prince to the war against the Cossacks, the evildoers, who had shed so much innocent Jewish blood.
Kamiński was received in Chaim's house like a true friend, and he had never spent such a few pleasant hours as now, with the family of his Jewish friend, in the Jewish lane, in Kraków.
The coachman sat here like a lord; before him on the table stood a bottle of the best brandy and various good things to take with it. Kamiński was not shy; he ate and drank and at the same time told stories about his friend Chaim, what a good man and hero he was; he also talked a good deal about the approaching war against the Cossacks.
— Our Prince will soon give Chmielnicki and his band a good thrashing and scatter them; we shall soon come home as victors. Meanwhile let us drink to the health of the pretty girl, and we shall all rejoice greatly at her wedding...
The gentile already had a little in his head, but he was still steady enough on his feet. He took leave of everyone, kissed the little children and earnestly begged that when Chaim came home he should not be kept here long, because he must soon go off again with the Prince.
But none of all those who listened to Kamiński's simple but honest words could have had any notion at all how many streams of human blood it would yet cost, on both warring sides, before Prince Wiśniowiecki would nevertheless succeed in having the expected victory, of which Kamiński had just spoken in such confident language.
Chaim's wife and the older children were now happy. They took great pleasure in the good, living greeting which they had now received from Chaim. The mother did indeed deeply wrinkle her forehead and pondered a good deal over her husband's desire to go to war, but she put her trust first in the Master of the Universe and then in her Chaim, that everything would turn out for the good.
Sarah, Chaim's girl, now, after Kamiński's departure, still sat at the open window and thought over the stories the gentile had told about her dear father; but among all these things a thought about Shimon kept flitting past her. She could not get it out of her head at all how strongly he resembled her father. She also kept on pondering over the terrible events which he, poor man, had had to endure.
(To be continued).
"Der Kokh-lefl" (The Stirring Spoon) — humour and satire, compiled by Ben Amotz

[Humour and satire — Będzin and Zagłębie. The weekly column "Der Kokh-lefl" ("The Stirring Spoon", i.e. the busybody who stirs every pot), compiled by Ben Amotz.]

A Frosty Plan.
We have had frosts —
frosts indeed;
one could not breathe,
it simply would not let you [?]...

What use are overcoats? What use are furs?
What use the heat of coal?
Tooth did not meet tooth,
I tell you — it is no joke.

Fine things — such a chill
we have never had;
people walked about as if congealed,
frozen through, faint.

Every limb frozen,
face, nose and ears —
except the hearts, which with the rich
are frozen anyway...

We already thought the world was ending,
that everything was coming to its end,
since greetings were reaching us
from the far corners of Siberia...

For it was stated plainly
that this cold beyond measure
really does come from there,
from deepest Siberia.

So the thing did not please me,
and I thought to myself then
that the terrible frosts are coming to us
from Biro-Bidzhan...

That the cold, the Siberian one —
so I thought to myself —
has brought great troubles
upon our region.

And while I was at it I reflected:
— Oy! it would do no harm
to the Jewish public of Zagłębie as a whole,
nor to the individual either,

if, out of gratitude, we were
(the sooner the better)
to send a few parnasim
straight off to Siberia.

Yekl ben Flekl.

A "Wolf" in the Radomsker Shtibl
Last Friday night, while a group of Hasidim were sitting in the Radomsker shtibl (number 2), a "wolf" burst in and savagely tore to pieces... a herring.

"Miss Zagłębie".
The "beauties" of Zagłębie, being "zazdrosne" [Polish: jealous] that "Miss Polonia" is a Warsaw girl, held a large meeting at which a special jury chose a beauty to be sent to the international beauty contest in Paris.
After a lengthy exchange of views, the old woman Altele [printed: אלטהלע] of the Będzin old-age home was elected "Miss Zagłębie".

An Urgent Meeting.
Because of the prevailing Siberian frosts, an urgent meeting will take place next Sunday, at which it will be considered whether to begin a coal campaign.

A Rare Phenomenon.
As we are informed from a reliable source, a rare phenomenon occurred this week which deserves to be made public.
It happened, namely, that a doctor from the Magistrate [the municipality] came to a patient one day late...

50 Degrees of Frost.
At the last minute we received a radio report from Bielitz—Biała [Bielsko—Biała] that 50 degrees of frost prevail there (25 in Bielitz and 25 in Biała).

A Revolution on Kowalska?
Among the "kuptses" [Polish kupcy — the merchants] at Kowalska 2 a revolution has broken out. The "tshlonkes" [Polish członkowie — the members] demand that the k.k. "King Ka" tender his resignation.
At the last minute we receive reports that the revolutionaries are steadily getting reinforcements and will certainly carry off a victory...

Afraid of Wolves...
The first report in the press that wolves have appeared in Zagłębie has cast fear upon:
— the Dąbrowa parnasim, and they are afraid to come to a meeting.
— the Będzin budget ["etat"] commission.
— the Będzin Endeks [National Democrats], who are running in fright to the "Eynsl" ["the Number One"].
— the board of the Będzin "Hazamir", which is afraid to call a meeting.
— the coal dealers, and they are not to be seen by the light of day.

A Remedy against the Grippe.
— Why on earth have you taken your mother-in-law into your home?
— The grippe, you understand, is going around just now; I reckon that when the Angel of Death catches sight of her, he will run away in fright.

—o—
Randkes, may they rest in Eden [a mock notice in a mourning frame]
We feel for the great suffering of those who were scorched by the frost on Saturday night while they were waiting for "randkes" [Polish randki — dates, rendezvous], of blessed memory.
May you find consolation in the spring nights.
A group of lads.
On the City-Council Elections in Czeladź (A Letter to the Editor)

[Czeladź — city-council elections; letter to the editor.] (A letter to the editor.)
Having read in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" that a union of the small traders and the artisans has been reached with regard to the local city-council elections, and so on, I have the honour, as a resident of Czeladź who is versed [?] in the local election struggle, to acquaint the broad mass of readers of the "Zagl. Tsayt." with the "political" maturity of the Jews of Czeladź, who no longer remember the "verdict" they received at the previous elections: because the Jewish voters went with 3 lists, not a single Jewish councillor got in.
As soon as it became known among us that the temporary commissioner, Dr. Parczyński [?], had been elected city president of Sosnowiec, it became clear that elections would shortly take place in Czeladź, and Mr. Abraham Gelbard took upon himself the initiative of bringing about a union of all the local voters, so that only one Jewish list should figure. Mr. Gelbard's work was a sincere one; it cost him much toil and labour with a number of stiff-necked people, until at last he announced that the work had succeeded and that the union rested on a compromise between the merchants and the artisans in the following manner: the first candidate was to be from the merchants' side, the second — an artisan, the third — a merchant, and the fourth — again an artisan.
According to the grouping and fragmentation of the Christian voters, and also because the Communist list will be disqualified, the Jews have a chance of getting 3 Jewish councillors through.
An election committee of 5 merchants and 5 artisans was also elected, whose task was to put forward candidates and to conduct the election campaign; but as soon as the committee met, the "bomb" burst — namely, a representative of the artisans declared that the first candidate must be a baker. The reason was that, since there are 4 Jewish bakers, they must have a secured candidate. Against this, naturally, both the bakers themselves and representatives of the election committee protested, but the demand caused the committee to dissolve at once, and the merchants made themselves a separate list; the artisans did the same.
Then the question of the candidates began, and out of the two lists a situation developed from which it is hard to find a way out, for over a number of years the only Jewish councillors were Messrs. Chaim Szwajcer and Mr. Rechnic. This is not the place to recount Mr. Szwajcer's successful activity for the public good: even before he became a councillor he always intervened in municipal and judicial institutions, and with success; the greatest antisemites respected him, and there is not a single Jew in Czeladź who has not turned to him for help. The same praise is deserved also by the present first candidate of the artisans' list, Mr. Rechnic, who together with Mr. Szwajcer made a name for himself by their activity in the former city council. The two Jewish councillors had against them a majority of 22 Christians, and the moment a Jewish question was at issue the non-Jews were spontaneously united against the Jews; and yet they achieved much for the benefit of the Jewish population.
Councillors as capable and able as Messrs. Szwajcer and Rechnic we shall not have again, and all the local Jews know this, even their opponents (if there are any such). From a logical standpoint all the local voters ought to have voted for one list headed by the former councillors; but something occurred which caused the two meritorious communal workers to stand each on a separate list. The result is that the voter who knows how to appreciate their activity, and who would have wished to see both as councillors, is now helpless. Both are dear to him, and both mandates are in danger. The one who caused this is Mr. Efraim Klajman [spelled Klajnman in the notice on the same page], whose sympathizers and friends put forward his candidacy in second place, after Mr. Szwajcer, and Mr. Rechnic in third place. The latter felt insulted and accepted the proposal of the artisans, who put him in first place on their list.
Because of this a situation without a way out has been created for the Jewish voter; this is thanks to party ambition, and both lists are condemned to one and the same verdict.
Therefore I have the honour, in the name of a larger group of admirers who know how to appreciate your merits for the public good — to turn to you, esteemed communal workers Szwajcer and Rechnic: be proud of your past, your conscience is crystal-clear; do not lose courage, and continue your deeds for the benefit of Jewish interests.
Abraham Epsztajn.
—o—
A Demand!
Whereas Mr. Efraim Klajnman, for the sake of grabbing a seat in the Czeladź city council, has publicly insulted me, I call upon him: if within 8 days he does not publicly apologize and give 100 zł. to the free-loan (Gemilut Chasadim) fund, I shall hand the slanders hurled at me over to the court.
Abraham Gelbard.
"Agudah" Councillors Help the PPS to Victory

[Będzin — city council.] Deck: A shameful betrayal by a Jewish councillor.
This Monday evening the honour of Będzin's Jewish population was stained. The great community of Jews received a slap across the whole face, and the pain is greater still because the slap was dealt by those who have already wrought enough ruin in the Jewish camp, those who bring more troubles upon us than the worst enemies of the Jews, those of whom the prophet said: "Thy destroyers and they that made thee waste shall go forth of thee" [Isaiah 49:17].
That evening 4 ławnicy [aldermen, members of the municipal executive] were elected to the local city administration. The Jews, who make up half of the total number of councillors, could without any effort have carried 2 ławnicy, so that together with the vice-mayor ["vice-president"] we would have had 3 Jewish votes in the city administration...
Along came the councillor of "Poalei Emunei" [Poalei Emunei Yisroel, the Agudah's workers' organisation], incited by the base, insolent fellows of the local "Mikveh rag" ["mikve-bletl" — a derisive name for a local paper], and put forward the claim: "We are due an Orthodox ławnik"...
The other Jewish councillors, hearing such a claim, put up for the sake of peace a compromise candidate in the person of the philanthropist esteemed by the whole town, Mr Sz. Fürstenberg, who declared explicitly that he would stand on guard and that the Jewish population would be grateful to him for his work in the magistrate.
But the "Poalei Emunei" councillor succeeded in catching in his net the councillors Rechnitz and Sztajer as well, who behaved to the last minute like that false mother who demanded "Gzoru!" — "Let the child be cut in two": if not an Orthodox ławnik, then let it by all means be an enemy of Israel, so long as it is not a Jew...
And the "Gzoru" was carried out. The councillors Gerszon Rechnitz, Mosze Sztajer and Herszl Erlich abstained from voting, and thanks to that the Jews lost 2 representatives: a ławnik in the person of Mr Fürstenberg and one more Jewish councillor [as printed].
Our "left" councillors too have spat upon [?] the Jewish collective; they too understood that it is better to support Hetmańczyk than Fürstenberg, and with their votes they enlarged the position of the PPS [Polish Socialist Party] and made the Jewish strength smaller.
Let the facts remain in memory, let Jewish society record it for eternal remembrance: thanks to the fact that the above-mentioned councillors followed the "politics" of irresponsible brazen-faced men, the merchant class of Będzin has lost a significant force in the present city administration.
———
A shameful betrayal also took place in the ranks of the 10 Jewish councillors (apart from the Agudah ones) who had given a written undertaking that they would support the candidacy of Mr Fürstenberg.
A struggle must be undertaken that will have the power to unmask the one who betrayed the Jewish collective, Jewish honour and Jewish interests.
Jewish Będzin must shake itself awake, organise protest meetings, demand of the Jewish councillors a public oath and various means of struggle, in order to uncover this traitor.
One may not be indifferent to such a villainy; the traitor must be boycotted by Jewish society, such a base creature must be put outside the camp, and he must be set at the pillory.
———
The session is conducted by the vice-chairman, Mr Fürstenberg. Before the agenda a declaration of the "BB" club [BBWR, the Non-Party Bloc for Cooperation with the Government] is read, which casts off responsibility and protests against the tactics of the city council up to now.
The item on electing the chairman of the city council and the secretary is moved to the last item, and the procedure of electing 4 ławnicy is begun.
On the proposal of councillor Mrs Ratner a recess of 10 minutes is made for the purpose of consultation.
During the recess the Jewish councillors of numbers 12 and 17 [apparently electoral list numbers], and in particular the vice-mayor Mr Rubinlicht, again appealed to the councillor of "Poalei Emunei Yisroel", Mr Erlich, and his comrades to give up the harmful, narrow party politics and vote for Mr Fürstenberg.
The latter himself also negotiated with the Agudah representatives. I shall — Mr Fürstenberg declared — defend Orthodox interests better than you, and above all as ławnik I shall be the representative of Będzin's Jewish merchant class.
But the words remained "a voice crying in the wilderness"; the would-be representatives of Orthodoxy would agree to no compromise whatsoever and with their ambitions broke a Jewish mandate.
———
Before the vote the "Poalei Emunei" councillor Mr Erlich reads a declaration from a scrap of paper, that "because of the tactics of certain Jewish councillors the Orthodox faction will not take part in the elections".
The elections take place and give the following result: the Jewish list received 9 votes, the PPS 10, the "BB" 6 votes, and one blank ballot.
As a result of this outcome the Jewish councillors received 1 ławnik (the ławnik until now, Goldsztajn), the PPS 2 ławnicy, Niewiara [?] and Hetmańczyk, and the "BB" 1 ławnik, the chairman of the city council until now, Mr Żebrowski.
The result of the elections struck the large number of Jewish visitors like thunder.
Of the 10 Jewish councillors one committed betrayal and handed in a blank ballot. The councillors Gerszon Rechnitz, Mosze Sztajer and Herszl Erlich boycotted the elections, and with the assistance of the Endeks [National Democrats] and the votes of Messrs Jakub Erlich, Jehuda Lejb Fajner and Mordechaj Berisz Rotenberg, there was elected, instead of the patron Mr Fürstenberg, the well-known enemy of Israel Mr Hetmańczyk.
At the end of the session the Left Poalei Zion submits an urgent motion that the magistrate should begin an action against the catastrophic situation of the coal shortage.
Mr Fajner argues the urgency, and the motion is sent on to the city administration.
The conduct of the 7 Jewish councillors during the election of the ławnicy has aroused great bitterness among the local Jewish population, and especially among the Orthodox Jews.
Councillor Mr Mosze Sztajer too greatly regretted his mutiny after the session. I am not at all to blame — said Mr Sz. — all this was caused by the rascals of the "Mikveh rag" with Herszele Shaygets at their head...
Butchers flay the hide

[Będzin — prices.] From a reliable source we are asked to draw attention to the fact that the butchers are permitting themselves to screw up the prices of meat.

It is a fact that in Będzin the price of meat is higher than in Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa.

One of the butchers, Mr. R., who did not want to join with the other butchers in the matter of raising the prices, was threatened by the butchers.
From the Small Traders' Union

[Będzin — commerce.] We are asked to announce that persons who have purchased trade licences (patents) for 1929, and also for 1928, in another person's name should report at once to the union, in order to change the registration at the starostwo [district office].

The merchants who have been penalised administratively by the starosta or by the magistrates' court [sąd pokoju] must also report.
Collision between 2 trams
[Będzin — accident.] Near the old station 2 trams collided with one another. The collision was a light one; only a few window-panes of the car were broken.
An incident

[Będzin — incident.] On Tuesday Mr. Yosil Kokotek was at the "Paryż" coal mine, from which he was to collect a quantity of coal.

When Mr. K. was standing by the "sortownia" [coal-sorting plant] he received a shove, from which he fell down and broke a bone of his left leg.

As it turns out, the Christian coal dealers wanted to take revenge, because Mr. K. disturbs their "pasek" [profiteering] in coal.
Wolves come to visit the ancestral graves...

[Będzin — miscellany.] On Sunday a wolf appeared among the graves at the new cemetery. The gravedigger notified the police station [komisariat] by telephone, from where several policemen were sent out, but the wolf, on hearing the first shot, vanished.
The bridge "falls" to its knees...
[Będzin — transport.] The bridge on Czeladzka Street has sunk somewhat. Because of this, tram traffic over the bridge was halted in the course of Saturday.
Battle between police and bandits

[Będzin — crime.] Several weeks ago a policeman was wounded by bandits at Ksawera. In recent days the police received information that the bandits were in Porąbka.

The little house in which the bandits were staying was besieged. The bandits, seeing that they were threatened, fired out.

The police fired back, and the result was that one bandit capitulated and the second, not wanting to fall into the hands of the police, shot himself dead.
Merchants, hand in your declarations!

[Będzin — taxes.] Today, the 15th of this month, is the final date for handing in declarations [zeznania] of turnover for the year 1928.

Declarations must be handed in by merchants holding trade licences (patents) of the 1st and 2nd category.

Whoever does not hand in a declaration loses the right to lodge an appeal [reklamacja].
Declarations of Income for 1928

[Będzin — taxes.] By 1 March all merchants and traders must submit declarations (zeznania) of their income in the year 1928.
—o—
From “HeChalutz”
[Będzin — Zionist movements.] In the premises of “HaShachar” the second meeting took place on reorganizing the local “HeChalutz”, with the participation of the following organizations:
“Poalei Zion”, “Hitachdut”, “Freiheit”, “HaShachar”, “Herzliya” and “Gordonia” (printed “גרדניה”).
A provisional secretariat was elected, consisting of comrades Brafman, B. Liwer and Majerowicz, whose task is to come to an understanding with the Central Committee of “HeChalutz” in Warsaw and to convene a meeting of the interested persons who will take an active part in “HeChalutz”.
—o—
A Lecture
[Będzin — culture.] Tomorrow, Saturday the 16th of this month, at 1.30 in the afternoon, a lecture will take place in the “Nowości” theatre by the well-known speaker Dr Yechiel Halpern of Warsaw, under the title “Trotsky — the Tragedy of the Soviet Union”.
—o—
A Concert
[Będzin — education and culture.] The orchestra of Elementary School no. 2 is arranging a concert, the proceeds to go towards buying and repairing the musical instruments.
The concert will take place in the “Nowości”.
—o—
A Discussion Evening
[Będzin — societies.] Today, the 15th of this month, a discussion evening on the principles of Esperantism will take place at the Esperantists' Society.
—o—
Lay Judges in the Labour Courts
[Zagłębie — courts.] On the basis of an understanding between the merchants' and the house-owners' associations, the following lay judges (ławnicy) and deputies have been nominated to the Labour Court in Dąbrowa and to the district (“rayon”) court in Sosnowiec:
In the Labour Court: Michał Lewin, Adolf Sercarz, Yeshaya Ratner [?].
Deputies: Elimelech Wrocławski, A. Szwarcbaum, Gustaw Weinziher and Adolf Zmigrod.
As lay judge in the district court: Kopel Kopłowicz.
Sosnowiec: Dr Weinziher — Chief Physician of the Jewish Hospital

[Sosnowiec — the Jewish hospital.] As the hospital committee informs us, Dr Weinziher has been engaged as chief physician at the local Jewish hospital.
Dr Weinziher has already been carrying out his functions in the last days of this week, and today the agreement between the two sides is to be signed.
—o—
Raised by 20 Groszy
[Sosnowiec — community.] The community board has an agreement with the eye-doctor Kołowski [?], that for a visit [of a patient] whom the community (gmina) sends to him he is to receive 1 zł.
The price was in force for a considerable time. This week Dr K. notified the community that he demands a further 20 gr. per visit.
—o—
A Victim of the Frosts
[Sosnowiec — the great frost.] At Ciasna [?] 7 there lived a certain Berman, 61 years old. In recent days, when the neighbours noticed that the old man was not showing himself, they knocked on his door, but no one opened.
The neighbours therefore called the police, and when the door was broken open Mr Berman lay dead on the bed.
As it turned out, the unfortunate man had frozen to death.
—o—
The Coal Campaign Is a Success
[Sosnowiec — relief.] Thanks to Messrs Czapnik, Zając, Gelbhaar and others, the coal campaign is a success. By the last days of the week several hundred korzec [a measure] of coal had been collected.
It is, however, worth drawing the initiators' attention to making it easier for the poor people to obtain the coal.
—o—
Meeting of the City Council
[Sosnowiec — municipality.] This evening, Friday, a meeting of the city council takes place. Among other things, the supplementary budget for the past year will also be dealt with.
—o—
Organization of Insurance Agents
[Sosnowiec — economy.] Next Sunday the founding meeting to create a union of all insurance agents in Zagłębie will take place in the premises of the insurance company “Port”.
—o—
3 Years' Prison for Killing a Child
[Sosnowiec — court.] In the month of July (“lipiec”) several children were playing in a field behind Sosnowiec. At that moment a 17-year-old Christian struck an 8-year-old girl with a stick, and she later died. The murderer was sentenced to 3 years in prison.
—o—
When Will the Schools Be Active Again?
[Sosnowiec — education; the great frost.] Throughout the whole week lessons in all schools were interrupted because of the terrible frosts.
On when lessons should be resumed, a conference of the school authorities took place, and nothing definite was decided.
As we are informed, the question was settled in the sense that if the frost is greater than 20 degrees, parents need not send their children to the schools.
New residence-registration rules

[Poland — registration of residents.] The Ministry of the Interior has drawn up a new draft concerning the registering and de-registering of tenants.
Under the new draft, a tenant who leaves will have to be de-registered only when no trace whatsoever remains of him. If, for example, someone goes away and leaves a flat behind, or a subtenant leaves belongings with his landlord, or when someone goes abroad to study (even if it be for several years) — in these cases the tenant need not be de-registered.
At the same time, however, the administrator of the house (in the case of a subtenant — the master of the flat) is obliged to know where the tenant is, so that at any time the administrative authority can obtain exact information as to where the tenant is.
The frost has eased and the official coal price — raised

[Zagłębie — the frost and the coal price.] As of Wednesday the official price of coal has been raised by 25[?] groszy per korzec [the customary coal measure].
— That is how the dearness of articles of prime necessity is fought in our parts.
A monthly ticket taken away from a schoolgirl because she was carrying a pair of shoes

[Dąbrowa–Będzin — tramway.] Miss Glezer of Dąbrowa attends commercial courses in Będzin, and on that account enjoys a reduced-fare ticket on the tramway.
Last Monday the pupil travelled home from Będzin, taking with her a pair of shoes that she had bought in Będzin.
Because of this the tram conductor took her monthly ticket away from her. After much inquiry and investigation she got the ticket back the following day.
Frost — has paralysed trade

[Będzin — trade.] Owing to the terrible frosts that prevailed for a whole week, trade has been completely paralysed.
Apart from ear-muffs and iron stoves, there was a standstill in every branch.
The Będzin magistrate in the fight against dear coal — 4 zł 60 gr. a korzec of coal

[Będzin — municipality, the coal price.] The Będzin town administration has resolved to open a fight against the dearness of coal, which in the course of the week reached as much as 7 zł per korzec of coal.
To this end the magistrate has bought a larger quantity of coal, which is being sold to the population at the price of 4 zł 60 gr. per korzec of coal.
The coal is to be collected at Kokotek's, Modrzejowska 11, telephone 2-39.
More than the above-mentioned price need not be paid.
—o—
Frozen in her bed
[Będzin county — the frost.] In Strzyżowice[?], Będzin county, a local 75-year-old Christian woman froze[?] to death in her bed.
The PPS's "housekeeping" in Dąbrowa — 400 thousand zł missing from the municipal treasury

[Dąbrowa — town council.] Under the chairmanship of Dr. Piwowar, a sitting of the Dąbrowa town council took place on Wednesday evening.
Before the agenda come greetings: in the name of the "BB" [the Non-Party Bloc for Cooperation with the Government] Prof. Kaczkowski gives a greeting, from the PPS [Polish Socialist Party] — Zieliński, from the ND [National Democrats] — Nowak, and from the Jews — Rechnic.
Then the president [mayor] Mazejski[?] delivers an exposé, in which he promises to work for the good of the local population without distinction of faith or nationality, and stresses that the main emphasis will be on reducing the expenditure of the municipal budget.
After the exposé the vice-president Kożak [Kozak?] takes the floor and declares that on taking over the administration it was established that about 400 thousand zł are missing from the municipal treasury.
Mr. Kożak proposes that a commission of 8 persons be elected, with all the clubs represented except the PPS, and that the commission carry out an exact audit of the books.
On this Mr. Cieplak (PPS) speaks, demanding that the commission be enlarged to 10 persons and that the PPS, too, have 2 representatives on the audit commission.
The vice-president is against this, giving as his reason that those who are being accused cannot at the same time be arbiters.
The PPS proposal falls and the vice-president's proposal is adopted.
On the audit commission the Jews are represented by Mr. Futerko.
Then 5 commissions were elected, on which the Jewish councillors are also represented.
On the commission for culture and social welfare — Mr. Strzegowski; budget — Mr. Rechnic; sanitary and complaints — Mr. Futerko.
How bills of exchange must be signed

[Economy — bills of exchange.] Although for a number of months now, on the basis of new regulations, a certain order has been introduced in writing out the texts of bill-of-exchange forms and in the signatures on them, many drawers nevertheless do not adapt themselves to the new regulations, which makes it hard for the holders of the bills to be able to discount them.
The banks do not accept any bill whatsoever if it is not properly written out and signed.
The drawers are therefore being reminded for the second time by the authorities that badly written-out bills will not be accepted by the banks; the signature of a firm on a bill must agree with the name under which it is entered in the commercial register.
Moreover, where there is a stamp on the bill one signature is enough; if not, 2 signatures. Nothing may be struck out on the bill forms.
Stoves in the streets
[Dąbrowa — the frost.] Because of the frosts the Dąbrowa magistrate has set up stoves in several streets, so that passers-by may warm themselves.
False rumours about rents

[Housing — rents.] A rumour has spread recently that the landlords have obtained permission to raise the rent — in line with the valorisation — by a further 72 percent, which the złoty has lost since the first valorisation.
From the most reliable sources we learn that this is not true: the government does not intend to permit rents to be raised; nor is it true that rents will become dearer because of the projected tax on premises [podatek od lokali]. For the time being the tax will not be introduced so quickly, so the matter is not yet so very topical. Incidentally, the new dwelling tax for building purposes will amount to only a few percent a year, and small flats will be exempt from it.
—o—
Meeting of merchants and industrialists.
Yesterday evening an urgent meeting took place at the "Merchants' and Industrialists' Association" in Sosnowiec, Kowakska [?] 2.
The meeting was called by a majority of the members of the institution, who are in opposition to the presidium, which took the liberty, without the members' knowledge, of nominating representatives to the Chamber of Commerce.
The meeting was stormy in character.

The Jewish Voter Has the Word! (On the Jewish Defeat in the Będzin City Council)

[Będzin — city council; leading article.] It is an old rule that among us Jews a vessel must be broken at every celebration in remembrance of the Destruction; it is a curse of exile that whenever we are privileged to have some little piece of joy in our small Jewish world, it must, alas, soon be drowned in a sea of suffering and sorrow. A few weeks ago our town celebrated a victory. Unexpectedly, given the situation that had been created, a victory was achieved at the elections, with as many as 16 Jewish councillors obtained. People rejoiced and placed great hopes in that strength. But the holiday did not last long. A bitter disappointment arose, and once again we became notorious for the division of hearts, for the rift in our ranks, which has led to such sad results.
Deep in my memory is engraved the picture of the "historic" sitting of the city council at the election of the ławniks [members of the municipal executive]. Seeing the terrible situation created thanks to our fragmentation, a quiet and deep cry of pain could not but burst forth from people of honest feeling. The result of the vote struck like thunder, and with bowed head and a heavy heart I left the sitting, seeing how others rejoiced at the price of our defeat.
However bitter the truth may be, it must nevertheless be said that a certain part of the Jewish councillors have shown by their tactics, plainly enough, that their voters cannot have confidence in them in the future.
Is it not a tragedy that at a time when an external front has to be defended, when our duty is to fight for Jewish rights, for Jewish subsidies, the right to work, Jewish officials. At a time when we must stand bravely on guard, not let ourselves be wronged, not let ourselves be oppressed, it turns out instead that personal ambitions and principles are placed higher than the affairs of the whole Jewish community. It turns out that people are even prepared to sacrifice 2 Jewish mandates, among them [one] as ławnik in the person of Mr Fürstenberg, who declared to the Orthodox councillors before the sitting that he would defend their interests honestly, just as well as the interests of all Jewish citizens.
Is it then not enough that the Jewish representatives give vent to their hot temperament in the kehilla, where they tear at one another among their own? They come to the city council, where they show the non-Jews that "from the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it", so that those can laugh at our tactless conduct and exploit our weakness for their own purposes...
The Endeks [National Democrats] understood differently how to fulfil their duties. Seeing that with their votes they could save a mandate, a non-Jew, they forgot for a while their anger at the PPS [Polish Socialist Party] and helped it carry through 2 ławniks. Let no one suspect them of too much sympathy for the PPS; no, they did it not out of love of Mordecai but out of hatred of Haman; they did it to strengthen the non-Jewish position against us. And the result! — that 5 PPS men have 2 ławniks and we, 16 Jews, only 1...
We have to do here with 2 categories of offenders: 1) open and 2) secret. The open ones are the Orthodox representatives, who by their wrong, irresponsible tactics brought about such a situation. But I do not wish to accuse here the whole body of the Orthodox, for I am certain that only a few ringleaders acted on their own responsibility. Were it possible to carry out a poll, we would surely be convinced that all honest and sincere Orthodox Jews would express their sharp protest and their lack of confidence against the decision of their representatives. The same would also be the case among the voters who voted for the left-wing representatives. For they too understand that if the left-wing councillors could not, on principle, vote for a bourgeois candidate, they ought to have had the courage to demand 1 left-wing Jewish ławnik, since 3 persons had the right to that. This is not the place to go into all the details; I leave that to public opinion, which will certainly know how to assess their deeds and give them their proper reward.
Sadder still, for me, is the betrayal within our own minyan [?], by the "10 sworn ones" on whom we relied. Sad is the matter of the "unknown soldier" who with his vote brought about the defeat, and the traitor is once again an honoured in-law at the Jewish "wedding".. Thanks to the traitor we slipped, and Jewish honour, Jewish dignity, Jewish interests were shattered. How strong the confidence in the 10 was is shown by the following fact:
Several times I turned to a representative of the artisans and told him how uneasy I was as to whether the 10 were certain; to this I received the answer that I should have no fear, because it was secured. But my foreboding did not deceive me. We were too naive, had too much faith in our own, in those who deliver fine speeches full of promises at the election meetings, but in reality do not pass the examination in the sense of responsibility.
Jewish society must now raise its strong voice! Not pass over such wrongs in silence; demand an accounting from its representatives and judge the guilty with the whole force of truth, fairness and justice, so that it be known in the future that Jewish honour is not ownerless property, that the duty of every representative is to fulfil sacredly and honestly his tasks with regard to Jewish municipal interests.
The Jewish citizen, the Jewish voter has the word!
City councillor Mrs G. Ratner.
Extraordinary General Meeting of the “Merchants’ and Industrialists’ Union”

[Sosnowiec — Merchants’ and Industrialists’ Union.]
A vote of no confidence passed against the old board.
(Sh—kh) In connection with the recent elections to the Chamber of Commerce, things have come to the boil among the “big” merchants (Kowalska 2). It began with a “February upheaval”. The opposition, headed by Messrs. B. Tencer and Y. Saper, collected 50 signatures (that number is required in order to convene an extraordinary general meeting), and last Thursday the extraordinary general meeting took place in the union’s own premises, with a large number of people assembled. The vice-president, Mr. M. Rajner[?], opens the meeting and invites to the presidium Messrs. Lejzerowicz, Lidzbarski and Goldman and, as secretary, Mr. Krumer.
After the reading of the agenda, which consists of the following items: 1) reorganization of the Jewish merchant class in Sosnowiec, 2) directives for the representatives in the Chamber of Commerce, and 3) free motions — President Kwiatek takes the floor and demands that the first item be struck from the agenda, because anyone wishing to reorganize the merchant class in Sosnowiec would have had to come to an understanding with the other unions that exist in our town, and this was not done. Mr. Tencer opposes Mr. Kwiatek’s view, and the agenda is adopted by vote. The first speaker on behalf of the opposition is Mr. Y. Saper, who makes a personal statement that he is not out to grab any “seat”. The speaker sharply criticizes the board and points out that the board, which has acted on its own authority without consulting the members at all, settles very important matters that concern the Jewish merchant. So it was, too, in the elections to the Chamber of Commerce. I personally — the speaker goes on — have the greatest respect for President Kwiatek, but in so important a matter as elections to the Chamber of Commerce the members should at the very least have been asked who should stand as candidate.
The second opposition speaker is Mr. B. Tencer, who delivers a longer speech in which he reckons up a list of sins charged to the board, which in fact consisted of just one man, in the person of the president, who acted on his own authority in all questions. The fact that we collected 50 signatures — says Mr. T. — is striking enough proof that the board has lost the confidence of the members. At these words an interjection is heard from Mr. Birman: “Forged signatures”. Mr. Tencer demands that Mr. Birman prove which signatures were forged. The tumult, however, continues, and the incident ends with Mr. Birman withdrawing his words.
Lastly Mr. L. Finkelsztajn also speaks; he says that in the elections people kept to the system of “shmor li ve-eshmor lekha” [“you look after me and I’ll look after you”].
On behalf of the board President Kwiatek replies in sharp form; he complains that instead of thanks for his tireless work he is, on top of it all, being given a vote of no confidence. Taking part in the discussion are Messrs. Kabak, Kac, Judenherc, Lubelski and Rozman. The last-named delivers a short but sharp speech (in Yiddish. Were it not for Mr. Rozman’s speaking Yiddish, one would have had the impression of being at a meeting of a Polish merchants’ union). Our union — says Mr. R. — is divided into three categories: the presidium, the board and the members. If the board still somehow knows what is going on in the presidium, we members have not the faintest idea of what goes on in the union. What are we, that there is no longer any need to inform us of anything? After a fairly long and heated discussion it is resolved to put forward for nomination as councillors in the Chamber of Commerce Messrs. A.[?] Lipszyc, S. Wolfsohn and L. Finkelsztajn, and those assembled pass a vote of no confidence in the old board. Until a new board is elected, the work is to be directed by the presidium of the general meeting.
During the proceedings the sad news arrived that the member Shabtai Goldfein had died. At Mr. Kwiatek’s request those present honour his memory by rising. The stormy, “historic” meeting dragged on until 3 o’clock at night.
