The Heart Bleeds with Pain

[Będzin — city council; article.] "The heart bleeds with pain" — with this sentence Dr. Rechtman ended his article in the previous issue of our paper, where he touched upon the political wheeling and dealing in Będzin's municipal self-government and the latest betrayal committed by our Torah-"faithful" when the matter at hand was a Jewish ławnik [alderman, member of the municipal executive].

Yes, it will soon be two weeks since the betrayal was perpetrated, and still one cannot forget this villainy. But who said it should be forgotten? On the contrary, the fire has flared up even more. At first they were apparently intoxicated; they wanted to persuade the public that nothing had happened, that in fact they had acted quite well. Later, when they sobered up and at long last saw what they had done, they truly began to be ashamed, and they cannot raise their eyes and show themselves before the Jewish voters.

The more one talks about the terrible deed, the more glaring becomes the disgrace that "our own" have inflicted on us; and wherever the question is so much as debated, it everywhere calls forth the most terrible results, which lead to the point of losing one's balance, and the end of it is that when people part, the heart bleeds with pain.

There are naive people in town who cannot understand what has happened here, how it could come to this: that Jews did not want to raise their hands when a Jewish ławnik was at stake — and they knew that by doing so they were deciding that in the place of a Jewish ławnik a Christian would enter, and, God forbid, no friend of Israel.

Honest people, naive people, cannot understand that there are such as push their way in by force as representatives of the public, and afterwards put at risk all those who elected them, all those whom they are supposed to defend. These people — no sooner have they pushed their way in than they reckon with no one and with nothing. Then they are out only for career, for making capital and for personal interests.

When one reckons with the community, when one reckons with the town, with the citizens' interests, then one acts differently; then one remembers that one's own interests and personal ambitions must be set aside; at such a moment one bears in mind that the general honour and the welfare of the population stand higher than one's own "I". A representative, a delegate, of whatever tendency or party he may be, must remember that once he is an emissary of the public he must, without any excuse, represent the community as a whole.

After all, we saw that when it was a matter of obtaining a Jewish vice-president, the Christians "farratn" [?; so printed — literally "betrayed"; perhaps meant "baratn", conferred] and wanted to bring it about that the "catastrophe" should, God forbid, not come to pass; and then even our left-wing representatives joined the bourgeois elements, and they did not allow the antisemites to carry out their wild orgies undisturbed merely because a Jew was concerned — thanks to which Jewish honour was saved.

Had the Aguda councillors been mature, they would have understood what benefit conscious Jews can bring to the municipal economy; they would not have danced after, and walked in the ways of, boyish ignoramuses who have as much to do with economic management in general and with Europeanism in particular as Ivan has to do with the blowing of the shofar.

Who does not remember how the leaders of the Będzin "Aguda" publicly declared before the elections that they have nothing whatever to do with their "Poalim" [the Aguda workers], that this is a party in its own right and that the one does not obey the other — although the truth was seen at once, on the very morrow of the elections... So why have the "Aguda" councillors now gone with the one and only "Poel" and not with the merchants, with whom they had concluded a bloc?

After all, Mr. Fürstenberg guaranteed these people that as ławnik he would accomplish much for them — as a merchant, as a property-owner and as a Jew. But all that was too little. Nevertheless one should not be angry with these helpless individuals, even though with their help there was pushed through, instead of an energetic Jewish ławnik for whom even the Christians must have respect — a Christian, an antisemite, from whom we shall have no joy. We should not be angry with them; at most we can pity them, for they are just like a blind tool in someone else's hands, and the hands that guide the tool are helpless cripples who have not yet seen the bright light before them. Can one really be angry with such people? Will anything come of it even if one does get angry with them? More than pity them we cannot.

It goes without saying that had their place been taken by a person such as Mr. Paltiel Unger or Kapłowicz, they would not have gone down these paths; they would not have let themselves be led by just anybody. They would have understood that a Jew like Mr. Fürstenberg is not only no danger to them, but that such a man is a gain, when there is the possibility of winning him as a partner in running the town's affairs.

After all, this Jew has given more for religious purposes than the rich Jews of the Aguda; and who helped to build up the Talmud Torah if not Mr. Fürstenberg, regardless of the fact that the institution is in Aguda hands? And did he not say at the first opportunity that he would support the institution a great deal as soon as order reigned there? Is all that too little? Must he necessarily be a declared Aguda man?

Can one really say that these people have any understanding of economic activity? Do they know how such an apparatus ought to be run? It goes without saying that their ignorance will weigh upon the Jewish citizens of the town.

Before the elections to the previous [printed "frirign"] city council we remarked, in discussing the situation of that time, that one can sometimes forgo a councillor, one can sometimes settle for one Jew fewer — but those whom we send there should be people with heads on their shoulders, European people, people of intelligence, people with a sense of orientation, and they should possess steadfastness and composure.

As proof: we previously had 11 Jews and now 16 — so how did we look then, with the smaller number, and what kind of face do we have now, with the enlarged number of councillors?

What is lacking is consciousness, intelligence, a sense of respect, crystallisation. If these immature emissaries of ours had at least let themselves be taught, we would not have had so [?] much trouble from them; but they think that as soon as they have got the mare they must ride her and exploit her with all their might. And our neighbours stand at a distance and laugh at our helplessness and warm their hands at the fire that is being kindled by our Torah-faithful — which they are surely also doing in the name of the holy Torah.

But this helping to bring in, for the sake of ambition and private ends ["tsulib ambitsye, tsvekn"], a Christian ławnik, an antisemite, in place of an energetic Jewish philanthropist who is esteemed by everyone and whom the town costs so much money — this stain, which they made upon us at the very beginning, Jewish Będzin will never forget, and incidentally we shall yet feel it in the future on our own shoulders; and that indeed is why the heart bleeds with pain.

How Do Matters Stand with Peace in the World?

There is a wonderful tale by van Eeden, "Little Johannes". Little Johannes has been transformed by some spirit into a tiny little creature, such a wee thing, smaller than a fly, and he sets off into the world... The world appears to him as he has never until now seen or understood it. He lives through thousands of fantastic experiences.
Once he came upon an old ant who was pasturing a herd of little flies, from which the ants get their honeydew. As the little flies are very placid, the herdsman had time to have a talk with Johannes and even showed him the capital city of the ants. It was a very interesting city, only it seemed that there was some tremendous commotion in the city: everyone was running somewhere, carrying something, chasing off somewhere...
The old ant related with a sigh that the people was now in deep anxiety: a military attack was impending... They had to hurry to annihilate a hostile ant-people, and all were busy preparing for it.
— But what are you waging war for? — asked Johannes — it is not good to wage war.
— Quite the contrary, this is a very necessary and useful attack! — said the ant — we shall annihilate a people of warlike ants and bring peace into the world.
— And you yourselves do not belong to the warlike ants?!
— Where do you get that from? Of course not. We are the most peaceable ants.
— Then how am I to understand that you are getting ready for war?
— Very simple. You see, there was a time when all the ants waged an unceasing war among themselves, not a day passed without battles, and then a good and clever ant turned up who understood that life would be better and easier if the wars stopped. That ant's agitation was successful: all the ants became peaceable. Only, since some held that they understand peace better than their neighbours, and the neighbours are, that is to say, not truly peaceable but warlike — war has to be waged on them, and now we are annihilating the 13th colony!
This wonderful story comes to mind when one reads how enthusiastically the nations took up Kellogg's appeal and resolved to live in peace.
All would be well, only everyone has a neighbour who does not understand peace the way one should
— No, I'll make you understand peace the way it ought to be: — shouts one; and launches a brand-new little mine-ship.
— Kellogg, let it be Kellogg! — a second one says with twinkling eyes, and puts into store a nice fresh batch of machine guns.
And the third feverishly corks up the little flasks of cholera and plague bacilli and thinks; "I'll show you all what a real peace is!"
That, in fact, is how it is now going everywhere. And it seems that only after Kellogg's pact have the nations understood what it means to arm in earnest.
The League of Nations, the good mother of the nations, is convinced that after Kellogg's pact everything in the world is now in order, and only a few trifles are lacking.. It has already prepared a project of various agreements on a peaceful resolution of all future international conflicts, as though mankind will no longer need anything else at all, and the League has put all its strength into seeing that the peace projects turn out exemplary.
But here Mussolini, on whom the eyes of everyone in Europe are now turned, has declared in parliament:
— "We have signed the Kellogg Pact, and if need be we shall sign whatever else is wanted, but we shall attain our goal, and let no one be surprised if we now bring our forces on land, on the water and in the air up to the very highest level!
And we shall pray God to bless Italian arms, and to grant him — Mussolini — to live to the day when he can see the result of it with his own eyes.
Only the other day news came that a new gas has been invented — cacodyl, with which one can annihilate a whole army just as easily as snuffing out a candle.
A naive person might have a thought: if there is a Kellogg Pact, what good is an annihilation gas? But naive people are not reckoned with, and there you have it: the pact is not yet ratified and there is already a gas...
Now Europe, so as not to fall behind, has to invent a second gas...
And so, in order to safeguard the peace pact, one must reckon that a war in the future is inevitable. The nations will not allow that in so holy a matter as universal peace anyone should permit himself to interpret it incorrectly!
And beside the coming war, to speak seriously, all the earlier ones will look like children's toys, innocent pranks.
The old days, when during battles men used to gallop about on white horses and generals or little corporals had time to talk about pyramids from which 40 centuries look down, and the like — those days have long since flown. Today no one bothers with such foolishness; all the fine gestures and heroic sayings have gone into history, and with history they have vanished. Life has not only cast them off but made them ridiculous. Life has shown that there is no poetry whatever, no romance, in war.
War today is not made on horseback, nor do generals make it, but chemists; there are no longer even any fronts. The last war already showed that the most decisive, the most effective blows were not dealt to the front. England calmly bore the blows to the army, but when the enemy aeroplanes appeared over London and the population had to hide in the cellars and in the darkness of the city, the explosions of the bombs flying down from the sky were heard time and again...
In future they will begin straight away from that end [?]. And if they release that same cacodyl, which according to its inventor's statement can within a few minutes envelop whatever area one likes, and with a full guarantee that not a living soul will remain in that district — it is now easy to picture the coming war.
Perhaps it will be enough to press a button somewhere for half of Europe to be wiped off the face of the earth.

What Contempt Leads To. (What Has Become of the „Hazamir“ of Old? Who Brought About the Present State of Affairs?)

[Będzin — culture; the „Hazamir“ library.] A few weeks ago readers of the Będzin „Hazamir“ library printed in our paper a letter to the management, with the request that it render an account of its activity and convene a general meeting.
Several weeks have passed since the letter appeared, and the management has not considered it its duty even to give the public an answer.
That is not tactful, that is vexing and perhaps even more than that — for what does it mean, that a communal institution should have no responsibility towards the public? And what did its readers demand? All they asked was that a general meeting be convened and an account rendered, something that has not been done for a period of "no more than" 15 years.
Let us say that nobody had turned to these people — how then does one not have, of oneself, enough sense of responsibility to reckon with the community, to such a point that for 15 years one does not come into contact with the readers and does not wish to hear a word from them? Not to talk things over with them and wish to hear what the reader has to say, what is going on [?] with the „Hazamir“ library?
Surely this is not some kind of autocracy [samoderzhavie] that must exist on the same terms as in Tsarist times. Incidentally, even in those times general meetings were called — if we are not mistaken, every year — so why should things be worse now? It would be interesting to know the true reason. Altogether it would be interesting to know what goes on there. If there is a deficit, then who bears the loss, and how much does the deficit amount to? If there is a profit, where does the money go? If books are bought with it, then which ones?
We do not wish here to suspect anyone at all of dishonest intentions, if only because we do not know who occupies the place at the head of „Hazamir“; but we do know that there were once people there in whom one could have confidence, and those people surely handed the library over to such as one may also have confidence in. But who are they, and why have they hidden themselves so? Why are they so afraid even to reply to a few lines that were addressed to them? After all, one must in the end reckon with public opinion. A communal institution is, after all, subject to public control, so why should it not reckon with public opinion? This is unheard of, this is simply not to be tolerated. These people must surely reckon with the fact that communal activity is not like a private enterprise, [whose owner] can do what he likes and how he likes; he need render account to no one. Communal undertakings must be answerable to the community.
Who does not remember what the Będzin „Hazamir“ once looked like? We shall not speak of the first period, when the music stood at a brilliant level; we shall not speak of those times when the society had such great musicians as Bensman, Kop and others. Let us turn to the later period, when the book began to take pride of place, when the theatre began to play an important role, when a juicy Yiddish word was to be heard, when lecturers came who dealt with the most important problems of human life.
Who does not remember the Saturday-night "question-box" evenings, the questions with their answers — how they sharpened the mind, what crystallization and consciousness those evenings brought into human awareness.
In those times philosophy, hygiene, politics and history were studied and discussed. National and international problems were treated with fire and fervour. In the premises of „Hazamir“ consciousness was concentrated.
And how much responsibility, respect and reverence prevailed then among the youth — and not only among the youth but also among the older members, for whom „Hazamir“ was an intellectual centre, a spiritual centre [merkaz ruchani]; and how high the book stood then, and what respect people then had for the printed word, for the press?
But that period is long past; those fine times have, alas, long since vanished into deep eternity. Yet when we contemplate that historical period — and it still stands among us as a memorial, that monument, like a tombstone — the heart aches when we see what has become of the fine institution in whose spirit many of us were brought up.
How badly we would need a second, new edition of that „Hazamir“ of old! How badly we would need a tiny literary corner where one could have a cosy talk about Yiddish literature, bring lecturers and take a loving interest in the Yiddish book; how one already longs for that which we once valued so!
And you — when you took over the „Hazamir“ of that time, the duty lay upon you to want at least to try to apply means in order to maintain[?] the needed institution. But you never tried to do so; the problem evidently did not interest you, and you have brought the institution to its present ruin, notwithstanding that more than once you had the possibility of reviving it.
You, the leaders of the present „Hazamir“, have however done more than nothing: you have destroyed more than everything; evidently it meant nothing at all to you that you are tearing away, piece by piece, at that memory. You reckoned with no one and did as you pleased.
But now, when people come and demand of you a general meeting and an account, and you pretend not to know — that is contempt, that is ignoring those who want to know how the Yiddish book and Yiddish literature are faring; and this must not be allowed. At the very least you ought not to have remained owing the public an answer.
R. Let.
The Secret of the Kugel…

[Rubric:] Small Feuilleton.
In our shtetl there once lived — long years to us — a Jewish woman by the name of Chava Gitl. This woman was greatly famed for her excellent kugels, which she made every Sabbath — truly a delicacy fit for a king.
And she made a point of making a big kugel every time and sending it round in pieces to the notables of the town, to taste.
So quarrels began between the householders and their wives: why can the wives not make such kugels as Chava Gitl? It even came to the verge of several divorces. But the wives could by no means imitate Chava Gitl's kugel; some secret was lodged in it there, which Chava Gitl did not want to give away. The wives saw that things were bad, and they began sending delegations to Chava Gitl — but in vain.
Then it so happened that Chava Gitl fell ill, and things became — Heaven preserve us — very bad. So, naturally, the women of the burial society [chevra kadisha] were sent for, that they should recite the confession [vidui] with Chava Gitl and everything a Jewish woman needs before the soul departs. The burial-society women held a meeting and resolved that as long as Chava Gitl does not give away the secret of the kugel, they will say no confession with her and will not go to her at all.
Chava Gitl's soul grew bitter. If she does not give away the secret of the kugel, she may yet die without confession; if she does give it away — why, the One Above may still help, so that she recovers, and all the women will know the secret.
After long negotiations it was settled that the burial-society women would say one word of the confession and Chava Gitl would say one word of the kugel recipe.
"Ashamnu [we have been guilty]," said the women.
"A clean kugel pot," said Chava Gitl.
"Bagadnu [we have betrayed]."
"Grease the bottom with a little schmaltz."
"Gazalnu [we have robbed]."
"A few raisins." And so on.
Then it so happened that at "Pashanu" [we have transgressed — one of the last words in the alphabetical confession] Chava Gitl died, and the women were left without the secret of the kugel and Chava Gitl without a confession.
I say this with regard to the fact that the 9 Jewish town councillors want to get to the bottom of the secret of the "traitor"…
We would make the same proposal as the one between the burial-society women and Chava Gitl. But we do not wish them the same ending.
Lemekh.
Cards (A Story)

[Literature — short story.] (A story.) By Yitskhok Blum [Icchak Blum].
The family troubles began after Mania started to notice that her husband had acquired a strong urge to play cards. The fact that he had taken to playing alarmed her terribly. She regarded it as simply a misfortune — not so much because of the money, which she was afraid he would gamble away, as from the thought that he would lose his interest in the home, in the family. Cards, she knows, are like a kelipah [an evil spirit] that draws you in more and more.
Through the eight years they had been married he had always been a good, warm-hearted husband, for whom the home was everything in the world. Coming home in the evening from work, he would joyfully snatch the children up in his arms, play with them, talk about everything that had to do with their home, with the children. That was his whole pleasure.
When guests used to come to them, the time was spent in talking, reading, singing, and so on.
But since Berman, their new neighbour, began dropping in at their house, the fine and cultivated way of passing the time suddenly ceased, and their house was, as if by magic, transformed into a card-playing den. As soon as a few people had gathered, they sat down to play, and played until late at night.
The remarkable thing was that her husband seized upon card-playing with such an appetite, as though he had long been yearning and waiting for something that would give him a new interest in life.
Mania suffered greatly from this. She kept silent, however, hoping that he would grow sick of card-playing; but when a longer time had passed and he had become still more engrossed, she began to protest.
— I don't want you to play cards — she argued with him.
— What does it bother you if I amuse myself a little? — the husband asked, annoyed.
— You've lived and passed your time without cards ever since we were married; you'll go on living without them too.
— When I had no desire for it, I didn't play. But now I do have a desire for it, so I play! And what do I deserve for it? What sin am I committing?
— You are sinning against me and against the children; you ought not to play any cards.
— The "big" dowry you gave me I haven't gambled away yet, so far...
— You... you... don't you go poking my eyes out with the dowry — the wife flared up.
— And don't you go giving me opinions about whether I should play or not — the husband answered angrily.
— I'm telling you that you will not play.
— I will play.
— You won't play.
— I will...
———
Once, when guests had gathered and they had, as usual, begun to play, the wife snatched the cards from the table, flung them on the floor and burst out shouting:
— I don't want cards played in my house; this is no "card-house"!
The husband fairly leapt from his seat. He had not expected such a public scandal. But he bit his lips and kept silent.
The guests were thrown into confusion. One by one they quietly rose from their places and, one after another, left the house.
From then on no more cards were played in their house.
It did not take long before Mania came to feel what it means when a husband goes away from the house and comes back late at night.
She knew very well that he was sitting somewhere playing cards, and it tugged at her heart. She had already begun to regret having brought it about that he should play somewhere else. When he played at home he had at least not been so distant and estranged. The way it was now was worse still.
She wondered what the end of it would be. To keep silent and let it go on like this — she cannot and must not. She must do something; she must save herself and the children from the great misfortune that is moving ever closer upon them. Later it will already be too late.
———
Her shouting and lecturing him did not help; her protests had no effect. He became even more embittered and irritated. He came to hate her, began to avoid her, came home very late.
One night he did not come at all.
That night she did not sleep; she tossed on her bed and writhed with pain and vexation, and when morning came and he was still not there, she very nearly went out of her mind with despair. Like a wild woman she ran about the house, tore her hair, wept and wailed as over a dead man.
In the evening, when he came, she — losing all control over herself — met him with such a hysterical outburst of screams and weeping that the blood fairly ran cold in his veins. For a long while he stood as if petrified and could not move from the spot. At last, gathering all his strength, he strode to the door, opened it hastily, and, without uttering a word, vanished.
A day later Mania received from him the following few words:
"I will not come home any more. I will send money every week for you and the children to live on. A heartfelt greeting to the children. From time to time I will come to see them, if you will allow me.
Marek."
With an aching feeling she read through those few words. She felt her throat tighten, tears choked her, and she broke into bitter weeping... — — — —
———
Some time passed, and he sent her enough money to live on. From time to time he came to see the children, played with them and brought them presents.
With her, his wife, he had little to do. Sometimes he exchanged a few words with her, sometimes not; having spent some time with the children, he left at once.
She was sad, very sad. Friends and acquaintances seldom came to her. And when they did visit her, they did not stay long either. The gloom that hung over the house like a dark cloud immediately took hold of everyone, and the mute sorrow that looked out of her eyes cast a funereal sadness over them all, and each one looked for an excuse to escape from the oppressive atmosphere as quickly as possible. So she was alone, and the gloom pressed on her, lay heavily upon her spirit; were it not for her two children she might have gone mad from gloom and loneliness.
Only now did Mania come to feel how bad it is for a married woman, a mother of children, to be left alone — even when there is no lack of bread.
———
One day several friends came to visit her. Mania was very pleased with their visit, and she wanted them to stay as long as possible.
She received them very handsomely, invited them to the table. She served refreshments, and when one of the guests later proposed that they play a round of "Thousand" [Tysiąc, a card game], she was not against it.
That evening Berman came in and found people sitting and playing cards; he remained standing by the table, watched for a while how they played, and afterwards took a hand himself.
That evening he was much more cheerful with his wife, talked with her more than usual, and did not even refuse to drink a glass of tea which she handed him after the game.
Since that evening, when he found guests sitting and playing cards, and himself joined in the play, it has not even occurred to him that with the renewed card-playing in his house his wife is preparing a net for him, with which she hopes, sooner or later, to catch him and bring him back home...
The Rabbi's Son — a Jewish historical novel by Yaakov Zimmerman (instalment 22)

[Serial historical novel — "The Rabbi's Son" by Yaakov Zimmerman, instalment 22; set in the time of the Chmielnicki massacres (1648–49).]
"That resemblance of his is no simple matter" — the thought would not let her rest — "and even he, Shimon himself, feels it too... Why, only this evening he himself told us here that she, Sarah, and her friend Blumele strongly resemble his own two girls, and that is indeed why he asked to be allowed to eat here over the holiday.
"Who can know what may yet come to pass here; may it all turn out for the good..."
———
Prince Wiśniowiecki received the Rabbi of Kraków, Reb Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller, in a very friendly manner. He acquainted him with the general situation here in Poland, and above all as regards the Jews. He told him a good deal about Chmielnicki and his bands, and he also spoke of his own plans for the near future.
"Rabin [Polish: Rabbi]," said the Prince with an earnest smile, "I have heard a great deal about you; I have been told that you too are a great hero — I do not mean with the sword, but with the spirit — that you are an outstanding fighter with spiritual weapons — you too are the leader of a great camp of several hundred thousand people, one whose word is holy and even more than a command. Therefore I ask you to give me your help.
"I want [?] to have your great influence, in order to help the holy cause for which I am ready to give away my life — for the liberation of my beloved fatherland. I want to have your support in the great struggle which I am now about to take up against Chmielnicki, and I am convinced that when I shall have won you to my side, I already have at my aid the whole Jewish people of Poland — which I now, before you, rank among all the best and bravest people that Poland possesses?!"
"I will do it," answered Reb Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller in an earnest voice, "but I wish, noble Prince, to ask you to bear in mind also that the Jews have long since forgotten how one holds weapons in one's hands. Because of the oppressions that have weighed upon Jews for so many hundreds of years, the Jewish people could no longer take part in wars, and therefore the feeling of courage and valour has grown weak among them. That is why I fear that the Jews who will join your soldiers will not be in a position to fulfil your great expectations, and that instead of a help they will in fact be a hindrance to you in your undertakings, and on top of that they will arouse a feeling of mockery and contempt among their fellow fighters.
"But as far as money and other help are concerned, I am sure that all Jews will give you everything that is in their power, if only to be able to serve you and to help in your holy struggle."
"All that I do not need for the time being," answered the Prince; "gold and money I have enough of for the present. My own fortune makes it possible for me to wage the war against Chmielnicki, although that bandit has already destroyed some of my estates. What I lack, however, is men, whom one could [as printed: "you could"; perhaps "I could"] train into good and capable soldiers. Necessity teaches a man many things, and even to become a good and brave fighter.
"I am not frightened off by your objections, honoured Rabbi — when the Jews in Poland know that they have only two choices: to be slaughtered and murdered by the inhuman robber bands, or to take up arms themselves in order to defend themselves and their families, then I am sure they will rather choose the latter. If one must fall dead, then a more honourable death is surely far better than to be slaughtered like cattle!..
"You mentioned earlier, dear Rabbi, that for many hundreds of years now the Jews have no longer held a weapon in their hand. But you have forgotten a much earlier period, the glorious times of the heroic Maccabees. You have forgotten to mention how a small handful of Jews, led by heroes, fought bravely against a very great number of Greeks and yet defeated them all... And later too. Did the Jews then show few deeds of valour against the Romans and other oppressors? Is it not easily possible that what once was should return again, and that the Jews should once more gain a name as a brave and heroic people, as they were in former times?!..."
The Prince spoke with so much earnestness and zeal that it seemed to the Rabbi of Kraków that it was not a Polish nobleman standing before him, but one of the ancient Jewish prophets, speaking words of rebuke to his people.
The Rabbi was carried away by these lofty and true words. He stretched out his hand and offered it to the Prince.
"You are right, my noble Prince! Many thanks to you for your trust and for the loving judgment you have just pronounced upon my Jewish people. You will surely have no regret over your words of today. I assure you, by all that is holy, that everything will be done as you demand. I shall do everything possible so that my people may ally itself with you and help you fight against the robber bands.
"If it is your wish, I am ready to follow you into your wars, so that by my presence I may give an encouraging example to all the other Jews."
"Bravo, Rabbi!" exclaimed the Prince with enthusiasm. "That is what I expected of you when I was told about you — that is just how a faithful shepherd of his sheep and a leader of his community ought to speak. Nevertheless, I think that it will not be necessary for you to go with us onto the battlefield; you can accomplish far more for our holy cause if you remain at home and are active here.
"In place of that, however, I ask something else of you, and this will perhaps be a great sacrifice for you — entrust your son to me... When other young Jewish men see that it was not hard for the Rabbi of Kraków to send his youngest son to defend the Polish fatherland, it will surely work upon them as an example, and they will do the same willingly and with devotion..
"But you need not, dear Rabbi, fear for the life of your son. I assure you that I shall watch over him even far more than if he were my own child... For that I give you my guarantee, on my princely word of honour!..."
The Prince spoke so loudly and in so strong a voice that every word was heard in the second room, where David and Shimon were sitting and waiting.
Now the door opened and David, all aflame and very red in the face, stood on the threshold.
"Let me, dear father," he cried out, "go to the battlefield together with the noble Prince! Are we then to let ourselves be slaughtered like a flock of defenceless sheep? Let me, father, enjoy this so rare good fortune — to be one of the first Jews who, weapons in hand, will repay the shameful murderers for the many murders they have committed until now."
The young lad fell upon his father, kissed him and hugged him round the neck. Reb Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller took his son by the hand and led him up to the Prince.
"My youngest son," he exclaimed in a solemn voice, "belongs from now on to the first Jewish army unit that will fight under your leadership for the liberation of Poland! I hope that he will bring the Jewish people much honour. I now place him under your command, and in my heart I pray to God that you may always be successful!..."
The old Polish Prince was deeply moved by this rare scene. He gave the Rabbi his hand once more and warmly assured him that he himself would keep watch over David.
Now they took leave of one another, and the Rabbi hurried home to eat his holiday meal in haste, so as to begin this very night, the holiday notwithstanding, the holy work of calling upon all Jewish men fit to bear arms to enter the Prince's army as soldiers and help him fight against Chmielnicki's robber bands.
That same night the Rabbi had all the Jews called together into the synagogues. Together with the Prince he went from one synagogue to the next. Both spoke warm and heartfelt words, described the sad and dangerous situation in which the land of Poland now finds itself, and both called upon everyone, whoever was at all able to hold some kind of weapon in his hand, to enlist as a soldier.
The words had the desired effect, and when, in addition, it became known that David, the handsome youngest son of their Rabbi, so esteemed by everyone, had already enlisted as the first soldier, it did not take long, and that same night over a thousand healthy and sturdy young Jewish men enlisted as soldiers with the Prince's secretary.
On the second day they at once received the order to set off for Lemberg [Lwów]; there they would all be drilled and taught the soldier's lore.
The Prince left that very same day for Gnesen [Gniezno], to hold a consultation there with the Archbishop.
Dovidl was getting ready to go and take leave of Ayzikl the baker's girl, Blumele..
———
It was a few days after Shavuot. Towards evening, when there was nothing to do in the house and it was still a little too early to set about the work in the bakery, the two families, Ayzik's and Chaim's, were sitting outside together with their children, and they were talking — as usual — about the fathers, who were due these days, today or tomorrow, to come back from their journey, from Warsaw.
Blumele, who was sitting close by the window, kept gazing at the little rose tree, on which the roses were at the height of their most beautiful bloom. She took this as a happy omen for herself, that her own happiness too would one day bloom like that and unfold...
But suddenly a strong shudder ran through her whole body, and she had to restrain herself with all her strength so as not to let out a cry.
Shimon, who as a kinsman had already become quite one of the household with all of them and used to come several times a day to have a look at how things were with his relatives, had come now too and brought the news that the Prince had sent an order that all the young Jewish men who had enlisted as soldiers should hold themselves ready to set out on the road today or tomorrow.
"And as I have heard," Shimon went on to relate, "Dovidl, the Rabbi's son, is already prepared to go along too..."

He Is Looking for Her... (Tragedy of a Jewish Father)

[Zagłębie — a story from life.] A certain Abraham Aaron Hechtkopf (העכטקאפ) of Nowy Sącz (ניי-סאנטש), Galicia, came to the editorial office and tells the following touching story of what happened with his daughter.
— My daughter Mirl is a girl of 19. Last year she went away to Paris to a "mother" [so printed: „מוטער“; apparently a misprint for „מומע“, aunt — the father's sister mentioned below], who had sent for her in order to set her up in life in the metropolis. In Paris the girl learned a trade in a large Christian fashion enterprise.
I was glad of the girl's going away — says the father — because before that she had been going about at home with a Christian, Jan of Hanisów [האניסאוו; doubtful reading]. Unfortunately the lovesick goy did not leave the girl in peace abroad either. He got hold of an address in Paris from somewhere and began to correspond with her. One day I get a letter from the goy Jan, who informs me that he wants to convert to Judaism on condition that I give him my daughter Mirl for a wife. I did not even answer the gentile "bridegroom". But he, it seems, was not much troubled by my indifference and went on working to carry out his plan. But neither my sister nor my brother-in-law knew anything of this, and so they wrote me nothing about it from Paris. All at once, some 4 months ago, I received word from Paris that my youngest daughter Mirl had left there. The Paris brother-in-law reports to me that he has learned that "someone" is said to have been waiting for her at the Polish border. On taking leave of the brother-in-law she declared to him that she was travelling first to Kraków, and only afterwards would she come home.
More than that — says the father — they did not write me from Paris. In the end I again received a letter from the goy Jan, who declares categorically that he must marry my daughter. For that price he is willing to become a Jew. My son travelled to Kraków, where he managed to have a meeting with the Christian lover of his sister, who was in hiding. My son offered the goy a sizeable sum of money to leave the Jewish girl alone. The offer made the treyf blood boil in the "kochanek" [Polish: the lover]. He shouted at this and demanded energetically that they go with him at once to the rabbinate and help him there to go over to Judaism.
Having no choice, my son went along with Jan to the Kraków rabbinate. There the matter was dragged out from one day to the next. The Christian finally realised that he was being put off, and so he wanted to travel to other rabbis; the brother of his Jewish beloved then proposed that he travel home with him. Jan rejected the proposal.
Out of despair the Jewish father wrote in an earnest tone that "he would be happy" to see him, the goy Jan, as the husband of his youngest daughter Mirl. The father's calculation in this was to see his daughter in this way and to talk things through with her.
Soon the "bridegroom" Jan did indeed come to Nowy Sącz with the bride Mirl. The "bridegroom" then asked his father-in-law-to-be to help him become a Jew. The Hasidic father consented for appearance's sake and to that end gave the Christian a letter to the Kraków rabbinate. At the same time the father wrote a letter to the Kraków Council of Rabbis (ועד הרבנים) and explained the whole tangle, asking them to drag out the conversion of the goy.
But the Christian did not grow weary. He engaged a doctor together with a mohel in order to carry out the operation. The doctor, on examining the "bridegroom", established that he would not withstand the difficult operation. Soon afterwards the Christian went off to Warsaw together with his beloved, and since then there has been no news of the abducted Jewish girl.
In his great despair the Hasidic Jew finally learned that his young daughter had in the end given up on her love for the goy; she left him and, as he heard, wanted to settle in Zagłębie, working as a modiste.
Meanwhile the old father did in fact receive from his vanished daughter a short note, in which she sends greetings and asks that she not be looked for, because she will not be found; she has taken upon herself a vow never again in her life to marry.
Anxious over the fate of his child, the old father has come here. He runs about the fashion shops, hoping in this way to find his vanished daughter.
Economic Antisemitism

[Article — economy; municipal tenders and antisemitism.] The economic situation of Polish Jewry is growing ever worse. The tax system, with all its consequences, ceaselessly diminishes our property and leads to the impoverishment of the middle class.

At the same time the class of salaried employees is being pushed out of its positions, both because of the prevailing étatism and because of the specific tactics of our entrepreneurs.

Sadder still is the fact that we are not admitted to the various works and supply contracts. Regardless of our ability to compete, the so-called economic antisemitism has lately spread, which applies against us in the economic field the same methods as in the political one. Thus, for example, to every tender [konkurs] for work or supply the clause is added "that the entrepreneur reserves the right to choose the supplier or the workman." With that, the whole sense of any tender is brought to nothing. But who pays attention to that when it is a matter of favouring one's own and fighting others? Every road that leads to that goal is then holy. A whole series of municipal administrations [magistrates] have lately taken this road.

We know a town with a large Jewish community where, with the silent consent of our "patented defenders", presidents of economic organizations, this system has been introduced. Thus, for example, the clause is tacked on to all announcements about supplies, and after our artisans and workers go to expense for bids, calculations, often with stamp-duty payments, along comes the "reserved right of choice" and one chooses: if it is a matter of tinsmith's work — half the work is given to the cheapest bidder and the other half — to an iron merchant from the Endek [National Democratic] camp. If it is a matter of painting work, the same thing happens. Our artisans get one half (because that is what the Jewish population amounts to), others — the other half. This despite the fact that they do not carry out the work at all, but merely hand it over to Jewish painters, yet the first payments they take as profit for their "hard toil".

The same also happens in other fields, and when some honest Jewish representatives come with reproaches against this unheard-of system, they are answered: "one must not be a chauvinist and want to grab all the power" (authentic).

No explanations help — that we Jews do not want to grab anything, but demand equal rights; that the bid clauses should be removed, and that the work should go to the cheapest bidder, without distinction of nation or religion. But at the same time the entrepreneur [here: the contractor] must give a guarantee for the work or the goods delivered.

Then the public will have no claims against anyone; even if cases occur in which our people fail to hold their own in this or that tender, it will be a warning to them to calculate properly; but the outcome will be that the danger of protectionism will be removed and the work will go to the needy and not to the brothers-in-law and brothers of officials, town councillors and aldermen [ławnicy], who supply stones, bricks, sand and various other supplies and work. Do the gentlemen who defend the percentage norm really not understand that they are placing themselves in the ranks of the most dangerous antisemites, who constantly preach that the percentage norm is actually for the good of the Jews? After all, these have been shouting for years! The Jews make up 10—12 per cent of the whole population, why do they want free access to the state schools, universities and the like? Do the Jewish representatives really not understand that with their tactics they are supporting the "numerus clausus" and the "numerus nullus".

One's heart grows sad when one reflects on certain steps of some municipal administrations, and often the question arises: is not the open enemy, who fights against us with a strong hand, better for us than the one who lulls our "clever" representatives to sleep with sweet chloroform words, in order afterwards, with their enthusiastic consent, to build with our money and create positions for others?

Is this not a little link in the great chain that presses upon us and that is called — "economic antisemitism"?

But the question arises: why are the citizens silent? Do they not see that the number of "representatives" who abandon their occupation in order to live at the community's expense is constantly growing? And who have the impudence to shout that they do it for the good of the poor citizens of the town?

Their situation forces them to give their consent to steps harmful to us, which they later decorate and proclaim as conquests and favours. Countless secrets bind them, and therefore in time of trouble the one does not touch the other [?], and with the help of the interested parties, with promises [?] of supply contracts [dostawy], posts, honorary offices and similar "highly ethical" means, they crawl to the goal over the living and the dead. Who cares that the number of the ruined keeps growing, that economic antisemitism is taking ever deeper root? The citizen is needed only at election time; afterwards they say: "The Moor has done his part, the Moor can go."

Al.
Będzin — Session of the City Council

[Będzin — city council.] [At the head of the section: the heading “Będzin” and the date box — Friday, 12 Adar 5689; Piątek 22 lutego 1929.]
At Tuesday's session of our “poor wretched” city council the PPS [Polish Socialist Party] once again won a victory, obtaining a secretary in the city council with the help of 9 Jewish votes. The same Jews who caused the defeat of Mr. Fürstenberg as ławnik [member of the municipal executive] supported the “friends”, the PPS, and helped them so that, besides 2 ławniks, they should also be honourably represented in the presidium of the city council.
The PPS have all at once been raised up, and Jews — are singing new Lamentations…
— —
The chairman, Mr. Fürstenberg, opens the session and declares that, because in the election of a chairman [“prezes”] he received no more than 13 votes, he renounces the chairmanship and remains, as before, in office as vice-chairman.
The chairman then introduces the councillors who have come in to take the places of the ławniks.
In place of the vice-president [deputy mayor], Mr. Rubinlicht, Mr. Michał Lewin has come in; in place of ławnik Goldsztajn — D. Lustiger.
The “BB” club [Non-Party Bloc for Cooperation with the Government] brings in an urgent motion that, since a flood is foreseen in the low-lying areas of the town, the magistrate should adopt precautionary measures.
The president [mayor] declares that the question has already been considered by the town administration, that a rescue programme has been worked out, and that today, Friday, a committee will be set up to deal with the matter.
Then they proceed to the item of electing a secretary. The PPS put forward the candidacy of councillor Laskowski, who is elected by 19 votes (among them 9 Jewish).
Before the election of the various commissions a recess is declared, during which an understanding is reached among all the clubs, and the commissions are elected.
On the Jewish side the following are represented:
Audit commission: Feiner, Dr. Rechtman, and H. Erlich, Klajman.
Budget commission: J. Erlich, Lidzbarski Lustiger and Feiner.
Roads and building commission: J. Erlich, Goldfeld, Hampel and Sztajer.
Health and social welfare: Mrs. Ratner, M. Lewin, Klajman and Rotenberg.
General affairs: Hampel, Sztajer, H. Erlich and Feiner.
Water mains: Dr. Rechtman, Jakubowicz, Goldfeld and J. Erlich.
There Will Be a Secretariat at the Rabbinate

[Będzin — Jewish community.] On Sunday the kehilla board held a session at which the budget for 1929 was dealt with. The chairman, Mr. Prawer, proposes that the budget be reduced by about 50 per cent. The proposal is defeated, and the majority is in favour of the budget total being the same as in the last year.
At the session Mr. Ryński [Rinski] put forward a proposal that a secretariat be created at the local rabbinate and that 3 thousand złoty be allocated for that purpose. The proposal was adopted on the 1st reading.
Our Town Will Soon Have Water Mains

[Będzin — municipality.] This week the first consignment of material arrived for the installation of the water mains throughout the whole town.
The work will begin in the spring.
As we are informed, the water supply will be installed in every house at the expense of the magistrate, and in the dwellings it will be according to the wish of the house owners.
A "Child" Floats on the "Przemsza"

[Będzin — local incident.] On Wednesday at midday the residents of Zawale Street noticed a bundle in the shape of a pillow floating on the "Przemsza" [the river]. "Experts[?]" were soon found who confirmed that a child was lying in the bundle. To the scene of the "occurrence" there also came the police, who, with the help of rescue appliances, with great caution pulled the floating bundle out of the "Przemsza".

With fear and trembling the bundle was unpacked, and instead of a child a bundle of rags was found.
The Tax on Real Property Raised

[Będzin — municipality; taxes.] This week the new town administration held a session, at which the tax on immovable properties was raised by 25 per cent; i.e., instead of 25 as until now, the house-owners will pay 50 per cent.

— That is the first "fruit", thanks to the Jewish representatives...
35 Years of "Malbish Arumim"

[Będzin — charitable societies.] Next month the "Malbish Arumim" ["Clothing the Naked"] society celebrates the 35-year jubilee of its existence. The jubilee will be celebrated with a varied programme, including also a sale of stickers [nalepki — charity labels], which will begin next week.

In the course of its long years of activity the society has won the broadest sympathy among the local Jewish population, and therefore it is to be hoped that the sticker sale will have the proper success.
Income Declarations — Until 1 May

[Będzin — merchants; taxes.] The "Merchants' Union" announces that the deadline for submitting declarations [zeznania] of income for the year 1928 has been extended until 1 May.

At the same time the merchants who have not yet registered their enterprises at the starostwo [district office] are once again reminded that they should do so at once, in order to avoid penalties.
An Evening

[Będzin — Labour Eretz Israel; events.] A group of comrades and sympathizers of the Eretz-Israel workers are arranging an Eretz-Israel evening on 2 March in the Góra Zamkowa ["Castle Hill"] hall.

The programme will consist of 2 parts. At 10 o'clock sharp there will be the literary part, with the participation of good performers, and later also Eretz-Israel dances, songs and the like.
From "Tarbut"

[Będzin — "Tarbut"; Hebrew culture.] "Tarbut" has renewed its activity. The Hebrew library, which opens next Sunday, has been enriched with the newest books from the Diaspora and Eretz Israel.

Once (1 time) a week there will be lectures in the Hebrew language, as well as papers on literature, art, the Bible and Aggadah.
Sosnowiec — Session of the City Council

[Sosnowiec — city council.] (Sh.) With an hour's delay, the 4th session of the local city council took place on Saturday evening. On the agenda are 16 items and many interpellations, among them an urgent interpellation by the Poalei Zion (P.Z.) club on suspending the enforcement seizures (executions) on 1- and 2-room dwellings until 1 April of this year. The urgency is argued by Dr. Liberman, who points to the hard winter we are going through, because of which the poor population must first of all provide itself with coal and potatoes. Vice-President Jarża [?] opposes and declares that even if the proposal is adopted, it will in any case not turn out to the benefit of the poor population, because when the tax is paid together with interest in the month of April the sum will grow, and it will be much harder to pay a larger sum. By a majority of votes the urgency is rejected and the proposal is sent to the appropriate committee. The Jewish Koło [club] and P.Z. voted in favour.

The supplementary budget was not dealt with because of several inaccuracies. On the item of the surtax on the state industrial tax a lengthy discussion develops, in which councillors Wolf, Dr. Rzadkiewicz [?], Judge Sałak/Sołak [?] and others take part. In the end the surtax is adopted. Also adopted is the statute on taxing cinema and theatre performances, various entertainments, etc. Dr. Melodysta introduces several amendments.

A heated discussion is conducted around the question of expelling councillor A. Hojka [?] (B.B. [the Non-Party Bloc, BBWR]) from the city council. The point is that the Endeks accuse councillor Hojka of abuses committed in the year 1918. The rapporteur, Bień, declares that at the meeting of the committee for general affairs the item was passed over and the committee moved on to the order of the day, because there was not enough evidence to expel councillor H. from the city council. This drives the Endeks out of their wits, and councillors Wolf and Eng. Durzki [sic; = Rudzki] make sharp speeches supporting the accusation. A very successful speech for the defence is then made by the chairman of the city council, Dr. Pawełek, who points out that the Endeks have already achieved their aim, if only by the very fact that they publicly accuse councillor Hojka of such grave sins. By a majority of votes the city council passed over the item to the order of the day.

The council proceeds to the item on electing 4 representatives to the municipal school committee. Chairman Pawełek declares that, since no understanding was reached among the clubs, the item should be dealt with at the next session. Against this, however, councillors Dr. Melodysta and Rotsztajn come out, pointing out that the 4th representative on the school committee belongs to the Jewish Koło, because the Jewish population of Sosnowiec is being wronged by having no representative on so important a committee as the school committee. The just demands of the Jewish councillors are also supported by councillor Wolf (N.D. [National Democracy]). The chairman, having no way out, puts the item to a vote, and by 26 votes Dr. Melodysta is elected as representative, and Dr. Liberman and Eng. Rudzki as deputies.

The city council then authorises the magistrate to conclude an agreement with the local district court on leasing[?] the park located by the court for the town's population.

It is further resolved to adopt the finance committee's proposal to obtain a loan of 290 thousand zł in order to cover an earlier loan of the same sum. With this the session is closed.
Customs Officials in the Dock — the Verdict on the 27th of This Month

[Sosnowiec — the courts.] Great interest has been aroused by the trial which began on Monday in the local district court. In the dock sat the inspector (rewident) of the local customs office, Hamczyk (האמטשיק), and the storekeeper Gołębiowski (גאלעמביאווסקי).

The indictment states that the above-mentioned customs officials caused great losses in that they did not publish the dates of the auctions of contraband, did not admit any bidders, but sold the confiscated goods in secret to a few merchants, and when other interested parties came to the auctions, they were told that the auction had already taken place.

Some 50 witnesses were summoned to the sensational trial, some of whom were heard in the course of Monday and Tuesday until noon.

The witnesses added nothing of interest to the charge, except Hamczyk's maid, who stated that Urbach (אורבאך) used to come quite often, especially at times when the "pan" [the master] was not at home.

In the middle of the proceedings the presiding judge announced that the trial is adjourned until Tuesday the 27th of this month, because several witnesses who play an important part in the trial had failed to appear.
The Board of the Small Traders' Union Had to Resign

[Sosnowiec — associations; kehilla; hospital; schooling.] For several weeks now the "birds on the rooftops" have been telling that in the local Small Traders' Union ("Kleinhendler Farein") dishonest [?] deeds are being done by several members of the board.

The "cheerful" news reached as far as the Central Committee of the Central Federation in Warsaw, which in recent days dissolved the board that had served until now.

Until the coming extraordinary general meeting the Central Committee has appointed a commission headed by Mr. Herman Marek (הערמאן מארעק) as dictator.

—o—

The community-tax assessment (etat-rozkład) raised by 52 thousand zł.

The kehilla board held a session at which the kehilla budget for the year 1929 was considered.

After a lengthy discussion the budget, which provides for an increase of 68 thousand zł., was adopted.

The assessment (rozkład) will be 52 thousand zł. higher than last year.

—o—

Session of the Hospital Committee

On Sunday the hospital committee, together with Dr. Weinzieher (וויינציהער), held a session at which a series of points concerning the economic state of the Jewish hospital was adopted.

It was resolved to engage the doctors Nunberg [?] and Fanst [?].

The department of internal diseases and the management of the household have been taken over by the chief physician, Weinzieher.

It was also resolved that the premises of the "Beit Yetomim" (orphanage) should pass back into the possession of the hospital.

—o—

"The deeds of the sons are inherited by the fathers"...

The school authority at the local magistrate dealt with 53 charges against parents who had not sent their children to the elementary schools, or who had not taken care that the children attend any school whatsoever.

The verdict was: 37 persons were punished with a fine or arrest, 2 persons with 2 days of unconditional arrest. Dismissed — 4, annulled — 5, and 5 charges were postponed.
The Watches "Walked" Over Here...

[Sosnowiec — crime; accident.] In connection with a series of jewellery thefts in Częstochowa and Upper Silesia, several secret agents arrived here from Częstochowa and Katowice and carried out a search in the jeweller's shop of Mr. Bugajski (בוגייסקי), where articles of jewellery were seized, and Mr. B. was taken away to Katowice, to the investigation office.

During the search Mr. S. Klapfer (קלאפפער) of Dąbrowa was also detained; 4 diamond rings were found on him.

—o—

An accident.

During the shunting of goods trains a worker received a blow, as a result of which he broke a leg.
A Great Fire on Podwale Street — 3 Jewish Families Left Without a Roof · A Car Runs Over a Jewish Girl

[Będzin — chronicle; at the head of the page: an election slogan for the residents of Czeladź.]

[Slogan in large type across the whole page:] Residents of Czeladź, remember to go to the elections on Sunday with a 4 in hand [?]

—o—

A Great Fire on Podwale Street. 3 Jewish Families Left Without a Roof.

On Wednesday at 9 [?] in the evening a fire broke out in the dwelling of Mr. Gelbard at Podwale 13 in Będzin. There was no one in the dwelling at the time, and because of this the fire spread so that within a short time the dwelling, which consisted of a kitchen and a room, stood in flames.

The firemen were notified of the fire, but they did not set to work at once, saying that without a signal from the "siren" they would not come. A little later the firemen did finally arrive and, together with the firemen from Koszelew, put out the fire.

When the firemen had already gone, the fire broke out on another side, and the little houses round about were in danger.

Only thanks to the energetic rescue work of several young people was the fire completely extinguished.

Those who suffered from the fire are the tenants Gelbard, Moszkowicz [?] and Mrs. Hendil Laufer.

The last of these is a "living widow": 15 years ago her husband disappeared and left her with 2 children to their fate.

She has her livelihood from [?] the children, but the fire destroyed her last goods and chattels, and she and the children have been left to their fate.

It is the duty of Jewish society to come to their aid and to provide the unfortunate family with a place of rest.

—o—

A Car Runs Over a Jewish Girl

Yesterday at 12 noon the car of the Klein Brothers in Dąbrowa ran over 11-year-old Blima Grinbaum in Będzin.

The accident happened under the following circumstances.

The car was driving along Małachowskiego Street. As it came up in front of the "Post Office" building, a Gypsy's child was standing in the middle of the road; the child probably did not hear the signal and stayed standing in the middle of the road.

The chauffeur, wishing to avoid the child, swerved to the side and drove hard by the pavement, where a group of schoolchildren from Elementary School No. 4 were walking.

At that moment the schoolgirl Grinbaum was passing, and she received a heavy blow from the car.

Covered in blood, the unfortunate child was taken to the municipal hospital. On the way to the hospital the child was conscious and cried "Mameshi, Mameshi" [Mummy, Mummy]; later, in the hospital, she lost consciousness.

As this issue goes to press we are informed by the hospital that the Jewish schoolgirl has died.

The car was detained, and a report (protokół) was drawn up with the chauffeur.
2,000 German Marks Stolen at the "Darmstädter Bank"

[Będzin — chronicle.] This Tuesday Mr. Friedrich sent a clerk of his to Katowice to collect 5 thousand German marks at the "Darmstädter Bank" there. At the cashier's window, while the clerk was counting the money, there stood an unknown Jewish woman who was ostensibly counting silver coins, and while counting she let several coins drop onto the floor [?]. Hearing the ring of the dropped money, the clerk bent down, and at that moment the woman snatched a packet of two thousand marks and vanished.

On the following day Mr. Pachter came upon an unknown woman in the P.K.O. [the Postal Savings Bank] who looked suspicious. Mr. P. reported it to the police, who arrested the woman.

On the same day that the theft took place, a woman had been in several banks in Będzin, where she wanted to sell German marks. She sold only 1600 [?] marks, in the "Aguda" bank.

For this reason the Katowice police yesterday brought the arrested woman here and went round all the banks with her in order to establish whether she is the same woman who had German marks to sell,

but nothing definite was proved, and the police are continuing their investigation.

—o—

Elections to the Chamber of Commerce.

On 3 March a conference of artisans' delegates will take place here in connection with the elections to the local Chamber of Commerce. According to the earlier [?] agreement, 3 Christians and 1 Jew will be elected to the council.

—o—

A Lecture by Dr. Tsipor.

Tomorrow, Saturday, a lecture will take place in Będzin, in the "Nowości", by the well-known man of letters Dr. Y. B. Tsipor on the subject: "New Art Forms in World Literature and in Yiddish Literature".
Olkusz — From the Court

[Olkusz — court.] At the session of the Sosnowiec District Court, the trial of the 17-year-old J. Feliks, a member of the local needle-trades trade union, and of a certain Żurek, for Communist activity, was held on Tuesday in the local [Olkusz] courthouse. According to the indictment, the accused Feliks met Żurek and gave him several illegal pamphlets.
In the search at Feliks's home the police found illegal items, which were confiscated.
The accused Żurek confirmed that Feliks had handed him the literature to distribute in the village.
The witnesses (mostly policemen) described Feliks as an active worker of the Communist youth. Feliks was defended by the advocate Barczkowski [?] of Sosnowiec. After a lengthy deliberation the court acquitted Feliks and sentenced Żarik [sic; i.e. Żurek] to 3 weeks' fortress confinement.
On the same day the trial took place of the local residents Janek, Świda, Reicher, Kezman [?] and others, for robbing the railway cash office. The court sentenced the accused Janek and Świda to 3 years' imprisonment and acquitted the rest.
Tomorrow a second Communist trial will be held.
—o—
From the coal campaign
The rabbi, may he live long, collected [money] for a wagon of coal and distributed 2–3 korzec [a measure] per family. It is characteristic: some of the wealthy men did not want to give voluntarily, only under compulsion — by having their prayer-shawls withheld in the study house.
A. B.
To Our Esteemed Postal Subscribers

[Publisher's notice — subscriptions.] Our esteemed postal subscribers are requested to pay in the subscription amount on the enclosed postal cheque form, so that we shall not be compelled to interrupt dispatch as of 1 March.
The dispatch office of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".
From the Yiddish Theatre

[Theatre — Sosnowiec and Będzin.] Last week Jonas Turkow staged 2 plays in Sosnowiec and in Będzin: one by the name of "Leidenschaft" ["Passion"], a drama of student life in 3 acts, and the second "Dos glikliche porfolk" ["The Happy Couple"], a comedy in 4 acts.
The first piece, "Passion", is a fairly strong one, and we see there fragments of student life and the most varied original caprices of dissolute youth, which lead to drunkenness and melancholy.
The second piece, by contrast, "The Happy Couple", is indeed a modern comedy but a thoroughly shallow thing; moreover the actors did not find themselves in their roles.
The audience was very dissatisfied — both those who needed to have their "hopke" [a lively dance, i.e. popular entertainment] and those who wanted to see a fine modern operetta. It was noticeable that "The Happy Couple" had been staged in order to fill out the evening... and not so that one should see before one Yiddish artists in their well-rehearsed roles.
There was disorder in the theatre: nobody was shown to a seat, everyone sat down wherever he wished, and the performance began an hour late.
When "comedians" come here and behave like this, we have no complaints against them; but when such talented artists appear as Jonas Turkow and Diana Blumenfeld, who already have merits on behalf of the modernised Yiddish theatre and are attended by intelligent people, it is vexing when people see that artists hold the provinces cheap and treat the spectators to "cheap effects".

[Announcement — Zionists, Będzin.] All persons who wish to provide themselves [?] in good time with tickets and tables for the Eretz Israel Evening can reserve them from Tuesday to Thursday, by telephone or in person, at the Zionist club in Będzin, at 9 Kołłątaja Street, telephone 701, from 6 to 8 in the evening.

What's new in Dąbrowa? — General meeting of the Merchants' Association

What's new in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza]?
General meeting of the „Merchants' Association“.
On Sunday, under the chairmanship of Mr Abraham Neufeld[?], the extraordinary general meeting of the local „Merchants' Association“ took place in the premises of the „Craftsmen's Association“.
The president, Mr Rechnic, described in his report the sad state of the institution, owing to the apathy and indifference of the members, who use the association only when writing appeals (tax appeals).
The secretary, Mr Trefer, gave the treasury report, from which it emerged that the association has a deficit of 700 zł.
A discussion developed over the reports, and those assembled resolved to express no confidence in the board and the council (except the president).
Finally a commission was elected, whose task is to reorganise the association on new foundations within 24 days.
Elected to the commission were Messrs: Abraham Neufeld[?], Dawid Józef Prezerowicz[?] and Jekl Friedman.
Taught a local landlord a „[—]“ (lesson[?])

Taught a local landlord a „[—]“ (lesson[?]).
In the house of Mr Sh. on Szopena Street, the widow Fajgla Berman lived in a little room with her child. Because the „premises“ had become dilapidated, the widow moved for the time being into a stable, until her previous flat would be repaired.
The repair was finished; meanwhile the landlord „forgot“ his promise and let the widow's flat to another tenant, a Christian. Mr Lerfeld and others took an interest in the matter; he intervened with the commissioner Mr Polia-Kapuski[?], who also helped a great deal, so that the landlord had to give several hundred zł. towards a flat for the widow, and for the time being he took her and her child into his own home.
Cheap light

Cheap light.
The local municipal administration [of Dąbrowa] has begun negotiations with the municipal power station in Będzin about supplying electric light to Dąbrowa at the same prices as in Będzin.
The negotiations are going well, and most probably an agreement between the two towns will soon be concluded.
City council takes a loan

City council takes a loan.
The local city council [of Dąbrowa] held two sessions, at which it was resolved to take a loan of 100 thousand zł.
Meeting of the merchants' district council

Meeting of the merchants' district council.
Next Sunday a meeting of the merchants' district council, in which all the Jewish merchants' associations in Zagłębie are represented, will take place in the premises of the Będzin „Merchants' Association“.
Among other things, the question of protesting against the plan to raise the rent of business premises will also be discussed.
—o—
A loan of 300 thousand zł.
The Sosnowiec city president, Dr Marczyński[?], has gone to Warsaw about a loan of 300 thousand zł.
With this sum the magistrate will buy shares of the power station in Małobądz.
—o—
Reserves of butter and eggs in Zagłębie.
The Ministry of the Interior has drawn up a plan to create reserves of butter and eggs in the industrial regions of Poland, among them also Zagłębie, where, according to the number of the general population, stocks of eggs and butter are to be prepared that must suffice for the winter months.
Per person, 10 eggs and half a kilo of butter will be reckoned.
—o—
A robbery in Katowice.
On Wednesday at 7 in the evening, when Mrs Gertruda Danel was near the P.K.O. building on Mickiewicza Street, she was attacked by a bandit, who struck her on the head with a blunt object, from which she fell down on the pavement.
Then the bandit robbed her of 3,485 zł. and vanished.
