Annual General Meeting of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association in Sosnowiec

(Sh.) The annual general meeting of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association, which took place last Saturday night (motzei Shabbat), drew a larger number of members and aroused great interest. The debates were very heated, so that one might have thought the meeting was about to break up; only thanks to the chairman did tempers calm down, and the meeting was brought peacefully to its end.
As temporary president of the association, Mr. Lejzerowicz opens the meeting and invites Mr. Kac to chair it, and as assessors Messrs. Rozman[?], Gelibter and Kenigsberg as secretary. After approval of the agenda, Mr. Kwiatek takes the floor for the report for the year 1928. Before delivering the report Mr. K. makes a statement that, despite the accepted custom that a board which is in resignation does not deliver reports, he nevertheless considers it his moral duty to give a report. It turns out that in 1928 there were 10 board meetings, and the secretariat handled 50 appeals with a certain success. As one of the most important points of the work — so the speaker holds — was the board's initiative to convene in April of this year [sic, 'f. y.'] a merchants' rally, whose task was to protest against the excessively high assessment of the turnover tax. Jewish and Christian merchants took part in the rally, as did delegations of the Częstochowa and Radom merchants' associations. The resolutions adopted, in very sharp form, were sent to the [?] tax office, to the Kielce Fiscal Chamber (Izba Skarbowa) and to the Ministry of Finance. The Warsaw Head Council, seeing the merits of the association, assigned it a place in the Upper Council; the Head Council also intervened so that a merger would come about between the two merchants' associations existing in our town, but through the fault of that other merchants' association (Piłsudskiego 12) the merger did not happen. In November a conference of all[?] the lawyers attached to the merchants' organisations took place in Warsaw, in which the association's director Dr. Oder also took part; he helped to a great extent in drafting an amendment to the turnover-tax law. The treasury report is given by Dr. Oder. Before presenting the report Dr. Oder makes a statement analogous to that of President Mr. Kwiatek, on account of which an uproar breaks out. The representatives of the opposition, Messrs. Safer, Tencer and Lejzerowicz, protest against this, because if a president may make such a statement, an office manager must by no means do so, since he is only an employee and by reading out the report he does nobody any favour. After the chairman's explanation people calm down and proceed to deal with the further points of the agenda. Here, however, an unexpected violent storm arose. It was about this: President Kwiatek takes the floor once more and demands that the assembly grant the old board an absolutorium. The opposition speaks out against this, starting from the position that after a vote of no confidence in the board had been expressed at the last meeting, no absolutorium can now be granted. Messrs. Tencer, Rozman, Kabak, Safer, Lubelski and others take part in the heated discussion. The chairman, seeing that there will be no end to it, puts Mr. Kwiatek's motion to the vote — and here it turns out that the twenty-odd newly joined members take part in the vote and vote against. The old board challenges [printed 'konstatiert', 'states'] their right to vote; Mr. Tencer, however, points out that according to the statute every member has the right to vote. The uproar grows ever greater and the chairman is forced to call several members to order. When things calm down a little, Mr. Jurenheric[?] takes the floor and says that the opposition used various 'tricks' (sztuczki) to strengthen the opposition, and for this purpose recruited new members. Such systems were once practised in 'Linat haCholim' (all of it, of course, in Polish). The speaker gets a fitting answer from Mr. Tencer, who says that he has not yet forgotten the days of the beit midrash; Mr. Jurenherc may well have forgotten it already, because he counts himself among the better society. Mr. Szpigel also speaks, who incidentally is also a new member, and demands voting rights for the new members. His speech, which was full of humour, somewhat calmed the overheated debaters. The whole 'storm in a glass of water' ended with the assembly granting by acclamation the demanded absolutorium to the old board. On the point of amending paragraph 11 of the statute Mr. Tencer reports; he points out that the amendment should take the form that 7 members be elected to the board and not 11 as hitherto. The speaker also proposes creating sections for all trades. Then the election of a board is held, with the following result: Kwiatek, Tencer, Kabak, Safer, Jurenherc, Lejzerowicz and Krumer. As deputies: Rozman, Szpigelman, Wajner and Lidzbarski[?]. Audit committee: Kac, Gelibter and Kenigsberg. Finally Mr. Kwiatek is elected an honorary member of the association, and at about 4 a.m. the meeting is closed.
The Eretz Israel Evening

Hardly were the great 'Keren Hayesod' days over, hardly had the housewarming of the Zionist premises been celebrated — and again last week we had a small Eretz-Israel attraction.
The long-announced Palestine evening, which took place last Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) in the hall of 'Góra Zamkowa' [printed 'Nora'] and was dedicated to the organised Jewish worker in Eretz Israel, showed with its numerous audience how great the interest in the national ideal is among the broad Jewish public.
The large hall, splendidly decorated by the painter Sh.[?] Altusz Winer and Abraham Erlich, was overflowing with people, and a very great number had to leave, being unable to obtain admission tickets.
The atmosphere was homely and genuinely Jewish. The sound of Hebrew, the pioneer songs and the 'Hora' dance brought in an Eretz-Israel mood.
The evening, which had a [?] fine programme, is opened by Mr. Mordechai Erlich with a short speech in Hebrew and Yiddish, in which he points out the heroic deeds of the Jewish worker in Eretz Israel, who remained loyal at his post regardless of the last hard crisis years.
Mr. Erlich calls for active work for the Halutz, who is building the Jewish home.
Miss Jasna of Sosnowiec recites very successfully a fragment by the poet Shimonovitz and sings very beautifully 'Yad anugah' by Shneour and the Yiddish folk song 'Der kremer' (The Shopkeeper).
The pianist Miss Har-Kochav performs several musical pieces by the composers Liszt and Chopin. Both the singer and the pianist are rewarded with applause.
10 comrades join hands and, under special spotlights, a 'Hora' is danced with great enthusiasm and Hasidic fervour to the accompaniment of 'Mi yivneh et ha-Galil' and 'Kakha kakha nirkoda'. The dancers, among whom Miss Szarf particularly distinguished herself, are warmly applauded.
The onlookers at the side are carried away, link arms over the shoulders, push their way into the dance circle, and also 'snatch' a little Eretz-Israel dance.
Until 6 in the morning the crowd enjoyed itself over a bottle of 'Carmel' wine and Eretz-Israel and 'European' dances.
The main thing: the evening passed with an enormous moral and material success, thanks to the good organisation and exemplary order.
M. H.

Zawiercie.
Activity of the Free-Loan Fund.
One of the less well-known, yet nevertheless most important institutions in the town is without doubt the Gemilut Hesed (free-loan) fund.
In the course of its existence, i.e. over a period of 14 months, the G.H. fund has given out loans in sums of up to 300 zł to 684 families. The total sum of the loans amounts to approximately 100,000 zł. The fund has its own capital of 20,000 zł, deposits (wkłady) which people lend to it without interest, and in addition 10,000 zł from the “Joint”. The fund is housed in its own building, in a very fine premises, and all this came about through the initiative of a few little-“patented” (not prominent) communal workers headed by Mr Yosef Liberman.
This important institution would have achieved much more if its capital were larger, for hundreds of families (as I am told) go away without loans because the fund does not have the necessary capital. And if the “notables” had supported such an important institution, such an institution could do much more for our helpless brethren, so that they could maintain their livelihoods.
It is therefore to be hoped that the Jews of Zawiercie in general, and the more well-to-do in particular, will in future too know how to value properly the importance of the G.H. fund and fulfil the commandment of acts of loving-kindness.

Housing Tax and Cheap Dwellings

[Poland and Będzin — housing tax and housing; editorial.]
(What can the projects lead to, and how should the painful question really be solved?)
At last the government has recognised how bad the situation is; at long last people here have come to the conviction that one cannot go on living in Poland under the prevailing conditions. The government had imagined that the housing hunger would somehow resolve itself, and so it did not lift a finger (literally: "did not put its hand into cold water"). But time has shown us, and at the same time the government too, that one cannot go on living like this; that every citizen must have somewhere to lay his head, must have a roof over his head, a place to rest his bones after hard day-to-day work.
True, here and there a little is being built in Poland, but how hard it comes, and who benefits — apart from the rich, of course — from building of the kind where one must own a fortune to get a flat in such a house? What use does such building bring the broad masses of the people, who cannot even dream of getting in such a building even the smallest little room? How, then, is the housing hunger to be stilled for the average citizens and the artisans, who at best earn their daily keep? Can a people live in such a condition? Does it benefit the state, the citizens, hygiene, the development and the health of a people? Perhaps here they have paused over all this; perhaps they have realised that living like this is impossible and sometimes leads to worse consequences that a country must reckon with; perhaps they have begun to look at the European states, where the poorest live in better housing conditions than the average citizen here.
But be that as it may, the government has apparently undertaken to solve the question, and, as we see, in the "high windows" it is meant seriously and sincerely; but the system is not a good one. For this purpose they want to raise the price of flats and shops, and incidentally the landlords of the houses will also profit from the surcharge — though for them it will nonetheless be no easy matter to run the administration of the houses then. But the question arises: from whom will the money for building the flats be taken? From average and quite small people, who live in rather cramped flats? So it is from the very people who cannot get any decent flat that they want to obtain the fund for building houses? Is this how they want to solve such a painfully felt question? It is simply incomprehensible. Can one take money for building houses from people who themselves are unable to get the kind of flat they need? Is this how cheap houses for the people are to be created?
Without any doubt modern people's houses must be built in the country, intended for the use of those who cannot get a flat being built in private houses. Do they want to build these houses by this system? Can the goal be reached in this way? Does it not mean that the average citizen will thereby reach the point of being evicted even from the small flat he already has? We know, after all, that the people will not be able to pay the projected flat-money; moreover, as usual with taxes, there will be a series of fines for not paying by the exact deadline; then, presumably, interest with penalties "for zwłoka" [delay] will be added, so that to the tax troubles we have had until today a fresh tax will be added, which will embrace all strata of the population, and the tax will be called "dira-gelt" (flat-money).
Certainly people's dwellings must be built in the country, and this work belongs unconditionally[?] to the government, which has every possibility of doing much in this field. But the fund must be created from other sources, which should not touch the citizens — in any case not the average and middling ones, let alone the small ones.
A government has the possibility of obtaining various revenues for this fund. Today's poor little Austria, after all, has built entire quarters for the broad strata of the population, whose buildings are to be admired when one looks at them. Whole towns have been created there that one must be delighted by — how splendidly and methodically the streets have been laid out, how fine, modern and airy these houses have been built. And this came from an ordinary housing tax that the government levies on house owners, so that with all this a flat costs a trifle. The Austrian government has worked wonders in this field, and if a small poor state could create so much without touching the inhabitants of the country, the present large and rich Polish Republic can surely, surely achieve much.
Yet it remains incomprehensible why a government wants to build dwellings for the citizens in such a way that soon everything in the country will become abnormal, that soon there will be dearness of everything; for when the official and the worker have to pay surcharges on their flats, they will demand higher salaries, which in turn will make products dearer, and so one thing will depend on the other, and the vicious ("witches'") wheel will keep turning from one to the next, so that life and the means of existence will soon become harder — and how will one then be able to dream of anything better and finer, when existence itself begins to totter? Why make life still harder, when the struggle for existence is complicated enough even today?
* * *
In all the newspapers of the whole Polish Republic this serious question is treated with full seriousness. The tenants' associations are calling consultations and conferences, which adopt protest resolutions that it must not be allowed to come to the realisation of the projects being laid before the Sejm.
In this connection a congress will also take place here next Sunday, the 10th of this month, which the Będzin "Tenants' Association" is calling for the Kielce voivodeship. The burning question has been placed on the agenda and will be treated with full sincerity and sense of duty for the good of the citizens of the country, and various resolutions will surely be adopted, which will be sent on to the proper authorities.
The Kielce voivodeship is the richest and almost the largest in Poland, so the government must reckon with the resolutions that will be adopted at such a congress. Care should therefore be taken that the question be unfolded there in its full extent, and that the logical arguments be voiced before as large a number of those present as possible, for, after all, one must reckon with Zagłębie in general and with the whole Kielce voivodeship in particular.
L. Sz.[?]
Floods.

"Flood" — that is the second frightening word, which has come after "coal".
This year Europe fears a terrible flood. Telegrams from the Balkan countries signal that the new catastrophe is approaching. And last year's experience in England, where several suburbs of London stood under water, proves that even the most cultured countries cannot properly protect themselves against such natural catastrophes as floods.
The overflow of the river "Karen"[?] [probably the Garonne] in 1875 caused France damage of 40 million francs. Several suburbs were completely destroyed and dozens of villages were wiped off the face of the earth.
During the flood in Holland in 1634, 7000 people drowned. No flood up to now can compare with the flood "Kangez"[?] [place name garbled; perhaps the Ganges or a Chinese river], where 300,000 people perished.
In Europe, and especially in Poland, people are very much afraid of a flood in the coming spring. Our spring floods always depend on the amount of snow that has accumulated during the winter months, and on the way the snow melts under the warmth of the spring sun. The more snow lies on the fields, the stronger the current in the river afterwards, and the higher the water rises even in the smallest stream — and this year we have certainly had heavy enough snowfalls.
And for one more reason the danger of flooding is so great. This year the snow fell only at the end of winter, at a time when the fields had already been covered with ice for long weeks. The earth will therefore not be able to soak up the water of the melted snow, because under the snow lies ice, which will not feel the sun's rays so quickly; thus the water, instead of going into the fields, will run off into the rivers.
One stroke of luck could happen: that the temperature does not grow warmer suddenly but very slowly. If that does not happen, and on top of it rain begins to fall, it may come to an enormous catastrophe. The towns lying in the lowlands by the rivers will be completely flooded.
The government authorities and the communal associations are making preparations to stand up against the flood. But if the disaster is great, all these preparations will help little.
■ ■ ■
The End of the World Already

[Feuilleton — science and technology, Soviet Union.]
Leo Koenig.
(Feuilleton)
A certain Russian inventor by the name of Zlotnikov has devised a new affliction for mankind (not for nothing do some wise men keep insisting that all troubles come from Russia) — a new evil wonder. Namely, he has found a means, by way of a wireless apparatus, to make all clocks run exactly right, to the minute and to the second...
All clocks — town clocks, wall clocks and pocket watches — are to run exactly right to the minute and to the second...
I imagine what a terrible thing it will be for mankind when all clocks run alike and all the "hands" point, at all hours of the day and night, to the very same little mark on the dial.
By nature I am no great believer in utopias, but of all utopias I always imagined that all clocks running alike was the least realizable utopian utopia..
It is so rare to find two clocks that show the same minutes and seconds; in every house where there are only a couple of clocks there are already different times.
You often go out into the street and you wonder: you come across clocks that take no account of your pace and show you the very time at which you left your home..
Have you ever been in a watch shop and found all the clocks there showing the time precisely? There are, it seems, no more anarchist-individualist institutions in the world than watch shops or factories; every clock there shows its own hour, quarter-hour and minute.
And whoever wants for once to know the correct time does not go to the window of a watchmaker or a watch shop to find out. In a watch shop I always have the impression of a madhouse: all the clocks are going, all are ticking, all wag their long tongues, all lash out with their finger-hands. And all these "wise" time-pointers point to a different hour and a different minute.
Just as if you found yourself in a madhouse or, to make the distinction, in a company of philosophers, where every one thinks that he alone is original and knows the true secret of world and time.
—
Clocks have played an enormous role in modern culture. I often have the impression that many philosophers, poets and, to make the distinction, "cracked" people were once watchmakers, or used to stare too much at clocks.
Our pious grandfathers, when they wanted to prove to us that "there is a God in the world", used mostly to argue with the clock: "Here, take the clock," they would say, "would it go if one didn't wind it?"
Who does not know of our small-town philosophers and mechanics who, with a special mania, would want to take clocks apart and pull out all their innermost springs and guts.
And in general everyone looked upon "his" watch as a kind of atlas, as a miniature globe... and each one's watch always showed each one's time, each one's world, although in truth they all ought, by law and by reason, to have shown one time — everybody's time.
—
The clock was also a symbol of human inequality, of human individualism. Almost like people's "fingerprints", their watches never matched one another.
All clocks are set alike, and yet each of them goes its own particular pace, with a particular beat. From the mechanical clock certain pessimistic philosophers concluded that equality among people is impossible.
See — they argued — even "set instruments", even mechanisms cannot run alike; how then do you expect all people to be equal?
And very rightly did a writer in "The Times" (in a splendid leading article) point to the terrible blow that this new Russian invention will deal to all our intimate habits, to our whole psychology.
One will not be able to turn the clocks back out of spite, one will not be able to excuse oneself by the clocks, to throw the blame on the watch for being late.. One will not even be master of one's own waistcoat pocket and of the little watch lying hidden there in the dark; your private, intimate watch will have to tick in step with the town clock, and should you want to reset it — you won't be able to.. The wireless apparatus in the town council will correctly set the watch lying in your pocket, the clock standing at your bedside in the bedroom, and it won't help you however much you may want to turn them back...
Now — the proud claims, questions and excuses: what time does your watch say? Yours is wrong... my watch shows the right time...
All those old, dear little chats will have to perish...
I do not know whether a bourgeois-capitalist government would not issue a patent for Zlotnikov's invention. I imagine that the European individualist societies too would not forbid it if one came to them with the invention that will make "all clocks run alike".
But it is surely characteristic and symbolic that this invention should be made now in Soviet Russia. They want, they say, all people to be of equal lineage; well, there you are, you bourgeois individualists — an apparatus that will make all clocks run alike to the minute and to the second...
And it may well be that this invention will mechanize and communize our lives and our psychology more than the various socialist experiments they have made and are making.. That they have already taken on the clock itself — that really is "the end of the world".
Communal Poverty

(The state of our institutions in general. What do the Talmud Torah and the town synagogue look like?)

When it comes to elections — whatever elections they may be, to the kehilla or to the city council, or when it is a matter of a rabbi — people climb onto tables and benches, one wants to annihilate the other, one party wants to uproot the other completely; but all these shouters are wished "a good journey": the morning after the elections everything is hush-quiet, everything is back in order, just as if nothing had happened yesterday.
So it has always been with us in Sosnowiec. I do not know whether to count this as a virtue or as a fault. One can say that it is quite good this way: what was, was; people quarrelled, cursed each other out, whatever one had to say to the other he said, and afterwards they are good friends again and nobody bears a grudge against anyone. Another looks at all this differently. It is true, he says, that no one bears a grudge against the other, but that still gives no reassurance[?] that such a tactic is sound. How is it — says the second one — that we have such a cat's brain that we suddenly forget what happened yesterday? Here people fought for life and death, for existence and ruin, and one day later they no longer want to know why they strained so much strength, why they spent so much energy.
At the given moment we are not interested in whether this is a virtue or a fault. It is a fact that the day after the elections everything is forgotten and everyone goes back to his own occupation — and this is what causes our communal institutions to stand at such a low level and to become, in everyone's eyes, a kind of ownerless thing: whoever wants comes and takes it, and when he wants he throws it away, and nobody can come and tell him: stop! The object is not at everyone's disposal; not everyone may touch it whenever he likes, and not everyone should be able to throw it away[?] at any time and have no obligation whatsoever towards it.
Just such an impression was made on me by the local Talmud Torah when I looked it over. A fine building, free space, a large yard with a garden, splendidly suited for a Talmud Torah; the premises — high, beautiful, airy rooms; there is room to breathe. But God, my God, to what state has this beautiful building been brought? What has become of this people's building? I have the impression that whoever did not know the building as it once was cannot grasp with his mind at all what has become of it. It is in no way possible to recognise the present neglected building in comparison with the former one.
Is it then so easy for us to acquire such huge buildings that we can allow ourselves to destroy them? Is the board of the Talmud Torah not committing a crime by having allowed the institution to be brought to its present state? Who and what profits from this dark situation? And in what condition are both the pupils and the melamdim there? The situation there is so sad that it is better, and perhaps also healthier, not to speak at all — so long as there is no intention of radically changing everything for the good of the pupils and the melamdim, in a way that would at the same time bring honour and benefit to the Jewish population of the town.
Can such a people's institution, as a Talmud Torah ought to be, be run any further under the prevailing circumstances? Can the town take an interest in the institution under the prevailing conditions?!
The town synagogue ("di shtotishe shul") is in a not much better state. For quite a long time now they began renovating this holy place, but beyond beginning they have not gone. And so, in the middle of the work, people pray in the synagogue and have forgotten that a renovation was begun — and it is a disgrace to leave a holy place in such a neglected condition.
Respected householders of the town always pray in that synagogue — so why should these householders not take an interest in having the synagogue renovated properly, as befits a community such as Sosnowiec?!
Only now has the kehilla board put into its budget a sum of 8000 zł. in total for renovating the synagogue — but when will they have the sum? One must surely see to it that the synagogue is finally completed and does not remain in its present state. And, by the way: what kind of renovation can be carried out for these 8000 zł.? One must not forget that the local synagogue needs a thorough renovation, which cannot be done merely for form's sake. And if no consideration[?] whatsoever is taken and it is done only to get it over with, it will turn out more expensive, because in a year or two it will have to be renovated once again.
One must therefore remember that a synagogue is not a private flat; so many, so very many people come there daily. A synagogue is open to everyone and is therefore also more worn, for which reason a thorough, massive renovation is required; moreover one must not forget that it is a synagogue, which must also be made aesthetic and with style — so that 8000 zł. for this purpose is a ridiculous sum.
If our sister-town Będzin could afford such a renovation that its synagogue was placed in the same rank as other beautiful synagogues, we too can afford the same.
One must not forget that it often happens that the authorities come into the synagogue — let us not, at such a moment, have to blush with shame.
Every effort must be made to apply all means so that the renovation of the synagogue is carried out properly, so that after its completion one may feel that one is in a holy place.
It is high time that we no longer remain indifferent to all our institutions. We are poor in communal institutions as it is — let them at least see to it that the synagogue is renovated properly. Let us bear in mind that even the smallest shtetl has a decent synagogue; let us at least measure up to the small shtetls.
When a stranger arrives and wants to get acquainted with our capabilities, he goes to visit the communal institutions, and by that yardstick he measures our communal maturity — it goes without saying that by that measure he will find nothing at all among us...
Dr. Papuri[?].
Ersatz

[Zagłębie — satirical feuilleton.] (Short feuilleton)
Once there was a war; the German occupied our region and brought in a new word — "Ersatz".
Instead of bread he fed us ersatz bread. Instead of meat — ersatz meat, instead of butter — ersatz butter; in a word — the whole of life became an ersatz.
What is this thing, ersatz? In our language it would be called — "as if", "almost", surrogate, but none of these words took root with us the way ersatz did.
That is exactly why we cannot shake this word off, and now, already more than ten years after the war, we still cling to ersatz.
And the further it goes, the greater a ruler ersatz becomes — it penetrates deeper and deeper into our life and takes over every field: politics and economy, literature and art — everywhere it is the master of the house.
Can you deny that our politics, both the general Jewish and the local, we conduct according to an ersatz method?
Can we achieve anything with the Jewish "majority" in the city council — once again ersatz.
About the kehilla, again. It is already agreed that it is the true ersatz.
And our businesses?
Which Jewish merchant today is not an ersatz merchant?
And our modern art? And the modern theatre?
And I will tell you a secret — why should I talk about me, about you, about others — that Her Majesty Nature herself, in person, has also acquired a weakness for ersatz.
In the month of Grudzień [December] it is warm, and at the end of Adar — 30 degrees of frost.
It is ersatz, and nothing more.
Only one thing, you see, is not ersatz with us — the taxes!
Taxes — we pay no ersatz taxes at all, and Jewish troubles are no ersatz troubles at all.
On the contrary, they are more genuine than genuine.
Apparently it is such a fateful game, there is no cheating in the world — if the winter is not a genuine one, then the mud is genuine...
If your earnings are small, pay big taxes for it!
If your life is empty, then the cup of your troubles is full!
That is the new system — according to the ersatz rite...
Onkelos.
Einstein and Trotsky

[Feuilleton — Jews and the world; essay.] Pini the Wordsmith.
Two names with which the world now rings from end to end.
And at first glance, it would seem, there is no connection whatsoever ("smikhut ha-parsha") between the two of them.
On the contrary — the first is ever more exalted, and the second ever more fallen.
Einstein [Albert Einstein] already wants to hide, so that nobody can find him, because he is tired of praise and enthusiastic applause.
Trotsky [Leon Trotsky], poor man, wants to show himself to the world, so that everyone should see him, but they do not let him, and they want to banish him to where not even a bird could reach him.
But when we remember that these two are both Jews, and we start to look at them with Jewish eyes — then we do find a connection between them.
They themselves did indeed mean to perform their deeds for the world not as Jews, but as human beings.
The world, however, regards these deeds not as those of human beings, but of Jews.
Einstein and Trotsky — two revolutionaries.
The first wants to make a revolution in the world of the spirit.
The second wants to make a revolution in the world of the body.
And the world already calls this "Einsteinism" and "Trotskyism".
Heaven and earths
And it is no news to us that the world grants us as much "heaven" as we ourselves could wish, but when it comes to "earth", there they won't let us take a single extra step...
— — —
Jews are known as the people of the air, the people that lives off air and in the air.
And not because we are like that by nature, but simply because we had no other choice.
The world decided for itself that the "earth" is theirs, and drove us out of earthly life by force, so we had to create an airy life for ourselves.
And that is why the world grants us our "men of heaven": and even our "heavenly revolutionaries".
And when a Spinoza comes along, or a Bergson [Henri Bergson], who clamber up into the high heavens and make an upheaval in the world of ideas, then, regardless of their being Jews, the world receives them with honour and they are praised to the skies.
And when an Einstein comes and creates a theory of "relativity", and another theory of lofty mathematical calculations about some "force of attraction", the world carries him around on its hands.
For what does the world care, and what does it stand to lose, if some little Jew busies himself there in the high, clever worlds?
On the contrary, if it really is an achievement from which the world can gain something, then surely all the better; and if not — let the little Jew addle his own head.
After all, since time immemorial even the greatest haters and oppressors of the Jews liked to keep a court Jew by their side, with whom they always took counsel and whom they could send on an important mission.
The little Jew himself did indeed starve to death with them, with the lords, but the Jewish head they loved...
Now all the newspapers all over the world have written whole heaps about Einstein's achievement, and people have already fantasised that it may yet come out of it that one day people will be able to stride through the air and not fall down — and everyone was overjoyed.
A mere trifle! The world would then have had a totally different face, and besides, the one world would then have become two worlds, an "earth-world" and an "air-world".
In short, the world thinks highly of our heaven-men!
— — —
But on the other hand, when it comes to the earth, there the world can no longer bear our "earth-men", and certainly not our "earth-revolutionaries".
Our "Ten Commandments", which teach how to conduct oneself on earth — of those the world does not think so highly.
Our prophets, who teach how man to man and nation to nation should behave on earth — they are not at all so welcome to the world.
If a Karl Marx arose among us, who wanted to teach a little justice — the world throws this disgrace in our faces at every opportunity.
Other Jews, who at various times of world history gave their lives for the good of mankind — their names are not even mentioned, as if they had never existed.
And everywhere, all over the world, if a Jew has done something good for a country, they will not even mention that he is a Jew.
But on the contrary, if a Jew sins, they will ring all the bells that the little Jew brings every misfortune...
— — —
The same is now the case in Russia with the Trotsky affair too.
However much we may disagree with Trotsky's theory and with his deeds, the fact remains a fact that he was no lesser friend of Russia than his comrade Lenin.
Both came and risked their lives for the good of the country, according to their doctrines and ideas.
Both of them liberated the Russian people from bondage and wanted to create for it a paradise on earth.
Be it that they made a mistake — the mistake was made by both of them and by their entire company.
And nevertheless — Lenin, the gentile, with all his faults, has remained a saint for them to this very day, and Trotsky, the Jew, has fallen into the nethermost pit.
And what is more, his own comrades, his own people, who made use of the "Jewish head" all the time, now want to drown him in a spoonful of water.
And it has come to the point that they cannot tolerate him even on Russian soil, and they dressed him up Turkish-style and packed him off to the devil [an allusion to Trotsky's deportation to Turkey in February 1929].
Even the gentile revolutionaries cannot bear the Jewish "earth-revolutionary".
That is how it is even in the high windows, and of the "common people" there is no need to speak. We read about it in the newspapers every day.
— — —
Two names with which the whole world now rings.
And these two names tell us a great deal.
Because they are two names of two Jews.
And this is not Einstein and not Trotsky, but "Einsteinism" and "Trotskyism".
Spirit and body, heaven and earth.
The "heaven" the world grants us. But the "earth" — a "no" with a fur hat on [i.e. an emphatic no], the earth they want for themselves. Jews have no right to it.
An eternal question, a story without end...
The Rebbe's Son (24)

[Serialized historical novel — Kraków, Ajzyk Jekeles and the treasure of the dream; installment 24.]
A historical Jewish novel by Yakov Zimmerman.

"Well, now, Esther my life!" Ajzyk began to speak. "Now you will surely believe in dreams — and just as Joseph the Righteous became viceroy over the land of Egypt through a dream, so too will Ajzyk Jekeles very soon become the richest man in all of Kraków."

"What do you intend to do in order to come by this wealth?" Esther asked. She simply wanted to sound Ajzyk out about what foolishness he meant to commit now.

"What do you mean? It's not hard at all, and there's not much work in it. I'll tear down the oven and take the hidden treasure out of it!..."

"And if you find nothing there?" Esther answered, shaking her head. "What will happen then? Who can promise you that because of it we won't lose our livelihood? Ajzyk, Ajzyk, Ajzyk! You talked yourself into a foolishness with your empty dream. With that foolishness you went away, and with an even greater one you have come back home. Listen to me: give up all these empty things, go back to your work instead, and you will see that the Holy One, blessed be He, will send you His blessing, you will prosper, and we will take in far more than we do now.

"Your journey to Warsaw, which was certainly foolish and in vain, cost me a fortune. Because of it I had to sell the last piece of jewellery I had inherited from my mother, may she rest in peace. But that, I think, is quite enough for your foolish dream. I will not allow your homecoming from Warsaw to cost me now the baking oven and our livelihood as well — the oven is mine, the little house is mine! And because I am a faithful and devoted wife to you, I am now, for the first time since we have lived together, making such a claim on my property, for I do not want us to be ruined over foolish and empty dreams.

"By the happiness of our only child I swear — and you know, Ajzyk, that I always keep my word even without an oath — that as long as I live you will not tear down the oven for the sake of a dream you have talked yourself into!..."

Ajzyk sat silent and as if utterly broken; he could not utter a word now. He knew his Esther well and knew what a strong and stubborn character she had, and that once she says no, it must always stay that way. But the dream of the treasure would not leave him for a single minute; he felt within himself that his fortune was so near — just reach out a hand and take as much as the heart desires — and yet because of the stubborn whim of a Jewish woman he would never get to it...

Ajzyk — and Esther too — still sat sunk in heavy, sad thoughts. Meanwhile a knock was heard at the door, and at once there appeared on the threshold the very person who had a good deal to do with Ajzyk's dream... — Dudl, the son of the Rabbi of Kraków, R' Yom Tov Lipman Heller...

"I have come now," he began after a short greeting, "to take leave of you here. You probably know that I have joined those hundreds of young men from our town who are now going to war against our enemy. It is, as it seems, for quite a long time. And so I felt it was my duty to say goodbye to all of you here and to thank you for your care of me when I had that accident a few days ago."

Blumele simply could not contain herself for so much happiness and pain. On her pretty face the colours kept changing: one moment she was pale and white, and the next she turned red as crimson again. But her lips were as if sealed, so that she could not utter a single word.

"Happy are you," Esther said now, "that you are able to go and help our brothers and that you can put your life in danger for the sake of our faith and our people. The Holy One, blessed be He, will surely be with you, and you will soon come home again safe and sound, in peace. Happy is your mother, who bore such a son, and happy will be the girl who will one day have the privilege of becoming your wife. May all the good angels accompany you on your way and guard you from all evil. We count ourselves fortunate and thank you for remembering us and coming to say goodbye to us. If only it were possible for us to be with you and protect you from all the dangers you will surely have to go through..."

"I'll do it!" Ajzyk now cried out. "Yes, yes! I am going with you to the war! I am a baker; the soldiers need bread, and I will help provide it. Esther, Blumele! Do you agree to it?"

"With pleasure!" Esther cried.

Blumele, who still could not speak, now found her tongue. She fell on her father's neck and in a weeping voice [printed "veygndikn"] cried out:

"Do it, dear father! And may God stand by all of you!.."

Some two days later several hundred Jewish soldiers marched out through the gates of Kraków. Among them were also our acquaintances Chaim the carter and Ajzyk Jekeles. Dudl had stuck a fresh, blooming rose in his lapel, and when, together with the others, he marched past Ajzyk's little house and noticed Blumele standing on the threshold, a handkerchief in her hand, wiping her eyes, he bent down to the rose and raised it to his lips...

— — — — — — — — — — — —

A splendid summer evening descended over the old city of Kraków. All day it had been very hot, and the sun had burned and roasted without any mercy, as if it wanted to show what it could do. But now, in the evening, a refreshing little breeze was blowing and had cooled and freshened up the overheated public quite a bit.

After a day of hard, strenuous work Esther sat outside next to her little house. Her thoughts were far, far away with her Ajzyk, of whom she had had no news at all for a long time. She also thought a good deal about her only child, her Blumele, who lately went about so lost in thought and so worried. There she comes out of the house right now — it is frightening to look at the child. One can hardly recognise her, and no one would believe that this is really the always so cheerful and merry Blumele... What can become of a person...

Since the day Dudl had marched past here and she had seen him kissing with his lips the rose she had given him, she had become someone else entirely. She had completely lost her former cheerfulness and always went about gloomy and worried. Nothing at all interested her, she spoke little, and all her senses were bent on one single thought: "He loves me!"

Often she even felt happy and her heart danced when she reflected on the great privilege that "the handsomest, best and noblest of all people" loved her. But soon she fell into great grief when she pictured the great dangers in which he constantly found himself.

And not only by day was the girl so pensive and worried, but even more at night, tossing sleepless on her bed. She kept thinking about him: whether he was still alive, and whether the sword or an enemy's gun had not already put an end to his young life; and perhaps he was now even worse off: he had fallen into the hands of the wild and inhuman Cossacks and Haidamaks, and they had found out who and what he was, and that by his example many thousands of Jews had joined Prince Wiśniowiecki's soldiers, and therefore they would take special revenge on him and torture him with terrible cruelty.. It was enough to drive one mad... Who could endure such constant torments of the spirit?...

Blumele stood lost in thought beside her mother and looked up at the sky and the stars. She was so saddened that she did not hear her mother ask her twice already to sit down beside her.

"Blumele, my child," Esther took her by the hand, "sit down beside me..."

Blumele now complied with her mother's request; she wiped the tears from her eyes and silently sat down beside her mother.

"My daughter!" Esther began in a quiet voice. "For several weeks now I have seen you going about always so worried and lost in thought. What is the matter with you? What are you suffering from? Why are you silent? And why do you shake your head? A mother cannot be fooled... You may hide it from the whole world, but a mother's eye can never be mistaken... No, my child, don't behave like this; be sincere and keep no secrets at all from me. If something lies on your heart, tell it to me. Talk it out a little and you will see that it will become easier for you; if only I can help you — let us at least share your sorrow a little.."

"You don't need that, dear mother! Leave me alone... Have you too few griefs of your own, that I should burden you with my foolishness?..."

Blumele even steeled herself and held back enough not to burst out crying. But it did not help her at all. Her feelings were stronger than she was. She began to tremble, she shook all over as if in a fever, and broke out into bitter weeping.

"I understood it at once," said Sarah [so printed; read: Esther] as if to herself, "my heart told me that it is not mere longing for her father that has so oppressed the girl's heart; she always has another soul on her mind, one that is so dear and precious to her, perhaps even more than her own father..."

Where Is Professor Voronoff?

[Feuilleton — humoresque.]
(Humoresque).
By Y. Weinstein.

You don't happen to know where I can find Professor Voronoff [Serge Voronoff, the surgeon famous for "rejuvenation" by monkey-gland grafts]?
Oh, I need him like life itself.
I am ready to pay the biggest sums, just to track down the famous professor.
You laugh? You surely think I need an operation? Then, begging your pardon, you are badly mistaken. Would that all my good friends, together with you, were — no harm to me — in as fine a state as I am. Are you playing games with me! Five little children, no evil eye, besides the two daughters already married off; the son, who is now a soldier, and the divorced one, who now lives in France.
So what is it, then?
My mother-in-law — may she at last have her bright Garden of Eden...
I have a mother-in-law — so I have one, never mind, it is after all an act of God... like measles, smallpox, toothache, typhus, cholera and the like. When God wills, one falls ill with a mother-in-law, that is, you yourself don't know how or when.
Only suddenly you get up with a... mother-in-law... and that's it — lost.
I would have bowed my head and suffered like thousands of other young men; after all, I am not the only one at the fair — there are other Jews punished by God with mothers-in-law, and still they live, still have little children (that's still on their minds too), do big business, etc.; no one has ever yet heard of somebody taking his own life over a mother-in-law.
But with me it is worse than with all Jews.
My mother-in-law surpasses every fantasy.
She meddles everywhere she is not needed.
What more do you want? She doesn't let us live, because we don't have a child every year. She is a great opponent [?] of the fashion of having only two children, let alone one child.
"May all my enemies," she says, "have only one child and one shirt on their back; better not to marry at all than to have one child. What kind of face does one show to people?"
So argues she, the old woman.
Once I come home from the shop and sit down on the sofa to rest. It was before noon. Suddenly my mother-in-law edges up to me and asks whether I want to go and eat already.
I stare at her goggle-eyed.
— Eat what, all of a sudden? And where is Anna? (my wife).
— Anna isn't here. She got angry with me and left the house.
My mother-in-law, you understand, had plagued her the whole morning [literally "gone after her years"] because she doesn't want any more children. She threw such a fright into her, she so ate her up, that Anna had to run away from home.
And my mother-in-law, you should know, is not one of those Jewish women whom one can win over with talk; once she seizes on a thing, you may talk to her to the very end [?], and it will help you like cupping a corpse.
And I saw that if it went on like this, if I let her go on with her antics, no good would come of it — either my wife would croak, or I would burst with vexation.
So I resolved on the last resort:
to turn to the famous Voronoff, so that he would intervene and put an end to our troubles.
And here is what I write in my letter to the Professor:
"Dear Professor!
"Surely you have heard of my mother-in-law. You must have heard of her, for she is one of the famous mothers-in-law in the whole world.
"Besides that she is, by her looks, a model monkey. Among all your monkeys you will not find another such specimen.
"Dear Professor!
"As I have heard that you buy up any monkey you can for your scientific work, and as our monkey is of great importance, I, and my wife as well, have the honour of proposing that you buy her from us. As for the price, we will come to terms somehow. A Rendl [gold coin] down, a Rendl up.
"At worst we are also ready to hand her over for no money at all, that is, completely free, but on condition that you perform one of your youth operations. We want her, the old shrew [kelipah], to become young again, and so young that she could marry once more.
"With this we want to achieve two things: firstly, we will be rid of her by her marrying somebody; and secondly, she should start bearing children again, this old witch. Let her have at least three or four children a year (science can do anything, after all) and let her taste what little ones are like...
With best regards,
Ch. Mother-in-law-Victim."
Well, what do you think? Will he buy her from us?
If not — that would be really bad, because it is already impossible to put up with her.
And then again, why shouldn't he buy her?
Do you think there are many such monkeys in God's world?
"Der Kokh-Lefl" ["The Cooking Ladle"] — Frost Golems

"Der Kokh-Lefl" ["The Cooking Ladle"]
Appears from time to time, by Ben Amotz.

Frost Golems.
Frozen solid are we all,
The frost chokes[?] and strangles at the throat,
The little wheel has come to a stop,
And tries[?]: — it stands still. Now everything.

No takings at all, no "pochontek" [Polish początek — the first sale of the day],
All the goods untouched,
The thermometer falls
And the quicksilver freezes...

What is there much to talk about,
Letting out words with the smoke [the steam of one's breath],
When even hot[?] love
Freezes in us too, poor thing...

Boys are freezing, girls are freezing,
The couples long since destined
With their eyes damp and misted
Go about weeping, in tears...

Nobody lets a word drop,
Because the words are cold,
And the ears and the noses
One hides in[?] the collars...

When one barely breathes and gasps ["zhipet", Polish zipać]
It is quite a great miracle —
Merchants creep about as if embalmed[?],
Stiff, like a government corpse [a "kazyoner mes" — an unclaimed body handled by the authorities]...

One is afraid to stick out
Into the world even a bit of nose,
Because there may remain of it
No trace, no sign at all.

We walk around in the streets
Really, as in a hen-yard[?] —
One talks only of the troubles,
A customer one does not see..
Yakl ben Flekl.
When Trotsky Will Take Leave of Comrade Stalin

When Trotsky Will Take Leave of Comrade Stalin.
You think it can't happen? It can! Imagine that a second "strong hand" comes, seizes power in Russia and sends Stalin, too, off to Turkey; there he meets Trotsky, and between them a conversation of this sort takes place:
Stalin: It seems to me I have met you somewhere?
Trotsky: It seems to me, too, that I have met you somewhere.
Stalin: Weren't you once connected with the Red Army?
Trotsky: Yes, it seems so... And weren't you some sort of regular visitor in the Kremlin?
Stalin: Yes.. I used to drop in there, but were you some sort of in-law of Lenin's?
Trotsky: Yes, I knew him, he was a decent goy, and you?
Stalin: Me? I was acquainted with him too, but... did you do anything for the Russian Revolution?
Trotsky: Yes, a little... according to my powers. And are you one of those Stalins? Perhaps a relative of that Stalin?
Stalin: Yes... a close person, one could even say a close relative; and did you know a certain Trotsky?
Trotsky: Yes, knew him from a distance... So what are you doing here among the Turks?
Stalin: Nothing... trifles... business... And you?
Trotsky: Me? Eh, trifles too, business..
Stalin: Perhaps you deal in tobacco?
Trotsky: You almost guessed it... not in smoking tobacco but in snuff.
Stalin: So that means you can still give the world a sniff?... [pun: "gebn tsu shmekn" also means "to show someone what's what"] (They part.)
—o—
A Speech by a Coal Merchant
Praised and hallowed be His dear name, that He has for once remembered us blackened merchants; they, the customers, no longer knew what to walk on in the world — they took coal on bills of exchange, in instalments with discounts, and who knows what else they bargained for. Now they have to come to us, and we shall teach them a lesson[?]. We will sell by the łut [a small unit of weight, c. 12.8 g], packed in little boxes and tied with a coloured string, like a bonbonnière; we will make the price a small one — 5 złoty for 4 łut of coal, box included.
We must found a coal association that will see to it that the frost doesn't break so quickly — no harm if it lasts a few more months. At the coming kehilla elections we will put up a list of our own, because we see that the Sosnowiec parnassim are beginning to meddle in our affairs.

Education courses at the PAI [Poalei Agudat Israel].

Tolerance of a non-Jewish ławnik.

The World Tells...

(Sayings[?] of great Jewish sages)
Retold by M. Lipson.
Jakob Eichenbaum, the head of the Zhitomir rabbinical school, once examined the students in writing the Holy Tongue. One student wrote the word „goy“ without a yod: „go“.
— You goy, you — smiles Eichenbaum — don't you know that a goy cannot manage without a Jew?..
———
R' Chaim Brisker [of Brisk] was a great giver of charity; his hand was always open — he refused no one. When he had no money of his own, he borrowed, took interest-free loans, and gave. In this way he became a great debtor.
— Rabbi — someone once asked him — where will you get [the means][?] to pay your debts?
— No matter — says R' Chaim — in Brisk there are enough rich men who are able to pay what I give out for their poor people...
———
All the years R' Chaim was rabbi in Brisk, he almost never ruled on ritual questions himself. For that purpose rabbinic decisors sat with him in the rabbinical court room, and they answered the questions.
Once it happened that R' Chaim was coming in from the street and met a girl coming out of the court room with a fowl in her hand.
— Excuse me — he says to the girl — show me the fowl.
R' Chaim examines the fowl from all sides — not a trace of any question. He goes into the court room and asks:
— How was the question decided?
— Kosher, of course — they answer him — it isn't a question at all.
— Go home — R' Chaim says to the girl — and bring the other fowl.
The girl went off and brought another fowl. The other fowl did indeed have a question, a serious question, and it was in fact declared treyf.
The people were left astonished. A manifest miracle.
— It is a simple matter — says R' Chaim — nobody sends to ask a question about a fowl that is perfectly kosher; so I concluded that they had probably slaughtered two fowls and a question arose about one of them. But when sending to ask, they mixed up the fowls and sent the perfectly kosher one.
———
R' Shmuel Mohilever, the rabbi of Białystok, was, as is known, a great activist in communal affairs of the whole people, especially in the settlement of the Land of Israel. With town affairs he hardly concerned himself. He often made long journeys, leaving the town for weeks and months, and even while he was in Białystok he had more on his mind the Jewish people as a whole and its affairs than the town of Białystok and its needs.
More than once it happened that R' Shmuel would leave the town notables, the „good men of the town“, sitting and waiting, while he spent hours in his room with a young man who was busy with the settlement of the Land of Israel.
So a saying went round the town:
— R' Shmuel is not the Białystok rabbi, but a rabbi in Białystok.
———
A maskil [printed „mashpil“], a provocateur, once came to the Malbim and said:
— Rabbi, I have come to ask you a hard question. We know that when one sees a rabbi one must stand up, and when one sees a dog one must sit down. But what does one do when one sees both a rabbi and a dog?
— There is no explicit law about it — answers the Malbim — it depends on custom. Let us both go out to the market, and we shall see how the people will behave...
———
A young man once came to R' Leyzer Kalmer to receive rabbinic ordination. R' Leyzer talks learning with the young man — quite a capable fellow, learned and well-read.
— What is the law — R' Leyzer suddenly asks him — when someone cuts his finger on the Sabbath and the blood is flowing?
— One moment, Rabbi — says the young man — I'll look it up in the „Shulchan Aruch“.
— No, young man — R' Leyzer tells him — you may not be a rabbi. Before you look it up in the „Shulchan Aruch“, a Jew will in the meantime bleed to death..
And he did not give him ordination.
———
R' Yaakov Yitzchak, the „Seer“ of Lublin, used to say:
— I prefer a wicked man who knows he is wicked to a righteous man who knows he is righteous.
———
When the Yiddish writer Jakub Dinezon [printed „Dinenzon“] died, a great crowd came to the funeral. People came from all of Warsaw and the surroundings, because Dinezon was renowned as a great writer and a good man.
At the funeral there were, of course, all the Jewish writers of Warsaw, among them: S. An-ski, David Frischmann and Dr. Gershon Levin.
As is usual at such big funerals, there was no order at all.
Walking behind the bier, in a great crush, David Frischmann speaks up to Dr. Gershon Levin:
— See to it, R' Gershon, that at my funeral there is a bit more order, [—] unless An-ski wants to go first — why not.
———
R' Yisrael Pilever used to sit down at the table with the people in the morning after prayers and drink lechayim.
Once the people noticed that the Rebbe takes off the Rashi tefillin and, before putting on the Rabbeinu Tam tefillin, goes to the table and sits down to drink lechayim with the people. The people wonder and [wink?] to one another: surely a great secret lies in this. A deep mystical intention, which not every man merits.
One hasid, one of R' Yisrael's intimates, took heart and asked R' Yisrael:
— Rabbi, what is the intention in the Rebbe, may he be well, drinking lechayim before the Rabbeinu Tam tefillin?
— The intention — answers R' Yisrael — is a simple one. Once I waited until after the Rabbeinu Tam tefillin, and there was no more brandy left...
The Fate of the Traders in the Old Market. Little by Little Trade in the Market Will Be Abolished

[Będzin — municipality, trade.]
For quite a long time now rumours have been spreading that trade in the old market would be transferred to the site where the magistrate's [municipality's] market halls stand on Modrzejowska Street.
The rumours were denied at the time by the city administration, which declared that “in the year 1929 trade in the market will not be disturbed.”
The promise, as it turns out, was not a sure one, and the decree against the Jewish traders is being carried out.
In the course of the last few days several small traders turned to us and related that the magistrate had even refused to let out trading places in the old market for the month of March.
We conferred on this matter with the vice-president, Mr. Rubinlicht, who explained that the question of disturbing trade in the market became topical because the 40 people who rented shops in the halls turned to the magistrate with a petition that, if the magistrate does not disturb the trade in the market, they — the magistrate's tenants — will not pay the bills of exchange they signed when renting the shops in the halls.
Mr. Rubinlicht explained that the city administration has come to the conclusion that part of the market stall-holders must absolutely be driven off. For this purpose a conference of the Merchants' Association, the small traders and the artisans will take place in the coming days, which is to determine whose lot it shall be to be the first who will have to leave the market.
For those who will be forced to leave the market, storage places and boxes for the goods will be arranged in the halls, so that the traders will not have to drag the packs of goods home.
The total number of trading places in the market amounts to 177, of them: clothing 14 places, manufactured textiles — 21, haberdashery — 46, linen — 19, hats — 4, leather — 7, shoes — 27, fruit — 6, smoked meats — 4, and various articles 29.
In any case it is a settled thing that the first “batch” of about 40 trading places will soon have to be cleared away.
The conference will only decide who shall be among the first..
The Struggle against the Raising of Rents.

[Będzin — housing, tenants' association.]
As we have already written, the board of the local Tenants' Association, understanding its task with regard to the tenants, decided to call a congress of the tenants' associations of the Kielce Voivodeship.
In the course of the week the association received reports from a number of towns that they are in solidarity with the action the local Tenants' Association has undertaken.
But on the last day of the week the association received a telegraphic request from the Central Committee (C. K.) in Warsaw that the congress be postponed, because on Sunday the 10th of this month a congress of tenants' associations of all Poland will take place in Warsaw.
On receiving the news, the board of the local Tenants' Association held an urgent meeting yesterday, at which it was decided to take the C. K.'s request into account and to send a delegate to the general congress in Warsaw.
As can be seen, the board stands on guard and fulfils its task beyond its means; if the tenants themselves treated the association more seriously, the board could achieve a great deal for the tenants.

General Meeting of the “Discount Bank”.

[Będzin — economic institutions, small traders.]
On Sunday, in the premises of the Small Traders' Association, the first annual general meeting of the “Discount Bank” took place; it was founded a year ago by several board members of the local Small Traders' Association.
The meeting aroused a satisfying interest. Interest not for the sake of opposition: the 120 members who came to the meeting were saturated with praise and acclaim for the bank's management; even the few individuals who had muttered that “they will come out with criticism” in fact told merry stories with hints at the “brilliant” leaders.
On behalf of the supervisory council, Councillor Lidzbarski opens the meeting, reports on the origin and activity of the financial institution and stresses that the greatest optimists could not have foreseen the colossal growth of the bank, which is run by the board headed by the tireless chairman Mr. Trapoifer [?].
The chair is handed over to Mr. Meir Cymberknopf. As assessors: L. Goldsztajn, Y. D. Lustiger and Fryde; as secretary — L. Rozenblum.
After the minutes of the founding meeting have been read out by Mr. Jakubowski, Mr. Y. Ehrlich delivers the report on the board's activity.
The most important item on the agenda was the approval of the balance sheet for 1928. Mr. Ehrlich reports on the balance sheet and we obtain the following figures: collections (inkasso) amounted to 6.901,065 zł. Total turnover 32.976,128 zł. Credit for 315 members 1,285,387 zł. Loans (halva'ot) for 89 members in a sum of 27,730 zł. Members 343, with shares of 50 thousand zł. Gross profit 91,933 zł. After all expenses a net profit of 10 112 zł. remained.
The report is adopted without any discussion.
The item on distributing the profits evokes a small discussion, and the board's proposal is adopted that 6 thousand zł. remain as reserve capital, 3.172 zł. to cover the organizational expenses, and a thousand zł. at the disposal of the council and the board.
The sum for which the bank may incur liabilities is raised to half a million zł.
The budget in the amount of 55 thousand zł. is adopted. To the question of some of those assembled concerning the item of 2,400 zł. which figures in the budget under the name “unforeseen expenses”, the manager Mr. Jakubowski explains that the item was inserted on the proposal of the honorary auditor Herman Pinkus, who on auditing the books established that the bank must have an iron safe in which all the valuable books are to be locked.
Before proceeding to elect 2 members to the board and 3 members to the council, a sharp protest was adopted, on Mr. Jakubowski's proposal, against the Central Cooperative Bank and the Auditing Union, which ignore the Jewish small traders and do not grant them proper credit.
The elections brought no change whatsoever.

Doctor Sentenced to 2 Weeks' Arrest for Refusing to Go to a Sick Child

[Czeladź / Sosnowiec — courts, medicine.]
A Christian woman came to Dr. Wiśniewski in Czeladź and asked him to go to her neighbour's gravely ill child. When the Christian woman came back home and said that the doctor did not want to go, the sick child's mother went herself to the above-mentioned doctor and, with tears in her eyes, begged the "merciful" doctor to go with her to give help to her child.

The flood of protests must be stopped!

[Zagłębie — economy; the middle class.]
An incomprehensible indifference prevails regarding our middle class, which is now going through a very severe crisis. Our middle-class merchants and artisans have suffered greatly in recent weeks, both from the frost and from the disruptions in transport. They had neither coal nor a livelihood. The only difference is that the merchants and craftsmen did not go, and do not go, to the relief committees, and above all, that on top of all their troubles they still have to pay bills of exchange.
It also turns out that in the days of the great frost, when for weeks people did not take in a single grosz, certain officials in some towns and townlets became particularly energetic [?]. Bailiffs found precisely this time suitable for carrying out tax distraints; inspectors went around checking the trade licences (patents) and raised every merchant's category; and, to crown it all, various commissions chose this time of great want to carry out sanitary inspections.
State officials, who ought first of all to have taken care to help the needy population, would not take into account the sad situation that had arisen, but instead set about performing their duties energetically, and thereby made the already hard enough life of the Jewish middle class harder still. Merchants who had nothing to live on for the day were saddled with heavy fines for not carrying out the sanitary regulations.
The Jewish middle class faces complete ruin, and on top of that all those whose duty it is to prevent it look on indifferently. We have merchants' and artisans' central bodies whose task is to protect the interests of the middle class. But where are they, and why are they so indifferent precisely now, giving no thought to rescuing their members from the threatening danger?
The economic organisations and small traders are now holding conferences about the planned rent increase. That is surely a necessary step, but no less important is to deliberate on stopping the flood of protests [of bills], on trying to halt the tax distraints in the present hard time.
Why do these economic organisations — the merchants, small traders and artisans — not call conferences to deliberate on the present situation and to help the middle class? Why do they remember the provinces precisely at election time and during other political campaigns, and not when they must undertake an important and necessary action to save the middle class from going under?
Protests of bills of exchange are now multiplying, and that means that by the coming season many merchants will lose their credit and be ruined as a result!
Let the merchants' and artisans' organisations, precisely now in this hard time, take the initiative and prove their right to exist. The duty of economic organisations is first of all to protect the economic interests of the population, especially now when many livelihoods are threatened with ruin!
B. G.
The performances of the little-art stage "Azazel" in Zagłębie

[Będzin, Sosnowiec — theatre; the "Azazel" cabaret theatre.]
Last Monday the Warsaw "Azazel" gave in Będzin a revue entitled "Hulye kaptsn" ("Make merry, pauper!").
The evening was a splendid success both morally and financially; the programme was a mixed, varied one, as befits a little-art (kleynkunst) theatre; it is only a pity that there were no printed programmes.
It is long since an intelligent audience has had such a good time in a Yiddish theatre as on this occasion; the audience laughed heartily and enjoyed itself enormously. The artists showed us original and healthy Jewish humour, permeated with sarcasm, from which the tragicomedy often looks out in all its magnitude.
We have before us talented artists, intelligent artists, who live along with the stage. In every movement, in every nuance one notices study and devotion. The people become embodied in every role and thus sweep the auditorium along with them.
How splendid is Ala Lilit in her "Don't hit me, mama", how beautiful are her movements and with what understanding she utters every word, how fine is her facial expression and how good are her nuances.
Very good was our Potashinski as a candidate for parnes (community board member); how aptly he attacked our kehilla's management, and how successful he was in his declaration.
Excellent was Strugatsh as the widow in the one-act sketch "Blessings and Curses", and Godik too was very good as conférencier.
Yesterday the same evening took place in Sosnowiec, and the audience went away satisfied.
It would be desirable for "Azazel" to delight Jewish Zagłębie with a few more such revues.
—o—
[Będzin — religion; Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin.]
Around the campaign for "Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin"
On Sunday at midday the Piotrków rabbi, Rabbi Shapira [R' Meir Shapira], came to Będzin to carry out in Zagłębie a campaign for his creation, the great building named "Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin".
At the railway station a large crowd gathered, headed by the Rabbi of Będzin [R' Tzvi Hanoch HaKohen Levin]. When Rabbi Shapira stepped out of the carriage he was greeted with cries of "Yechi!", and the Rabbi of Będzin and Rabbi Shapira kissed each other.
Later, under the chairmanship of Mr. Shmuel Piekarski, a reception took place at the "Merchants' Association", with greetings from a number of public and philanthropic institutions.
The distinguished guest, in his reply to the greetings, stressed that Będzin must give the "coin of fire" (matbea shel esh), i.e. 53 thousand zł., which it will cost to install central heating in the yeshiva building.
On Tuesday Rabbi Shapira gave a lecture in the "Nowości" theatre entitled "The home for Torah youth". The lecture, which was delivered in a worldly (modern) form and with fine content, made a very good impression on the listeners.
After the lecture one of the attendees said Kaddish.

The chairman of the supervisory board, Mr. Pres, opens the meeting, and after some formalities have been settled Dr. Chain[?] is unanimously elected chairman; he invites Messrs. Ptak and Kajzer as assessors and M. Czarniecki as secretary. Two proposals are put forward as to which language the meeting should be conducted in. Messrs. Pres and Blum stress that, since Christian members are also present, the meeting must be conducted in Polish. The writer of these lines demands that the meeting be conducted in Yiddish, because hundreds of Jewish members need not take into account that only two Christians are present in the hall. On the chairman's proposal it is resolved to conduct the meeting in both languages. After the minutes of the previous general meeting have been read, the chairman [of the management], Mr. Muskat-Blat, gives a report on the bank's activity for the year 1928. The report shows that the bank keeps developing, and compared with previous years the bank's operations have grown manifold. The total turnover amounted to 6,638,195 zł. 15 gr.; discounts and loans came to a sum of 270 thousand zł.; share capital 15 thousand zł.; deposits 44 thousand zł.; collections (incasso) 810,810 zł.; profit 1,670 zł. The budget for the year 1929 is set at 15 thousand zł. Mr. Pres gives the report of the auditing committee, according to which everything is in the best of order. The reports were adopted without any discussion. A longer discussion was provoked by the use of the profit. A. Banker demanded 25 per cent for the free-loan (gemilut chesed) fund, and A. Brauner 10 per cent for the Keren Kayemet (JNF). It was resolved that the profit should remain as reserve capital. Re-elected unanimously to the management was Mr. Muskatblat, thanks to whose brilliant abilities the bank is developing very well; on his appearance in the hall after the elections he was showered with long-lasting ovations. Messrs. L. Pres and M. Ch. Cukierman were likewise re-elected unanimously to the supervisory board; by secret ballot 2 new members of the board were elected: A. Banker and M. M. Wajcman. Finally it was resolved to make a banner for the bank.
On Sunday night [10 March] a banquet took place in the new premises of the "Folks-Bank". At a richly laid table the public, consisting of representatives of merchants, artisans and small traders as well as invited distinguished guests, spent a very pleasant time. The chairman of the banquet was Dr. Chain[?], who in his toast delivered his credo in beautiful Yiddish: that he is a proud national Jew, and he stressed with enthusiasm that as long as his pulse beats he will not desist from his truly Jewish national activity in all fields. Toasts were further given by the head of the bank and "lirer" [?, probably "leader"] of the Jewish town councillors' club, Mr. Wajslfisz; the chairman of the supervisory board, L. Pres; the chairman of the management, Mr. Muskatblat; Kerner, Rapaport, Kozma, Parasol, Lowik[?] Blum; the chairman of the artisans, Glikstejn; Szwarcberg, Wajcman, Dafner, Brauner and others. When the company had grown merry with wine, a genuine Hasidic dance was struck up, accompanied by music from A. Rapaport and son.

An All-Polish Convention for Working Eretz Israel

[Eretz Israel — Labour movement.]
(A communiqué sent in by the World "HeHalutz" Organization.)
The Executive Committee (Va'ad HaPo'el) of the General Jewish Workers' Organization in Eretz Israel has decided to convene in the summer of 1929 a World Congress for Working Eretz Israel. In connection with this, special delegations have travelled from Eretz Israel to Europe and America. In January of this year there took place in New York, with the participation of Messrs. Bloch and Mereminski, the trade-union campaign conference for Working Eretz Israel, and in Berlin, with the participation of Messrs. Sprinzak and Rubashov, a convention of all friends of Working Eretz Israel. At both conferences the idea of calling and taking part in the World Congress for Working Eretz Israel was solemnly accepted.
Some time ago Mr. Sprinzak arrived in Poland in the name of the Executive Committee of the General Jewish Workers' Organization in Eretz Israel, in order to prepare the ground here too for convening an All-Polish Convention for Working Eretz Israel. In a series of meetings with the participation of Mr. Sprinzak and representatives of all groupings that stand on the basis of Working Eretz Israel, as well as with the existing Central Committee for Working Eretz Israel in Poland, all the differences of opinion that had made themselves felt at the first conference, held last year, were removed[?].
General guidelines and conditions were worked out under which the convention is to be called, and the foundations on which the joint, intensified work is to be conducted. It was unanimously decided to set the time of the convention for the month of May. All preparations must already be made to secure the participation of the broad Jewish masses, who are close[?] to the idea of Working Eretz Israel, in the convention and in the work of the Leagues for Working Eretz Israel.
In the coming weeks a special delegation of members of the Executive Committee of the General Workers' Organization in Eretz Israel is coming to Poland, which will direct the preparatory work for the convention.
