Do not ruin Jewish families

Barely a few weeks have passed since the Będzin municipal self-government constituted itself. In fact, to this day it has not yet set about any positive work. We therefore still know almost nothing about its plans in all areas of municipal life.
In recent weeks, however, quite unexpectedly, the question of clearing the trade off the Old Market has surfaced.
Apparently the problem is recognised as very important, since they have set about carrying it out with a severity that would have been far more useful in other neglected areas, such as housing construction, popular education and the like.
Did the initiative really come from the thirty-odd merchants in the market halls, or from the "Rozwój" circles, which have long been striving to remove the "Jewish hubbub" from the centre of the town and to strip well-known Będzin of its "specific" character?
Incomprehensible, however, is the energy with which they have set about carrying out the plan!
Do the town's managers really believe that those concerned will not react against the project? Did they make sure beforehand that the professional organisations will keep silent and that the press and the public will not say a word on the matter?
After all, there is a danger that several hundred Jewish traders will suddenly lose their livelihood and their families will be left without bread.
We therefore consider it necessary to protest publicly against the implementation of the project at the present moment, and we believe that the overwhelming majority of the population is on our side.
The supporters of the plan come to us with arguments:
1) that the thirty-odd merchants who have rented shops in the market halls demand that the trade be removed from the Old Market and transferred into the halls — otherwise [printed "negnfal", for "kegnfal"] they threaten not to pay the bills of exchange which they gave as rent;
2) that the street trade in the market obstructs traffic; and
3) that aesthetics demand that the market be turned into a garden.
The first argument is truly interesting, because it proves that when the shops were let, a promise was made to clear the trade from the Old Market, i.e. the hall shops were let together with the customers, the market stallholders and the petty traders of the Old Market.
But who was entitled to give such promises, especially when the town council has not yet considered the matter at all, and under the present order the highest authority in the town is the town council alone and nobody else?
Could the whole initiative of the hall shopkeepers be a pretext, and the real reasons quite different? How much truth lies in the various rumours circulating in town about this matter.
We understand the situation of those traders who paid enormous sums in rent and now, because of poor trade, find themselves in hard circumstances.
It is, however, inadmissible [printed "underlazbar"] that because of the fatal calculation some 200 market stallholders and dozens or perhaps hundreds of petty traders in the surrounding shops, cellars and dwellings should suffer.
There is surely no doubt that at least in the first months the customer will not look for the trader, but will buy elsewhere. Those few months will be enough to ruin hundreds of petty traders whose entire fortune is the bit of merchandise, often itself obtained on credit.
Let the calculation of the hall shops be reduced, let the amortisation term be shortened — then the price of the shops will also come down, and those concerned will not feel wronged.
The second argument of the supporters of clearing the market trade — because it obstructs traffic — recalls that "philosophical" opinion that human life would be very beautiful if one did not need to eat..
Every town, after all, bases its existence on trade. The bigger it is, the stronger the traffic and the concentration of people in the streets and squares, the more it creates the town's wealth.
For whom is this an obstruction?
Very important is the third argument: the demand of aesthetics.
Every one of us knows very well that the hygienic-sanitary state of our town is not an elevated one; there are almost no gardens, very few open spaces, squares and the like, where the town dweller might have the chance to breathe a little clean air after his hard work.
But every one of us also knows very well what the damp and dark cellar rooms, shack premises and similar "dwellings" look like, where dozens of families live in terrible conditions — families who get their livelihood precisely from the market trade.
The question arises: do aesthetics demand that these families first be deprived of their livelihoods, or that care first be taken that they get out of their "flats", which ceaselessly supply clients to the hospitals, infirmaries and the like — something that burdens the municipal budgets for social aid and popular education more and more?
Perhaps such a tactic is merely a fine means to an end: take the bread away from the families, and they will leave their flats anyway... One shot will bring down two hares.
We have great understanding for aesthetics. But tell the poor man to adapt himself and suffer aesthetically!
Transferring the trade from the Old Market is indeed an important matter, but its implementation must absolutely be postponed for a long time.
The economic situation of the Jewish petty trader in general, and of the market stallholder in particular, is so critical that all these fine projects must be put aside.
The étatism of the state and the specific economic and tax policy of the government agencies in the towns have brought petty trade to real ruin.
The slightest wind [?] blows dozens of livelihoods off the arena and enlarges the already long enough ranks of the "Luftmenschen" [people without a steady livelihood].
The question is too serious to be solved within a few weeks, and with draconian means at that.
The Jewish representatives in the Będzin self-government will surely [printed "dikher" for "zikher"] not allow the plan to be carried out now, because public opinion — the true "control" over our steps — would never forget their indifference towards the weakest stratum of our people.
Perhaps some local politicians and journalists will try to belittle the matter as a petty phenomenon in our "local hubbub [?]", but we must not forget that this concerns several hundred livelihoods — and exclusively Jewish ones at that!
We are sure that if it concerned others, the language would be quite different.
Around us they know how to apply a "load-pouring" [?] in order to burden [?] our shops, or to set one brother against the other, because from this the third party always profits...
Dr. H. Rechtman.
Times will come...

[Feuilleton — satire.] There are people who long for the times of old, for the years that have passed, because they think that the old times — those were the good and easy ones.
And I, on the contrary, long precisely for the times to come, because I am sure that the good and easy times are yet to come.
Upon my life, gentlemen, more than once I sit [?] and contemplate our time with all its wisdoms and its antics, and it pains me to the heart that I was born so early and not a few decades later.
Ah, what precious times will come into the world — it will be a real delight to live, truly.
I am not speaking here of a select few, chosen and well-established persons — for them the world is already easy even now, a lot easier than it used to be.
To make a career is already now as easy as spitting; to become famous — is already a nothing of nothings; to become a "great man" — that you can do in one-two, not like in the old days.
In the old days, for example, when you wanted to become a public worker, you had, in those hard times, to work for years on end, to give away money and time and strength, and only when your head was covered with grey hair did you become famous — today, however, two or three borrowed speeches with a couple of paid notices in the newspapers are enough, and you are a well-known public worker.
In the old days, for example, when you wanted to be called a "rabbi", let alone a "gaon", you had to sit and study, produce novel interpretations, show acumen, renounce this world and indeed be wholly immersed in the "upper worlds" — today, however, a couple of sermons seasoned with a bit of midrash are enough, plus a little kehilla politics, and you are a ready-made "ha-Rav ha-Gaon".
In the old days, for example, when you wanted to become a leader, a "Führer", you had to sacrifice your own interests for the idea, ruin your health and neglect your own life for the sake of society — today, however, it is enough to get a fat post with a hefty salary in a big organization, and one is a ready-made "leader of the generation".
In the old days, for example, when you wanted to earn a name as a charitable man, you really had to give away your last penny, throw cash about right and left — today, however, it is enough to give a few złoty and a few hundred promises, and you are already the famous philanthropist.
In the old days, for example, when you were a socialist, you really had to devote yourself body and soul to "the humiliated and insulted", go hungry yourself and be blackened, forget your own "I" and work only for the workers — today, however, it is enough to snatch yourself a warm nest, buy a little house of your own with a little Ford, and make a nice living purely off "workers", and you are already a ready-made servant of socialism.
You understand, gentlemen, I am not speaking of all those upper persons; for them our time is also very easy and good already, and on the contrary — what helped them was not the progress of "science" but of "un-science".
What I want to talk about here is our plain, simple man; about him I think — what will science bring him in the times to come.
No small matter — what comforts the man of the future will have! What fear [?]: he will not have to toil at all, and he will be as well off as in the Garden of Eden.
Just consider what science will accomplish:
For example, the man of the future will no longer have to walk; he will not break his feet, he will not push and shove on the trains — he will simply fly. Everyone will have his own little aeroplane that will cost next to nothing; he will get in and fly wherever he needs to. A flight here, a flight there, snatched a little profit — and done. Then one will be able to see a little picture like this:
Two Jews will meet in mid-flight and strike up a conversation like this:
— Hallo, Berl, where are you flying from so early?
— I am flying from Katowice; I bought a house there — a bargain!
— How much profit do you want to grab on it?
— Twenty thousand, not a penny less.
— Fifteen thousand I'll give you, deal?
— Eighteen, not a penny less, just for you.
— So be it.
— In a lucky [?] hour!
Both Jews shake hands in the air, money is paid and papers are taken, all while sitting in their little aeroplanes, and they fly apart again...
Or, for example, going to the theatre: one will not have to push in the queue to buy tickets and then quarrel over the occupied seats, or even over a banana peel thrown down from the gallery — all that will be spared too; one will just use the radio. Everyone will have a radio set at home, through which he will hear and see the actors of whichever theatre he likes. And then one will be able to come upon a little picture like this:
— Maria, switch on the radio and let us see "The False Husband"! — the wife will say.
— No, Sasza, let us rather see "The Devilish Woman"! — the husband will answer.
And the end of the saving will be that everyone in the house will have a separate radio and will hear and see his favourite theatre.
Or, for example, a thing like beauty: should nature, God forbid, bestow on someone a coarse face, an ugly nose, too tall or too short a stature — no danger: off to the doctor, hop onto the operating table and it gets fixed in one [?]-two: a cut — off with the old skin and a brand-new one stretched on; a chop — off with the ugly nose and another one made [?], according to the fashion journal; a cut, a twist — and the stature is just as you wish. And then a story like this will happen: a father is blessed with half a dozen daughters, all pure ugliness — he will not have to wear himself out [lit. be torn apart] collecting big dowries for them; he will only need a little money to pay for the operations:
— Listen, my wife, it is time to make the girls new faces!
And they will fly off to the doctor with a squadron of ugly girls and come back with nothing but "beauties", and they will be snapped up like matzah water — and the troubles are gone...
Or, for example, a story like this: a couple will want to know the real "truth" about each other [?] — it will be as easy as pulling a hair out of milk:
— Tell me, Chana Gitl, whom did you spend time with at the dacha? — the husband will ask.
— And what were you up to in town, Berlu? — the wife will ask back.
And both will give each other a few "truth drops", and it will be "and he opened his mouth" — both will confess all their sins...
And even better: people will not grow old at all and will have no fear of the Angel of Death, because the "remedies" for long life will lie ready at every doctor's.
The Angel of Death will come to a little old man and say:
— Come, good brother, it is time already, enough living and sinning!
The little old man will twist out from under his hands and up onto his little flying machine, straight to the doctor:
— Doctor, quick, give me a "youth prescription", that fellow has come for my soul!
The doctor will at once make the little old man young, and the Angel of Death will be left standing as if thrashed — he will be fooled "in Turkish".
The long and short of it — happy times will come, easy and good times.
Times will come when science will progress so far that the man of the future will no longer be a man at all. —
Upon my life, gentlemen, it is worth living and living to see all this!..
Pini Ba'al Lashon [?]
Let Us Too Lend a Hand!

(The Jewish community of Zagłębie must come to the aid of our brothers in Russia.)

Last week the Warsaw press informed us that alarming cries of woe have arrived from Russia from our brothers there, who are simply perishing of hunger; they beg that we take pity on them and supply them with matzot for Passover, for otherwise they will have to go hungry the whole festival.

It is tragic and it hurts very much when one begins to consider what a situation our Russian sisters and brothers are in. A trifle, the troubles they have endured since the terrible war broke out until this very day! After all, since the year '14 a bloodbath has poured over these unfortunate people, and with every change of power in Russia Jewish goods and property were plundered, Jewish daughters were violated and pogromed, the finest and best people were slaughtered worse than sheep — and nevertheless they died beautifully and proudly. They breathed out their holy souls and perished like righteous men for the sanctification of God's Name (al kiddush ha-Shem).

Bravely, like heroes, they fell upon the holy altar; proudly, as our Russian sisters and brothers understand it, they departed from the world, and amid all these troubles, amid that terrible chaos (tohu va-vohu), they did not lose themselves. We never heard that they stretched out their hands and called for help. Proudly and beautifully they lived, and no less so did they wish to take leave of our world.

Russian Jews were always dear to us, and more than once we took pride in them. After all, it was from Russia that the finest and strongest Jews came forth, from whom we once drew our spiritual nourishment.

And if we now hear a cry of woe from these people, and they stretch out their hands to us for help, it is little enough that we fulfil their requests. It should simply be a privilege for us when we can do something for them, and therefore we must employ every possible means so that the help is given to them in its full measure. We must lovingly stretch out our hands to theirs, press them warmly [—] and come to their aid with whatever they need.

Actually, we Zagłębie Jews are the most fortunate in that we did not suffer the exile of war, as happened to all other Jews of Poland. We knew nothing of all sorts of evacuations; just as the Germans entered here on the first day of the outbreak of the war, so they stayed until the birth of Polish independence, and therefore we perhaps cannot form any idea of how much the population in general, and the Jews in particular, suffer when governments change.

After all, we have heard so much about Jewish troubles and torment in Russia that the hair on our heads stood on end with fright; we were shaken[?] with grief for our Russian brothers. At first we did not believe that there could be such a terrible hell on earth; we thought it had been greatly exaggerated. Meanwhile the opposite turned out to be true: it has been established that to this day the great artist has not yet appeared who would be capable of depicting with his mighty pen all the details of what our Jews suffered in Russia during the whole time of the war.

Let us not be embarrassed; let us say openly and freely that the finest Jewry we had was in Russia; our pride before the war was Russian Jewry. And did they really help the Polish Jews so little? Did they not come to our aid on every necessary occasion, both materially and spiritually? Were they not concerned with the fate of the Polish Jews?

And if today Jews come to us and say that they need our help, shall we receive them coldly, or toss in a certain sum just to fulfil the obligation? Would that not be called ignoring them? Would that not be called slapping ourselves in the face? And this is precisely the point: that we should not think of the question of how to get[?] a burden off our heads. As said[?], we must consider it a privilege when we have the opportunity, with whatever it may be, to repay[?] the Russian Jews.

We now have in Soviet Russia two and a half million Jews who cry out that they will have to go hungry the whole of Passover if they are not supplied with matzah for Passover, so that the Polish Jews must send them at least 20 wagons of matzah.

We Zagłębie Jews, who are better situated than other towns in Poland and who, incidentally, are not petty, must take a broad part in this campaign. We would not want to specify how high the campaign should come to, but if we set about the work intensively, we will certainly carry out a fine relief campaign for the Russian Jews, of which we will not have to be ashamed compared with all the other, larger towns in Poland.

And here it would be only right to organise already now such a relief committee for the whole of Zagłębie, with every town having its own branch departments. In the central committee for Zagłębie all strata of the population must be represented, so that no faction whatever should have the possibility of wriggling out and saying that it must "make its own Sabbath", that it will carry out a campaign by itself — for this is not a matter of parties; here one must simply make it possible for Jews to have something to eat at Passover. And which Jew can stand aside from this? Which Jew will be able to sit down at the Passover Seder knowing that his brother in Russia is perishing of hunger the whole of Passover? Surely no one will exclude himself from coming to the aid of our Russian Jews.

And therefore it is important that Będzin–Sosnowiec should set about organising the committee right now, and that Dąbrowa and Zawiercie representatives should also be represented there; the surrounding vicinity too must lend a hand here. Nor should one forget here that Jewish Katowice will gladly come to our aid in this useful work.

We thus have the best chances of carrying out a rescue campaign on a broad scale, so that we may take an honourable place among the donor[?] towns of Poland.

The most important thing, therefore, is not to put the matter off for any longer time, because now is the best time to set about the organisational work, which demands time, energy and will.

Helping Russian Jews to have food at Passover will mean fulfilling a holy mission, thanks to which we will celebrate our own Passover with a quiet conscience. Let the necessary work be done first of all, let the committee be organised, and no Jew, either in Zagłębie or in Upper Silesia, will refuse to lend a hand to this great mitzvah.

Y. S.[?]

Letters from Home

[Będzin — Feuilleton; city-council elections.]
B"H, Będzin, week of the portion "In the sight of all the house of Israel" [Pekudei].
My friend R' Shlomo, may his light shine.
I have received your letter. I see you have grievances against me for not having written to you for so long. Truth to tell, your complaint is quite justified, but the blame in this matter must be thrown onto the tramway. You wonder, eh? "What has the Sabbatical year to do with Mount Sinai" — what connection has the tramway with my not having written to you for several months? That is surely what you will ask, so let me make the matter clear to you.
As[?] in Western Europe, a "Strassenbahn" now runs in Zagłębie too; here we call it the "tram-way" ("tram-woe")... a very fitting name, for many families already suffer great "woe" because of this reform... For there is a supposition that the initiators of the tram-woe sympathise with the new method discovered by a certain professor in America. This professor is a strong opponent of Professor Voronoff's "rejuvenation" system; this American professor holds the view that prolonging a person's life is a plain crime. Why torment oneself in the world? On the contrary, the professor even "proves" that a person need not live longer than 35 years; it is the greatest curse — he says — for a person to live longer...
The new method is "supported" in deed by the tramway firms in Zagłębie; they are strong adherents of the shortening system and cut short young lives.. They are very "angry", the woe-drivers, at the woman who rides to a shoemaker or comes back from a shoemaker...
— — — — — — — — — — — —
And now, my friend, I will answer you on the first point first and on the last point last.
— What fruits did the victory in the city-council elections bring?
— Hard to give an answer to that. In my opinion it would be very useful to print a brochure entitled "Lamentations of the Jewish Councillors of Będzin". The brochure should be illustrated with the Jewish public delegates who brought about the Jewish defeat...
After the elections, when the Jewish population came out victorious, obtaining no fewer than 16 Jewish councillors, every Jewish voter swaggered and boasted everywhere. Look — he said[?] proudly — "what Będzin can do", 16 Jews! Why, the gentiles will convert to Judaism out of fear... such Jewish power...
And, between ourselves, the Jewish councillors did suddenly become great notables; for a smile from a Jewish councillor the greatest Polish "moustaches" bowed and asked:
— "Panowie [gentlemen], what else? 'Up to half the kingdom'... Perhaps 'the little plate from the sky'?... Say it, panowie."
"Neighbours" worked for both sides, "Swedes"[?] rang out, "turkeys" puffed themselves up, "the wise and the clever" conducted the politics, and — — what have we achieved? — you ask?
Then have a little patience; first, R' Shlomo, I want to tell you a little story.
A poor Jew, who was perishing with wife and children from hunger and cold, made up his mind to become a highwayman. Since childhood he had heard plenty of stories of robbers who attack people on the road, take from travellers whatever they carry and so on[?], while those who were robbed are still glad if they are left with their lives. It seemed a very easy living! For what could be easier than to plant yourself on the road, show everyone a piece of iron or a stick, and get his whole fortune?
The Jew did just that: he got up very early, said his prayers, took a stick in hand and went out onto the highway.
He did not have to wait long. Here come Jewish merchants, riding to a fair and carrying money with them.
Our Yankel "the robber" plants himself in the middle of the road, stops the horses, makes a terrible face and shouts:
— Jews, give money!
The merchants look at him and shrug their shoulders.
— Crazy or mad? What's come over you, Yankel? The "robber" tries to raise the stick; the Jews are not frightened, they only laugh. In short, they begin to bargain, and the "deal" ends with the "robber" getting
— a pinch of snuff...
Almost the same thing repeated itself with our "Jewish politics": the "ascenders" have become "descenders", yesterday's notables are tossed about like balls, yesterday's "friends" have become today's enemies; even the "turkeys" who had been so "fattened" by us no longer know us and "bite" us at every city-council session...
Our councillors are confused, they have simply lost their senses; the best of them curse the day of the elections; even the chairman himself, in person, has gone off to distant parts out of great sorrow; if you happen to meet him, comfort him with the proverb: "Who lies down with dogs gets up with fleas"...
Such "victories" we Jews also celebrated in Sosnowiec and especially in Dąbrowa. In Sosnowiec the 4 Jewish councillors got a ławnik [member of the municipal board]; they could not elect more. Evil tongues even say that had the "BB" [Non-Party Bloc] not wished thereby to win credit with the Będzin Jewish councillors, so that they would consent to their match, there would have been no Jewish ławnik in Sosnowiec at all. But why philosophise — we have an established rule that "all depends on luck"; it was fated to have a ławnik, and that's that. The Jewish councillors in Dąbrowa, on the other hand, obtained broad rights for their voters...
The whole agreement is not known to me, but as authoritative sources report, the agreement assures the Dąbrowa Jewish voters that they may stroll on the local pavements without any payments, that Jewish children shall have admission to the Polish "powszechne" [public] schools, that every councillor of the "BB club" shall greet the Jewish councillors with a smile, and after all these — a cemetery of their own"..
———
In the national-cultural field — not to sin. The camp of the national youth grows larger and stronger by the day; a "Leib" [lion; allusion to Leib Jaffe] came here and gave such a roar that everything woke up; the "dry bones", which for years had rolled about behind "foreign" tables, bowing down and kissing the hem of every non-Jewish garment — rose up in a "resurrection of the dead", straightened their bent backs and cried out loud:
— "Jews we are, and for Jews we want to build"...
The national force has already overpowered the opposing camp. The "Aguda" circles, who always laid worlds waste and poured pitch and brimstone on the sinners, on the Zionists and Mizrachists, who walk "in the statutes of the gentiles" and among whom every undertaking is carried out "like all the nations".
True, the greater part of Jewish Orthodoxy has remained of the opinion that a Jew's ways must be modest: not to provoke the nations of the world, to bear the heavy yoke of exile, not to paste up loud posters in the streets when one finishes tractate Beitzah, but to study Torah for its own sake and to support Torah study in the old way; if a yeshiva finds itself in a bad state, emissaries go out, sermons are delivered and the supporters of Torah give money.
Such to this day is the way of the "backward" Orthodoxy, which does not go "with the stream"; the Aguda leaders, on the other hand, have taken over the whole "Shulchan Aruch" of the Zionists. What the Zionists do[?] today, one sees tomorrow at[?] the "Aguda". On the same train on which Jaffe came, the Rabbi of Piotrków came too. And what not — the same posters, reception committees, even an appearance with a lecture in the same theatre where Jaffe spoke. Believe me, R' Shlomo, if the Zionists "let down" something from their programme and the "Aguda" adds something, it will not be long before R' Itche Meir Levin holds the third Sabbath meal at R' Yitzhak Grünbaum's...
May we both live to see it, as wishes you your friend
Ben Amotz.
The main thing I forgot: I quite forgot to wish you mazel tov. In the night of the 6th to the 7th of March, the 25th of the month in which joy is increased [Adar I], peace was concluded between the warring powers: Grünbaum–Lewite. The two "war ministers" have halted the frontal offensives and demobilised the armies...

Who's talking yet of whether peace will come in the Będzin Zionist Organisation too — then, R' Shlomo, only then will the verse be fulfilled: "And peace upon Israel"... The above.

[Serialized historical novel — the 1648 massacres, Chmielnicki and the Cossacks; installment 25.]
A historical Jewish novel by Yankev (Jakub) Cymerman.

"Come here, my child!" she now said a little louder, "and confess to me that you are a little in love... You love Dovidl, the son of the local rebbe [?]..."

"Yes, dear Mother," Blumele answered, "him I love with all my heart and from the depths of my soul, so much that I am quite unable to put it into words..."

She rested a little and then went on:

"Ever since I first saw him, when he was going with his father into the synagogue one Friday evening, it seemed to me that I was seeing the holy Shekhinah before me, so beautiful, a heavenly delight for the eyes... Since then my heart keeps telling me that one day I will yet be granted the merit of having him, and that the two of us will be united for our whole lives... This thought has not left me all this time and has made my sorrowful heart happy. But now, since he went off to the war and we have heard not one single word from him, nor from Father [printed "shunem saten", apparently a misprint for "funem tatn"], my heart is nearly torn to pieces, my mind works, it gives me no rest, I imagine the most terrible pictures, until I feel my heart bursting inside me..."

At these words she fell upon her mother's breast and wept pitifully.

Esther let her cry herself out. Her mother's heart told her that these tears would bring her child a good measure of relief; she kept silent and stroked her head with great love.

When Blumele had calmed down a little, her mother said to her:

"Blumele, my child, rely on the Master of the Universe, trust in Him, and you will see how well He guides His world and everything will turn out for the good... Be patient, keep up your hopes, and you will see that soon they will both, Father and Dovidl, come back home in peace, alive and well..."

"If only it may come true!" Blumele answered with a faint smile, "but meanwhile a good few weeks have already passed and we have no news of them at all, and such terrible rumours are going around town that when I think of them my blood nearly freezes..."

"Mother," Blumele went on, wringing her hands, "I have obeyed you and poured out my grieving heart to you. You have even given me a little comfort and hope, but now I beg you, fill up the measure of your goodness and grant me one more, my only request: let me travel to Father and to Dovidl on the battlefield, so that..."

"Child! Child!" Esther interrupted her and did not let her go on. "What do you want? What are you saying? It seems your grief has taken away your reason... You, a girl, and a frail girl, want to leave home and go among such terrible and savage people? And me you have forgotten altogether? Have you not considered at all that I would surely waste away here from longing and brooding?"

But before Blumele had time to answer her mother, terrible voices and wild cries were heard in the street from afar.

Blumele, who had sharp hearing, at once made out the words and in fright burst out [printed "oysgerisn", doubtful]:

"The Cossacks are coming! Now may God help us. It seems [printed "soet", doubtful] those were true and not empty rumours that went around town these last few days, that our men have been badly beaten and that the robbers are already approaching our town."

"Calm, be quite calm, my child, don't lose your head at all!" her mother soothed her. "Come, let us find out what is happening here [printed "du", a misprint for "do"]."

They did not have to go far, because the crowd, screaming and shrieking people, was coming ever closer, and among them Esther recognised quite a few acquaintances. She went up and heard the rabbi speaking to the people and trying to calm them all. What exactly the rabbi said she could not hear, but she noticed that his words had a great effect on the crowd, which began to thin out and disperse.

Esther and Blumele, however, still stood there; they wanted to find out properly what had happened.

The rabbi now noticed them and came closer.

"Rebbe! What has happened?" Esther cried out.

"Sad news has reached us," answered R' Yom-Tov Lipman Heller. "As you know, the country is now full of bands of Cossacks and Haidamaks. Wherever they come they wreak terrible destruction, they murder, burn and spare no one. Just such a band has now suddenly appeared in a village only four hours away from here; they left few people alive there and sent the whole village up in smoke. The surviving [printed "gretere", doubtful] people have now come here and brought the terrible tidings that tomorrow the Cossacks will already be before the gates of our town..."

"And Wiśniowiecki?" Blumele asked, almost out of breath.

"From the Prince there has been no news at all up to today," was the rabbi's answer, "but as it seems, no decisive battle has yet taken place to this day. Had our side already won, such good tidings would have reached us at once; had, God forbid, the case been the reverse, Chmielnicki would surely have hurried to come and take our town. Probably the two camps already stand not far from one another, and as far as I understand, the decision will come in the next few days."

"But I am afraid," the rabbi went on in a quiet, strained voice, "that the Prince has far fewer soldiers than Chmielnicki, and if he gets no help from somewhere"

"And where could he get it from?"

"Then we are lost. If the Cossacks besiege the town, and they will surely do it at dawn, then we must all prepare for death. The only rescue left to us now is to flee, and the sooner the better..."

"And where can one flee to now, dear Rebbe?" Esther asked in a strained voice.

"That I do not yet know myself. The terrible news about the nearby Cossacks struck me like thunder from a clear sky, and I have not yet been able to think about it at all; but since I knew this news would frighten you badly, I hurried to come here and calm you a little. Meanwhile gather together everything you can of what has value and is dear to you, and get ready to flee from here this very night.

"But you may be sure that wherever I turn now, I will not forget you and your child. Because of your sufferings and those of others, which we all share, I will, as far as I am able, always protect and shield you both..."

"I have," the rabbi went on, "ordered everyone to come into the synagogues, so that we may take leave of the holy objects and the precious buildings that we must leave behind here for the time being [printed "derveyhe", a misprint for "derveyl"]. Go now for this short while and get ready [to leave] the town with us this night... and let us trust in the Master of the Universe, who has helped us until today, that He will not forsake us now either..."

Grieved and worried, the rabbi went away. Mother and daughter remained in a single terror; they did not know at all what to do now or what to start with first.

Although Esther had always been a brave and strong-willed woman, now she trembled after all. The events of the last few weeks, which had cast fear and terror on all the Jews of Poland, had had only a slight effect on her and on her strong spirit; but now, when she heard from the rabbi's own mouth the terrible news, how far things had already gone and that they would have to flee from here this very night, it affected her so strongly that she lost heart, became helpless [printed "ophengig", dependent] and very nearly broke down completely.

A Little Piece of Herring.

[Literature — sketch; short story.] By K. Michał.
(Sketch)

It began with a kind of weariness in the bones, a lack of appetite and a little fever. Later a cough was added, and once the teacher Yankev (Jakub) Goldman suddenly spat blood.
To his wife, who had gone away to recuperate a little, he did not write about it, but to his mother he did say:
"I am ill, we must call our doctor."
The house doctor tapped and listened to the teacher for a long time, tapped over his sunken chest, tapped over his bony, lean back, listened to the chest cavity all round, and afterwards slowly folded up his stethoscope with the long rubber tubes and said:
"There is nothing to be afraid of; of course, the work at school will have to be interrupted for a while. The best thing would be to go to Zakopane."
He spoke the last phrase not quite firmly. As a good acquaintance of the Goldman family he knew that their finances did not allow it. Nevertheless he still considered it his duty to say it.
"I saw blood and clots [?]," Goldman complained.
"Nonsense!" the doctor waved his hand, taking [?] his hat. "With you it comes from the throat... not from the lungs."
And so indeed everyone was told that the teacher Goldman had fallen ill with his throat.
For whole days he lay like that, swallowed little pieces of ice which his old mother chopped for him in the kitchen, took punctually the prescriptions the doctor had written for him, obeyed everything he was told.
But he did not get better; on the contrary, with every day he grew weaker and weaker. At night the sweating tormented him, nightmares tortured him...
To the friends who came to visit him in his sickness he said something with a questioning smile:
"Here, out of nothing at all I fell ill... blood... it is from the throat..."
And everyone agreed that it was from the throat.
When he coughed, he put the handkerchief to his lips and then studied it for a long time.
His wife came home six weeks later.
A healthy, plump, fresh, blooming woman — she looked like a bright contrast compared with the pale, sunken and tormented face of her husband and with his whole emaciated, bony figure.
Seeing him, she actually clapped her hands:
"Oh, woe is me! Why didn't anyone let me know that he is so ill?..."
And instead of the old mother, she was now the one chopping pieces of ice in the kitchen.
The doctor came every day; earnestly and in detail he questioned the teacher whether he had slept at night, how he felt and whether he had had a fever. He tapped, listened, wrote a new prescription and left.
Many times he whispered with the sick man's healthy, red-cheeked wife, and every time after such whispering she would come out with red eyes, but still just as healthy — blood and milk — as always.
She seemed somehow ashamed of her high bosom, of her healthy, bright-coloured cheeks and of her whale's appetite.
The thin little old mother complained of only one thing: that the doctor was tormenting her son with hunger. "How can he get back his strength, when they don't give him a single thing he likes, but precisely such dishes as he has hated like pork ever since childhood?..."
Two weeks later the blood burst out again — from the throat, of course.
He lay flat, stretched out on the bed, and looked even more deathly pale in the presence of his healthy, blooming wife.
"Don't be afraid, my dear," she said, stroking his cold, sweaty forehead, "don't be frightened, with you it is from the throat."
"Yes, I know," the teacher said in a weak voice, "only something quite... right here..."
"Perhaps you would take [?] something into your mouth," the old mother spoke up. "Tell me, sonny, what kind of food [?] would you fancy?"
"I would eat now... a little piece of herring..."
"Really?" the old woman rejoiced. "I am going to bring it right away!"
"No, mother-in-law, first we must ask the doctor whether he may," said the wife, and ran to ask the doctor by telephone.
Soon she came back with the answer that the doctor had strictly forbidden herring and spicy things in general, God forbid!...
The sick man gave in. Only the old mother went on grumbling for a long time, cursing the doctor, who would yet — may it befall her enemies — kill her son...
The next day the doctor again conferred in secret with the sick man's wife. She came out with eyes even redder than usual and said:
"Mother-in-law, you know, the blood may after all be from the lungs too..."
To the old mother it made no difference at all where the blood came from — from the throat or from the lungs; she wanted only one thing: to see him healthy, the sooner the better.
But the daughter-in-law said:
"I am going right now to the director of the school to ask that something be done, that Jakub be sent to Otwock..."
Having powdered her face so that she would not look so healthy and red, she left. And the old woman sat down by her son's bed, sat quietly, looked on with pitying eyes and shook her head. In her heart she blamed the doctor, and the daughter-in-law, and her own bitter fate — everything, everything..
And a day before the departure for Otwock, this is what happened:
The blood from the throat — or from the lungs — burst out with such force that the doctor forbade the sick man to move at all.
"When he becomes a little stronger, then he will travel," the doctor said. "Now he needs rest and more rest."
The wife — full-figured, blooming, with red eyes — did not leave the sick man's side. She gave him small pieces of ice to swallow and tended him with tenderness.
The sick man lay gloomy, indifferent, with closed eyes. Only once did he open his eyes and say:
"A little piece of herring..."
"Right away!" the mother rejoiced. But the daughter-in-law stopped her sternly:
"It's not allowed! God preserve us! It could, heaven forbid, harm him!"
The old woman could not bear it, and when no one was looking she quietly brought in a piece of herring on a little plate. But she was caught and told to take it back.
And towards evening he died.
The wife lay on the sofa and wept, trembling with her whole massive, blooming, healthy body.
And the old mother wept in her own room, lamented bitterly and wailed aloud!
"Oh, how they neglected him! My heart told me so! Robbers! He begged so desperately for one more little piece of herring... perhaps that is exactly what would have helped him!.."
A Jewish industrialist shows the German government how it can be helped

(Special from our Leipzig correspondent).
For the first time in the history of the German state, Germany has begun to take up a project worked out by a private person, an industrialist — and a Jew at that.
True, Germany has had many Jews from whom it learned a great deal in economic matters. It is well known, for example, that Ballin [Albert Ballin], the late Jewish director of the Hamburg-America Line, was Kaiser Wilhelm's best friend, and almost all of Germany's economic projects were worked out by Ballin.
Walther Rathenau could surely have prevented Germany's entire economic decline had the antisemites not put an end to his life.
Germany has had more than enough great Jewish economic personalities; but that the government should officially take up a project worked out by a Jew, a private man, and moreover by someone who tells the government to its face that it has neglected the country until now — that is a rarity worth recording.
At the last Leipzig Fair, which has just been held, the Jewish industrialist Philipp Rosenthal, head of the world-famous porcelain firm Rosenthal, declared publicly, before the assembled German ministers and parliamentarians, before the diplomats of all the countries of the whole world and before some 300 journalists from the four corners of the earth — clearly and plainly, openly and honestly — that Germany will not get out of its economic distress as long as the government does not begin to think of increasing the export of economic goods and products, of which Germany has an abundance.
This plan is quite a simple one. Everyone who knows a little about economic conditions knows it, and anyone could have said it. But it had not yet occurred to anyone to say it with such openness and clarity that it makes everyone open their mouth and eyes, as Rosenthal did.
Rosenthal further shows that even states with great economic successes, such as America, England and the like, became great only through their export economy.
On the basis of official statistics Rosenthal demonstrated that Germany can be helped only once the government's entire foreign policy is directed towards creating economic relations with all the countries of the whole world.
Rosenthal proposes that the Leipzig Fair, the greatest economic fair in the whole world, together with the German embassies and consulates, should concern itself solely with developing Germany's economic relations with other countries.
He further shows that Germany's exports are declining from year to year, and unless something is done about it, the people that has always played the greatest role in the commercial world will disappear from the world of commerce.
"We all know that here in this country we are going to ruin economically. And as soon as a merchant, even the smallest shopkeeper, sees that his business is not going well and recognises the reasons why the business is not going well, he looks for every means in the world to improve his business at once. We would be bad merchants if we went on standing and watching our competitors from other countries conquer one market after another, and did not immediately do something about it. We have already missed a great deal, and if we do not soon begin to do something, we will never be able to make good what we have neglected until today."
These statements made such a great impression that the German Minister of Labour welcomed the plan in the name of the government and promised to see to it as soon as possible that the plan be carried out.
The German press of all parties is dealing at length with the plan, which it considers the best yet put forward to help Germany out of the severe crisis it has been going through since the Versailles peace treaty.
Z. Hager.
The Legal Position of Tenants Sentenced to Eviction

Because of poverty, small earnings and unemployment, many tenants are in no way able to pay the overdue and current, enormously high and already considerable sums of rent.
Most landlords, however, do not wish to take any feelings or circumstances into account, and bring eviction suits against such indebted tenants.
If the defendant tenants cannot prove that at the time they offered their landlord a certain sum on account of the said basis, the courts [printed "ne-courts"] sentence them to eviction.
Judgments of the first instance are almost never delivered in a final form, so that the defendants in any case have no possibility of appealing.
In the worst case the court sets a 6-month moratorium, i.e. the execution of the eviction judgment that has been delivered is postponed for a term of at most 6 months.
Hundreds and perhaps even thousands of families thus live in constant fear, expecting that after the term has run out [printed "afgeshapegem"] they may be thrown out onto the street at any minute.
Understandable, therefore, was the great joy that seized these unfortunate people when they learned that the competent organs of power were preparing a regulation that would annul, or at least hold up, the execution of all eviction judgments delivered so far.
Unfortunately, however, the hopes that all these desperate families had placed in the expected regulation have not been fully realised.
The amendment ("novela") to Article 23 of the Tenant Protection Act, published in Dz. Ustaw [Dziennik Ustaw, the Journal of Laws] No. 100 of 15 December 1928, takes into account exclusively the unemployed, and takes no interest at all [misprinted] in the fate of tenants of the other strata of the population who have been sentenced to eviction.
Moreover, even with regard to such unemployed persons the amendment has created no new legal situation, but merely clarified the one already existing, so that Art. 1 of the Act of 28 November 1928 is to be regarded only as an implementing law for the said Art. 23 of the decree on tenant protection.
Under that same Art. 23, point 1, an eviction judgment concerning unemployed tenants of 1- or 2-room flats was in any case not once carried out unconditionally. In such cases, at the proposal of the sentenced tenants or on official initiative, the moratorium rules were always applied, in the form of suspending the execution of the eviction for a term of up to 6 months.
In other words: if the tenant had paid the overdue sum of rent within the given time, the eviction judgment delivered against him became automatically void.
According to the text of the cited article it was not at all clear in what manner the adjudged sum of rent was to be paid, and how the eviction is annulled.
Article 1 of the amendment of 28 November 1928 to the decree on tenant protection has regulated the matter as follows:
Every tenant who has remained in arrears with rent and has for that reason been sentenced to eviction — as soon as he invokes a certificate from the State Labour Exchange Office that the arrears are a consequence of unemployment — is granted a moratorium in the said form.
If the same tenant obtains work during the moratorium granted, and begins to pay separately [?], with each current instalment of rent, 25 per cent on account of the overdue debt, the eviction judgment in such a case loses its legal force, but not automatically — only upon the intervention of the tenant concerned.
These tenants must apply with a proper petition to the court that pronounced the eviction.
To the petition must be attached a certificate from the State Labour Exchange Office, a certificate from the enterprise that one is already working, and the receipts for the debt paid off.
The court then, by a corresponding decision, annuls the eviction judgment that was delivered.
As for tenants of the other strata of the population sentenced to eviction — insofar as the overdue debt is a consequence of extraordinary poverty, or even unemployed persons, but from larger flats — their legal situation has not changed at all in connection with the publication of the amendment.
With regard to them the moratorium rules provided (in Article 23 of the decree on tenant protection) remain valid, but no longer in the form of a suspension (zawieszenie) of the execution of the eviction judgment, as with the unemployed in 1- or 2-room flats, but only in the form of a postponement (odroczenie).
Y. Infeld.
Jewish Tales

On kings, queens and princesses.
Frederick the Great and Moses Mendelssohn.
The German Kaiser Frederick the Second once came to visit the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn.
But Mendelssohn happened not to be at home. Frederick wanted to play a joke on the Jewish philosopher, and he wrote on his door: "Mendelssohn is a stupid donkey."
When Mendelssohn came home and saw the inscription, he at once recognised the Kaiser's handwriting. Mendelssohn then added under the inscription: Frederick the Second.
Now it came out like this: Mendelssohn is a donkey and Kaiser Frederick is the second donkey..
When the Kaiser came to Mendelssohn again and saw what the philosopher had done, he was beside himself. This was, after all, lèse-majesté, and for that a severe punishment is due.
But Mendelssohn argued that he had merely signed the Kaiser's name, so that people would know who had made the inscription...
Once Frederick the Second met Mendelssohn in the street and asked him:
— Where are you going, Moses?
— I don't know! — Mendelssohn answered.
— What do you mean, you don't know? How can a person not know where he is going? — the Kaiser grew angry.
— I don't know — Mendelssohn answered again.
The Kaiser ordered Mendelssohn to be arrested.
While Mendelssohn sat in prison, the Kaiser nevertheless came to visit him.
— Tell me, Mendelssohn — the Kaiser said to him — you are a wise man, so how come you answered like that?
— I answered correctly, Majesty — Mendelssohn exclaimed. — Did I know, then, that I was going to prison?
These are only two out of a whole sea of jokes and plain stories that Jews tell one another about Moses Mendelssohn and Frederick the Second.
The apple, the mirror and the carpet.
One of the most beautiful stories that Jews tell in connection with kings, queens and princesses is the story of the mirror, the apple and the carpet. It must be noted, though, that similar stories circulate among various peoples.
Three brothers decided to set out across the world, each one to a different country. Then, after a certain number of years, they would meet again and see what each of them had found in the distant places.
When the time had passed, the three brothers met and each of them told of his experiences. One had found a mirror in which, if you look into it, you see what is going on at the end of the world. The second had found a carpet on which, if you sit down on it, you can fly away in a moment to the most distant country. The third had found such an apple that if you give a sick person a bite of it, the sick man at once becomes well.
The one who had brought the mirror meanwhile took a look into it and saw that in a distant country a princess was gravely ill, and her father the king had had it proclaimed that whoever made her well would receive the beautiful princess as a wife and half the kingdom besides.
He at once told the other brothers about it, and all three sat down on the carpet. In a moment they were at the sick princess's side.
The third brother, the youngest, that is, gave the sick princess a bite of the apple, and she at once became well.
But when it came to the reward, the king did not know what to do: to whom does the princess belong as a wife, and half the kingdom besides?
The eldest brother argued that but for his mirror, the other two brothers would not have known at all that the princess was ill. The middle brother argued that but for his carpet, their knowing would have been of no help at all — for they could not have reached the princess anyway. The youngest brother argued: what good would it have done that they knew and flew to her at once, if not for his apple — neither the mirror nor the carpet would have been worth anything.
It was truly a very hard riddle for the king and his advisers. In the end they had to cast lots, and the one who won[?] the lot received the princess as his wife.
But the story itself is a good parable for all kinds of human deeds, which are knotted and bound up with one another so that it is hard to determine which of them is the more important.
How Jews devised a punishment for Wilhelm.
A company sat and pondered: what punishment should be devised for Wilhelm [Kaiser Wilhelm II]?
An Englishman proposed hoisting him up and down a ship's mast.
An Italian — that he be stuffed with macaroni from morning till night.
A Cossack — that he be lashed with a nagaika [Cossack whip] "into a thousand pardons"[?].
Some proposed hanging; some — beheading; some — cutting into pieces.
Among the company there was also a Jew.
— And what punishment would you propose for him? — they ask him.
— I, — the Jew answers, — would give him my passport...

Conflict between the choir conductor and the community

Będzin.
Cantor Żupowicz threatens to leave his post.
In the winter, when the choir conductor Mr. Kalmus was engaged, the kehilla promised him that it would come to his aid in the matter of a flat.
In the meantime relations between Cantor Żupowicz and the conductor have become strained, and consequently the kehilla board has for the time being declined to look after the conductor regarding obtaining a flat.
The conductor is supported by a group of worshippers of the main synagogue (the „shul“), who resort to impermissible means to take revenge on the cantor, and last Sabbath several of the synagogue worshippers already had a plan ready not to let Mr. Żupowicz go up to the prayer-stand (amud).

Outside meat — insiders have a permit

Uproar among the butchers — meeting at the gmina.
It is well known that the local rabbinate forbids outside slaughter! The prohibition, however, does not apply to certain sausage manufacturers, who have a permit to buy outside meat.
Because the permit prevents the butchers from keeping their fixed price for meat, they are greatly agitated and demand of the rabbinate that the prohibition of outside meat should apply also to the insiders who produce sausage.
The conflict is taking on a serious character, and it has already come to the point that the other day a butcher threw himself with an axe at a „gamen“ [?].
The president of the kehilla is therefore calling a meeting, to take place next Sunday with the participation of the rabbinate, representatives of the board and council, and the butchers.

Sosnowiec — A lump of ice falls from a roof and kills a man.

Sosnowiec
A lump of ice falls from a roof and kills a man
On Saturday at 11 in the morning a tragic incident occurred in Warsaw at Grzybowska 27, which cost the life of a local resident, 37-year-old Michał Ejbeszyc.
The tragically killed man had travelled to Warsaw last Friday on business matters.
On Saturday morning, as he was walking along Grzybowska Street, a lump of ice fell from a roof and struck Ejbeszyc on the head.
The blow was fatal. Ejbeszyc instantly felt severe headaches and, after saying the words: „Telegraph my wife“, he lost consciousness. In this state he was taken to the Jewish hospital on Czysta, where he was operated on. A few hours later Ejbeszyc died.
The tragic death made a shattering impression on the whole town.

From the Sosnowiec City Council

From the Sosnowiec city council.

(S) The latest session of the city council proceeded in great disorder. The reason: the president, the attorney Pawełek [?], was on leave, and the session was chaired by the first deputy president, director [Sajur?]. The opposition (N.D. — the Endeks) exploited this, attacking the magistrat at every opportunity; the Jewish councillors and the "Koło" (the bloc) also felt uneasy. The deputy president and acting head of the council, Dir. Pazur [?], opened with an announcement that several interpellations had been submitted, which the magistrat had answered properly.

The first item on the agenda — taking a loan of 150,000 dollars to speed up the sewage works (canalization) — aroused a lively debate. Messrs. Michel [?] and Wolf opposed approving the loan, arguing that the city council knows almost nothing about the work of the [contracting] company, which swallows sums in the millions, and that approving a loan before learning the course of the sewage works would be an absurdity; they proposed referring the project to the special committee for examination. Deputy president Parża [?] delivered a long speech and showed with figures what benefit the city would gain from speeding up the sewage works, and demanded that the council approve the loan. But the Endeks, seeing that they would not defeat their opponents, left the hall before the vote; no quorum remained, and the item was removed from the agenda.

The second item — adopting the regulation on the capital tax on buildings — was referred to committee for amendment. After settling several unimportant items, they moved to the item concerning the application of the retirement law (emerytura) to the president, the deputy president, and the ławniks. Councillor [Datsztejn?] appeared as rapporteur and supported the proposal; after a stormy debate the project was approved by a majority. Then the committees were elected: for examining the appeals (rekursy) of taxpayers on undeveloped plots — P. Wieszarek [?], T. Rudzki [?], and L. Piątkowski [?]; and for payment matters — radny Dzieczkowski [?], Opel [?], Wolf, Tobiasz [?], Limewka [?], and one representative each from the Jewish and Polish merchants' associations.

The last item — granting the outgoing president compensation equal to three months' pension (9,000 zł in total) — was brought by councillor [Datsztejn?] in place of the formal rapporteur, Dr. Rządkiewicz [?], who was absent. The opposition came out sharply against it, arguing that the outgoing president is at the same time a Sejm deputy, so his pension is assured. A stormy debate developed, and for the first time the Jewish ławnik Dr. Fuks [?] took the floor; he rejected the accusation that "the project brings the presidents under the retirement law", and stated that the whole question had never been discussed in the city-administration sessions. (As is known, president Michel [?] belongs to the Endek club in the Będzin city council, which has already adopted this project, and Michel supported it.) Deputy president Parża [?], seeing that the item would drag on, proposed removing it from the agenda and left the session in agitation; when they proceeded to the vote, chaos broke out — people voted for and against until the chairman could make no sense of it. The [Polish/PPS] club, seeing no chance of success, left the hall; no quorum remained, and the chairman was forced to close the session close to two after midnight.
On the Way to the Land of Israel (Travel Letter by M. Hampel)

The international express train carries hundreds of passengers at lightning speed, and of them only a few are traveling to the Land of Israel. We, the immigrants to the Land of Israel, occupy a special place in the carriage, from which a cheerful Hebrew song can be heard. The immigrants differ from one another: there are wealthy Jews traveling to buy land in the Land of Israel and settle there for good; there are students of the Hebrew University; journalists; mothers [traveling] to their children; and ordinary pioneers, who entertain the whole company with their cheerfulness.

After Vienna, and making use of the free hours left to us before continuing the journey through Italy, we toured the most beautiful sites of the great and magnificent city: the former imperial palace at Schönbrunn, the largest zoo in the world, the parliament, the university, fine museums, and interesting places — where the Będzin Jewish students studying at the "School of Commerce" (Hochschule für Welthandel) in Vienna kindly accompanied us.

From there we travel on, through the Alps, to the Italian border, where the warm weather is already felt and no trace can be seen of the last hard winter. In Trieste, which has 3,000 Jewish residents, we visited the fine kehilla and the synagogue — a magnificent and beautiful synagogue, except that we could not manage with the beadle, who speaks Italian and Hebrew to us but knows no Yiddish. At the office of the "Palestine Office" (Palästina-Amt) in Trieste, which handles the final formalities for the journey to the Land of Israel, I met the "Keren Hajesod" activist so well known to us in Zagłębie, Mr. Leib Jaffe, who left Poland after his successful tour and is traveling home, to Talpiot, to his wife and children. Mr. Jaffe asked after the Jews of Będzin, and requests that they be given once again his heartfelt thanks for their friendship and warmth. He is especially grateful to the "Zagłembier Cajtung", which assisted the successful "Keren Hajesod" campaign in Będzin.

On the ship "Carnaro" [?] many immigrants from Poland are traveling. As they say, the sea voyage will be pleasant, since the sea is calm. The ship, sounding its departure whistle, is interrupting my further writing. In future letters I will share with the readers my impressions from the ship, and from the life of Zagłębie's Jews in the Land of Israel.

M. Hampel. Trieste, [X] March.

In the Name of the Holy Torah

In the name of the holy Torah.

It is unbelievable how far licentiousness has gone in our day, and it is sad that this "zealotry" is spreading into every sphere of our life — wherever you turn you hear complaints about the wantonness penetrating every vein of our soul. It is to be attributed to those brazen "wanton ones", experts in their insolence in every field, who plant their filthy hooves everywhere. They gather around themselves an irresponsible band of youths, with whose help it is easy for them to slander and incite against anyone who brings benefit to the public — "in order to increase the [noise]". And youths, as is known, are but inexperienced children, dragged along without knowing themselves where to or what the true aim is of those in whose hands they are a blind plaything.

A few years ago these people took to tormenting a refined and pure personality like Dr. Weinziher [?], whom those few brazen ones dared to insult at every step — first as a representative in the Jewish kehilla, and later when his candidacy for Sejm deputy was put forward. But Dr. Weinziher [?] is not one to enter into battle: he said, "neither your honey nor your sting", I do not wish to look at you and I do not wish to hear your lies — and he withdrew from public life, like one fleeing a fire.

Now a new, clean personality has stepped onto the stage, wishing to serve us in the public field — the great industrialist Firsztenberg. These "politicians", instead of seeing to it that Mr. Firsztenberg be elected ławnik, brought it about that an antisemite was installed in his place; and apparently they are not satisfied even with that result, and have taken to attacking and insulting the man everywhere. These zealots cannot bear that Mr. Firsztenberg also employs Jewish workers in his zinc factory — and of course they curse him, since by this he "causes" them, so they claim, to work on the Sabbath. And as a result they have begun to cut back the Jewish workers one by one.

78 Jewish workers are employed today in Firsztenberg's zinc factory. Last week a delegation of the working families came to us at the editorial office and described their grave situation should they be forced to leave the factory. See to what a state the irresponsible loudmouths bring people by their repugnant deeds.

Everything is done "in the name of the Torah" — but if they truly meant it in the name of the Torah, the Torah would not serve them as a tool, but would be a true ideal, and they would see to it that Jews receive work with their Torah-observant friends. So why do they not do this? Why do they want Jews specifically to starve? After all, there are well-to-do Hasidic Jews in Zagłębie who indeed do not employ Jews on the Sabbath — but their places are taken by Christians; why do these "ideal leaders of the Torah" not take pains with their friends to employ Jewish workers, who would rest on the Sabbath instead of on Sunday? If the Torah were their true ideal, of which they boast at every opportunity, they would take better care to employ Jewish workers in their small factories.

But it is all a lie: there is really no intention of helping a Jew because one wants him to remain a Jew. After all, the workers of the Firsztenberg factory, if they were assured that they would not work on the Sabbath, would accept it — so why do the loudmouths do nothing in this field? The moment they want to enter into the "pose" of public representatives — why does it not concern them that Jews should observe the Sabbath properly? This was their task: to see to it that Jews employ Jewish workers; but they do nothing — except to raise a noise, so that the naive crowd will think something is being done. For the loudmouths seek nothing but that it appear as if they have an "opinion" in the Jewish street.

True, Mr. Firsztenberg is still innocent, naive enough to believe that they will not prepare against him all the schemes and libels that these people need in order to stir up commotion in our home life. Had he understood this, he would not have entangled himself with people who are responsible to no one and are worth nothing to the nation. Whoever knows the [band] knows well that they would sell everything for a groschen. Indeed, even the good and understanding ones in the "Agudah" want nothing to do with their groschen-and-boy politics, and even many Agudah activists keep away from their world.

Licentiousness in the Jewish street has reached its peak. But it is to be hoped that the blind crowd will at last coalesce and recognize the lies for what they are — for to use the holy Torah, which brings benefit to all, for evil is not proper at all.

R. Let [?].
Dr. Chaim Zeitskowski [?]: A Look at [Social] Life

Dr. Chaim Zeitskowski [?] — a look at [social] life.

Esteemed reader, I wish to offer a few thoughts on assimilation, which still has many devout adherents. Have you already noticed that the assimilationist ideal — of merging culturally and linguistically into the foreign language and culture — has almost entirely vanished from our public consciousness? Have you already felt the fact that, while assimilation tears the young generations away from us and casts them into the European melting pot, a sharp protest against this process is growing among our intelligentsia?

Whence comes the protest? And what draws us — I mean those who once believed in the assimilationist ideal — back to the Jewish people, to its language and culture? It seems to me that all this stems from the fact that assimilation deceived us, the progressive Jews. It did not keep its promises; it issued "notes" that it could not redeem. In a word: the assimilationist ideal went bankrupt. It came to us with the claim that if we gave up our Jewish people, our language and culture, and joined the nation, the language, and the culture of the country — antisemitism, the heavy blow from which we had suffered so much, would in the end disappear.

And how did this promise hold up? For more than a hundred and fifty years assimilation ruled Jewish life in the most advanced countries, and afterward also in enlightened Russia. Did antisemitism weaken anywhere? No — the opposite: the more we assimilated among the ruling peoples, the more Jewish children in their youthful energy broke through into the foreign culture and, with their Jewish talent, began to compete with non-Jews for privileged positions — in commerce and industry, in art, literature, and science, in all the free professions — the sharper grew the peoples' resentment toward us, and the more bitter and unashamed became Jew-hatred, even in circles that had once been friendly to us. On the matter of halting antisemitism — assimilation went bankrupt.

And with yet another ringing promise assimilation came to us. Among the great Jewish masses the simple Jew became, through many hardships of life, bent-backed; and yet for generations he was a proud man, with a spark of human pride in his breast — who let every idle squire spit in his face, crawl before him like a dog, and lick the dust of his feet. Assimilation said to us: "When you adopt the squire's language and culture and are counted among his sons, your bent back will straighten; proud and self-aware you will look the squire in the face, and he will declare you his equals."

And did assimilation keep its promise? Look at our assimilated children, the graduates of the gymnasium and the university. How many proud and self-aware people will you find among them? I do not wish, heaven forbid, to insult anyone — but people already complain bitterly that among them are people of suffering soul, plate-lickers of the foreign culture, unscrupulous careerists ready to spit out their Jewish soul and forget their Jewish name so that the squire will not recognize that they descend from Jews — provided only that he admits them to his table, for which they yearn. Instead of straightening the back of the man and the Jew, assimilation bent them still further — both as man and as Jew.

I could enumerate several more "notes" that assimilation issued and did not redeem, but I will mention one more point. The level of foreign culture and education was, compared to the old Jewish people, higher, and assimilation said: "Cross over to the higher foreign culture and to the foreign language, and the whole cultural level, the Jewish one, will rise." And what came of it? Assimilation took from us our most talented children and dragged them into foreignness; the home remained culturally poor, and the level of education among the mass of the people sank deeper and deeper. Only when a large part of our educated ones returned home, felt themselves members of the Jewish people, responsible for its fate, and began to work for it culturally in its Jewish language — only then did culture in that Jewish language rise wonderfully high and win the recognition of the entire educated world.

When all this is before your eyes, you will no longer be surprised that our new generation protests with fervent energy against assimilation and raises against it the sharpest war. However strong its influence in life may yet be, we hope to overcome it: our people has stood in even greater adversity and emerged from it in victory. We will also defeat this serpent, which seeks to swallow us whole — the three-headed serpent that bends both the man and the Jew, that seeks to undermine the foundation of our free human-cultural development. And our call is — to war against this serpent, for our free and independent culture and for our Jewish people!
What About the Matza? (Article)

What about the matza?
(Dos Yidishe Zaglembie — Jewish Zagłębie must take an interest in the question in good time.)

After the long and terrible winter, after the harsh cold, comes the pleasant spring; little by little the heavy, long nights vanish and give way to the short, delightful spring evenings and the warm, sun-drenched days. From this we learn that the harsh weather has passed into the past, and in its place come the warming rays of the sun, which awaken to life not only man but every living creature. Spring is the herald that announces to us that winter has passed. True, the harsh weather still does not wish to part from our world and tries once more to show its "might" — but these are its last powers, and it has no strength left; sooner or later the spring winds begin to caress us until the heart grows merrier.

Never, it seems, has humanity so longed to part with winter as this year; never did winter "torment" us so strongly as this year. And so it is no wonder that we already wish with all our might to part from it. But as we come to rejoice in spring, we must picture to ourselves under what conditions the lower strata of the people are forced to live. How can human beings live when they were unable, for money, to obtain even a little coal in our Zagłębie region — and these people had not even a potato? And they have nothing to cover themselves with, and do not always have a roof over their heads for themselves and their households.

Is it not a wonder that the winter dragged on so, and that many await the bright, warm days when the sun's rays will warm them? And immediately upon the arrival of spring — we must remember that Passover is near; and while many gladly welcome the spring festival, upon us falls the concern for the poor strata of the people, for the [poor and needy] of whom we must think — so that their matza box too [will not be empty] at Passover.

In Zagłębie it was always the custom to organize excellent Passover campaigns for those who cannot celebrate the festival properly. But lately they have somehow become cold and indifferent toward philanthropic work — and perhaps the institutions themselves are also to blame, keeping less to their responsibility to fulfill their tasks. It cannot be accepted that the charitable institution should remain "standing on high" while it brings no benefit to the needs of the small retailers and the needy, for whom it was founded in the first place.

Therefore — a fine Passover relief campaign should be launched even now, to distribute [flour and matzot] to the needy families. Do not put it off for long, for now is the right moment. "Dos Yidishe Zaglembie" — our Jewish sisters and brothers in Zagłębie — do not let a single Jewish family go hungry at Passover! [Signed:] Dr. Papori [?].
