To the Headmaster and the Entire Teaching Staff of the 'Jawne' Gymnasium in Będzin

To the Headmaster and the entire teaching staff of the 'Jawne' gymnasium in Będzin.

For the children of 'Jawne' a Purim ball was organized. Very fine — let the children rejoice, and let the joy of childhood be engraved in their souls for long years, and let the memories sweeten, in the hard days to come, the moments of despair and bitterness. The parents and children set about preparing for the ball, each according to his own way: rich fathers, for whom tens of zloty for a single evening play no part, ordered money and with a calm heart had magnificent costumes sewn for their children — turning their daughters into marquises and their sons into medieval knights or into historical and mythological figures. Other fathers, for whom a few zloty play a considerable part in these hard days, and others who have no light head and, besides the hard work at home and in the business, must still earn a living — did it more simply, and told the children: 'you shall have a new suit for Passover, and also a costume for the Purim ball.'

On the day of the ball the children's excitement reached its peak. But immediately upon entering the hall the joy turned into tragedy: two friends chanced to meet — Chanele and Chajele, who have already studied together at 'Jawne' for a few years and even sit on one bench. Chanele came in a new dress and nothing more, and Chajele — as a 'marquise'. Chanele remained standing there insulted, and her little heart filled with bitterness and tears.

Headmaster and teachers of 'Jawne'! Did your pedagogical vision not grasp that dividing the children into 'beautiful' and 'ugly', into 'rich' and 'poor', is not permissible, that it is anti-pedagogical and liable to cause harm? Or is this a method with you — perhaps you wish to make 'Jawne' into an 'institute for well-bred young ladies'? Parents must know this and draw their conclusions.

And further: already at the threshold of the ball a part of the children found, instead of joy — bitterness. The children were divided into two categories: privileged 'costume-wearers' and 'rightless' ones without costumes. With the privileged they busied themselves, with them they danced and rejoiced, and the 'simple ones' they set aside and hardly even looked at. The privileged received gifts — nice candies, and the simple ones — a 'fig' [nothing at all]. And when a child with an aching heart ran to one of the teachers and asked for a sweet, he received the answer: 'Without a costume — get lost'...

Headmaster and teachers! My children went to the ball happy and glad and in new clothes — but without a 'costume', and returned crying and embittered, a living protest against the peculiar 'fairness' that hurt them at their own ball. The children leveled sharp criticism at their teachers and instructors who treated them with such 'fairness', and we the parents were compelled to act — and had we spoken against the teachers in order to correct it, it would have been even more anti-pedagogical.

Headmaster and teachers of 'Jawne'! My children will return after the vacation to the threshold of 'Jawne', but they will cross the threshold with an embittered heart, and instead of respect and trust they will carry in their hearts a suppressed hatred. And I ask: how do you intend to repair the enormous harm you have caused the children and the whole class? What will you do to restore the trust and the respect — or will you fall again onto that same slippery slope and punish the 'offenders' — the children who dared to tell about the 'cheder' (the classroom), or the father who dared to write these words? This is not a question of an individual but of the collective, and the manner of education at 'Jawne' concerns all the parents and children, who want the school to educate their children into healthy human beings and not into cripples of the soul.

With respect, a father (of un-costumed children).

Enough Shnorring! (Editorial on Funding the Institutions)

Enough shnorring! (Away with the 'shnorrerai'!)

All our public work rests on 'shnorrerai' (the collection of alms). No Jewish public institution has a healthy financial basis. An institution's expenses are usually covered with the help of organizing 'evenings', academies or balls — more or less successful; then tickets are sold, people go from house to house to sell them, and in the peak season sometimes several balls succeed; and from time to time emissaries also appear who collect money to maintain or establish a yeshiva. These are almost the only revenues from which our public institutions cover their necessary expenses. The method of collecting money door to door has taken root so deeply that no one thinks of any other way.

And nevertheless this 'shnorrerai' — I cannot call it otherwise — morally corrupts both the givers and the receivers. True, we must turn to the Jewish public and demand money from it in order to maintain our schools, the orphans and the charity societies — since the government understands only how to pile on taxes, and does not wish to know of our cultural needs. On the one hand we must wage a struggle for our institutions to be maintained by the government, and on the other — as long as our demands do not succeed — we must ourselves maintain our cultural and charitable institutions. These are facts we must reckon with. From this standpoint, our public institutions have the full moral right to demand money from the Jewish public for cultural and charitable needs — and with that I fully agree. What I do not like is the manner in which the money is taken from the public — for collecting money from house to house corrupts, as said, both the giver and the receiver.

The receiver is not only the chance individual, but the institution for which the money is collected. Every institution must first of all cover its expenses from ordinary revenues. An institution whose existence is justified has a certain number of members whose duty it is to maintain it through their monthly payments. And it is interesting how the state of the monthly payments looks in our public institutions: do the managements act educationally upon their members to accustom them to pay their membership dues willingly each month — which is the first duty of every society-member? Unfortunately they do not, and this corrupts the members. Therefore nowhere can one see any Jewish institution flourishing; all the Jewish societies 'gasp for breath', and so it will continue as long as the 'shnorrerai' for the public institutions does not cease. The honor of the institution should be as dear to every member as his own honor; and once they understand this, they will know that just as it is a disgrace to shnorr for oneself — it is also a disgrace for the public institution to shnorr.

There are, however, institutions that could not at all cover their expenses from membership dues alone, and which have the moral right to turn to the broad public — in order to ease the distress of the poor and the sick, to educate orphans, to establish Jewish schools, and so on. But such an institution should not turn directly to the public: the kehilla (gmina) should subsidize such institutions — on the one hand the kehilla finances, and on the other it guarantees once and for all to the subsidized institution [the right] to collect from the public. The distress, the poor, the sick, the schools and the orphans cannot wait until we reform our kehillot — this must be dealt with already now. True, but that does not justify organizing balls to ease the distress.

There is a Latin expression, 'res sacra miser' (the poor man — a sacred thing), and in Warsaw, on the building of the Polish charity society, it is written 'distress is a sacred thing'. What a corrupt and conscienceless society this is, that finds no other way to support the most wretched of the wretched than through low amusements — so that the poor man may receive a glass of hot tea, whole bottles of champagne are drunk, a large hall is rented for several hundred zloty a night, a first-rate orchestra is engaged, flowers, serpentines and confetti are bought; the committee wishes to scatter money with a lavish hand so as not to be ashamed before the buffet at the ball. How much is spent at home on the preparations for the ball — of that I shall not speak at all: the haberdashery trade makes a 'fortune', the workshops sew the dresses, and the magistrate collects the high entertainment tax — all so that the poor man may receive a glass of tea. Is there really no shorter and cheaper way to ease the distress?

And one more thing: who supports whom? You keep shouting all the time 'the public supports the poor'. It is a lie: the poor support the public — of all the merriment he receives a glass of tea, and the fine portion the public receives. Nor is it clear why we receive no financial accounting after each amusement; the figures themselves would speak, and would teach us to seek other ways to ease the distress, not in such a brutal manner. The method of collecting money is also wrong because only a tiny part of the public is burdened with this unsympathetic tax, while the rest are exempt from everything. Usually one turns to the old-time notables, who still live on the central streets — those of whom it was said during the war that 'were it not for the old-time notables there would be no poor' — and it is precisely they who are not truly the ones capable of sustaining the institutions; whereas the truly well-to-do are exempt from any burden, and have still not been educated to take upon themselves a share of the public expenses.

Only the kehilla is the one that can and must put an end to this ugly way of maintaining the cultural and charitable institutions. As long as we do not obtain from the government and from the communal tax equal rights for our national and cultural needs, we must see to it that the kehilla be the only body authorized to tax the entire Jewish public for national and cultural needs. For that there is no need to 'reform' the kehilla, but only to see to it that people with a public sense sit in it — and to that I shall yet return.

One thing is already clear now: the balls for the benefit of the distressed must cease, since they corrupt the entire public, insult the needy one who still has in him a grain of dignity, and humiliate him. Wounds must be healed gently; our public institutions must act educationally upon the whole of society. Therefore the 'shnorrerai' for the public institutions must cease once and for all.

Dr. P. Wiezerman.

Responsibility Toward the Public (The Sosnowiec Budget — 18 Million Zloty; What Do We Get from It?)

Responsibility toward the public.
The budget of the local self-government (Selbstverwaltung) of Sosnowiec stands at 18 million zloty. What do we get from it?

The local authority in Sosnowiec has closed its budget at the sum of 18 million zloty. One cannot say that the sum is small — and if a city can raise such a considerable sum, it is worth managing on it. It is no wonder that at a time when various quarters point to the real necessity of thrift, the public institutions do not understand [the situation of] their citizens. And here we see that our authority understands, rather, how to increase its budget, without noticing that in the previous budget too the cities were burdened quite enough — and the question arises: what is the reason for the increase? Is the city really in a better position, has its economic condition improved? Have the poor strata grown richer, have their interests expanded? Or was the previous budget collected so easily that they saw fit to increase it to 18 million zloty? It is well known that the population must economize and cannot spend even [the essential] — so why not set an example and manage thriftily, so that the population can breathe? Why not show that with good management one can save money and be more economical?

And if we take everything into account nonetheless — that we save on nothing — the question arises: what does the local authority give us as Jewish citizens? It is well known that when it comes to the distribution of the taxes, we Jews are counted among the first-rate citizens — so how do we benefit from the taxes we help pay for the good of the local interests?

Note that the budget has no intention at all of subsidizing the charitable institutions properly. Only the Jewish hospital is to receive 15,000 zloty; all the rest are treated with utter indifference. We have enough institutions in difficult conditions, many of which barely survive and into which life can barely be breathed. The 'Talmud Torah' is in the cruelest conditions; the other institutions cannot subsist on the municipal commitments — so why should they not be properly supported by a well-off authority? And that 15,000 zloty are allotted to the hospital — is that a subsidy? It is like tossing, for a formal reason, a crumb to such a useful institution; otherwise it would be entitled to a respectable subsidy, since the other institutions were not taken into account at all.

We have our representatives on the city council — true, in a minuscule number — but they should not be deterred by that: they must remember that these four councilmen represent all of Jewish Sosnowiec, and as such they have the full right to speak in the name of the entire Jewish population. Therefore a sacred duty rests upon them to fight for the institutions in need of support to be properly subsidized; they must not be permitted to content themselves, for a formal reason, with waiting for a [crumb]. An authority that allows itself a rich budget of 18 million zloty can allow itself to subsidize all the institutions from whose citizens it draws a large part of its revenues — and to subsidize not only philanthropic institutions but also cultural, economic and professional ones.

In the magistrate there is a municipal library with all sorts of newspapers and periodicals, but not a single Jewish newspaper is to be seen there — so why should the Jewish newspapers not enjoy equal rights? Why should a Jewish worker or educated person not be able to enter there and read a Jewish newspaper? Such a phenomenon must not be passed over with indifference. Our representatives must remember that, after all, they represent the municipal interests, and they have the right to claim the debt and to demand what is due to Jewish Sosnowiec. With pride our representatives can demand that we be given what is due to us — for that is what our public institutions need. There is an old rule: he who gives is entitled to demand that the institutions he needs be subsidized. Our councilmen must not make light of this important matter, and let them all be present at the session at which the budget deliberations will be discussed.

Dr. Papori.

What Happened to the Vanished 'People's Groschen'? (Article)

What happened to the vanished 'people's groschen'?
(How should one react to the outrage?)

There were times when such people had no way whatsoever to dare to prove their existence and prosperity, and lacked the audacity to stand openly in the street; today, cloaked in the counterfeit 'atara' [crown of the Torah], they have grown bold. In Będzin a 'new star' appeared on the horizon, and salvation had supposedly come to all Israel: the Torah had been 'rescued', posing as 'guardians of the Torah', as an 'organ' of the 'Agudah' that would not allow the 'criminals' — who had taken such root in the Jewish street — to go on being 'pious', while in the same breath uprooting everything that is genuinely Jewish.

The reference is to the rival newspaper ['Unzer Tog'], which pretends to be built on other 'foundations' but in fact arose 'without itself knowing what for'. For what role can a newspaper fulfill among the public while it itself does not know what it wants or why it came? Who can reckon with an organ that has nothing to say to anyone — or the reverse, that perhaps says 'yes' to everyone? And what worth is there in promises written last night by certain people, and by the next day found already on the other side of the door, their places taken by others? For there the editorial managers are replaced daily with the speed of moving pictures. A saying already circulates in Sosnowiec that only 'young men with a dowry' find a place there.

And every issue takes on a different face. Every issue cries out: 'You can buy me' — everything in the world can be had, only not honor. Whoever places an advertisement gets to see his articles printed for free; and you understand — instead of articles they print advertisements, and everyone can praise himself to the very heavens... And since the printed word has fallen to so low a rung that any mortal [can buy it], the thing has lost all sanctity.

But they went even further. They laid hands on public moneys — and what moneys? Such as were intended to warm, in the great cold of winter, the poorest of the poor, the widows and orphans who cannot afford to buy a piece of coal. In Sosnowiec the communal activists gathered and created a drive to supply coal to the aforementioned poor. And now the editorial office [of that newspaper] informs us that it is not responsible for the member who took the coal funds, since he has already been 'removed' from the office — and those removed declare that they took no funds at all. It goes without saying: even had they in fact taken them, the office is responsible for its people. And the question arises: to whom did the committee report on those sacred moneys taken from the people? How did the committee even allow itself to touch such moneys and use them, while decent people were engaged in the drive?

For our part, [our newspaper] is not responsible for the men of that issue, who have nothing to say to anyone and do not know what decency is — and who dared to lay hands on such people's groschen. We cannot, then, keep silent in the face of an outrage that must not be silenced. Today they have grown bold and brazen enough to touch other people's money, without fear; but today the world is different — and we must not allow the matter to pass in silence. A day will come when the committee will be required to render an accounting of the coal drive, and the town will know how it conducts itself in such a shameful affair.

Selekt.

What Are the Future Prospects in the Będzin City Council? (Editorial)

What are the future prospects in the Będzin city council?

When one studies the [reports] from the Będzin city council, and observes the negotiations and all sorts of dealings that are tied together in one bundle — one understands from afar, and in the face of the intrigues, the maneuvers, and the slanders, one feels a desire to flee far, far away, for the air is stifling and it is hard to breathe. We understand that one can engage in politics, and that at times one must 'maneuver' behind the scenes — but all this is fine when one knows how, when one has a grasp of it; one cannot do it while one has not yet gone through 'school', is inexperienced, errs incessantly, and fails at every step.

The Jewish councilmen intended to play first violin in the city council. And what do we see instead? At every opportunity — a failure, in every negotiation — the greatest defeat. And the question arises: what is the reason? Why do these losses keep occurring? No great expertise is needed to understand this: it is plain and clear, most of our councilmen have no notion of how a municipal economy is run — they have not learned and do not wish to learn. Besides that, they are divided and splintered on every question, each acting on his own judgment, taking responsibility alone, and reckoning not at all with the collective.

These people have no awareness that as representatives they must reckon with the public and remember who sent them. The impression they give is as though they were sent to the city council, entrusted with the [mandates], in order to sit upon them and do whatever they please, as is convenient and pleasant for them. And this is a colossal loss, given a figure of fifty percent Jewish councilmen — for at every local-government election we pointed out that we need enlightened and more knowledgeable representatives rather than many people 'taken off the street', who understand nothing of the town's affairs and have no notion of how a local economy is run.

True, it is good to accept people off the street who are 'something', who let themselves be taught and want to understand, and who over time will learn — these are the capable elements we need; but the trouble is when people are convinced that already now they are the 'last word', that all their deeds are good and fine, and that they bear no responsibility toward the public. Therein lies our tragedy.

If this continues thus — if these people go on acting each on his own responsibility as he pleases — then the prospects are not brilliant at all, and we have every reason to fear for our fate in the sphere of communal economy. Our better representatives must not allow the matter to be run 'like a ship without a rudder', with everyone doing as he wishes. The people must be taught by force and convinced that continual failures cannot be tolerated; and if they will not foresee what is coming — they must be told that they are responsible for the whole town, and if not, a day will come when they will be forced to render an accounting before the voters. Let them take upon themselves 'a measure of sense', let them unite — as the Christians unite, 'black and white bound together' when it is a matter of unseating a Jewish position. And if not for their own sake — if these people do not feel our harm and reckon not with the failures caused by them — let them at least feel shame before their Christian colleagues, who exploit every opportunity as we lose position after position and stand idle.

R. Let.

A Mother and Child on the Tram (A Feuilleton on Chivalry Toward Women)

A social feuilleton. The customs of social life differ; seen from outside they seem to be refinement — yet there is in them tension, artificiality, and fawning upon the external; and at times it is not so. Those very same customs, when applied in the right place and at the right time, become a moment of true humanity.

This is a preface to the 'virtuosity' that we men display toward woman: we always give her precedence. In society, in the street, at the theater, in every public place — we make way for her, open the door for her, let her go first, meet her [courteously] at the post office, at the bank, at the office, and even pick up the handkerchief she has dropped so that she need not bend down... In short, we do things that are not always pleasant and more than once betray a blind politeness. And when the 'readiness to serve' oversteps ordinary courtesy and turns into a pretended 'kindness' toward woman — then we are not so quick to display our nobility, and our 'chivalry' hides away somewhere.

This is felt especially by us Jews, members of an ancient, Eastern race with deep-rooted habits and customs — a true people, which cannot be superficial and affected in its attitude toward woman; a people whose conception of woman as mother, as human being, and as wife has been crystallized in its culture over thousands of years; and a people whose tongue is too simple and straight to [serve] for inflated rhetorical flourishes in the relations between man and woman. No; we Jews were never accustomed to this — and herein lies a great error.

All this was once; today — it is a disgrace. When Jewish life changes like a kaleidoscope, not according to need but according to fashion, according to time and place; today, when we seize so ardently and hastily upon the customs from Europe — our attitude toward woman has become affected, unnatural, and has taken on caricatured forms.

The author illustrates this with a scene: we board a tram. The car is crowded, there is no place to sit. It stops at a station, and a woman gets on with a child in her arms. Everyone is young, no one gives up a seat. Among the passengers there are young people — the young men sit, and the mother with the child stands. The tram sways, the mother clutches now at the rail, now nearly falls — but the public sits and does not give up a seat for her. And behold, an old man rises — an old man, of all people — gives the woman his seat and offers it simply, humanly. The woman thanks him and sits down, the old man stands and sways; while the 'polished' young men, in their fine neckties, dressed in the latest fashion, the educated ones — sit serenely.

And let it not be counted against us to our shame: in 90 out of 100 cases it is precisely young Jews who remain seated, even when the woman with the child is Jewish. Whereas young Christians would indeed hesitate to rise before the 'Żydówka', but — in 90 out of 100 cases they would nevertheless rise and give up their seat to the woman, to the mother with the child. Whence does this come? That is the [question]...

Something Has Stirred...

(Voices about the "fine" deeds of those who hang around the so-called[?] newspaper "Unzer Tog" ["Our Day", a Yiddish paper in Sosnowiec].)
A few weeks ago we printed in our paper, in the name of the coal committee in Sosnowiec, a demand to the editors of "Unzer Tog" that they return the money paid in by a number of donors who had supported the "coal ring" (koyln-ring).
The demand — as it turned out — had little effect on the editorial board (at least, so to say[?]), and there was neither voice nor answer: they made themselves deaf and wanted to hear nothing.
For some time, in our paper's column "From the Public to the Public", we gave space to former staff members of "Unzer Tog", Messrs. Dr. Kaufman and Y. Feiner, who made clear to the public various low deeds being done around the said newspaper.
The revelations naturally caused a stir in Sosnowiec, so much so that even the few dozen loyal readers of the said newspaper dared[?] to take the little paper in hand... Messrs. the "editors", seeing that they were "in a trap"[?], fell back on the well-known invention — "Stop thief!"...
And so the heroes[?] came out with a reply under the title "The vile lies and slanders of the 'Zagl. Tsaytung'". In the reply they stagger about like a drunkard. Gentlemen — they shout — "we are not guilty; the guilty one is precisely the coal committee, which out of negligence or ill will did not want to collect the money at the administration office. Then[?] they tell stories that the coal money was "grabbed" by Messrs. Dr. Kaufman and Feiner, who, poor things, are slandering them"...
Until now we have not taken a position on this question, because we have not yet, God forbid, sunk to the level of polemicising with "international businessmen"; above all we refrain from it so that nobody should get the impression that we are doing it for the sake of competition (woe to such means of competition). We therefore turned to the coal committee, asking them to speak out on the question.
And here is what they write:
To the hypocritical statement printed in "N. Unzer Tog" no. 52, that the coal committee out of negligence and ill will did not want to collect the 67 zł. that donors had paid in with them, we declare that this is a base lie. We, the undersigned, were at the editorial office of "U. T." 5 weeks ago, where we demanded that they deposit the sum of the coal ring in the "Bank Kupiecki" [Merchants' Bank], and to this day they have not done so.
By the way, it is worth noting that according to the information we have, the editors took a larger sum from the "ring", and they deny it.
Respectfully,
Itshke Zaks [Iczke Saks], Reuven Tshapnik [Czapnik].

„Aryeh“ I — „Maccabi“ I 7:1 (2:0).
Because „Orzeł“[?] of Melnowice[?] did not turn up, „Maccabi“ played a friendly match on Saturday [6.4.1929] on the „Ruch“ ground against the local „Aryeh“. 23 P.A.L.[?] (Będzin) — „Victoria“ I 1:6 (1:2).
On Sunday [7.4.1929] the 23 P.A.L. of Będzin played a friendly match against „Victoria“ Sosnowiec. Among the players of 23 P.A.L. were such players as Jaszke (1. F.C. Kat[owice]), Lubelski („Maccabi“ Sosn.), Margula and Dymański[?] („Victoria“ Sos.), etc. The course of the game was very interesting. In the 30th minute Jaszke managed to score the first goal for „23 P.A.L.“, to which „Victoria“ immediately equalised through the inside-left. But shortly before [the end of] the first half „23 P.A.L.“ managed to score the second goal (Margula). Theatre and Music

Leivick's "The Golem".
Last week the Jewish theatre-goers of Będzin and Sosnowiec had a true artistic holiday: the well-known artists of the Vilna Ensemble, such as Nachama, Kash, Kadish, Shriftzetser and others, performed Leivick's mystery play in 3 acts "The Golem", staged and directed by Mark Arnshteyn. The performances were a huge moral and material success. The artists carried the whole audience along with their acting. Although the theatre was overfull and the "gallery" was heavily "occupied", the performances passed in exemplary order and complete quiet, which is a rarity in the Yiddish theatre.
Finally, heartfelt thanks to the artists Kadish (the Maharal), Kash (Tanchum), Grodner (the Golem), Shriftzetser (Tadeusz), Litvina (the Rebbetzin), Yedina (Dvorele) and others, for the figures they created so masterfully in Leivick's "Golem".
Worth mentioning too are the mass scenes with the participation of the Będzin "Muza", which came off brilliantly.
"Parisian Love".
The same artists gave in Będzin the operetta "Parisian Love" (Bayadère) and this time too enchanted with their versatility. Particularly outstanding were Mr. Kash and the temperamental, gifted Malwina Rapel. The splendid sets and costumes — a sensation of their own.
Today — "The Thought".
The famous Jewish artists Ida Kamińska and Zygmunt Turkow, who toured in Będzin last week with colossal success, give a farewell performance today in Będzin at the "Karso" theatre. "The Thought" by Andreyev will be played.
In the leading role Zygmunt Turkow has no rival. His acting electrifies the spectators.
It is therefore to be hoped that, as every time, the artists will be warmly received.
Concert by Kranelli.
Next Monday a concert will take place in Będzin at the "Karso" theatre with the participation of the singer Mr. Kranelli, well known in Zagłębie, who appears with a rich programme of European musical works and Yiddish folk songs.

I.
Esteemed Mr. Editor!
The management of the "Yavne" gymnasium in Będzin most politely asks you to give room in the next[?] number of your esteemed paper to the following statement:
In connection with the open letter by an anonymous author, which appeared in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" No. 13 of 29 March of this year, the management and the pedagogical council of the "Yavne" gymnasium in Będzin declare the following:
We find that the open letter of the "father of non-'kastituirte'[?] children" is a highly unpedagogical way of criticising the school, because it frivolously undermines the authority of the teaching staff in public opinion and among the children; and precisely for pedagogical reasons we do not intend to conduct a polemic in the press about the matters touched upon in the above-mentioned open letter.
Were we to pay measure for measure, i.e. to answer on the merits the reproaches, which were written perhaps in a moment of anger, we would commit the same pedagogical error as the author of the open letter, and we would then provoke the same negative consequences for the youth in the school that the writing of the above-mentioned author has no doubt provoked.
And therefore, taking into account the above-mentioned reasons and striving to preserve and cultivate the atmosphere of harmonious living together at home as well as at school — we wish to avoid any discussion on the merits in the press and announce that the director of the "Yavne" gymnasium is ready to give all interested parents, or groups of parents, detailed explanations concerning the matters touched upon in the open letter.
For the above reasons we will also not answer further voices, should such appear in the press.
The management and pedagogical council of the "Yavne" gymnasium.
II.
Esteemed Editors!
For the sake of truth I am compelled to return to the sad affair of the charity money at the "Nayer Tog":
Wishing to wash themselves clean, the gentlemen of "Unzer Tog" keep confusing[?] the public's minds, as if I were the one to blame for everything, and the proof: I have already "made a name for myself" at "TOZ" and the Jewish hospital.
First, everyone knows that working both in the hospital and in "TOZ" I committed, God forbid, no abuses whatsoever; the boards of both institutions can confirm this.
And second — what has the Sabbatical year to do with Mount Sinai? What connection does the hospital have with the charity money that vanished in the editorial office?
It seems clear enough to everyone how badly the gentlemen of the "Nayer Tog" have come out of it; they are already seeking to return "all the money", even that which I supposedly took.
But that is not the main thing — even if one were to force[?] the editorial office to cover the money, the ugly affair[?] will still not be healed thereby.
There is therefore a duty on our communal representatives in general and on the Coal Committee in particular to take measures so that in future such a thing should not occur.
Let them as quickly as possible create a commission and establish how much money was collected and by whom, and also why it was not handed over at once. Otherwise suspicion must fall on the above-mentioned institutions or on the persons connected with this or that campaign that "their hand too was in it" and that they are interested in smearing the matter over...
At long last the matter must become clear, and honest people should finally know where the truth begins and where the lie ends.
Dr. Ch. Kaufman.

Self-Humiliation

[Sosnowiec — community; the town synagogue; opinion.] (How do we manage our money? — The straying path.)
And yet we had thought that these spectacles would at long last come to an end; we reckoned that, whatever might be and whatever might happen, our Sosnowiec kehilla leaders would resign. We could by no means understand that conscious people, people endowed with understanding, could sit there calmly, occupy public positions and do nothing at all. True, the situation is such, the circumstances so tangled, that even with the best will nothing can be achieved — and for that very reason we had thought that these people would understand that they must resign from their responsible posts.
Meanwhile, however, we were mistaken. The people sit on, and their whole housekeeping [?] consists of drawing up new budgets year after year; and such a budget has just been dealt with: as is the way of the world, the board submitted it and the council cut it. Well, such things happen; what is interesting and characteristic is only how the cuts were made and what they wanted to save on.
Thus, for example, they went after the Gemilut Chasadim (free-loan) fund and tore off half its subsidy (out of 10 thousand zł. they made 5 th. zł.). For the healing of the poor sick they also cut 5 thousand zł. You understand — they went to take revenge on those who keep silent [?], on those who will not have the courage to come forward and show themselves in broad daylight; for what Jew who takes a loan from the free-loan fund will blacken his own face and show how far he has been wronged, when at once they would reduce his loan or not give it at all? And the poor sick, too, will not come with their weak hearts to cry out about all kinds of scandals. That is why it was easiest to go after the institutions mentioned.
It is quite different, however, with the party subsidies: there one gets through somehow, because each is afraid of the other. "You tear off my subsidy and I'll throw out yours altogether" — and so one hand must, even unwillingly, wash the other... It is a wonder: with party subsidies one hardly looks at all whether they are needed or not, but simply shares them out like Sabbath fruit: you give to me and I'll give back to you.
It is interesting: the necessary minimum sum of 12 thousand zł. was proposed for repairing the town synagogue (Stadt-Schul); and since that is not a party matter, there was nobody to be afraid of — so this sum, too, was not accepted.
The synagogue is a real ruin; one is frightened to go in there, and it demands a thorough repair — yet no more than 8 thousand zł. were assigned. It goes without saying that this is a laughable sum for such work, which must be done properly and not for 2–3 years. A synagogue is, after all, a public building; one should not look to save 4 thousand zł. on a repair, because of which the assigned 8 thousand zł. may be thrown away. Our synagogue is in a considerably worse state than the Będzin synagogue was, and nevertheless that one was decorated beyond recognition — while here they want to save 4 thousand zł. and strike a bargain. The sum is simply laughable: does it really matter, in a budget of a quarter of a million zł., to put in another 4 thousand zł. for a synagogue meant for the whole town?
Let us not fool ourselves: Sosnowiec is undoubtedly a better-situated town, and yet you will find in the smallest shtetl a finer synagogue than ours.
When some celebration takes place and the authorities appear in the synagogue, one turns red with shame; we fall in our own eyes when we show what our sanctuaries look like. And what notion of us do the authorities get when they step into our holy place — is that no disgrace for our kehilla leaders? Does it [—] not need, first and foremost, a holy place that would impress people from outside? Should the synagogue not be a building such that reverence and decorum arise the moment one steps over the threshold? Have they never yet felt this need, both for our own world and for the outside? Why, we are ashamed when anyone at all comes into the synagogue. How many times have we already been made aware that we are diminishing the dignity of the synagogue? Because of the ruin, children run around there as on an open square — so how are these children to learn that in a synagogue decorum and quiet must reign?
We get nothing from our kehilla administrations. They cost the town so much money, and what it ought to do, what belongs to the whole town — where our honour before the outside world and before our own world is concerned — there of all places they become stingy, and a few thousand zł. play a role. Is that not ridiculous, is that not simply banal?
A Jewish community must, after all, first of all have a decent synagogue. Sosnowiec has no public buildings whatsoever. So why should we not try to save what can still be preserved — what we need both for our children, whom we often take there, and for the authorities, who send their representation on every occasion?
Has Sosnowiec really sunk so low that it cannot, or will not, allow itself a town synagogue that one can enter? Have we really become so indifferent to everything, or do things simply run like this, without order and without a path? It is nonetheless interesting to analyse this train of thought.
Dr. Papuri.
The Power of Money and Cooperation

Money is power, money is strength — this, regrettably, is an old and ever-new truth.
We see it both in the relations between states in the international arena and in narrow social life.
Everything is done for the sake of money; money is the dominant and most important factor, and power and strength follow it.
The same happens in social life too. Here too money takes the top place, here too money is a mighty force, before which democratic slogans and principles often give way.
Everyone knows that whoever has money is thereby a man of standing (baal yikhes); he is shown honour, he becomes a "prezes" [chairman] everywhere, he is clever, he is right, people listen to his word, his word is law — as the saying goes: "Who has the hundred [the money] — has the say."
But should he lose his money, it is the end of standing, the end of honour; he also loses the chairman's seats and his cleverness, and remains the same ignoramus (am ha'arets) he was before.
In the field of cooperation money plays the same role. Financially strong cooperatives are powerful factors in social life, only with this difference: a cooperative, as an institution of self-help with a certain ideological colouring, is a power of the many against the individual; here the power must be used to protect the members against the individual who bases his power on money. That is how it ought to be, but regrettably we often see exactly the opposite phenomena: cooperative institutions are exploited by individuals against the interests of the many.
The cooperative movement has developed strongly of late and is beginning to penetrate every little chamber of economic and social life. Some persons — crafty individuals — have understood this and have seized the chairman's seats; from then on everything runs "in good order".
With the help of smaller or larger little loans, or little "favours", one creates for oneself a little circle of "friends" who nod along[?] when necessary and when not necessary, and so the cooperative becomes an instrument of power for one individual or a few individuals.
A very sad phenomenon!
Yehuda.
I Settle Accounts with the World.

(A legend) by Pompadour.
Who is sicker — Trotsky or the world? That is the question.
I ask myself a question: who is more ill, Trotsky or the world?
And I answer: the world!
At the moment the world refused the sick Trotsky a home, a health resort for his weak lungs — it showed that it is a more serious invalid than he.
At that moment it made plain that its own heart is affected...
Yes, yes, I take the liberty (khutspe) of throwing the accusation in the world's face:
World, you are dangerously ill!
World, you have shown that you have no strength!
What does it mean — a whole world is afraid of one man?!
And a sick man at that?!
And is it not the clearest proof that the world is very sick, that it is afraid of a blow from a consumptive?
At the minute when the world said to Trotsky: I won't let you in! — it admitted[?] itself that it suffers from senile weakness, that it is played out...
World! I cry out — you had no right whatsoever to show your weakness.
A sick man knocks at your doors — let him in!
That should have been the world's attitude.
Give the sick man a bed in your hospital, set a nurse by his bed to watch him so that he does not jump out in the middle of the night and start a fire, or throw something at somebody's head, from fever..
Caution with invalids never hurts.
But let him in you should have.
With an invalid, and a dangerous one at that, a world should not keep accounts.
And taking revenge on a sick man is certainly not becoming for a world.
Our capitalist world, may it forgive me, has made a fool of itself.
Through Trotsky it should have, and could have, given the new Russia a lesson in humanity.
"Look at the difference between me and you: you drive out your best sons — I take them in! You make them sick — and I heal them! (because my order has the best doctors[?])..."
The capitalist world made a fool of itself, because it would have lost nothing by Trotsky.
Did the England of old lose anything by "uncle" Kropotkin when it gave him a home? — Not at all.
Kropotkin did England no harm whatsoever and perhaps even brought it something.
Trotsky too would not have harmed Germany.
Nor Czechoslovakia.
And any other state in the world — certainly, certainly not.
Indeed, my dears, the world is sicker than Trotsky.
And when a world is sick, it is a greater danger than when an individual is sick.
The world has lost its hospitality (hakhnoses-orkhim).
And that is much worse than having consumption.
A world must not lock itself against a [—?] (unclear word, printed "נעקושיחודיטן").
A world must not display collective cruelty.
A world must show consideration for a persecuted man...
And the main thing: a world must not be afraid of an individual, even when he is a Napoleon or a Trotsky.
And above all it does not befit a world to refuse a man when he asks for a cure.
Even a man sentenced to death is given a doctor.
And Trotsky after all has not yet been sentenced...
When Trotsky settles accounts with the capitalist world, it is a sign that it has not yet entirely condemned him.
I say to myself: when the individual sometimes acts foolishly, it is forgivable.
But when a world acts foolishly — that may not be forgiven.
And the world has acted foolishly regarding Trotsky.
The world should have said to the former leader of Soviet Russia:
— By all means, comrade, come to me!
With me you always have a home: whether when you fled from the tsarist nagaika [Cossack whip], or when you flee from your brother Stalin's "Chrezvychaika" [the Cheka].
And "samoye glavnoye" [Russian: the most important thing]: I want you to know that I, the world, have no fear of you!
My capitalist throne stands firm on its golden feet.
So what then: you are sick? — By all means, come and take a cure with me!
Cure your body and perhaps your spirit too; heal yourself of your world-overturning madnesses (meshugaasn).
I will give you a home — only don't try to remake me.
Better sit down and write the memoirs of a revolutionary...
I, the world, love memoirs.
You write — and I will pay you well.
Because I, the world, delight in such stuff...
But the world, as said, made a fool of itself.
The world, as soon as it heard that Trotsky was coming, at once began clutching its head, feeling its pulse — and sweating.. sweating...
And the world, as far as Trotsky is concerned, also showed itself a great coward.
Hearing that Trotsky was coming — it slammed shut door and gate, locked itself with all its locks.
— We are afraid of you!
— Even your illness makes you dangerous to us!
— — — — — —
Well, am I not right then? Say it yourselves: is the world not a greater invalid than Trotsky
Medical Aid for the People — What is local self-government doing for the public in the field of medicine, and what could it do?

[Article — Zagłębie, health and municipality.] (What is local self-government doing for the public in the field of medicine, and what could it do?)
Several months ago we began to take up the question of a "Pogotowie" [emergency first-aid/ambulance service] for Zagłębie. The matter was discussed at length in the columns of our paper, and the conclusion reached was that rapid aid for Zagłębie is an urgent necessity — if only because the tramway network is branching out ever further in our district, and the victims and accidents [?] have already been, relatively speaking, quite numerous. Besides, Zagłębie finds itself in the same conditions as all other large cities, and we hold that this question is one of the most topical, one of the most urgent, so that it must be solved as quickly as possible.
It appears, however, that the matter is not yet ripe among our self-governing bodies in Zagłębie, on whom lies the duty of realising this ideal; they still treat it with coldness and apathy.
Had they at least tried to be more active, they would have had to learn something, become more practical and bring as much benefit as possible in the field of saving the sick — giving medical aid so that the poor population would derive the greatest possible benefit from it. Unfortunately we do not see this being improved, nor any effort to make the aid more universal, more popular, more accessible.
In the past the philanthropic sick-care institutions sent out doctors and had their own outpatient clinics. Today this hardly exists any longer, and all medical aid is concentrated around the self-governing bodies. And that is right, too, for the magistrates [municipal councils] tax the citizens with larger sums of money, and it is their duty to see that medical aid is provided through them as well as possible; indeed, in the municipal budget this heading takes up a fairly considerable position.
True, every poor man gets a doctor free of charge through the magistrate. But what use is this support to the poor Jewish population? Here is how, for example, a resident of Będzin obtains a doctor through the magistrate.
It is said simply: "a doctor through the magistrate." In reality such a Jew goes through the seven circles of hell before he sees the doctor before his eyes. First of all he starts wandering about until he finds out everything he needs to have for the doctor to agree to come to him. Thus, for example, the magistrate demands a slip from the Jewish "Dobroczynność" [charity board] that the Jew is a poor man. But the "Dobroczynność" works in the afternoon, while the magistrate works in the morning, so that, having the slip from the "Dobroczynność", he must in any case wait until the next day to obtain from the magistrate the slip for the doctor; and once the doctor has the slip, one must still wait for him a whole day. So this is a matter for a healthy person — and meanwhile, meanwhile a healthy person can fall ill and a sick one can recover.
Moreover, we hear more than once that the magistrate's doctor does not treat the patient properly and feels as if he were going for nothing — regardless of the fact that for every visit he is paid [printed "געמט"] by the magistrate.
It turns out that such a family sometimes urgently needs medical aid, and when the institutions are closed, then there is certainly [printed "אװראי"] no question of being able to get a doctor.
Since the medical aid costs the magistrate so much money, since this item occupies such an honourable place in the budget, such defects must surely be remedied. Let the doctor not take the patient lightly merely because he is sent by the magistrate; let him remember that he has before him a sick person whom he must examine and heal, without regard to who called him or who pays him for the visit.
The same with the slip procedure: is it really such a great thing to arrange for the "Dobroczynność" to work in the morning, so that obtaining slips from two institutions need not take two days? That requires nothing more, we believe, than a little diligence and good will. Nor is it any better with the doctor: he must not take things lightly merely because he goes on behalf of the magistrate and it seems to him that he is going for free. He is, after all, paid by the magistrate for every visit separately. And public money is no worse than private money — it is collected from all the citizens of the town.
The so-called "Opieka Społeczna" [municipal social welfare] occupies an honourable place in the large municipal budget, and it indeed does a great deal for the poor strata of the population; precisely for that reason the city administration has the duty to keep improving the system of giving aid to poor sick people. Small shortcomings must be removed; big ones should not exist at all. Nevertheless one must not forget that medical aid is not something that can be put off from one day to the next; often the patient's life depends on a doctor's visit. More than once people have departed this world only because they did not manage to get a doctor.
If for the time being we have no rapid aid, if we cannot achieve a Pogotowie in Zagłębie, then at least let it be seen to that the free medical aid is improved. Let it be run with more speed and punctuality, so that it can occupy its proper place. Let it be possible to get a magistrate's doctor at any time; let medical aid not come with so many difficulties and so much torment. Let it not be forgotten that a poor man does not need a doctor in order to chat with him. Let our public activists remember that punctual medical aid means for a poor man the true salvation, which more than once revives the dead in the cramped and stuffy cellars and attic rooms.
And therefore: let the public medical aid be run with more punctuality and more responsibility.
R. Let.
The Woman of Yesterday and Today.

[Essay — the position of women; women and society.]

In prehistoric times men were idlers and the women worked. The men loved to roam about hunting and fishing, and took pleasure in breaking one another's bones. In the evenings they would lie around the caves, gaze into the fire, think how good it is to live in the world, and shout at the women to bring the food.

All the work was done by the women: they pounded the grain, sewed fashionable costumes for the men and children out of bearskins or similar materials, made the fire, cooked the food, and occupied themselves with all the other primitive industries.

Since those distant, distant times the wheel has turned completely: the prehistoric world was man's paradise; the modern world is a women's paradise.

The men of our time, however rich they may be, have lost the ability to enjoy their time. But the women — as soon as the men begin to earn reasonably well, they at once take servants and become complete idlers.

And what does the intellectual European woman do?

To this day she is the most restless person in the world. She is a woman with education, often with higher education; women's suffrage does not satisfy her as it did her sisters of the previous generation. She knows that she wants a husband, a home, children. She longs for love and also for social life, and wants, in her own words, "to do some serious work". And all these demands fight one another. She is a tireless visitor of women's clubs, political leagues and endless committee meetings. She keeps straining to accomplish something, but nothing at all comes of it.

She is less happy than her unintelligent sister. She is tormented by too many demands.

When these women, who are so rich in free time that they have nowhere to put it, talk sentimentally about woman's place being in the home, they are not honest with themselves.

When a married woman works, or studies to obtain a diploma, or gives lessons, she is always reproached with doing wrong — with neglecting her home. But if, instead of going to work, she went off to play cards with a company of idle women, that would not be called neglecting the home.

But surely it is foolish to think so, and it is an injustice to make this reproach to the working women, who strive so hard to make married life interesting and many-sided.

In time the way of life of women will change. It will be considered a disgrace to go about idle and empty-handed. When well-to-do women have finished bringing up their children, they will take up other useful occupations. One sees that many women of high society [do so], and from experience one knows that every fashion among the aristocratic ladies passes in time to the women of the bourgeoisie.

Klara Lewin.
„Guard me, and I'll guard you...“

(Dedicated to the „extra editions“ of the Będzin communal activists.)
... There they sat, the two communal activists, pondering how one becomes popular with the broad masses — so that people would learn of their „holy“ activity, and after a hundred and twenty years their names would be inscribed in the list of the „immortal men“.
— I have a plan — the president says to his „prefier“[?] of the „naked“ institution. — The great honour I have been longing for these several[?] years, which has cost me money and blood — I can attain it if I publish an „extra edition“, a sort of newspaper of the „Somekh Noflim“ [„Upholder of the Fallen“] institution, in which I occupy the president's chair. For the members, for the so-called blind mass, the „extra edition“ will serve as a report on our activity, but at the same time I will have a broad field to popularise my name, to publicise my deeds and...
— Ua! Truly a fine plan, panie prezesie [Polish: „Mr. President“] — the vice-president of the „naked ones“ is delighted to the marrow — but from what means will you cover the costs of the edition? Don't forget that almost every week we drum it everywhere that the institution is collapsing, that it is facing a catastrophe — and suddenly we spend hundreds of guldens on editions purely for the sake of advertising?..
— I must tell you, brodershi Kroyn[?], that in matters of advertising you are a great idler and still possess a great measure of naïveté. First, who cares that it will cost a couple of hundred guldens — am I then obliged always to work for the common good? Let me at least have the satisfaction that my name will be immortalised in the „extra editions“. I'll actually write a couple of articles too, interwoven with sayings of the Sages — ah, there will be some who will roll with laughter reading my quotations from the Gemara — so what's all the fuss? There are — I say — bigger „ekhloys“[?] [probably: ignoramuses]; believe me, I can swear to you [„bekhiyen“[?]], that there are rabbis who draw big pensions and don't even decide a single ritual question. And secondly, I have a good opportunity: with the „extra edition“ the fund can also rescue a lost debt of several hundred guldens.
— What? Collect an old debt with the help of the newspaper? How so?
— Just what you hear. Don't be a dolt and don't be so amazed — do you know the „editors“ of the mikveh rag [„mikve bletl“]?
— What a question, whether I know them! I have to give them a gulden of „go-away money“[?] every month; if not — they threaten — they will write me up in their paper...
— Then listen to me, what I had with those ugly pętaki [Polish: „good-for-nothings“]: as soon as our „Somekh Noflim“ fund was founded, they, the „Vayakhel-Pekudei“ [inseparable pair, like the twinned Torah portions] good-for-nothings, made me a „mi sheberakh“ [blessing] every week in their paper, sang my praises and glorifications, until they succeeded in catching me in their mikveh-net and getting a tidy sum out of the fund...
They paid the first instalment — and stop. When we tried to dun them for the debt, they explained to us that they are „working off“ the debt with articles... Well, I thought it over: what good is a „kezayis“ [olive-size morsel] every week to me, when I can „eat up a whole challah at once“... They'll have to give me a whole newspaper, where my name will shine on „all four pages“...
— Hm... hm... I understand, but excuse me, Mr. President, one more question I want to ask you, panie prezesie: apart from your Talmudic articles, what else do you intend to put in the „extra edition“?
— Don't be a sucker [„frayer“]! You don't yet know the „trick“ of how to become popular. I guarantee you that as soon as we make the first trial this year and the „naked society“ also puts out an „extra edition“, it will become a fixed statute, and year in, year out the „naked“ institution will be clothed in a „newspaper“...
— Yes, comrade, there is no other way; we must behave like that tavern-keeper with his wife.
There once was a tavern-keeper, a very great drunkard. His wife would not let him drink so much, and because of that quarrels broke out between the tavern-keeper and his wife.
All of a sudden the tavern-keeper hit upon this invention: he called his wife and said to her: Chana! Do you want us to have blessing and success? Then listen to me: I have a dreier [three-groszy coin]; here, take the coin, and pour me a glass of vodka...
The tavern-keeper's wife took the coin and gave her husband a glass of vodka. A little later the husband says to her: give me back the dreier, and here, have a glass of vodka too.
The „trade“ went from him to her and from her to him, until the barrel of vodka was „sold out“...
We shall do the same — says the president — I, as president, will thank the vice-president; the vice-president will thank the president back; then the president will thank the board, the board — the president, board, vice-president, board, vice, and so on.
— Ha, ha, ha, it will look, panie prezesie, like little children sending each other shalach-manos on Simchas Torah!... What will people say about it? Nothing else but that it's like children playing: „you'll send me back, I'll send you too“, „you tickle me, I tickle you“...
— Oy, sucker ben Gimel[?] — the president of so many institutions, and you come preaching morals?! David! Go right over to the „Vokhnblat“ [„Weekly“] and tell them that if the „extra edition“ isn't ready by Purim, a demon will get into their f... f... [probably „father“]...
— — — — —
In the month of March in the year 1929 two „extra editions“ appeared in the town of Będzin, which announced: 7 notices of thanks to the untiring president, 4 „yasher koyekh“s [well-dones] to the devoted vice, 3 „mi sheberakh“s to the secretary, and 2 „marble tablets“ with golden letters for all those who busy themselves with public needs.
— May it do them good...
Yoshev Beseser [„He who dwells in secret“].
To and from Eretz Israel.

The Italian ship „Carnaro“, sailing to Eretz Israel, presents with its Jewish travellers from the most varied countries a Jewish state in miniature. On this ship, which is carrying several hundred olim [immigrants] to E[retz] I[srael], German Jewish excursionists are travelling on the initiative of „Agudath Israel“ in Frankfurt, under the leadership of the rabbi of Cologne, as well as many journalists, headed by the well-known Zionist leader, editor of the „Jüdische Rundschau“ in Berlin, Dr. Robert Weltsch.
The Jewish passengers of the „Jewish state en route“ feel on the ship just as if they were at home: there is public prayer, Sabbath candles are lit, zemiroth are sung and, above all, one eats from a special Jewish kitchen. It is worth noting that the shipping company „Lloyd Triestino“ takes pains to treat the Jewish travellers with the greatest tolerance and respect.
The halutzim [pioneers] from Congress Poland and Galicia make the long, tedious and hard six-day sea voyage pleasant and entertain the crowd with their dancing and singing. The song „HaAvoda kol hayeinu, mikol tzara tatzileinu“ [„Labour is our whole life, it will save us from every trouble“] resounds over the stormy water.
On the Adriatic Sea, as far as the port of Brindisi, the water was very calm, but on the Mediterranean, near the Greek islands of Crete and near the newly built Corinth canal, the sea „played up“ and the waves tossed the ship, so that the passengers suffered badly from seasickness.
Everyone hid in the cabins; only the halutzim stayed on deck, paying no attention at all to the „raging“ sea. Meanwhile a halutz quoted the „Songs of Zion“ of R' Yehuda Halevi:
The sea storms
In fire and flame —
Yet my soul is happy:
To the sanctuary it flies,
Ever nearer it comes
To the Temple of God!
Only on the sixth day did we approach Jaffa, and seeing the city from afar everyone, even the sick, went up on deck and greeted E[retz] I[srael] with loud „Hurrah“ cries and a „hora“ dance.
Having gone through the formalities at the „Immigration Office“, the customs and the quarantine procedure, I finally arrived in Tel Aviv, where a fairly large number of Zagłębie Jews who live here were awaiting me, wishing to hear a greeting from home, from Zagłębie. I am looking quite closely into the situation and life of the Będzin Jews, about which I shall write in my next letter.
In today's letter I pass on, through the columns of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“, warm greetings from the Zagłębie Jews who live in the towns, villages and colonies of E[retz] I[srael].
All the former Zagłębie residents whom I looked into expressed their satisfaction with their situation. They all speak of E[retz] I[srael] with enthusiasm and fervour and are very optimistic about the development and future of E[retz] I[srael]. After the last re-emigration a large number of people from Zagłębie remained, who after prolonged difficulties have settled in and are already thinking of not leaving the country they have come to love. Many of them have even already acquired local citizenship. All are already fully acclimatised and speak Hebrew, which is a living everyday language here.
All are thirsty for news and follow events in Poland and take a particular interest in life in Zagłębie; they read — so they say — the „Zagl. Tsayt.“, which informs them of all the details of Zagłębie Jewish life. On this occasion all these Jews from Będzin, Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa send, through the „Z. Ts.“, warm greetings to their relatives and friends.
I visited the colonies around Tel Aviv as well as those in Samaria and the Valley [Emek]. In Nahalat Yitzhak near the Borochov quarter a Będzin „farmer“, Pinchas Cin, is working; I met him at work in the field when I came to „Nahalat Yitzhak“. Mr. C. explained to me that he has already been through all seven circles of hell and has succeeded in settling in. He owns a live „meshek“ [farm stock] (inventory) of 3 cows and up to 30 fowl, which his wife looks after; Mr. C. has no land and works in private orange groves, and is nevertheless content with his quiet life.
In Bnei Brak I visited Mr. Natan Fuksbrumer from Będzin. Mr. F., a carpenter by trade, works with his 2 sons, carpenters, from which he draws a respectable livelihood. He also owns „nichsei dela nayedei“ [immovable property]: 2 small houses built of brick and a few dunams of orange grove. His wife, who showed me her henhouse, spoke to me in the following characteristic Yiddish: „Azoy, do iz der ‚lul‘, kh'gib ‚gre'onim‘[?] di ‚efrohim‘...“ [„So, here is the henhouse, I give grain to the chicks...“ — Yiddish studded with Hebrew words].
In „Binyamina“ I met Mr. Avraham Weinryb[?], the son of the Sosnowiec Zionist leader Mr. Israel Moshe Weinryb[?]; he came to the country 8 years ago. Mr. W. works in the PICA perfume factory. He earns a living and does not complain, God forbid, about his situation. For Purim Mr. W., his wife and children came to Tel Aviv, wishing to enjoy a merry Purim too. He is striving to have his father, the ardent Zionist, settle in Eretz Israel.
All who wish to have news of their relatives in E[retz] I[srael] can get in touch with me through the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ at the address: Hotel Sternfeld, Tel Aviv, Lilienblum 36, Palestyna.
M. Hampel.
Tel Aviv, 2 April 1929.
Where Are You, Spring?

By Graf Kali.
Dear God! It is already spring,
Yet the cold reigns — what a fright!
Oh, the winter, like a watchman[?] [„dozor“],
Won't get off its bench...
Long will this winter be remembered
By the merchant and the peasant alike —
This one's nose was frostbitten,
That one is missing[—] a bit of an ear...
This one caught the grippe,
That one — a long-term catarrh...
Winter lodges in the bones
Like a wicked sequestrator...
Dear God, it is already spring
According to all the calendars —
So harness the sun in the sky,
Don't make fools of us people.
I long for dew and forest, and for flowers,
And above all for the old nag-cart
That will take my whole „kapelye“ [my whole gang, the household]
And will celebrate the „rite of the dacha“ [the move to the summer house]...
The Rebbe's Son (29)

[Serialized historical novel — Kraków in the time of the 1648 massacres; installment 29.]
A historical Jewish novel by Yakov Zimmerman [Jakub Cymerman].

Now our men already had an easy job. They no longer even had to exert themselves much in order to pursue the fleeing enemy. They ran by themselves. We now busied ourselves with two things: first, to free all the captives whom the oppressor Chmielnicki [printed "Khmelnitski"], may his name and memory be blotted out, had dragged along with him on all his plundering raids; and also to gather up all the many and precious things that the enemy had thrown away, or that he had left behind in his flight.

Among the captives — Shimon concluded his report — I had the privilege of finding my two dear daughters, but my wife I found no more; she is dead!...

At these words Shimon burst into tears, and looking at him many wept with him, especially the women, up in the women's gallery.

Almost every one of those assembled there had someone — a child, a bridegroom, a husband, a relative or simply a friend — among the Jews who had voluntarily joined the prince's troops; although they had won a great victory and the enemy had for the time being been driven off, quite a few had fallen dead or been wounded. Who could know what that one — the son, the bridegroom, the husband, the close relative or friend — was doing there? Was he still alive, and would one yet have the privilege of seeing him alive and well? And the assembled crowd wept bitterly and lamented.

The rabbi, the wise and worldly-experienced "Tosafot Yom Tov" [R. Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller], although he himself also had reason enough to fear and tremble for the life of his beloved son, was nevertheless the first to collect himself, and at once he took courage and hope. He now turned to Shimon with the question:

— On your way here from the battlefield you surely had to pass through the village of Piaski. Where the Cossacks were gathered — how then was it possible for you to get through there in peace?

— Of course I rode through the village of Piaski — Shimon answered — but the Cossacks were no longer there. Before I reached the village, which was after I had already been riding for over two hours, I was, to tell the truth, very frightened that I might, God forbid, fall into the hands of the vile Cossacks. I very much wanted to announce to you, Jews of Kraków, the happy tidings of the great victory that we had today, and therefore I kept well on guard and stopped every few minutes [?] to look around and see what was happening around me.

When I was in the forest, not far from Piaski, and the moon was shining clear and bright, I suddenly heard a clatter of horseshoes. At once I went with my horse under a very thick tree and hid myself so that those riding by would not be able to see me.

Soon I saw how the Cossacks who had been in Piaski arrived at full gallop. By the light of the moon I even recognized their leader. It was the Cossack Bazyl Petrash [?], the former coachman of Prince Wiśniowiecki.

As they rode past right next to me, I also heard their talk and shouts. They were very angry, and it vexed them that they were not destined to enjoy "such a fat morsel" as Chmielnicki had promised them — to rob the Jews of Kraków, the richest in all of Poland.

— Let us hope — Shimon concluded — that they will not come back here any more, and that with God's help Prince Wiśniowiecki will succeed in destroying Chmielnicki and his robber bands.

— Yes! — said the rabbi in a solemn voice — we must thank and praise the Lord, blessed be He, who never forsakes His people Israel, for having now saved us from our bloodthirsty enemies, and let us hope that so it will be further on as well...

— When do you think — he went on to ask — will we have the privilege and the great pleasure of being able to see our loved ones again, who are now fighting on the battlefield?

— According to what the prince told me — Shimon answered — the Kraków Jews, because they were the bravest and most heroic of all on the battlefield, will already be able to return home tomorrow, so that they can rest from the torments they had to suffer in the camp. But they will not be able to stay here long, because the work is still far from finished. There will still be much to do until Chmielnicki and his robber bands are entirely rooted out.

— Now, dear Rabbi — Shimon concluded — allow me to withdraw; nature demands its due. I have lived through a very hard day and I am very tired from the excitement and the long ride. I urgently [?] need to lie down and rest.

Shimon took leave of the rabbi and went away. His example was followed by all the men, women and children who had been gathered in the Great Synagogue. Everyone hurried home. The house which only a few hours earlier they had had to abandon, not knowing whether they would ever again have the privilege of stepping over its threshold, had now become doubly dear and precious to everyone.

Half an hour later the synagogue was completely empty and again wrapped in darkness, as always in the late night hours.

LAST CHAPTER.

Lively activity reigned the next day, early in the morning, in the Jewish streets of Kraków. Almost all the Jewish inhabitants were already on their feet and looked with curious eyes and great suspense in the direction from which the heroes were soon to arrive — the Jewish soldiers, the young men who had voluntarily joined Prince Wiśniowiecki's soldiers.

But everyone's patience was put to a hard test. The town clock had long since struck twelve. It was already rather late in the afternoon, the sun was already about to set, but everything remained quiet. Of the returning soldiers there was still no sign, and not one of them had yet appeared.

Among all the impatient ones, who had not left even for a single minute the street leading to the gate through which the Jewish soldiers were to march, was Shimon. The whole time he stood straining his eyes hard. He kept on looking in a straight line toward the gate. He very much wanted to be the first to see the first Jewish soldiers, but unfortunately, for the time being, his effort was in vain: no one came...

[Commentary — Warsaw; assimilation and conversion.] We know them, the young careerists with doctor's diplomas in their waistcoat pockets. They are no new faces among us. They were there in Russia in the days of the Tsar, and they are still here now as well, in all the lands of the Diaspora.
While he studies at the university he is a nationally minded young man, belongs to a Jewish students' corporation. He is a Zionist or a Socialist, and should anyone insult the "pintele Yid" [the Jewish spark] in him, such a fellow can flare up like fire and even challenge his Christian comrade to a duel.
Surely this ought to be good; surely Jews ought to rejoice that Israel is not widowed — that there is growing up, no evil eye, a Jewish intelligentsia with national pride and national consciousness? But it is not good, because it is bad, and it is bad because their nationalism stems from forced nationalisation. This youth is Jewish because it cannot be gentile; they are Jews under duress, nationalists against their will, and Jewishness is for them an affliction, a nuisance that clings, which one has to put up with because there are others who will not release him from it. The Polish students' corporations are locked to him with seven locks. No assimilation helps, and even after conversion one is still not a welcome guest in the Polish student family. Having no choice, one must resort to a corporation of one's own, an own one, which one cultivates because one must have it, but which one does not love. For the average Jewish student it is the yellow patch, which he would very much like to be rid of. But he cannot free himself of it.
A yellow patch one wears; one mends it when it wears thin, one cleans it when it gets soiled, but at the very first opportunity one tries to free oneself of it. It is a garment one does not want, only one is forced to walk about in it. And when an opportune moment comes, such an opportunity that one can shake it off — then one indeed shakes it off.
Such a shaking-off took place these days in Warsaw. Twenty young Jewish lawyers, national "young men", were admitted to the Bar Chamber, and on this occasion had to take an oath. It turned out that 12 of these young Jewish diploma-holding intellectuals had to take the Christian oath, because... they are converts.
Twelve young Jewish lawyers, national young men, who played a role in the Jewish student organisations, and... converts. This is no product invented in the imagination of a newspaper reporter, but a fact, a real fact, which happened not in old Tsarist Russia and not during the epidemic of conversion in Germany, but only a few days ago in Warsaw. In the city where the pulse of Jewish national life beats, in the city where one need not resort to the artificial Jewishness of a Frankfurt or the charity-box Jewishness of a New York. It happened in the city where Jewishness is a natural growth that has no need of artificial means.
In Jewish Warsaw there is a natural Jewishness; there is a Hasidic Jewishness with all the fervour and ecstasy of a Rebbe's court. In Jewish Warsaw there is a deep Jewish workers' movement with national élan and consciousness. There is Jewish political life, and Jewish culture grows out of every stone on Nalewki and Karmelicka. This is no Jewishness of necessity, no forced nationalism, this is no yellow patch. This is a Jewishness that bursts forth from the depths of reality. Therefore it is strong, therefore it breathes élan, is animated by readiness for sacrifice, sanctified by self-sacrifice (mesirat nefesh).
This is a Jewishness that can be humiliated and bent, but never broken.
This is a mighty oak that sits firmly in the earth.
The Jewish man of the masses, the toiling Jewish merchant, the oppressed Jewish artisan, the benighted Jewish worker loves his Jewishness. He does not regard it as a curse from the Admonition (Tokhehah) and an affliction for the parents' sins.
It is different, however, with the young Jewish diploma-holding intellectual. His Jewishness is to him a yellow patch, and he wears it only until a violent tear comes into it.
The Jewish diploma-holding intellectual has from time immemorial and in all countries been the one who jumps and runs over foreign fences; the pull of a career has always been very strongly developed in him, stronger than religious and ethical feeling and mightier than national consciousness.
For a long time people tried to close their eyes to this; they wanted to persuade themselves that today's young generation of doctors and lawyers is different from their former brethren before the war.
Thus people wanted to deceive themselves.
Then came twelve young Jewish lawyers and showed that the old pot of peas [the mess of pottage] has not lost its value even today, and had themselves baptised — in order to be admitted to the Bar Chamber. Merely because of the hope that in this way they might perhaps get to the pot of peas..
Y. B. Gips.

[Sosnowiec — court, crime.] The degenerate from Sosnowiec before the Court of Appeal.
On Saturday the Warsaw Court of Appeal heard the case of Gershon Fiwszkiewicz [?] of Sosnowiec.
This Fiwszkiewicz lived with his brother-in-law Yaakov Kaptan, who had 2 girls, one, Rachel, 13 years old, and the other a younger one. F. chose a moment when nobody was at home and raped the 13-year-old girl. At the same time he threatened her with death if she told anyone.
In time the girl began to feel different, but she told no one. Some time passed and the girl gave birth to a child. Nobody was at home then except the degenerate Fiwszkiewicz and the two girls. The criminal gave the little girl a few groszy and told her to throw the newborn child out onto the rubbish heap. A woman neighbour heard the crying of the little child and took it out of the rubbish.
The Sosnowiec District Court sentenced him to 8 years in prison, but he appealed to Warsaw. Because some witnesses did not appear in court, the trial was adjourned.
