Będzin's Former Rabbi, Rabbi Yehutiel Grojbart, on the Tragedy of the Agunot in Poland

Będzin's former rabbi, Rabbi Yehutiel Grojbart, has published in the New York newspaper 'Der Tog' an extensive article on the tragedy of the agunot ('chained' wives) in Poland. Because of the importance of the subject, our paper brings selected passages from the article.

Rabbi Grojbart writes: The world war ended long ago, but its consequences are still felt. In Central Europe, where thousands of Jewish families remain torn apart and scattered 'across the seven seas,' a particular wound stands out in the Jewish organism — the tragedy of the agunot. Thousands of Jewish women have been abandoned by their husbands; they are left with small children, helpless and unprotected, unable to locate the husbands who have vanished and to obtain a divorce (get) so as to begin a new page. Some of the husbands emigrated to America and remarried there; others perished in the war, died as prisoners of war or as hostages in Russia — and their wives are 'living widows,' whose plight is harder than that of actual widows.

The article presents several real cases: (a) A man named N. Welber [?] left his wife in Poland in 1902 and went to Chicago; he was recently located and summoned by the Polish consul at his wife's request. He claimed that he had divorced her back in Warszawa before a certain rabbi whose name he had forgotten — but the rabbinate in Warszawa investigated, found this to be untrue, and now demands that he grant a divorce. (b) An aguna who could find no way to locate her husband, who had disappeared to America and married another woman — the husband's family helped obtain a divorce. (c) A man who was conscripted into the army in Poland in 1912 and of whom nothing further was heard; after rumors that he had fallen, his wife turned to the rabbinate in Warszawa, and through the examination of formal testimony it was proven that a man of the same name had been killed in Russia; the rabbinate was about to issue a permit [for her to remarry], when it was suddenly learned that the husband had been seen strolling through the streets of New York.

It is further related that at the convention of 'Agudat HaRabbanim' (the Union of Rabbis) in Poland a central bureau was established which collected material and documents on the missing husbands, and made contact with world Jewry in order to save these unfortunate women. The writer cites the saying, 'Whoever rescues one aguna is as though he rebuilt one of the ruins of Jerusalem,' and warns against levity in granting agunot permits [to remarry]. In conclusion he calls on the Jewish organizations and communal activists to give a fitting response to the great emissary Rabbi Elijah Lifszyc, the Rabbi of Grójec ('der Gritzer Rov'), who has come to America with the documents and material in order to create the means for this work — and asks whether American Jewry, so generous, will not allow the superstitions of the war years to go on devouring the remnants of these lives.

Matzah — Why Is the Poor Man's Matzah So Expensive? Who Is to Blame, and Could It Have Been Prevented?

Matzah. Why is the poor man's matzah so expensive? Who is to blame, and could it have been prevented?

As has happened more than once before — today there is no longer any limit or distinction: everything runs along as usual, and no one bothers to ask whether it must be so or could be otherwise. Things are so 'arranged' nowadays that lawlessness reigns in every sphere of our life — wherever you turn there is no responsibility anywhere, and everyone is left with a free hand to do whatever he pleases; no one considers his fellow, no one wishes to have pity on the other or to 'play along with him' at all.

And against what is all this said? Against the [high cost] of this year. As is well known, the most important question for the Jew is the piece of matzah he must bring home — and which costs him dearly. A Jew came to our editorial office asking to be heard: he himself is a matzah baker, and according to him matzah is not baked in order to 'take an interest' in kashrut certifications and in profiteering. He relates: I pay the rabbinate the takse (the tax) on the flour's being 'kosher for Passover', and they charge for the baking of the matzah as well; and after all that I sell the flour at under 75 groszy a kilo — no shop made any profit on it — and yet the bakers charge for the flour a price above the one just mentioned.

It is impossible to understand how the rabbinate and the community board allowed a kilo of matzah to reach 170–180 groszy! And if the population was thus 'squeezed' — is it to be precisely over the bread of the poor? Was kashrut observed to such a degree that a kilo of matzah simply had to cost so much for the sake of the certification? After all, [grain] is not as dear as it once was. So why did such an exceptional percentage have to be added to a kilo of matzah? You understand: the bakers cannot justify it, and in the end they say that the rabbinate grants certification to 'foreign' (imported) matzah as well, so that no one can compete with them — and then they are 'sole rulers' and charge as they please.

Matzah, after all, is a commodity of the very first necessity, which even the poorest person needs — so why did the rabbinate and the community board not join together to see to it that matzah would not become dearer? We ask nothing of our community board except that it at least take into account the concern that we should have cheap matzah for Passover; and if it did not wish to deal with the matter, then at the very least it ought to have influenced the rabbinate to take an interest in it. It is not enough to lift the ban on 'foreign' products so that the locals can 'clip a coupon' from it. We live in hard enough times, the groschen earned is stretched to the minimum for the average Jewish merchant — all the more so for the retailers and the artisans. This class ought to have been kept in mind — so why should the bakers be given a free hand to charge whatever they please for a commodity of first necessity?

Fish and other products, too, became dearer 'in honor of Passover' to an unheard-of degree. Had we a healthy economic society that understood the necessity of leading a normal, healthy life, none of this would have been so lawless. Today it is hard for the Jew, in any case, to bring the Passover necessities home — his difficult situation ought to have been eased, whereas we see, to our great regret, the opposite: everyone grabs for himself as he pleases. There is no economic leadership here to cry out: it must not be permitted that the population be squeezed because it needs matzah and festival products.

From the practical standpoint and from the Jewish standpoint — the rabbinate ought to have seen to it that the matter be conducted [properly], so that [the Jew] would not have to pay so much for products bearing the certification; it must not be permitted that under the name of 'kashrut' a [squeezing] of the poorer classes should reign. Kashrut must be put in its proper place, so that it does not fall upon the backs of the poorer classes. It is clear that such people, who do not conduct public affairs according to truth and honesty, [deserve condemnation].

R. Let.

Who still calls for justice? What has the "pagan" gemilut chesed (free-loan) fund [of Sosnowiec] done, and how does Sosnowiec respond to it?

Sosnowiec — so the [scandal] tells us — the gemilut chesed fund [—] took the money for itself. And not for the first time: whatever the reason, it is done knowingly, on the calculation that it is more 'profitable' this way, with no regard for anyone. What can such a phenomenon teach us? What respect can we show for public institutions and their heads? How is the prestige of our public institutions to be preserved while their representatives behave with such crude, petty-shopkeeper cunning that it arouses disgust?

This is the result of public negligence and of moral [decline]. There was a time when such license was unheard of — the community was taken into account. No institution would have dared to use such improper means, and it would have been pointed to as [an unacceptable] phenomenon. Now it has come to the point where one institution does not consult its sister institution. That private individuals do not consult one another is understandable — those are private matters; but a society, however little it may wish to consider others, still stands under the scrutiny of the community, and must, willingly or unwillingly, reckon with public opinion.

In the face of such vast public license, one might have expected our institutions to lose all sense of tact, decency and respect toward the community. But they are not the guilty ones; the guilty are those who know that it ought to be otherwise, that this must not be permitted. We, the public representatives, will earn respect only if we do not allow license to advance on every front. Around our gemilut chesed fund are gathered people worthy of respect in the town — so how do these people allow themselves to compromise so?

The heads of the gemilut chesed fund must respond to this license; failing to respond to such phenomena only helps to foster what is unhealthy and improper. Every institution is subject to public scrutiny, before which it must conduct itself with propriety — all the more so a gemilut chesed fund answerable to the central office in Warszawa, which must surely reckon with public opinion. Let the heads of the Sosnowiec gemilut chesed fund bring the 'pagan' members to a public trial and prove that there are no [improper] acts for which they are responsible — and if not, then they have nothing to show but deeds that are [unseemly]. Y. Ben-Zvi: The Palestine Workers' Fund and the Histadrut (on the Occasion of Mr. Ben-Zvi's Visit to Zagłębie)

An article by Y. Ben-Zvi (Yitzhak Ben-Zvi), on the occasion of his visit to Zagłębie.

"Zionism can be realized only through the Jewish working class" — an idea that 23 years ago was considered outright heresy, both among Jewish workers and in general Zionist circles, and that was finally acknowledged by the entire organized working public of the Land of Israel — and not only in the Land of Israel: all the parties and non-party bodies, in Europe as in America, that embrace the building of the Land of Israel must recognize that without the workers and their own efforts the Jewish national home will remain a vain stronghold.

The first concrete result of this idea was the founding of an economic apparatus for the workers' activity in the Land of Israel. Today there is in the Land of Israel a workers' bank with founding capital of one hundred thousand pounds, as well as a series of the workers' constructive cooperatives (HaMashbir, Solel Boneh, Nir, Kupat Cholim, the Committee of the Colonies). It is hard to grasp what the establishment of such a first institution meant in its time; but 19 years ago, in December 1909, when the representatives of the united socialist federation "Poalei Zion" decided for the first time to found the "Palestine Workers' Fund" (Palestine Arbeter Fund), it was an unprecedented novelty in the history of the Jewish workers' movement. The Fund gave expression to the unity of the Jew and the Jewish worker in class consciousness — for the building of the Land of Israel.

About 6 years later, in Elul 5673, the Labor Bureau was in fact established as the executive apparatus for all the Fund's work. The Fund became a tool of work and struggle in the hands of the entire Jewish working class in the Land of Israel, and a tool in the hands of the worldwide Jewish workers' movement for the Land of Israel. As long as the working public in the country was not united in a single class organization, the connection between the Fund and the working public was indirect.

The situation changed fundamentally with the founding of the Histadrut: about 9 years ago, at the founding convention of the Histadrut in Haifa, "Achdut HaAvoda" and the Fund's management announced that they were prepared to hand over to the Histadrut their place and rights in the Fund. After negotiations (and with the agreement of the Histadrut on the one hand and Poalei Zion on the other), it was decided that the property of the Palestine Workers' Fund would pass into the possession of the Histadrut, and that the Fund (Kapai) would be registered as a subsidiary of "Chevrat Ovdim," like all the institutions of the Histadrut.

The Significance of the General National Exhibition in Poznań (by Dr. St. Wachowiak)

The Significance of the General National Exhibition in Poznań.
By Dr. St. Wachowiak (president of the Exhibition Committee).

A whole literature has already been written about the economic and cultural significance of the great exhibitions organized abroad. Their influence on the development of nations is immense. It is enough to point, as a typical example, to France — of which one may say without exaggeration that, thanks to its magnificent exhibitions, it turned Paris into the metropolis of the entire world.

In a Poland awakening to life, the General National Exhibition is a supreme first achievement in two senses: first, that the exhibition was erected in an astonishingly short time — not even two full years; and second, that it arose with meager means relative to its scale. That the exhibition answers our living economic and cultural needs — to this all of Poland has responded, taking an active part and not sparing considerable funds.

The exhibition arose on the basis of a general national understanding of the matter. In the last ten years there have been few instances in which such striking enthusiasm prevailed among all strata and all regions of Poland. Our national character tends toward momentary outbursts that pass quickly; we are less accustomed to coordinated work. The General National Exhibition is, as it were, proof that something is improving in this respect. The [mobilized] front and the whole population gave moral support to the initiators of the exhibition to complete the greatest constructive enterprise created in the ten years of liberated Poland — all the greater for being the fruit of a period of economic depression, which reached its peak precisely when we were finishing our hard work.

The economic aim of the exhibition was to raise domestic consumption and exports, and to improve working methods and propaganda abroad. The rich French and German literature provides a series of proofs that exhibitions had a decisive influence on domestic consumption — something we shall easily understand considering that consumption in the various parts of the Republic is by no means equal (it is enough to compare the consumption of Upper Silesia with that of the eastern regions). Thanks to the exhibition, hundreds of thousands of Polish peasants will come from those parts of the country where consumption is meager, and the exhibition will serve as a healthy factor in this respect — especially if government circles and the local authorities, appreciating its significance, organize tours from all the decisive circles, and above all in the economy of local self-government.

As for exports — until now foreign countries have had no opportunity to become acquainted with our export possibilities as they can at the present exhibition. In Poznań all of Polish industry, crafts, and agriculture are now represented. The exhibition will also help not a little to improve working methods: a peasant, for example, will be able to see for himself the usefulness of artificial fertilizer and to see agricultural machines he has never seen before; and in industry, already during the organizing stage a certain movement toward concentration was felt — new associations were formed, and people banded together around the achievements — which will inevitably lead to the removal of the old boundaries that had held back the development of industry and commerce.

And what more is there to say about propaganda — no field in Poland has been so neglected as this. Foreign countries did not know us and did not have confidence in us — and that is why it was so hard to obtain foreign loans, which all rest on trust. Even before the exhibition opened, it is being talked about all over Europe; there is no language spoken in Europe in which nothing has been written about the exhibition. From all of Europe and from America many visitors are preparing to come to us; tours to Poland are being organized on an enormous scale — for the first time since Poland came into being. I am convinced that the economic circles, which have invested so much for the sake of the General National Exhibition, will feel its good influence in all fields of their work.

Dr. St. Wachowiak.

The Budget Question in Communal/Municipal Self-Government (Editorial)

The budget question in communal self-government.

More than once we have already had occasion to speak of the economic affairs of Zagłębie, of the failures and losses caused with the help of our 'city fathers.' There were times when we wondered how the local authorities are run, and we came to the understanding that half of their members only 'train themselves' after they have already taken up the [office]. Once they have gone through this 'school' — will they be better or worse? Will they understand more or less? We want well-trained representatives who will understand how to create great, important, and useful things — things that will benefit both the town and its inhabitants.

And what do we see instead? At every opportunity — a failure; in every negotiation — the greatest defeat; and so it is among the councilmen in general, and especially among 'our brethren, the children of Israel': among them the matter is especially [grave]. We are occupied only with mutual squabbling, and each one knows only how to 'play tricks' and to trip up his neighbor. And while matters that concern us little can still be endured — it is hard to endure this in important questions that concern us directly, in which no agreement is reached and the potential is not used for our benefit and our honor.

Now we stand before the municipal budgets of the towns of Zagłębie, and at such an important moment — to set about discussing budgets of millions at a time of such division is surely and certainly useless, and even dangerous. Let us not forget that the budgets now reach into the millions, and that the great majority of them is covered by Jewish money — so which of the councilmen will give an account of how the budgets might be drawn up in such chaos? Which of our representatives will take into account what consequences all this may bring upon the Jewish public?

Once we had a Jewish 'Koło' (bloc), in which people would gather and decide how to act on this or that economic question concerning the Jewish public — and they acted in unity and together, so that the unity itself commanded respect even among the non-Jews, who were compelled to reckon with it, and not seldom even identified with the Jewish merchants. Now there is no longer such a Jewish club: no one gathers, and on an important question each pulls in his own direction; no one knows anything decisive and unifying — and precisely at such a moment, in such chaos, they set about discussing the budget question.

It is understood that the Christians, however divided they may be, the moment a question concerning the Jews is at hand, unite into a common front against the Jewish public. Who grasps the harm that Jewish Będzin may suffer if it sets about discussing the budget question under the prevailing conditions? Surely [precisely] now we ought to have a Jewish association, to discuss every question sensibly and to adopt resolutions from a proper position. Our representatives need not fear a bloc — they themselves know how to act, and know their place well. But when one observes how the sessions are conducted — how each looks only to 'snatch' at his neighbor and trip him up — one may conclude that the situation in the city council is not brilliant, and that those who wish to act are able to achieve very little in such division, in such chaos.

Let us not forget that this concerns the drawing up of a budget covered by the urban population — and above all by the Jewish middle class, the artisans and the retailers; therefore one must not remain divided. One can already picture what such an economy looks like: the impression is as if they were playing lotto, and we are left to fate without knowing how it will be 'drawn'...

With the passing of the city council elections we trumpeted the great victory, having won 16 Jewish mandates; and the victory is indeed great. But how do we look with this 'great victory'? They are divided, and how little understanding they have of joint and fruitful work, of managing a sound economy. The people lose their balance, do not know at all where in the world they are, take no account of their Christian colleagues (who derive no less enjoyment than they do from these 'performances'), and take no account of the spectators, the gallery, the voters who sent them to the city council. It seems that they are not conducting politics and not leading agitations — but simply administering the municipal self-government, defending just demands and protecting class interests. But who bothers to defend interests and safeguard civil rights, while the people forget where they are.

And as an illustration — a small example: before turning to the ordinary work, almost every faction read out 'declarations,' containing — as is well known — loud demands upon the self-government; only a single class read out no declaration and raised no demand — and that is none other than the merchants. Understand: Będzin is, it would seem, a town of merchants, whose representatives surely had something to demand and request of the city council. In the elections 'work was invested,' the merchants played first fiddle, formed a bloc and got representatives through — and now there is nothing, as though no one were sitting there and there were no demands. And that the merchants have no representatives there can be seen from the fact that when the matter was the reduction of the excessive tax on goods shipped by rail — there was no one to support the motion, and it was accordingly rejected. That is what the merchants' representation in our city council looks like.

Dread seizes one on watching how our representatives manage the [affairs] of the town — not for the town's benefit, and at the same time suppressing Jewish prestige. A Jewish bloc (a klub) must once and for all be formed, so that whoever sits on the city council comes as decent people and as Jews. The heart aches to see how such work — which once absorbed so much attention and was bound up with fine ideas and lofty ideals — is being reduced to a bagatelle. Once, when educated Jews sat on the city council, they were a thorn in the eye of the little clique, which invented [slanders] against their integrity; and now that the 'gems' have been removed, there is no one to hinder them, and everything is open and free — and there we have a picture of what the activity of these 16 councilors looks like.

We lack the educated, learned and experienced public representatives who would not permit the present chaos; we lack the personalities who would have the courage to bang on the table and say: Enough! This far you have been allowed — no further; we cannot permit such deeds, so that Jewish honor not be harmed. But, alas, we do not now have the powerful personalities who would understand that public activity must be guarded like the apple of the eye. It must be understood at last that one stands 'on a stage,' and one must not allow oneself to be mocked as a person. The representatives must understand why their voters sent them to the city council, and what tasks are laid upon them in administering the municipal self-government. Our councilors must finally pull themselves together and create one unity — one that will not [break down] like the [orchestras] that play only when they are paid.

R. Let.
Our Foundation Capital (Article)

Our foundation capital (grunt-kapital).

The upheaval reigning in our economic life can be well recognized [through] cooperation. One might think that in this respect we have won a great victory: we have a large, purely Jewish bank that employs dozens of clerks and finances almost all Jewish commerce and small industry. And it is indeed one of our great [riches].

Before the war the banks were mainly private, apart from the State Bank (the 'Crown Bank'): one financier, or several financiers, would invest a large sum as foundation capital, on the basis of which they received credit from the State Bank; and once they developed, the private bank financed itself through credits, dealt with other towns in the country and conducted [operations]. Today it is different: no one has money. All our banks that play a role were built from the outset on donations, on loans from the American philanthropic institutions — chiefly 'the Joint,' which gave [almost] the entire sum for the capital. In a word: a cooperative. And in this respect [—], and the growth of the banks is the fruit of recent years. A few tens of thousands of dollars from 'the Joint,' together with the [members], would surely not have created the great wonder that developed.

In this cooperation the Jewish combinatorial abilities are revealed: the Jew shows his 'miracle-power,' to create 'something from nothing,' and the [secret] is laid bare. The loans of a few hundred zloty are turned over several times in trade, and the result is that the member [is taxed beyond his means]... He repays the loan [in notes]; and the whole [maneuver] is perhaps only 'sorcery,' without a real basis — you do not see it with your own eyes: [the notes] are turned over, rewritten, discounted, re-discounted... 'super-Jewish scribblings' [—].

One must reckon with the bank management: here, with the merchant, he is not [certain] to pay, and in the present situation — day after day, week after week, month after month — a 'balance' is already being drawn up. And since Poland is [in crisis], the merchant has nothing every month. The merchant [turns] to the banks, and to the loan fund (lei-kase) for merchants, and the retailer — to the traders' fund; and the banks [lend him] a few thousand. There is no room for tenants in the banks — they [cannot] pay rent...

The banks are as if 'public,' since the society — which gives the foundation capital — is the [owner]; and before the war, when a bank was [created] on real foundation capital, the aim was that the foundation capital should not be a 'miracle-power' but a genuine basis for the bank. Today's foundation capital, as said, is the public [foundation]. It is no wonder that we have a bank on a public foundation — and not a fiction of foundation capital. The democratic [maneuver] [created] the 'something' that [accompanies] us in Jewish [trade]...

P.K.

The Question of Education (in Light of the State of the Talmud Torah) — Can the Indifference Be Changed? (Article)

The question of education (in light of the state of the Talmud Torah). The question of education among people and among the [nation] — can the indifference be changed?

It is no novelty that the question of education is among the most delicate problems of the modern worldview. Education demands the greatest minds, people who will study and toil to develop the idea. Among modern peoples the 'world of children' occupies the highest place. Who does not know that the education of children is the finest, dearest and most exalted thing, and that every person of understanding is engaged with the delicate matter called child-rearing? And who are the educators, the teachers, the leaders? People who have merged, body and soul, into the world of [children], who study the child's physiognomy and penetrate deep into children's souls. The higher a people stands, the more culturally developed — the better the people it obtains to educate the future. The children, the school, the teachers — among the nations of the world these form an entirely separate world, and this little world struggles by every means to be insulated from the great 'world of adults.'

Parents discharge their duty before God and man once they have handed their children, here or there, to this school or that; the only thing that interests them is that at the end of the school year the children should not be left to sit back in the same grade. And how little interest is shown, among [people], in the children of the secondary schools — and this is nothing compared with the great interest a people takes in the children of the elementary schools, in which are concentrated those from the middle strata down to the very lowest. The children are kept like a treasure more precious than fine gold; care is taken that they should have the best educators, the best opportunities to develop their talents, and the finest, most comfortable premises.

And here it is instructive to cast a glance at how the children of the poorest class are educated among us, and who their educators are. Take, for instance, our Talmud Torah, in which the poorest children are supposed to be educated. Who does not see in what condition our Sosnowiec Talmud Torah appears, and who its educators are. Can one speak of the institution at all as an educational institution? Every conscious person — or, more precisely, anyone with any modern education — must blush with shame if he has to speak of the Talmud Torah as an educational institution. In fact we see that there is nothing there, neither teacher nor melamdim, it is chaos; the melamdim do not receive their wretched pittance of a wage, and the matter has been brought to the point of liquidation.

The question then arises: can Sosnowiec not maintain even a single Talmud Torah? We know that in the smallest little town Talmud Torahs are maintained; but here is the flaw: the Talmud Torah, which ought to be municipal — is not so; otherwise Sosnowiec could maintain such an institution and afford a larger budget, so that the melamdim would not go hungry. For partisanship in politics rules over everything, and one faction gives the other no quarter, until the institution becomes a kind of 'private shop' in which no one has any regard for his fellow. That is why our institutions, which once held an honored place, are brought to such a woeful state.

It would seem that for an educational institution like a Talmud Torah one need not have hesitated [to exert oneself] on its behalf, and meanwhile the institution has been brought to such a dreadful state that one must hang [padlocks] on its doors. Can such a thing be imagined among other peoples? Can other peoples even form the notion of bringing a people's institution for children to such a dreadful state?

If people really want a Talmud Torah worthy of a town like Sosnowiec — it can most certainly be created; one must not tremble before the bright light and the rising sun. Let them make the institution public, let them understand the task such an institution must fulfill toward the broad masses, let them demand that the whole town come to the aid of its upkeep, let a general meeting be convened — and everything will become clear, and then the institution can be reorganized, and in it all strata of the population will be concentrated. It is a desecration of the Name that in a town like Sosnowiec the Talmud Torah should be in such a dreadful state. The Jews of Sosnowiec give money to maintain a Talmud Torah, they surely want it — but they must receive the guarantee that the institution is municipal and admits all the poor children. If it continues to be a 'private shop,' one cannot demand that the whole town maintain it. The present leaders of the Talmud Torah must therefore come to the town with clear demands — what they want from it and what they will give it.

Dr. Papori.

The Fruit of the Evil Inclination? — Why Does [the Merchant Class] Not React to the High Cost of Living? (Article)

The fruit of the evil inclination? Why does the merchant class not react to the wanton lawlessness?

Economic conditions in Poland are not good at all, as witnessed by the waves of dishonored promissory notes and the great number of bankruptcies, which have become a routine and ordinary phenomenon. We live under harsh conditions of existence: expenses in these times are so large, taxes weigh heavily, the housing question and the various outlays oppress and choke the small and middling merchants.

But it is characteristic that, for all this, business is not conducted on a normal footing. Today one must, on the one hand, be careful in buying goods; and on the other, earnings must be calculated so that one can be both competitive and still make a profit after deducting the [enormous] administrative costs. And what do we do? We are neither the first nor the last: no one tries to be competitive, no one earns according to a normal reckoning. Instead: either they trade without profit at the expense of the Jewish [conscience] — "What do I lose?" — or they slash the price with no calculation at all.

The war years bred disappointment and demoralization in every corner of our life; the war threw humanity off the [track], the wheels came off the rails and cannot return to the right [road]. And so today such a terrible chaos reigns, and people lose their balance. As human beings we trade and wander, we trade and turn the world [upside down] — while knowing full well that not a single earned penny was invested in the business, that almost nothing is earned on the goods; whereas real merchants stand and watch how goods are "thrown" about without end, and the result is that one man goes bankrupt, takes the goods for cash and reckons with nothing and no one.

Such people have no respect for anyone, no fear and no responsibility, and so they "play lotto" and do not calculate at all how the matter will "come out" in the end. And the question arises: can a real firm hold out under the terms and prices given by some new "star" that has just sprung up? Can it compete with those who are themselves lawless and who also make free with other people's property? Understand — in such trade the legs are cut out from under the real and honest firms, which understand the rule "live and let live".

And just as the lawless lotto-speculators, with their swindling combinations, sink the solid and genuine firms below the surface — so too the reverse: there are swindlers who stand on guard and wait for the "opportune moment", and at such a moment they "tear" a price out of whatever the world depends on. Thus, for example, we know that in honor of Passover the price of fish began to climb to 8 zloty a kilo — and the price holds. The question arises: what has happened that there is such a "shortage" of fish? Have the fish emigrated from Poland? The answer: it is not that the fish went away, but that the fishmongers simply, "in honor of the holiday", set a price that "flows over the mouth". It is understandable that the evil inclination for money is great, and that raising a price is surely easier than lowering it; and so it is more convenient for the crowd and for profit to charge as high a price as possible — and the [butchers] and poultry dealers followed in their footsteps.

And the same with bread: as is known, coal has grown dearer these last few weeks, and the price of bread rose by a few groszy; and the bakers do not want "to know anything" when flour is cheap, but they immediately raise the price of bread the moment flour grows dearer. It must not be forgotten that in the magistrats there are committees whose task is to set the prices of first-rank foodstuffs — that is, to stand guard so that the population is not exploited on articles of prime necessity. So the question arises: where are these supervisory committees, which are supposed to see that the population is not cheated in buying bread or other basic foodstuffs? These are unheard-of doings; and the sad thing is that the committees of our local authority remain indifferent to such a scandal — that the population is forced to pay dearly for a "luxury" like bread.

R. Let.

Social Obligation — How Are We to Understand the Lack of Interest in a Professional Association? (Article)

Social obligation. How are we to understand the lack of interest in the professional [association]?

Time and again we come up against it: at every opportunity we see our own dividedness, our meager understanding of our own affairs, of our most painful questions. We convened a general meeting of the "Merchants' Association" in Sosnowiec. One might have thought that important questions would be raised, questions touching the members' own interests. But who says so, who thinks that a professional association is obliged to take an interest? And indeed the question was raised — whether the association should exist at all, or whether it ought to be liquidated entirely.

Do you understand — a question? The "Merchants' Association" supposedly has nothing to do on the Jewish street; the people of the merchants, of the shopkeepers and retailers, are so "orderly and calm" that they have no need of a professional association, the matter does not interest them in the least, and it should simply be cleared out of the way — for it is a nuisance, a superfluous object that no one looks at and no one needs to carry on his shoulders. Thus we see our dividedness, our helplessness, our failure to understand for what purpose professional institutions are created.

It would seem that Sosnowiec holds Jewish merchants; but only at first glance does it seem that there are merchants, and that the association belongs to the middling merchants, to the average Jew, to the people — to the one who is exploited at every step, who cannot help himself, whose only recourse is the [need] for a patron-adviser, for a lawyer to go and defend him and speak on his behalf. It is impossible to grasp where this category of people gets so much coldness, so large a measure of indifference, which causes so much trouble in the merchants' world. How common are the scenes in which such Jews walk about as men pursued by a tax seizure, complaining that they will have to give up their place if the decree remains hanging over their heads.

One might have understood that at such a moment one should come to the association and examine the situation, deliberate on the future of this or that merchant, of this or that exploited man on the brink of ruin; and if such an institution is done away with — to whom will those helpless Jews then turn, who cannot even defend themselves or say two words? And if there is no "Merchants' Association" — who will intervene on behalf of the merchants as a whole when there is need to speak in the name of the merchant estate?

We know that, sadly, we have very few of our professional institutions, and fewer still of merchants' associations as such; and for that reason the merchant thinks he has no need of an association, that it is superfluous to him, since he derives no benefit from it — so what is it for? No one analyzes the fact that such an institution is as vital to the merchant as life itself; no one tries to understand that if the association brings him no benefit, that is no proof that the institution is superfluous — but rather the opposite: it must be raised to a level from which the proper benefit will grow. Do we ever pause on the thought of what colossal benefit we could draw from our professional institutions were they standing at their proper height? No, we do not render ourselves such an account, otherwise we would see to it that we had sound professional institutions; otherwise the ridiculous question would not arise — whether to keep in existence, or more precisely whether to liquidate, the institution that ought to be the "ABC" of the merchants' method.

People do not want to understand that nothing comes of itself, that everything must be created, that every thing must be built systematically, and that sometimes years pass before the benefit becomes apparent. With us everything is simple and primitive: there is no benefit from this or that institution — let it be cleared away, removed from the Jewish street. With an indifference — we would say, a criminal one — we treat matters of the common good; how banal we are when public deeds are to be considered. We must finally understand that nothing comes of itself, and that with folded hands nothing will be created. For the more worthy and understanding ought to come and educate their fellows, to plant in the masses an interest in the society, and to show them the great thing that lies in concentration, in the understanding of public tasks and public obligation.

Selekt.

Our Institutions — The Downfall of the 'Small Traders' Association' in Sosnowiec and Its Rebirth (Article)

Our institutions. The downfall of the Sosnowiec "Small Traders' Association" and its rebirth.

Just how much is left to chance among us, how indifferently and with what criminal banality we treat everything — the sad events of the "Small Traders' Association" (Kleinhändler-Verein) in Sosnowiec can serve as an example. The scandals that occurred there, the unheard-of and impermissible deeds, were reflected in such a way that it came to the point where the association went completely bankrupt, and the institution was ruined and shattered. It is, after all, unheard of that an institution numbering close to a thousand members could crumble in the blink of an eye; and we measure the usefulness of an institution by the size of its membership — the more members an association has, the more esteemed it is, and the greater its chances of taking a leading place and fulfilling a public role in our life.

So it is among us: whenever an institution attains a justification for its existence, whenever it shows that it deserves to take a place in our public life — suddenly a storm and tempest come and reduce everything to trifles. For when a body reaches a thousand members, at a time when our economic interests are at so low a level, the Jew who is a member of a "traders' association" needs so much public support and so much enlightenment of public spirit — that the moment he is a member, and has some support from the institution, and the moment it collapses — it is for him a real catastrophe.

We are certain that an association must be a "guide" to its member, a "guide of the way" who shows him along which line to continue on his life's path and how to struggle along his hard road. We constantly urge upon the common people that they must be united in a public institution, that they must have the "authority" that will look after their tangled present and enable them to reach a better "tomorrow." For we feel at every step how hard life becomes for these people: on the shoulders of the broad common people lies the burden of continuing to maintain their meager existence; and there are those who seek to spoil their way, to block the narrow path they have. And so it comes to the point where, even if they sell their little bit of poor merchandise — they still cannot pay what is demanded of them.

We know how helpless the Jew is left when he reaches such a stage. The question arises: who will speak on his behalf at such a terrible moment? Who will be able to fight for him and see that he is not broken? We know that a Jew cannot do this alone. And hence the division. But nothing compares to the great usefulness of public concentration at such a serious moment. We understand the importance of the institution when it can intervene on behalf of its members; an institution with a larger number of members has the power to demand justice with greater force. Can we estimate the great value of an institution numbering close to a thousand members? We cannot imagine the might and power that such a body holds on behalf of the community. Such an institution must be seriously reckoned with — both by the [authorities], the headquarters in Warszawa, and by the community as a whole — which looks upon such a united body as a giant that must be reckoned with, whether willingly or of necessity.

And when the institution crumbles, when such acts of corruption are committed in it, one must respond as befits unheard-of deeds that humiliate the Jewish community as a whole — and thereby the retailer is orphaned, with no one to turn to who will protect him. It is therefore fitting to welcome the fact that the institution has now been reorganized, and a fresh stream of life has been poured into it: the guilty parties were removed, and in their place came people who took upon themselves the labor, the initiative, and the will to act on behalf of the broad strata of the Jewish common people.

Let the institution, then, be properly reorganized — for the [need] exists and is "standing and asking"; there are members who support such an institution, provided it protects their dignity when they need it. Let the "Small Traders' Association" henceforth show signs of life, signs of activity, and signs of awakening — and this will give the proper satisfaction. Let the new board show us that it understands how to manage so vital an apparatus in our economic and public life. We wish, therefore, to place great hopes in the new board, which must understand its important tasks on the new path of life.

Selekt.

How Zagłębie Looks to Foreign Visitors — Part II (Impressions of Israel Kahan)

How Zagłębie looks to foreign visitors — Part II.
(By Israel Kahan, editor of "Lodzer Tageblat.")

Będzin derives no great honor from its Jewry — one might say the opposite. Here in Poland people have not come to judge public phenomena objectively; they do not want to know that "a single standard" can apply in public and economic life. The "favor" of the decisive circles has turned its back on Jewish Będzin, and the "favor" is bestowed more and more upon neighboring Sosnowiec. A year ago this place was a village, known for the beautiful pine forest of Sosnowiec, nothing more; and from the word "sosna" (pine) the town's name is supposedly derived. And the "-wiec" (the sting) came only now...

Sosnowiec — where the Jews reach [a considerable proportion] — now receives constant preference at Będzin's expense: a Chamber of Commerce for Zagłębie was created — and its seat is not in Będzin but in Sosnowiec; the districts for the labor courts were established in Sosnowiec; the great Polish joint-stock companies set up their offices there. In short — Sosnowiec is becoming the "kitchen" (di kikh), the one that sets the tone, and Będzin is left behind, reduced to a "town of a distant firm." There is method and design in this — though there is no Jewish heart [there] to what this means in practical terms.

Zagłębie has grown greatly over the last ten years and climbs ever higher on the ladder of industrial and commercial development; the borders between one town and the next are being erased. Dąbrowa–Będzin–Sosnowiec are indeed today one great center: a single power plant supplies current and light to all three towns, a single telephone exchange serves the three points, and a single tram line (operating only for the past year) connects them. As you travel from town to town — it is all one, by tram or by train — you must be an excellent expert in local conditions to determine where Sosnowiec ends and Będzin begins; along the whole line — one long row of industrial plants, a dense network of chimneys.

And yet there is a difference. Dąbrowa and Sosnowiec are mighty industrial centers; whereas Będzin concentrates the commercial nerve of all Zagłębie — a commerce that flourishes and grows, in which wonderful Jewish energy, Jewish initiative, and enterprising spirit are shown. Zagłębie is today the liveliest and most seething place of commerce in Poland. It is the link that binds [—], connecting the rich textile region of Łódź with the rich industrial Upper Silesia. An enormous [commerce] of the towns of "Kongresówka" as far as Katowice, Królewska Huta, and even up to the German border; and in the present bitter-hard time it feeds tens of thousands of livelihoods that the economic crisis has brought upon them.

[The fair:] A fair, as far as the eye can reach — a crowd of people, the [peddlers], the bank one link, [—], merchants and peddlers tug at the skirts of one's coat, drag the passersby into the shops, promise "bird's milk." Commerce in Poland is in full bloom...

[The street:] I stand on the "ragged" Modrzejowska Street in Sosnowiec — the "Nalewki," the "Nowomiejska" of Zagłębie. A strange picture that captivates the eye: the crowd that so densely fills the street is rare and unusual; young and old, men and women — more women than men — all in [modern] dress, neither urban nor rural, something distinctive and special. These are the "Ślązacy" (the Silesians); one recognizes them at once. This is not the human material of the Polish heartland, of "our Poland": missing here is the [ostentation] of the Łódź population, missing is the primitiveness of the "Krakowiacy," and there is here also none of the old-fashioned townsfolk of the "Kongresowiec." The people and their dress — gray, monotonous, precise like the industrial structures, from which they radiate like the coal mines and the [factories] whose fists [spat] them out, or spat out their fathers — and which will soon swallow them up again for long, long hours...

And this strange, wondrous crowd, speaking the characteristic "watery Polish" (Wasserpolnisch) and flooding itself like water, fills the town, drawn in long, almost unbroken rows from the station to "Modrzejowska" Street and back to the station...

[The heart of the matter:] Once, in very ancient days, the old chronicles tell, Zagłębie was the point toward which the [invasions] of the "Ślązacy" were directed; they came here armed, [—] avid, to rule these neglected but blessed provinces, which had the ill luck to lie near the Prussian border. And today they come here again in their thousands, whole camps — an "invasion" of a new kind, good, beloved, and welcome: day after day they stream to the shops, empty the shelves of merchandise, but as they leave they leave the shopkeepers full cash drawers. This is [something] that brings an abundance of livelihood, a rain of good fortune — golden (now only "silver").

Tragic Death of a Jewish Woman — Rachel Steinitz Run Over and Killed

A report: a tragic accident occurred on Friday afternoon on [Bóżnicza (Synagogue)?] Street in Będzin. Along the street walked Rachel Steinitz, aged 52, the owner of a fruit shop on ul. Warszawska. As she was crossing near the "Warszawska Confectionery," a passenger car of the "Tapiasz" company came along in the same direction; from the other side came a droshky (dorożka), and the driver, wishing to avoid a collision with the droshky, rapidly backed the car up; at that moment Mrs. Steinitz found herself close to the car, and from the strong shove she fell against a tree and suffered a concussion. She died in the hospital. The funeral took place on Sunday; the wailing reached to the heart of heaven. The funeral procession passed by the house of Mr. Tapiasz and stopped there as a sign of protest. The deceased left behind several unmarried children; tragically, on the day they lost their mother fell the anniversary (yahrzeit) of their father's death, who had passed away a year earlier. The Small Trader (Article)

The small trader (the Kleinhändler).

What does the retailer want? What does he demand? It is hard to put in a few words what a person of this kind suffers, what pains him and what he demands. Wherever you turn — troubles; and when there is no 'sound limb,' how can one point to a single spot, to a single fact? It seems the situation can be characterized thus: the retailer struggles to be recognized for what he is — that it be established once and for all, and legally acknowledged, that there exists in the world a type of person, a type of trader belonging to the category called, in economic language, 'retailer' (Kleinhändler), and that he should be treated accordingly.

On the ladder of economic life there are various rungs. The government has recognized, for example, that there is a peasant — an ordinary farmer — and there is a squire (pryc), the owner of a great estate. Among landowners there are certain categories for the purpose of paying tax: thus, for example, we know that a peasant who holds 15 morgs of land is considered a poor man and is entirely exempt from tax. That same 'poor man' is, by our notions, a wealthy person — since his property is worth some fifty-odd thousand zloty — yet in agriculture it is held that his income is minimal and that he cannot pay tax. In the urban economy, by contrast, there is no 'minimal income' for which one is exempt from tax; at most there is a [ceiling], but even that is so low that only someone truly starving to death is exempt from tax.

And worst of all is the situation of the small 'trader,' toward whom there is no consideration whatever. He is immediately taken as a 'whole' in full. And herein lies the retailer's misfortune: it is a misfortune when a man is made into a 'rich man' so that he can be treated as a 'poor man.' Walk into the retailers' association in any town you like, and hear what they say about the turnover-tax assessments (Aufsatz-Steuer) for the past year — and you will see that people are being made 'rich' by force, into big merchants doing enormous turnovers. From almost everyone you will hear that his turnover was assessed at twice or three times that of the previous year: a grocery shop assessed last year at 18 thousand zloty — this year already 36 thousand; a second grocery assessed last year at 25 thousand — this year a full 60 thousand; one butcher was raised from 50 thousand to 135 thousand zloty. Such examples could be brought without end.

One sees that a tendency prevails to 'drown' the retailer type, to make everyone into big merchants. This would be well, and one could understand it, if it were truly seen that turnover — and all the more, profit — had grown. But by recording a large turnover on paper, one makes a man at most into a 'great rich man,' but not into a great merchant; and all the [wrath] is poured out only on the trader, the shopkeeper and the small retailer — for the big firm keeps books, it cannot simply be led 'up the garden path,' it cannot be cheated — and so all the anger is vented on the retailer, who keeps no books and cannot defend himself.

And the question arises: where is the fairness? True, many merchants who keep books have been seen whose turnover doubled within a year — but there it is not 'seen with the eye,' there it does not [suit]. It must be understood that a small trader and shopkeeper, a branch that suffers greatly from competition, is unlikely to have his turnover grow so much. The retailer struggles for recognition: he demands that a minimum for the trader be fixed once and for all, just as it was fixed in agriculture, and that the minimum be stable — not dependent on the good or ill will of an 'informer' or an official; that it be known that the fourth category pays at most such-and-such, the third such-and-such — so that the assessments and the surprises may cease.

This is how we understand the retailer's demands, and we believe that the deciding authorities must heed these demands — for one does not wish to ruin a large stratum of the population.

A. Sz. J. Stupnicki.

Joint-Stock Companies in Poland

Joint-stock companies in Poland (Akc. Gez.).

In countries with a high economic culture, joint-stock companies are enterprises that pool [scattered] capital. Big industry rests on this basis too, and in commerce as well much is gained from this form of capital organization. Compared with other countries, the companies and banks in Poland are [developing]; after the crisis of 1925/26 they [came] to a strengthening of their finances. There is an urgent need to publish an information book for those who require it. The book 'Akc. Gez. in Pojln' (Joint-Stock Companies in Poland) fills this need, and provides information on all the companies in Poland: place of seat, branches, year of founding, purpose, [capital], management and supervisory board; and the book appears also in French, English and German, so that those who do not know Polish may make use of it as well. The book can be obtained from the publisher.

An Institution for Honor or for Benefit? — What of the 'Linat HaCholim' in Sosnowiec? (Article)

An editorial on the responsibility of public institutions. The writer recalls a report that appeared: a porter (Treger) in Sosnowiec complained that the local 'Linat HaCholim' had refused to lend him a bathtub (Wanne) for his sick wife, even though he offered a pledge; the president reasoned that he could not grant the request because the man is not a member of the institution. The writer asks: does the institution serve only its members? Does it supply its equipment only to those who maintain it? If so — the institution is superfluous, since those who can pay have a bathtub at home. He argues that philanthropic institutions exist precisely to serve the poor strata who cannot afford such things; and he criticizes the lack of transparency of the 'Linat HaCholim' — one never hears what it does and what its activity consists of. Little Feuilleton: A Difficult Eulogy

[Little feuilleton — 'A Difficult Eulogy.'] A humorous feuilleton on the difficulty of writing (and needling) about life: the writer thought one ought to write precisely about the living — 'and let the living take it to heart,' and perhaps 'he will take it to heart and it will have an effect'; but his 'close neighbor' warns him: 'Ah, why touch him? He has a note due on the exchange, his daughter is being matched, and simply — a living man. Don't you know? Dread and fear — leave him alone!' The writer muses: perhaps he is right, for 'with a living man one must not begin: as long as a man is alive one cannot be sure of him — he himself may yet turn out to be...' A biting feuilleton on the feuilletonist's self-censorship.
A Letter from Krynica (Impressions of the Spa Town)

[A letter from Krynica — impressions of the spa town.] The correspondent describes Krynica, the most popular spa town in Poland (among Christians and Jews alike): situated 740 meters above sea level, ringed by mountains that purify and refine the air; but the main thing is the mineral waters and springs (carbonic acid) and the mud baths, which are considered the finest in Poland and draw many visitors from abroad as well. The correspondent notes that Krynica is very expensive in material terms — the baths and the boarding houses cost 'a pretty penny' — and describes the crush of the peak season, the question of antisemitism 'then and now,' and the difficult season on account of the crisis in the country. A detailed travel letter from the spa town.
Greetings from Home, from the Land of Israel (Continuation of Hampel's Journey — Będzin's Zionist Standing)

A continuation of the travel letter of M. Hampel from the Land of Israel. Every week he meets yet another Zagłębie Jew he had never known before; every post brings him letters from landsleit asking him to visit their relatives or to reply to them through the newspaper, as well as letters from 'homefolk' now living in the Land of Israel. He concludes that the Jews of Zagłębie form a large enough 'kibbutz' (community) in the Land of Israel, and that despite the recent re-emigration they occupy an honorable place in the building of the country. Among the many human sacrifices offered on the altar of pioneering in the Land of Israel are also several pioneers from Zagłębie, older and younger, who fell in the labor and the conquest of the land for the sake of the Jewish people — may their memory be holy!

He stresses that Zagłębie in general, and Będzin in particular, are known and famous in the country not only as a large Jewish settlement, but as a stronghold and a strong Zionist center. Half a year ago, in connection with the Keren Kayemet (JNF) campaign, Będzin (which was the topic of the day in the Warsaw press) won praise in the Land of Israel too; special telegrams were sent from Poland to the newspapers of the Land of Israel, reporting that of all the cities of Poland — even of Warsaw and Łódź — Będzin had distinguished itself in self-taxation for the Redemption Fund. And just now Będzin has again been mentioned in the Hebrew press: in 'Davar' there appeared a large item stating that Będzin had once more proved its understanding of the Land of Israel, by imposing on itself a tax for the 'Palestine Workers' Fund' (KPAI) during Ben-Zvi's visit there — to the sum of a thousand dollars. The item aroused great satisfaction in local pioneer circles and among the members of the 'Histadrut' and 'Hapoel Hatzair,' with pride that it is precisely the 'plain-folk' city of Będzin that one can boast of. The writer met Leib Jaffe in Tel Aviv, at a gathering devoted to the eminent Zionists of Russia; Jaffe too took pride [in Będzin]. (A travel letter; the OCR is garbled — expanded translation.)
How Zagłębie Appears to Foreign Visitors — Part IV (Impressions of Israel Kahan)

How Zagłębie appears to foreign visitors — Part IV.
(By Israel Kahan.)

Sosnowiec, they say here, is 'the crown of Zagłębie'; and the gems that give the crown its charm and its worth are set — in no small measure — by Jews. The Jews, the Jewish merchants, may perhaps not know much about all those 'seven wisdoms' called economic science — and therefore they understand a great deal more about commerce. They know the craft of exploiting the conjuncture and of creating [profits] and trading possibilities. And the Jews in Poland have, in addition, a dear 'rebbe' (oh, a very dear one!) — cruel poverty, the shaky economic ground, and the [dissolving] hopes for improvement and equal rights...

The bitter times of the constant economic crises drove the Jews to seek rescue from their distress. Their healthy commercial instinct directed them toward Upper Silesia and toward — Zagłębie. Sosnowiec has grown in recent years, grown greatly, commercially and industrially. In industry, too, Jewish initiative, Jewish diligence and the Jewish commercial spirit contributed much to the prosperity: small, backward workshops developed under Jewish leadership into flourishing enterprises, employing legions of workers and paving the way for Polish products abroad as well. So it is in Sosnowiec, so too in Będzin.

But the Jews' chief [contribution] to Zagłębie is in the field of commerce — not only in 'Jewish' Będzin, but also in Sosnowiec, where the Jews make up barely 15 percent of a population of over 100 thousand souls. Naturally the antisemites do not [like] this: by every [ruse] they seek to undermine the economic positions — but they succeed little; on the contrary, more than once they 'break their own necks.'

In the heart of Modrzejowska Street (ul. Modrzejowska), the liveliest place of commerce in Sosnowiec, a fine [—] was 'displayed': not long ago a plain hall (hale) stood on this spot; poor Jews stood there with 'stalls' and by hard toil wrested their livelihood from the [place] — and this was a thorn in the eyes of the people of 'Swój do swego' ('buy from your own'). Partly by Jesuitical ruses, partly by thuggish tricks, they drove the Jewish shopkeepers from the place, destroyed the [stalls] and cleared away the hall. A fine and splendid bazaar was erected — with a row of 'purely Polish' shops under the sign of the Jew-hating 'Rozwój.' Now the champions of the boycott hold the [bazaar], and the whole [affair] is put on display, to shame and to scorn.

After all, the commerce of Zagłębie too lies in the earth — deep in the earth. Not 'nine cubits deep,' as the saying goes, but far deeper — in the coal mines... There, in the belly of the darkened, depleted earth, human toil and human resourcefulness bring up, in sweat and labor, the black diamonds. The coal mine is the [source] of all activity, the energy of all economic life.

To arouse interest among the members, personal invitations were sent out, and the 'experiment' succeeded relatively well — a comparatively large number of members came; a rare sight: the hall full of 'half-dead people,' lifeless, with dulled senses, human shadows who no longer have the strength to assess any question, indifferent to everything, nodding their heads in a sign of assent. An Understanding of Development and Obligation Toward the Citizen (article)

An understanding of development and of obligation toward the citizen.

Everything ultimately comes down to the same question, the same interests, the same duties toward the population, toward the broad mass of the people. These would seem to be questions that concern every city citizen; and yet he is not taken into account. We know that the city's citizens — merchants, retailers and artisans — pay colossal sums into the state treasury; we know that they pay taxes constantly, and as such, as citizens on whom the country and the crown rely, they ought to be consulted, to be engaged with. Unfortunately we see nothing of the sort — no thing and no one is taken into account.

Obviously it would be entirely different if the citizens were taken into account, and the public institutions would wear a different face if the citizens reacted to undesirable phenomena. We of Będzin have in recent years been going steadily backward — without noticing that the town is growing, that various concerns are being opened and new streets cut through; and yet none of this is taken into account, and we are not given what is due to us.

Thus, for example, before the war we had a district court here in Będzin; today we have none. We know that an important case is heard at the district court (okręgowy) in Sosnowiec, and the Będzin merchants must travel there every time. Had the citizens of Będzin reacted in good time to such a wrong, the town would have obtained its due. Furthermore: in Sosnowiec there is a labor inspectorate (Arbeitsinspektor), to which one must constantly turn — both employers and workers — and so again the people of Będzin must travel to Sosnowiec; and the labor courts, too, were established in Sosnowiec. Thus Będzin is bypassed entirely, and the people of Będzin are left orphaned in this respect. We are treated like stepchildren, as if nothing can come out of Będzin, and therefore we have nothing to demand of anyone.

They have begun to build a post-office building here — but the plot for the post-office building was chosen precisely behind the town. We understand that when one wishes to enlarge a town one builds various public concerns outside it, for two reasons: first, the plot is cheaper; second, so that the new quarters become more settled. But that holds for other institutions — not when it concerns so popular an institution as a post office, to which all strata of the population flock several times a day. Who does not need to deal with a post office nowadays? Who does not need to send money, redeem bills, send registered letters, dispatch parcels? The post is today the true nerve of life among all strata of the population, and therefore the whole town should have taken an interest in seeing that the future post-office building be located in the town center; and if they wished to build it on a new street so that traffic there would become more popular, a kind of midpoint could have been found, one not far from any side. But here nothing and no one is taken into account, and so nothing is done for the benefit of the citizens and their interests.

Furthermore: we have no institutions or representative bodies that would react when nothing is done for the benefit of the citizens — otherwise they would react to every wrong, and would not make mistake after mistake. Będzin is without doubt a town of merchants — and there is no one to defend the merchants. When "declarations" were read out in the city council a few weeks ago, every group solemnly proclaimed that it would defend its own interests and guard its voters at every step — and no one even knew that there live in Będzin such people called merchants, who have no defenders, and no one said he would defend the merchants' interests. But when money is needed, when a campaign must be carried out — the merchants are the first to be remembered, those who stand behind their shops looking for customers. Yes, this is the best proof that among us everything is still fragmented, and that we are still far from an understanding of our duties. We know only that it hurts us when we are struck; but the moment the pain stops for an instant, we have already forgotten that we lost a shred of position and grew weaker. And because our memory is so short and we never recall our weaknesses — for that reason what could be repaired is not repaired, and what vigorous activity would have removed is not vigorously removed.

R. Let.

How Zagłębie Looks in the Eyes of Foreign Visitors — Part V (Israel Kahan)

How Zagłębie looks in the eyes of foreign visitors — Part V.
(By Israel Kahan.)

When wages are paid (on the 1st and the 15th of each month) — everything comes alive, commerce awakens, and the bustle seethes throughout Zagłębie; the wheel turns round and round. But when the workers receive only "advances" (zaliczki), or when working hours are cut back — this is reflected in every corner of the whole region. Invisible threads stretch from the industrial [plants] to the most refined shops, to the cafés and the places of amusement. Here coal not only heats the stoves and the factory boilers directly — it is also the "accumulator" for the engine of all economic and public life, the driving force of the commercial pendulum as well. Coal regulates not only the temperature and the heating system, but indeed the entire economic system.

Zagłębie is black with masses of people. There is here a kind of "migration of peoples": the traffic is enormous and many-sided. The trams, arriving in convoys from Katowice and from the neighboring towns and townlets, disgorge at the appointed hour the thousands of "Ślązaks" who descend upon the town, buy all sorts of goods, wrap everything up, and, laden with parcels and baskets, return to Upper Silesia across the nonexistent border.

The "Ślązak" is the key to the economic problem: when the "Ślązak" comes — a livelihood comes; when he does not come — everything dies... Everything rests on the "Ślązak", everything revolves around him. And he, the enormous consumer, though he is constantly incited against the Jews by the Jew-baiters and their organ (a paper resembling "Der Stürmer" of the antisemite Bielaszewski [?], "Kurier Zachodni" [?]) — buys, for the most part, from the Jews, in whom he places his trust, and from whom he gets cheap goods at prices that are not too high... The merchant has already grasped what the "Ślązak" needs and what suits him; they strive to make the goods cheaper, adapting them to the taste of the Silesian buyer. He is no longer seen on Modrzejowska Street as a dignified Prussian "presenter"; they knock on the shop doors, adapt to the taste of Upper Silesia — goods [—] light in color, elegant, especially for him, so that he will buy...

When one observes this commerce and sees the [enormous] role the "Ślązak" plays in the local trade, Upper Silesia grows in the imagination into a kind of monster-creature, incomprehensible and endlessly mysterious. Upper Silesia appears like a bottomless maw, unsatisfied and unquenched in its needs; it swallows everything, digests everything again and again, and with its juices [nourishes] tens of thousands of local and foreign shopkeepers, peddlers and "abzug" (wholesale) traders, strengthens them and gives them new energy, new capital...

Katowice is the "poylishe parada" [Polish ostentation] — a relatively large city when compared to a European [city], and in its wealth, though from the center the immense industrial momentum is [evident], it still has something small-town about it. And Katowice, the capital city of Upper Silesia, concentrates within itself Polish production policy: it sets high prices for all-Polish consumption, as well as for export across the Baltic Sea. Katowice is realistic; the politics are materialistic, as is the characteristic outward appearance of a relatively large industrial place — revealed in the [roar] of the machine halls; a conscious, materialistic energy, so that in the fine architectural buildings one sees the visible energy of industrious labor.

Conscious Calculation — Prepare Now for Winter (article)

Conscious calculation. The hard reckoning is preparing now, in summer, for the winter.

Economic conditions, the method of thrift, reckoning and calculation — these have no place at all among us in the public sense. We have no authority to instruct us on the necessary steps in such a case. To this day we live, sadly, for the most part under the psychosis of the war and the years of hatred, when money was like [ashes] — and however terrible and depressing it was, it has been forgotten in a deep oblivion. This is not taken into account, and people do not want to remember that we have long been living in other times, and that life and the whole system must be arranged on a different basis. We were schooled in war, and we did not occupy ourselves with thrift and economy — even after the war no one tried to take up the matter; so that none of us went through the 'routine' or the 'training,' and it is no wonder that we remained thus, neither on this side nor on that; harder times befell the Jews at intervals, until [uncertainty] set in among us — people did not know how to reckon. The far-sighted view was lost entirely, and people began to live without any system and without any conscious calculation; and to this were added enormous burdens of taxes, which drove wholly respectable households to catastrophe — once they lost their balance they fell from the [arena] and lost their connection to economic existence.

Clearly, had we undergone economic training that would teach us the proper guidance, we would not have 'slipped' in the event of a catastrophe: we would have reacted in good time, and the situation would have been saved on the spot. But now, given such a state of affairs, we must not go on behaving this way, and life must be arranged differently — to live by reckoning, to be economically aware and to be well oriented on the ground.

In government circles too people are beginning to regard economic reckoning as a first-rate matter. Not long ago we received a circular (cyrkularz) from the Voivode in Kielce, appealing to us to devote a few articles to the question of the necessity of stocking coal for winter during the summer months. At first glance one might laugh — that we, the residents of Zagłębie, should now stock up on coal for winter — after all we are surrounded by it all year round. But when one considers the question seriously, one arrives at the conclusion that we too must lay in coal for winter in these months. There is no need to look far: last winter there was a frost, and then we received no coal from any part of Poland; merchants paid for coal day by day and received it in railway cars, whereas we here in Zagłębie could not obtain coal, since it was more convenient for the coal merchant to sell his coal to the outside dealer than to bring it into town; and at that moment a slice of coal could not be had at any price — even though we are steeped in this commodity at all times. This proof shows how much we too here in Zagłębie need to lay in coal for winter in the present months.

Of course we are not saying that it is easy to stock coal in summer for winter when it is hard to get through the day and one cannot cover current income; of course the situation is very bad — but this is not said of everyone: there are people with good reckoning and precise calculation who [can] save and prepare a stock now for winter, and they must do so by every possible means. For from this both those who can prepare a stock will profit — since they will have goods ready at a cheaper price — and, later on, those who had no possibility of preparing a stock, since in the great frosts there will be fewer private [speculators] among us, and the small buyer will have a chance to obtain a slice of coal. We must live by reckoning; we must know how to calculate both in commerce and in private family use; and therefore now is the right moment to lay in coal for winter. Conscious calculation must now embrace the important positions in the Jewish middle class.

R. Let.
