How Zagłębie Appears to Outside Visitors — Part VI (Israel Kahan)

How Zagłębie appears to outside visitors — Part VI.
(By Israel Kahan.)

Upper Silesia is an astonishing and interesting region, and its capital no less so. It is more than a 'voivodeship,' more than a 'province' — it is Upper Silesia. One may well doubt the claim of the 'local patriots' that the 'Ślązak' is a special 'ethnic type' — but distinctive he is: the local German is not a full German, the local Pole is not a full Pole, and the 'local' Jew too is kneaded of a different sort than the rest of the Jews. More than anywhere else, on the western fringes of Poland (in Poznań and Pomorze) 'interesting' anthropological types leap to the eye; the broad faces of the 'Ślązaks' are very Slavic. The historical placement of German and Pole face to face is here a fact that even the most ardent German patriots do not deny. During my visit to Upper Silesia there was still an uproar over the arrest of the president of the 'Deutscher Volksbund,' Mr. Ulitz, who was charged with high treason by the Polish authorities. From all my conversations with the German 'extremists' I concluded that the alarm about a German 'irredenta' in the Polish part of Upper Silesia is, at least on the 'theoretical' side, 'much ado about nothing' with no real basis; the most distant ideal is territorial autonomy — but that already touches on the tangled and complicated problem of multinational Poland.

The first thing that leaps to the eye when you come to Katowice is the colossal traffic and the enormous bustle in the streets. A babel of languages rings out here every day; people gather from all corners of Poland and also from abroad — merchants, industrialists, factory managers, commission agents, [—]-legionnaires, travelers of every kind, and plain 'visitors.' Amid the Polish, German and English one can meet at every step a hearty Yiddish as well. Upper Silesia is Poland's 'Eldorado' commercially. In this wonderful, nature-rich corner one does not feel so much the attendant phenomena of the prevailing economic crisis; the dreadful shortage of ready cash is not so acute here, and here they do not know the mysterious 'paper bridge' — the promissory notes — which makes commerce in Poland flimsy, insecure and dangerous. Other standards govern commerce here, and the whole manner of operation is different — more solid and more secure. There is something in local life of the breadth with which nature has endowed this region, a region holding inestimable wealth in mineral treasures.

Upper Silesia is one of the few mineral-rich places in the world: the coal mines here combine with other underground yields — lead, zinc and iron — all in deep mines of the finest quality and of a productivity hard to find elsewhere. Here are located no fewer than 75 percent of all Poland's coal industry, two-thirds of its iron industry, and all of Poland's zinc industry. Of the 36 mines that operated in 1920, before the partition, 50 mines fell to Poland's share with a workforce of 130,000 men; today the mines operate at greater intensity, and the workforce employed in them reaches more than a quarter of a million. Katowice is the seat of this marvelous region, the richest province in Poland. Thousands upon thousands of hard-pressed and squeezed people in Poland aspire here, seeking a prospect and a hope; this is the last life-belt for those drowning in the present bitter-serious economic situation in the country.

Katowice numbers some 125,000 permanent residents, and about as many outside guests on average are present in it for a period of [?] days; so that in fact Katowice has a population of close to a quarter-million. It is the city with the greatest transient traffic, relatively, in Poland. The cafés, the variety theaters and the night-entertainment houses flourish here better than in all the other cities of Poland — perhaps the only feature that justifies the nickname 'the Polish Paris.'

The voivodeship of Upper Silesia is not among the largest in Poland: its population is some 1,130,000 souls — far smaller than Łódź, Kielce, Lublin and most of the other voivodeships; but thanks to its great, flourishing industry, its population is economically far better established. Conceptions of life here are different, the needs of the population higher; the worker's wage here is almost double that in our parts, and so the standard of living is broader — more humane, I would say. The worker, and especially the urban dweller and the middle class, is well dressed, lives with dignity, 'nothing human is foreign to him' — he can and wants to allow himself this. And hence — the enormous consumption of goods in Upper Silesia, and hence — the flourishing commerce, and hence — the general prosperity.

In Light of the Facts (Editorial)

In Light of the Facts.

There is a parable: A father, shortly before his death, calls his son and reveals to him that a treasure lies buried in the garden, one that must not be uncovered except in a time of severe distress; and as a marker he placed a large stone there. The son, who lived well and had no need of the treasure, told the same thing to his eldest son before his own death, but to make sure — he added a second stone; and so in every generation a stone was added, until the treasure was forgotten entirely, and all that was known was that one must place a stone. Why do I tell this? A similar impression came over me when, in the last issue of the 'Zaglembier Tsaytung,' I read the open letters defending the 'Zionist' councilmen from Dąbrowa. I say to the esteemed authors: 'Enough stones — tell us something about the "treasure" too' — the defenders try to defend Mr. B.R. but leave Mr. L.P. out.

Let me put it briefly and clearly: Was the conduct of the Zionist councilmen in Dąbrowa correct? Did they fulfill at least the necessary minimum toward their voters? And did they raise their voice at all from the rostrum of the city council? I shall give an objective answer to this. The Zionist Organization in Dąbrowa decided at the time to go to the city-council elections independently; because of the intervention of several Zionist activists the decision was changed, and a bloc was formed of Zionists, Mizrachists and a few non-partisans. The first candidate was put forward by the Mizrachists and the non-partisans, but was a member of the Zionist committee; the second — a declared Zionist, put forward by the Zionists. The first gave a public declaration that he would act according to all the decisions of the Zionist committee, even though he was the non-partisan candidate, and that he wished to work on a Zionist list.

After the election results it turned out that the Zionist councilmen could be the 'tongue of the scales' (the deciding vote): by uniting with the 'BB' club [PPS] they could form a stable majority on the city council. Indeed a rumor spread that the Zionist councilmen were negotiating with the 'BB' club; and how great was the surprise when it became known one day — not directly from the Zionist councilmen — that an agreement had been signed under which the Zionist councilmen undertook to vote for all the 'BB' proposals, and in return received a [vague] promise that the local Jewish population would be recognized as having equal rights...

Under the agreement, the Zionist councilmen voted together with the 'BB' club — thanks to which the entire city administration came to consist of 'BB' members, and the multi-million budget and the club's expenditures were approved thanks to the Zionist councilmen. The single ridiculous sum of [—] 5 zł allotted to Jewish obligations was rejected in the plenum — thanks to 'our allies.' Our councilmen, without regard to the [insult], did not walk out of the session in demonstrative protest but remained in the hall and, as faithful instruments, voted for the 'BB' proposals. It is worth noting: in Olkusz, where there is no 'BB' at all, the local city council decided to grant Jewish obligations a sum of 9,300 zł. And the 'BB' proposal to merge the neighboring villages with the town was carried thanks to our councilmen. What the 'BB' could not push through in the Sejm — they pushed through in Dąbrowa with Jewish votes. At a city-council session a 'BB' member insulted Jewish honor in a [crude] manner and came out against the Jewish [people] with vile words — and our councilmen, faced with the antisemitic [attack], did not demand that the antisemite [retract], nor demand that he withdraw his words addressed to the Jewish people.

All the Jewish voters demand that the councilmen show what they have done for the Jewish public: did they intervene on behalf of a Jewish public elementary school, on behalf of a Jewish institution subsidized by the magistrat? It seems they will be the last to do so. The verdict: lay down your mandates!

Jechiel ben Menachem.

The Terrible Sanitary Conditions We Live In. It Is High Time to Remedy Them.

The terrible sanitary conditions in which we find ourselves. It is high time to remedy them.

At last the weather has turned warm; and immediately with it, diseases that bring bad consequences have begun to spread. Contagious diseases are beginning to spread, and under the conditions in which we live there is fertile ground for terrible and dangerous results. Doctors confirm that in Będzin, for example, there is a [shortage] of water in the largest buildings in the town center; besides this, we know of many houses that have no water at all — not because no water line was installed, but because the landlord does not want to carry out the repair the house needs, or does not want to give the tenants the same conveniences they once had. He especially does not care that the tenants will be forced to leave...

It is not enough that the landlord is punished if he [repairs] nothing in his house — they only draw up a protocol and a [fine], and all this is as nothing in the face of the general hygienic-sanitary conditions in which we find ourselves. In small towns that have a 'magistrat,' at every step [there is] a little fresh air; whereas here there is no possibility of [cleaning/watering] the streets. And the children, our next generation, whom we want to grow up healthy and strong, cannot play under the green trees where the fine scent of nature would blow. Open squares and parks free for all — we have none; we do not even dream of what natural beauty is, the pleasure of strolling among trees and grass, the shade from the sun. We, the residents of Zagłębie, have no notion of any of this.

And when the great [heat] comes, one cannot even breathe: there is dust upon dust, and every time the tram passes it raises a cloud of dust that settles on the passers-by and penetrates into the shops and the open rooms. From this dust people fall [ill] countless times, since the tram [passes] every few minutes, and the cars too do not clean the air. There is good reason to fear dangerous diseases when dust rules the main street — and no one even tries to prevent this danger. The police punish every citizen for the smallest trifles — why do they not see to it that the local authorities, which collect taxes, properly attend to the citizens' health question? Why do the authorities not [plant] gardens for the town and [water] the streets with clean water? If these problems are not solved, the diseases will spread. It is high time the local authorities dealt with this seriously: that people should drink clean water, that the streets should be watered with clean water, and that gardens and parks should be provided for the poorer classes.

R. Let.

Citizens and the Crisis — Increasing Expenditures (article)

Citizens and the Crisis — Increasing Expenditures.

Everywhere and on every occasion, the decisive circles take pains to show that things are good here and that "largesse" prevails, and that a better situation is impossible. Were these things said merely for their own sake, no one would be troubled; but on the strength of this, people permit themselves to increase expenditures — and that is already dangerous; it begins to "smell of mortal peril."

When it is only a matter of drawing up budgets, they say that everything in the country is advancing, business is flourishing, enterprises are developing, the workers in the workshops are laden with work — and therefore we may permit ourselves anything, may compose budgets as we please, enlarge them as much as possible, and the population will pay it all with a light heart. When the municipal authority in Będzin was setting its budget, its Christian representatives said that things were good in Będzin and that they had plenty of money, and therefore a large budget could be drawn up. Now, when a budget for the municipal authority has been drawn up in Sosnowiec, they again claimed that everything is perfectly fine and that the economic crisis in Poland "has already passed," and therefore we may permit ourselves larger budgets and the citizens will be able to pay. And by the same method other budgets are composed, which increase the expenditures of every citizen.

But if an accounting were made with common sense, one would finally have to look at how we stand in the world, and weigh honestly: can such heavy budgets of millions be permitted everywhere; can the population really pay this; and is it in fact paid without coercion, without distraints? The economic situation in Poland is not good — how do we know this? In what does the [ill] manifest itself? It is known that the situation in Poland is not brilliant, that the crisis is steadily growing and taking on ever more serious forms: this is evident in the world of commerce and in the credit institutions, where instead of bills that are honored come protests; it is evident, too, among the artisans who have no work; the workers are being cut back, and there is a large number of unemployed without occupation.

The truth must be told: in this case Zagłębie and Upper Silesia are the fortunate ones — our corner is among the richest and most flourishing in Poland — so that here we have so far felt very little of the crisis prevailing in Poland. But now Zagłębie and Upper Silesia are beginning to "dance along" with the Polish crisis: here, too, workers are beginning to be cut back, the artisans have no work, and the merchants cannot pay their obligations.

We have grown accustomed here to looking at the small taxpayers who at every step clutch their heads, and by this measure they gauge the whole citizenry and conclude that all is well and good, that everyone has work; and they do not see — or make themselves out not to see — those who yearn in the darkness, those who do not stick out their heads, who have no garment to wear and who go hungry in silence. Let those who present that "everything is flourishing" conduct a survey, study the condition of the whole, and reach the conclusion that things are not as brilliant as they superficially present; and even if there are a number of well-to-do people and a number who make a living, one must not judge the whole population by the small percentage.

Can one go so far in shutting one's eyes and saying, "I see nothing, all is fine and good"? Whom does such a method benefit? We believe the question is serious, among the most important and topical that must be dealt with as quickly as possible. The consequences of an error here could be very grave. We must not persuade ourselves that all the citizens are well off, for taxes will be piled upon them beyond their strength. A clear accounting must be given once and for all, so that the population does not arrive at the dreadful thought of the beginning of a decline — one that could lead to an abyss for which there is no longer any remedy.

R. Let.
Greetings from Home, from the Land of Israel (Hampel's journey continued — the Jezreel Valley, Nahalal, Ein Harod)

A continuation of the travel letter of M. Hampel. The writer has just returned, a few days ago, from a tour of the most flourishing and fertile region in the Land of Israel — the Jezreel Valley — which makes a great impression with its natural wealth. The valley, which not long ago was a region of infected swamps and fever (malaria), is today once again a region of blessing; the valley, which lay desolate for two thousand years, is today covered with great green fields stretching mile after mile, and is today the pride and crown of the Land of Israel.

On the way to the valley, in Haifa, he was met by a fellow Będziner, Mr. Abraham Sznajur [?], who emigrated with his mother and brother to the Land some years ago and settled in Haifa; Sznajur, who has command of the country's three languages (Hebrew, English, and Arabic), works at the [magistrat] on Mount Carmel as a correspondent. In the workers' moshav of Nahalal — whose principle is individualism, that is, each family works on its own responsibility but is bound by "self-labor" and "mutual aid" — he met the colonist Mr. Szliwka from Dąbrowa and his wife Perl [Fajgenbaum?], who worked for many years as a nurse at the "Hadassah" hospital in Tel Aviv. He also met the former activists of the Będzin "HeChalutz" — Mrs. Frida Rozenberg and her husband Mr. Jacob Szliwka, who live in Haifa. From his conversation with his former townsfolk he learned about the way of life in Nahalal and about their contentment; Mr. Szliwka cultivates about 100 dunams of land which he purchased from the Keren Kayemet, and with Keren Hajesod funds he built a house on the farm. In the large kvutza "Ein Harod," whose members drink from the spring waters that gush from the mountain slope, he met Mr. Moshe Dov Palec [?], who came from Będzin.

It Is a Disgrace… (article)

It is a disgrace…

In Łódź, "Oświata" published a very interesting article about parents and children — highly relevant to the school question. Our mothers would do well to read its contents, devoted chiefly to arousing attention and prompting a moment's reflection on whether we are truly failing to fulfill the sacred duty of raising the young Jewish generation to Jewishness.

It is a disgrace that the Jewish father, who devotes so much time and energy to his daily work, does not remember — or neglects — his important duty to want for his child a school in which a healthy education will be given. The Jewish mother, who has the free opportunity to decide on her child's education, bases her decision not on the pedagogical value of the school to which she wishes to entrust her child, but on passing impressions and on purely outward appearances. Often parents send their children to whatever school is "fashionable" at the moment — the one to which industrialist Mr. X sends his son and Dr. Y his daughters, and to whose "good tone" one must conform…

It is a disgrace that many respectable parents, sending their children to "elite" schools, choose a school whose spirit, life, customs and ideals are utterly foreign to Jewish society; they send Jewish children to a school where they are taught to look with contempt upon their own community and upon everything Jewish.

It is a disgrace that Jewish parents allow themselves to be carried away by fine words, lofty phrases, etiquette and outward glitter, behind which hides an empty superficiality. It is a disgrace that Jewish parents actually want their children to be "pale and colorless"; they care about the complexion and not about the soul, the heart, the mind of the child — about what is "Jewish" in him: Jewish feelings, Jewish ideals. This they call "chauvinism": to remain what you are and not an aping "monkey"; "chauvinism" they call the guarding of one's own ideals and the refusal to chase after the foreign; "chauvinism" — to know your people and your culture; "chauvinism" — to bear self-respect, national pride, to think of the past and to yearn for freedom… Away! Away with the "sidelocks"!

It is a disgrace that some Jewish parents are content that the [Hebrew] language is not taught at school; that the child still does not understand or feel the language, the religion and the Jewish culture, and is no Jew… There are parents who do not even care what the child learns of the "[Polish] religion." And the Jewish parents are right: with the language come pain and sorrow… and if there is no learning and no religion, then it is all the same; then what good is the whole comedy?

It is a disgrace that all this takes place before our eyes while we keep silent; no one blushes with shame, no one cries out in a true and sacred outcry and calls for a return from the mistaken path. It is dreadful to think that soon it will be too late… Look around, Jewish parents: do you not see how your children slip and slide out of your hands, how they grow estranged from you — and may one day become your enemies?…

At the Shomrim Summer Camp

On the Shomrim camp.

The "Hashomer Hatzair" in Sosnowiec undertook this year, for the first time, to organize Shomrim camps during the summer months. Eighty shomrim are at the camps: the older shomrim at [—] beyond Wolbrom, the younger ones at [—]-Jacob; and the last group, which is simultaneously running a leadership course, is at Prusicko [?] (near Łódź). In the mountainous region of Harli [?], about 20 km from Gielek [?], the first group is stationed — 32 young shomrim and shomrot, the "fit ones" — in two small village houses: one house for the boys and the other (a few steps away) for the girls.

At dawn, around 6 a.m., the Shomrim "state" bustles with cooking, running and commotion: they prepare for the first morning assembly, at which the camp instructor Zvi Fernericht [?] reads out the daily "daperim" (announcements) and divides the work among the [members] for the given day. This does not last long, and after the singing of the Shomer anthem they set out for the forest for gymnastic exercises. It is a real delight to see how the tiny "nekudim" (children of 12–13) perform difficult gymnastic exercises. Between meals they sing songs from the Shomer repertoire, and the whole company immediately joins in — happily.

I experienced a characteristic incident: as I was strolling with my companion, the "commandant" [Blawic?], among the splendid "fields," a shomer turned to us with a question in the Polish language; whereupon little Shoshana, a girl of about 10 whom we had not even addressed, jumped up and cried to her friend: "Hebrew! We speak Hebrew!" I later learned that the language in the camp is Hebrew, and that those who are not fluent in Hebrew must devote their free time to studying it. At the end of the meal the group of youngsters sits down on the grass in the nearby forest and takes up the Land-of-Israel custom of the traditional "Oneg Shabbat" — the study of a chapter and reports on various subjects. I had the chance to hear a very interesting report on our great leader Dr. Theodor Herzl, the 25th anniversary of whose death falls this coming Sunday. The young listeners drink in every word thirstily. The "discussion" is interesting too; and afterward they link arm in arm in a lively "hora," which the peasants of the area watch with great curiosity. The impression of the Shomer group, full of life, we shall remember for a long time. S. Strauch.

Bankrupts (bankruptcies) and recklessness.
A reply to a painful question — to the Radom merchant Mr. M. B-r.

In one of the previous issues of our paper we touched, in the article "Bankrupts and Recklessness," on the painful question of our economic interests, and reached the conclusion that even if our merchants struggle and suffer with no way out, one must at the very least draw a distinction between involuntary bankrupts (owing to enormous tax burdens and customers who failed to honor their promissory notes) and voluntary bankrupts, who do so with a light heart. We proposed that firms which go bankrupt because they were broken should not be put on the same level [as the rest] — whereas the voluntary bankrupts should be identified at every step: if they cannot prove that understandable causes compelled them, they should be branded on a "black list" as voluntary bankrupts, individuals who let no one else live and make themselves lawless. We therefore proposed to create a kind of committee that would fight against voluntary recklessness.

And it is telling: it seems the question is so painful that one could write about it endlessly — yet, to our regret, not one of our aware and intelligent Zagłębie merchants took up the word on the matter; only a Radom reader took up the word, and his article was printed by us in "Zagl. Tsayt." no. 26 under the title "This Is Not the Way Out." The Radom merchant Mr. M. B-r. does not agree with our view that such a committee can be created at all, one whose judges would be [pure] and able to decide on the solidity and honesty of others; nor, in his opinion, can such a committee determine who is a voluntary bankrupt. It was, the merchant says, high time to remove the mask and tell the plain truth, however sad it may be.

Does the sad truth lie in the fact that the judges themselves have already been "caught"? No, the situation is not yet so grave; and precisely because we want the air not to be poisoned — so that an honest merchant can remain upright and true — precisely for that reason one must not shut one's eyes to reality, but rather see to saving the upright and pure and to fighting the lawless and the vile, which sometimes takes on even more terrible forms that no honest person may permit.

You claim that, because times are bad, an elemental "crash" has come, catastrophically ruining commerce, and protests begin, "klauzes" [postponements]; naturally in such a case the merchant is brought to a terrible state and left helpless — so why call him a "voluntary bankrupt"? Voluntary bankrupts we call those who take up as much merchandise as they can and flee with it "to where the pepper grows," and afterward one [hears] such things again and again. Of course, in this case no less to blame are those who extend unlimited credit to such reckless people. Voluntary bankrupts we also call those who throw merchandise right and left at unreasonable competition prices — cheaper than the original source gives — and afterward, having traded for a few years, pull off the great "crash." There are various illegal schemes to which no honest firm can stoop — and the result: a genuine firm is forced to freeze (collapse) because of the recklessness of the [weeds] that have sprung up, who bear no responsibility toward anyone.

Of course, had our merchants' and retailers' associations stood at the proper height, the recklessness would not have reached the present dismal state — for at the given moment the member would have been obliged to explain to his association how he intends to sell below cost, or why he gives merchandise to irresponsible people. But we do not yet have this; such tribunals must be created, such committees, that will not allow merchandise to be thrown about recklessly, and whoever throws it about — it will be possible to hinder him. In any case the question is topical and painful enough, and worth discussing; and it is desirable that everyone who has something to say should utter an upright and sincere word. The idea that the best and most radical means would be to fight for the abolition of the "numerus clausus" in every field, to be admitted to government posts, and even to establish free emigration — that is certainly good; but there are many old matters that cannot be realized at all, and certainly, at a moment of urgent need, one must not enter into fantasies and utopias.

R. Let.

The Social View — The Jewish Councilmen in Sosnowiec (Article)

The social view.
The Jewish councilmen in Sosnowiec — unity, responsibility, a lesson.

Public work, political activity, the interests of the community — all this must be weighed and measured, and calculated down to the smallest detail. Every little mistake, the slightest wrong step, causes troubles and disasters, pain and anguish, and brings misfortune to every corner of our meager life.

We have a gratifying phenomenon to note in our Sosnowiec society. Small and insignificant as it may be, it is a gratifying phenomenon that must be reckoned with and deserves to be blessed. It concerns the Jewish representation in the local authority. True, the number of Jews there is not large and one cannot accomplish much, and yet we see, on attentive reflection, that it is a great thing. We had, for instance, in the previous municipal administration two Jewish representatives who, with the best will, could accomplish nothing; no one listened to them, and so they lost heart; they did not have the courage to demand, as they should, a large and strong representation, no one wanted to hear them and they had no one to talk to. Why was the situation so bad and bleak? Because in those city-council elections there was no proper response — Jewish votes were lost, many did not even get onto the roll — and only with difficulty, by a miracle, did we obtain two representatives; and what role, what significance, can a representation of two members fulfill in the Sosnowiec city council?

In the last city-council elections the situation changed for the better, and now we have — apart from the two representatives of the Left Poalei Zion — five representatives of the bourgeois elements; and a representation of five people can already be reckoned with, and with a group of five representatives one can already [act]. And this, we say, is a great victory: the Jewish voice is now heard in the city council with far greater force; when there is an injustice, its bitter expression is heard. It makes no difference whether our bitter words are heeded or not — it is enough for us that with such a small representation no opportunity is let slip, and that what needs to be said is said.

And behold, last week the Jewish councilmen held a public report meeting, at which we had the opportunity to hear what our representatives had done in the city council and what had not been done, on what it had been possible to respond and on what not. After the weak previous representation, the present one has great significance — also because the representatives take their voters into account and see fit to be in contact with them and to tell them what they can and cannot achieve for Jewish Sosnowiec.

It goes without saying that unity among the few Jewish councilmen must be assured unconditionally, and that each should support the other on every occasion; this is one of the most important conditions. Unity is such a hidden power, such a strong force, that it can never be fully appreciated: only occasionally does the opportunity arise to see the combined power of unity, and then we marvel at the beneficial results — which appear as if they came about by chance; but on deeper reflection, in full seriousness and with understanding, one sees that the victory grew thanks to unity and to a clear view of the present and the future.

In public activity every movement plays a part, every step — everything must be calculated and purposeful; whereas the smallest mistake, the tiniest miscalculation, brings enormous harm to the community for long years. This must be taken into account, and conscious representatives must think it over well. Not seldom do we speak of "public trust," of quarrels over nothing — which bring so much bad blood into our life and strengthen the split... and it comes to the point where one cannot breathe, one finds no place of joy, and at such a moment one becomes so beaten and depressed that one loses consciousness and balance, ceases to believe in the community; one sees only loneliness, division, indifference and endless pessimism. At such a moment it would never occur to one that not all is lost, that division does not reign everywhere, and that bright horizons may yet appear over our gloomy sky.

And now, when we see that our small representation brings unity to the citizens of the town and takes into account the demands of its voters — this is to be blessed. May these deeds show that the good will of public representatives is an important factor in daily life and can accomplish much for all strata. May the activity of the present councilmen be a lesson to all who wish to work for the community and its interests; let them remember that unity, energy and good will are the strongest driving force, and can sometimes achieve more than one imagines. True and sincere public servants must keep this before their eyes.

Dr. Papori.

The Community President in Będzin — Rise and Downfall (Article)

The community president in Będzin — their rise and downfall. When will they see fit to give up their chairs?

We were convinced that the [matter] was so naïve, and that it already had an end — but no: only now is it beginning, only now are they starting to sit down at the "green table" and conduct the politics on which the world rests. We thought that the moment the president of the Jewish community administration in Będzin resigned his post, the administration would be finished, the "head" would go and the whole order would fall apart. But it turns out that we are not good politicians, and that we were too naïve to think so: we could not imagine that, in the present gloomy state of the community administration, the events would not be the "opportune moment" to dismantle the institution, to put an end to the unheard-of things being done there. We could not reckon that people would be found who would actually want to "fish in troubled waters."

We did not know that the Jewish community administration in Będzin now needs a president in order to "save Judaism" — otherwise they would not have made such [efforts], they would not have brought the rabbi all the way [from Otwock] and pushed through what they wanted, what was needed for the "Agudah"; they got a president of their own and their position is secured. Of course, toward the man himself, as a private person, we have nothing — on the contrary, a most respectable Jew, an honest man, a householder in the town; but one thing should have been understood: the virtues just listed are still too few for a man to become a public servant, and he barely represents anyone — all the more so when he becomes the representative of the entire Jewish community, the president of the Jewish population of Będzin.

Now, when the man begins to represent us, we have the right to demand of him that he be worthy of representing us, that he be able to speak in our name; and let us be permitted the candor to say that the man, with all his virtues, is not able to speak in our name. The man does not understand at all what "public" means, public interest, public responsibility — he has never dealt with such matters. This is a simple Jew of the old generation, and he will honestly admit to you that he is not versed in "the matters of the day." It is an impudence on the part of people when they provoke in order to push this through, when they persuade such a Jew that it would be fitting to entrust him with the responsible and high office that today, in every city, is held by the most educated and capable personalities — the office that among us was held by the national Sejm deputy Dr. Weinziher, and afterward by the president of the Polish zinc industry, Mr. Szepsel Firsztenberg.

So we sit here in one "serenity," so we sink and fall ever deeper each time — and no one sees, no one feels. It may be that some see it, it may be that many understand how far we are going backward — but they make nothing of it, remaining indifferent and cold as ice to everything. Therein lies the deep tragedy.

In any case, one cannot understand at all what for they sit there in the community shtibl when it becomes a plain social shtibl. An institution costs the town so much money — and who gets anything from it? If the community were a social shtibl, it would cost no one anything; but since it is no more than a social shtibl, why does it draw so much money from everyone who pays? Yes, Jewish Będzin has the right to demand something from such an institution.

What, then, do we have today from our community administration? Whom does it serve and what does it do? Upon our representatives, you who represent us, rests a responsibility; and unless you give up your chairs — the high time has already come for you to give up your chairs, which you have held for far too long.

R. Let.

The crisis. — The tax question. — What ought to be done at the present moment?

Zagłębie is considered one of the wealthiest corners of Poland. The [tax] district knows this well, and therefore taxes here fall considerably more heavily than in other, [agricultural] regions. The government knows that we earn materially far more here than elsewhere, and has therefore made [demands] of us not for nothing. Let us say, then, for the record, that the taxes are unbearable and that we are burdened by them too heavily. As long as business goes well — one manages, the taxes are rolled over and somehow paid. It is worse when business begins to fail, when income turns bad, when a crisis sets in — and then there is nothing to count on and nothing to take from, and then it is bad, bitter, very bitter.

In fact the crisis in the country is no longer news; it has prevailed everywhere for some time. But from the moment it took hold here — among us it was not felt, or we felt it little. At first we felt it [indirectly]: the world of commerce [weakened]. Whoever had no export business, whoever traded [locally] in Zagłębie alone — for them the general crisis did nothing, or next to nothing. Now the situation has changed: at every step the heavier crisis strikes directly, so that already everyone feels it — the small and the weak, but also the strong and the great. [Factories] have less [work]; large-scale industry, like small-scale production, is beginning to collapse.

The merchant no longer knows from where and with [what] to take, does not know what tomorrow will bring him. The worker does not know whether he will be able to work. — These are the hard 'crisis days' we are passing through. And at such a time, of crisis and hardship — what ought to be done? We must look closely and see: the hour is not favorable, and we are not [meeting] it properly; counsel is needed. We believe the [tax question] must not be taken lightly, for it is quite simply a question of survival of the first order. We must demand relief — and at the same time we must organize: the community must not be treated as individuals and separate persons, but as one single, unified body; for the individual alone is nothing, and the interest is shared. The professional [organizations] ought to unite everyone, so that they stand in mutual defense of one another. — The community must be organized as one man, as a single unit, for only thus is there strength and weight.

What Will Become of It There? [?] (Article)

What will finally become of it there?

They keep on conducting 'high politics'. — Jewish kehilla property is left ownerless. We ask about the [council members].

Tell me, you will say, with my plain common sense I simply cannot understand what is going on here. I do not [understand] what this thing is — the present Jewish kehilla in Będzin; it is a riddle, a mystery that cannot be grasped. From every side you are shown that everything there is rotten, that what was created over the course of several years is systematically sinking — not because nothing real is being created now, but because the good and healthy that once existed is being liquidated one by one. And a person asks himself: why, under the prevailing conditions, is such a large staff kept on? Why is it not reduced when there is no work for it? Why maintain so large a budget when it could be cut? Why load onto a town of Jews so great an expense when it could be reduced? Such questions the householders of the town ask, and there is no one to answer them, no one to talk to.

And it is characteristic: precisely at the hour when conditions press upon us and we do not understand why the kehilla now needs so large a staff — the fresh 'Agudah' president comes with an entirely new method of enlarging the bureau staff, and has taken on a new clerk, one of his own men, close to the 'court'. And people ask: what is the point of it? What does it give our kehilla administration, which has already lost all decency and takes no one into account? Otherwise Jewish money would not be left ownerless; otherwise it would be reckoned that a president has no right to employ his own people merely so there [should] be someone there to [drain] the till... It is unheard of — to be so tyrannical, to ask no one and to reckon with nothing. Is Jewish money really so ownerless that our own brothers will not reckon with it? Can 'partisanship' really so blind a decent man that he sees nothing true any longer?

Why are new people needed now in the bureau of the kehilla administration? What additional work has arisen that the present staff could not cope with? What is being done there is unheard of; no one would have imagined that a few people would dare to run the affairs of a whole town this way, before everyone's eyes — and that the other representatives, like the whole town, would not respond to it as they should. In fact all the activity there comes down to 'making politics' alone, whole days and nights, and the end — that everything comes out of the town's treasury.

[The writer recalls earlier affairs: two years ago they leaned on the kehilla treasury; the appointment of a cantor and a choirmaster who impressed the town; and disputes between the cantor and the choirmaster over [income/coal], which only stoked quarrels in the town.]

The Jewish population needs no showcase representation, but one unified and responsible leadership. — That is what such a population needs at such a time.

R. Let.

The Jew as Co-Builder of Poland's Economy

It is a fact that economic life in Poland is increasingly held in Jewish hands. No wonder, then, that [the ruling circles] seek to push the Jews out of their economic positions. The "economic boycott" waged by the ruling circles in Poland is bringing the Jewish population economic ruin and a steady [statistical] decline. The Jewish economic malady grows worse from day to day.

For this reason — and these are no empty phrases — one must approach with a clear, cool understanding the diagnosis of the present sickness and search quickly for the means to arrest and cure it. The Jews' poor training for the various trades means that the earning capacity of the Jewish population is hurt more quickly during a prolonged or passing economic crisis; and bound up with this faulty economic tendency are also the artificial economic envy that is cultivated and the relations of the Jews toward the other peoples living in the land. How Should We Treat Public Institutions?

How should we treat public institutions?

Subtitle: How should we treat the institutions that bring benefit to society — and those that do not?

Not long ago a report appeared here concerning [the gemilut chesed (free-loan) fund]; and now the same thing is being reported again — that certain people, and precisely the [capable] ones, wish to take revenge on the free-loan fund that helps a considerable number of people. What does it mean to take revenge on a gemilut chesed institution, one meant to save a person just as he is about to lose the ground beneath his life, just as he is about to fall? How is that oppressed person to blame if [—] someone has wronged him? Whom do you harm with such revenge — the poor and oppressed Jew? After all, [striking at the fund] will only expose the institution in its true light, and the distress of the people who turn to it for loans.

Obviously there can be no comparison: [the worth of] a useful institution is not on a par with a useless one. Can one not understand how people would be saved were they guided to the better path? It is a rare thing for an institution among us to be run properly. Among us, on every occasion, we give with the left hand and take away with the right. No one takes care to strengthen the Jewish kehilla — because it is "worthless," because it is utterly rotten, because we get nothing from it. In this case we do not seek to protest — but rather to stop replacing the leadership, and to take an interest that something be done [—].

By contrast, when a useful institution like the free-loan fund exists in Sosnowiec and helps people — not to let those fall who could be saved by a small loan — would you not at such a moment support such people, and yourselves as well? Surely you would. There is, then, no one who would doubt the necessity of the gemilut chesed fund — and especially in the present crisis, when so many oppressed people need to be saved by a loan. On the contrary — sensible and practical people in the field of public activity must see to it that the scope of this blessed institution be enlarged; for lately the number of the distressed who need it has grown, and it is evident that the crisis among us is steadily worsening. People need saving.

It is therefore fitting to take an interest in the institution, to examine its work, to see whether it needs broader powers — for we understand that it must grant larger and more numerous loans; and for that the involvement of the town and the warm attitude of respected citizens are required.

At the same time we must give ourselves, once and for all, a clear reckoning: institutions — whatever they may be — so long as they bring benefit to society, it is our sacred duty to sustain them and give them every possibility to act. But when we hold institutions that bring no benefit at all — it is one of two things: either one must go into them deeply, examine them, impose order and bring them to a properly useful state, so that they benefit society; or, if not — they must be recognized as superfluous and useless, and then society must free itself of them. For in the end one must remember that public funds are not ownerless property, and must not be treated with abandon.

As for our kehilla leadership — we all know full well what state it is in, how low it has fallen and how little it gives to society; and it is self-evident: when the members are burdened with large sums and one sees the kehilla giving nothing for the common good, for Jewish Sosnowiec — this rightly arouses indignation. It is therefore high time that our Jewish kehilla leadership be dissolved. This is what must be demanded, and on this serious steps must be taken.

Dr. Papori.

One Must Learn to Walk

[An allegorical editorial.] There was a time when it was taken for granted that a child had to be taught to walk. How much effort the whole family put into it, and how much wisdom it required. Everyone would take the child by the arm, pull him along, and want to set him on his feet; 'On his own, on his own he'll walk!' — the mother would sing, and everyone held on to him. It was not only people who helped the little one to stand on his feet — machines, too, were invented for the purpose: baby-walkers and contraptions bought so that the child would learn to stand on his own. Today we already know that there is no need to teach a child to walk — just as there is no need to teach a kitten to walk. Who teaches the foal, the calf, or the dog to walk? When the hour comes, they walk of their own accord.

But if a child in the cradle need not be taught to walk — then with grown-ups, with adults, one must indeed learn the art of walking. And it is a great art: from time immemorial the soldier was taught how to place his foot; the placing of the foot was always the first and eternal wisdom one had to learn. It had to be so, for if everyone placed his foot the way his father taught him — it would be impossible to build an army: one would tread on another, one would stumble over another's step, and at a critical moment, when they had to run forward or backward, more would fall to their own comrades' feet than to the enemy's sword. Once, only the soldier was taught to walk; today everyone must learn the maneuver, for today we all find ourselves on the battlefield. Today the street is an arena of war. The larger the city, the greater [the danger]...

It is even beneath one's dignity to reply to attacks of this kind; and yet we wish to make one thing clear: their hatred of us does not stem from the fact that we do not buy Sosnowiec meat, but from the fact that we do not buy Sosnowiec meat [precisely from them]... (We have several butchers who have more than once sold Sosnowiec meat as local slaughter.) And in this whole matter of the meat we have already made clear to the rabbinate that in no town does a meat consignment arrive without [supervision], for the sausage-makers as well; and had this been instituted, we would without doubt have been among the first to support it — for if supervision were enforced, half the sausage businesses of the factory owners in Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa Górnicza, Częstochowa, and Wolbrom would close down...

We therefore already have as much fear of Heaven as truly exists, and in all sincerity on every side. As for the piece of non-kosher meat — we would add that this cannot happen: 'young and old' already know that every piece of meat is stamped with the rabbinate's seal, and besides is marked in each factory with a special name.

Will We Have [a New Communal Institution]? — Why Is the Institution Not Being Established?

Will we have a 'Pogotowie' (emergency medical service)?

Subheading: For what [reasons] is the institution not being established? Can we go on waiting?

We have dealt with this question more than once in the columns of our newspaper. In recent months we published several articles on the matter, and proved the necessity of establishing such an institution — but nothing has been done. None of our 'city fathers' here in Zagłębie was moved; we showed that the high time has already come for a rapid-aid institution to be established in Zagłębie, yet no one so much as paused over this important matter to consider what is possible and what is not.

It is an old rule: the moment an article's author sees that his words have no effect, that they 'stick to the wall like dust,' he loses heart and says to himself — better to wipe one's mouth as if one had said nothing. But how many times have we already pointed to this very fact and established the necessity of setting it up? We already proved, in our time: Zagłębie must have a rapid rescue service.

The situation here is worse even than in Warsaw or Łódź; for here many accidents occur in the factories, which are not properly arranged for rapid aid to workers. Besides this, our traffic is heavy, the railway lines branch out in every direction, and the road network too is extensive — hence the multitude of accidents in everyday life.

True, this is not visible to the eye: barely a line appears in the local press, one sees an accident here and there and no one pauses over it. People are injured, killed, and all the events pass as though they had never been. But things look different when one reads attentively through all those accidents and disasters — then a horrifying picture emerges. When one studies all these, one sees that our city administrations ignore great crimes as they look on at everything with indifference. Many times we have seen accidents that ended in dreadful tragedy — owing to the fact that there is no rapid aid, whose task is to save the unfortunate at once.

Here is an instructive case: two weeks ago a young man came to the editorial office and told us that, as he was walking in the street in the evening hours, two unknown young thugs attacked him and stabbed him in the head. The young man cried out, but — as usual — everyone is deaf to cries for help, and a policeman, of course, was nowhere to be seen; so the wounded man ran with open, bleeding wounds until he reached the hospital, where they [agreed] to treat him only after he promised to pay 5 zl.

And the question arises: what would have happened had the unfortunate man been so badly wounded that he could not have dragged himself along the street? What then becomes of the fate of such a person? How many times do we hear of people passing away simply because they did not receive medical aid in the right place and at the right time? This is nothing new; and if we try to study such cases, we shall come to the conclusion that many people die in this way.

The question therefore arises: can one remain indifferent to such grave events, when a matter of life and death is at stake? When it costs a human life? Can an organ of self-government [cast doubt] on the necessity of the possibility of saving a person in time of disaster? Who, then, should be concerned with saving a citizen's life, if not it — when sudden circumstances place life in danger?

We insist on this with all force and demand: establish a 'Pogotowie' (rescue service), organize rapid aid that will be ready to save a person at once in a time of grave danger.

Dr. Papori.
Make Your Children Productive People

Make your children productive people.

The fate of children is today the concern of most Jewish parents — not only among other peoples, but among us too, and in other countries. Take, say, America, England, France: there it is no concern at all. There the rising Jewish generation has open doors, alongside the rising generation of the ruling nation; there it has broader possibilities, political and economic, to settle down, to build a life, to earn not only bread but also a better life.

True, even there the young generation's path into life is not always the right one — a surplus arises in certain professions and branches; but in the end, one way or another, they arrive there at a secure existence. Among us, by contrast, the failure to fit into real life is a mass phenomenon, and it brings it about that the declining middle class steadily loses its standing, and the youth grow up as a downtrodden stratum, without ground under their feet and without life's content.

And this can be seen in all classes of Jewish society — among the artisan, the merchant, the shopkeeper, and the worker. Take, for example, a German artisan, say a shoemaker: how does he think about his child's future? Although he himself is a shoemaker, he takes pride: 'My son will be the best shoemaker in Germany!' And so too the German merchant, the scholar, and so on — he raises his child with a ready living in life, a 'ready-made shoemaker,' a 'ready-made merchant.' He does not think that his son will be anything 'lesser' than he himself.

Among us it is otherwise: a Jewish shoemaker, tailor, tinsmith, locksmith, carpenter, merchant, or contractor already resolves in advance not to bequeath his trade to his children — that very trade from which he himself makes a living. He wishes his son to be anything at all — a doctor, an engineer, [a lawyer], a professor — so long as it is not what he himself is; as though his own trade were the family's disgrace, a shameful craft to be ashamed of.

Thus the young generation is uprooted from productive life and falls into the downtrodden element that cannot integrate into life — even if it studied, even if it acquired an education. And this after the young generation has been uprooted from work, from standing on its own feet — so that it [shapes] its life as it should not be.

Education must not be separated from a trade; intelligence must not be separated from a livelihood. The two must be joined together. Let this be the parents' watchword: children should indeed be given an education, and schooling too — but it will do no harm if it is accompanied by a trade. The more you raise your child along the right path, the better it will be for him. Impart to him your own trade — for that is the real thing, that is the secure thing; from familiarity with your shop and your surroundings, he will know how to manage better than a stranger.

A. J. G.

The Land of Israel Bleeding

[Lead editorial, signed Sh. Y. M.] [The murderers] have already filled the measure. Such provocative conduct could not have been anticipated, and it has now overflowed the cup. In the Land of Israel blood is flowing. The news swept like fire through the whole Jewish world — everywhere a Jewish pulse still beats. Regardless of party or movement, the news aroused grief, fury and protest. In our history we have grown accustomed to bloodshed and persecution; there is no corner of the world where Jewish blood has not been spilled. The holy soil of Jerusalem is soaked enough with Jewish blood — but all that happened in the grey days of old, or in lands held by wicked rulers and dark despots; that such a thing should happen in our own day, under the protection of the "gracious kings," no one expected. And for that reason the indignation is so great, and for that reason the protest is carried with such force throughout the world.

An ancient Indian legend tells that the lion, king of the beasts, comes forth from its mother's womb dead. But when the mother sees her cub lying dead at her feet, she lets out such a cry that all the trees of the forest tremble, and from that cry the cub is roused to life and grows into the mighty lion before whom all the beasts of the forest quake. So too "the lion's whelp of Judah" appears in the world as if born dead: with it everything proceeds so slowly, so drowsily, so hidden away. But when it raises its voice, when the "voice of Jacob" is heard in the world — all the beasts of the forest will tremble, and even the English lion will be forced to awaken and shake off its phlegmatic repose and its indifference.

In Jerusalem blood is flowing. It is very sad. We have no words to express our grief and our fury. But we do not fall in spirit, and in this case we believe in the old "In thy blood, live" that the prophet spoke. And we must honor with respect the heroic defenders of Jewish honor and of Jewish right. If until now the Wall was called "the holy Wall," "the Wall of Tears" — now it has become "the Wall of Blood," and its holiness is doubled, for blood is stronger than tears. — Sh. Y. M.

[Analysis:] For weeks and months now a struggle has been waged around the Western Wall. It began when the Arabs started to erect a structure behind the Wall, with the intention of opening a passage through the Wall and thereby desecrating and injuring the ancient Jewish holy site. But that is only an outward and criminal pretext on the part of the Arabs and of those standing behind them. In truth the matter concerns things far graver and deeper: it is that precisely now, when the building of the Land of Israel is taking on gladdening forms, when matters have reached the point where all of Israel must summon its strength for the building — precisely now the Arabs want to stir up a scandal and bring the question before the great public opinion. Until now the provocation has succeeded, unfortunately. In the streets of the Land of Israel demonstrations rage, and blood is spilled.

And where is England? Where is the great power that has proven to this day its ability to conquer and pacify the wildest peoples in Africa, Asia and Australia — why is it suddenly so helpless in the Land of Israel against the Arabs? The question is surely being asked by many Jews the world over — and not only Jews. In what does the tragedy consist? To this one must give thought. The English government did indeed give the Balfour Declaration, did indeed make promises; but the English government was then waging a war, found itself in a difficult position, and was ready to accept help from any quarter that might come. Then Jewish help and Jewish sympathy were important to it. Today the war is long over, long forgotten; today England has entirely different interests; today it is important for it to live in peace with the Muslim world, since eighty million of its best subjects in India, [Turan] and the various islands are Muslims. And in such a situation the English government is in no hurry to fulfill the obligations it gave in the Declaration; it is in no hurry even to fulfill its duty as the mandatory power — on the contrary, it seeks every means and exploits every opportunity to delay and drag things out. And in this policy of the government lies the great disaster, and this the Arab agitators in Palestine know, which is why they permit themselves so much; but the last word...

Shabtai Weiss (Jerusalem)

Shabtai Weiss (Jerusalem).

[Editorial note: The author of the article, Mr. Weiss, considered one of the most esteemed and active public figures in Zagłębie until his emigration to the Land of Israel, is known to our readers. Mr. Weiss will contribute articles to our newspaper from time to time, chiefly on life in the Land of Israel.]

Dear friends,

For many years now I have been bound to you: here I spent a considerable part of my life, here I passed through many vicissitudes and changes. For more than ten years I lived among you and with you; for more than ten years we struggled together for the [—] of the town, and surely also for Jewish-national life; for more than ten years we labored together at national posts: in the communities, in the city councils, in the field of education, in national and political-social work, in organizing the strata of the people, in the Keren [Kayemet] and in communal life. Ten years of shared aspiration, of creation — a [privilege] that I guard zealously.

Out of the interest I continue to feel for the development of your public life and its tendencies, permit me to dwell with a critical eye on the "face" of your public life today — and to draw a few conclusions from that observation.

I ask you, old comrades: where have vanished the energy, the storm and the enthusiasm that then characterized the public-national work of those fighters? What became of the esprit de corps that was then beginning to develop? Where have the "chevreh" vanished, who grew up through toil and hard struggle? What became of the national youth, who were then so finely organized? Why have you remained standing halfway along the road? Do you even know where your road is leading you?

Week after week I read in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" details of your public life in various fields, and from these details I assemble for myself a picture — and it reveals to me the plain "face," the characteristic, the stereotyped; the countenance of the society. And the face — is terrible.

Allow me to dwell on a few facts that have remained in my memory from the recent issues of the newspaper — chiefly on the descriptions of general meetings, for their course and their level always serve as a barometer of the public development and the cultural height of a given community:

At a general meeting of the artisans in [the town], the organization's activists were torn to pieces and criticized in language rare even in the marketplace; at another general meeting, of merchants, the opposition throws the board and the president "up and down" as one throws a playing ball; at the general meeting of [the Zionist group] in Sosnowiec — which only recently won governmental rights — only a handful of the old-timers come, and the "meeting" can barely muster a chairman, tellers and a secretary. The participation of the six holders of rights was considered "progress," since in previous years even fewer came. The president of the Zionist Organization in [the town] resigns his presidency over a certain formality — and in the newspaper he explains that he will no longer take part in any Zionist work there (but rather in London...).

I could cut a whole string of "pearls" from similar facts: from the electoral process, from the work, from the "leaders of the generation" in the rabbinate and the city councils, and so on. But the situation is too grave — in its public and national weight — to be content with isolated illustrations.

And permit me the question: if such is your attitude toward the matters of everyday reality, toward the problems and needs of the hour of emergency you encounter daily — what room is left in your heart and your thought for the idea of the nation and for the enterprise of building the Land of Israel? And especially now, when by the decree of Jewish fate the [riots] cast the question upon every part of the Jewish people in our era — and many, out of shortsightedness, treat it as something outside the circle of the immediate reality of exile.

When your absorption in courtyard affairs and in love of the local nest is so deep — that you no longer feel the [national] force, which alone gives meaning and significance to life; when you lay not one stone upon another for the building of the Land of Israel, for the building of the Jewish people in its national home, for the new edifice that is liable to collapse — and when you [neglect] Jewish cultural life and the future of your children... — this is the tragedy of a whole tribe.

In this difficult hour you must unite as one, mobilize all the public and national forces — for this is no time for division and courtyard quarrels. Bind together the fracture, and reopen anew the broad national aspiration.

Shabtai Weiss.

What Is Heard in Zagłębie? — Great Protest and Mourning Rallies Against the Bloody Riots in the Land of Israel

[Local news section; Friday, 24 Av 5689, 30 August 1929.] Subheading: Great protest demonstrations against the bloody riots in the Land of Israel; as a sign of protest Jewish shops close; the Sosnowiec community sends telegrams of protest to the League of Nations.

The bloody riots in the Land of Israel aroused — as throughout the entire Jewish world — sorrowful echoes among the Jewish population of Zagłębie as well. The central topic of conversation, without distinction of class or movement, was the bloody slaughters in the Land of Israel. Many families with children and relatives in the Land of Israel sent inquiry telegrams there, but to this day no one has received any reply.

At the Zionist premises there was held on Sunday evening, with the participation of Rabbi [of Wodzisław?], a large youth assembly of the [young people] of Będzin, Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa, which resolved to organize a demonstration outside the British consulate in Katowice. On [Monday] evening, in connection with the sad riots, the community leadership held an urgent session of the "gmina," at which a sharp protest was adopted and it was resolved to organize a mourning rally in the synagogue. The organizing committee issued a proclamation to the Jewish population, which was asked: 1) to gather at half past five in the afternoon in the courtyard of the "gmina," from which the procession would set out to the synagogue; 2) at six o'clock all the shops would close as a sign of protest.

At the appointed hour hundreds of Jews of all strata gathered in the courtyard of the "gmina," and from there the march set out to the synagogue. At the head of the procession walked members of the local rabbinate: Reb Yehoshiele, Reb [Dan] and Reb Henech [Direktor?]. Behind them, in closed ranks, marched hundreds of Jews; the crowd kept growing, until in the Old Market the number of participants reached thousands. Except for a few Hasidim, all the Jewish merchants in the Old Market closed their shops and left their everyday occupations.

Men and women, old and young, hurried to the synagogue to take part in the memorial service. The crush was enormous, the heat dreadful, and yet each one stood like a [firm wall] and expressed the sharpest fury against the English government, which had allowed such sad results. The memorial service opened with the recitation of Psalms, from chapter 74 to 79. The first chapters were recited by the aged synagogue beadle Reb Abraham Kaplan; the last chapter — by a member of the synagogue choir, Mr. Danziger, who after the Mincha prayer recited "El Male Rachamim" and "Yizkor."

A terrible panic broke out in the middle of the memorial service, when the Rebbe [of Aleksander], Reb Yehoshiele, who had stepped up before the Holy Ark to speak, fainted. The women in the women's gallery screamed and wailed dreadful wails, and some time passed before order was restored. It later turned out that Reb Yehoshiele, in touching the electric lamp, had received an electric shock and was saved by a miracle.

After the memorial service, eulogies were delivered. The first to speak was the Rebbe Reb Yehoshiele, who called for repentance and for the daughters of Israel to dress modestly. Then, on behalf of the Zionist Organization, spoke Mr. [Winad?], who drew a comparison between the pogroms of old against the Jews of Russia and the heroic defense now by the Jewish youth in our land. The speech of Mr. S. [Rinski], who spoke on behalf of the Jewish community about the sad riots, moved the audience to tears; when Mr. Rinski mentioned the terrible slaughter of the 45 yeshiva students murdered in Hebron — a wail broke out.

Afterward, in the synagogue courtyard beneath the open sky, a youth assembly was held, at which Yehuda Finer (Poalei Zion Right) and Zelkowicz (Brit Trumpeldor) spoke. At the assembly, resolutions of protest and appeals against the English government, which bears heavy guilt for the riots, were adopted. The members of "Ha-Tikvah" organized a youth demonstration that marched, headed by blue-and-white flags wrapped in black, from the Old Market through the streets to ul. Małachowskiego, where the demonstration was dispersed with the intervention of the police. The demonstrators went to the premises of their organizations, and there it was resolved to travel together on Wednesday to Katowice to demonstrate outside the British consulate.

From the morning, special trains set out with the [young people] of Sosnowiec and other Zionists. In Katowice the demonstrators were dispersed and placed under surveillance. At 12 noon, when the factories began [work], some 600 people suddenly gathered near the British consulate, calling out various protest cries. Someone [threw an object], and in the consulate's apartment two windowpanes were shattered; a strong police force was present, which politely asked the demonstrators to disperse quietly. This happened after the singing of "Hatikvah," and the demonstration was dispersed without further [incidents]. A few young men who did not immediately obey the police order were arrested.

On Wednesday the Jewry of Sosnowiec too expressed its sharp protest: on Tuesday evening, at the "Mizrachi" premises, a consultation of all the Jewish national organizations was held on how to express the protest over the bloody riots against the Jewish settlement in Palestine. [Dr.] Meladista, [Dr.] M. Weinreb and others spoke on the matter. It was resolved to hold a protest demonstration throughout the town on Wednesday: the shops would close from 6 o'clock in the afternoon, and a memorial service would be held in the synagogue. At 7 o'clock in the afternoon a special session of the community leadership and council was held, under the impression of mourning. The chairman, Mr. L. Zendel, opened the session and gave the floor to Mr. Weinreb, who described the riots in a few warm words, and at his proposal they paid honor by rising in memory of the souls of the heroic victims who had fallen in the Land of Israel. Mr. Weinreb also proposed sending telegrams of protest to the League of Nations and to the English government via London; the proposal was accepted. Then the head of the community, Mr. Meladista, spoke [on behalf of] [the Orthodox] with great pain about the heroic pioneers who had fallen victim, who with the blood and sweat of the heroic pioneers had built the Land of Israel, and that the world must give support so that the enterprise not be uprooted. At the appointed hour the procession set out with [the rabbis] to the synagogue — all in mourning, in black attire: members of the community, [the directors], lawyers and a large number of Hasidic Jews, "Ha-Tikvah" with a flag wrapped in black, [marching] in closed ranks. Delegations from Czeladź, Modrzejów, [Wojkowice] and [Będzin] took part in the procession, coming to the synagogue.

[At the Sosnowiec synagogue:] In the women's gallery too the crush was dreadful. Mr. Leichter, one of the members of the choir, recited a chapter of Psalms; after Mincha "Mi Sheberach" and "El Male Rachamim" were recited. Rabbi Szwarc also spoke, as did Dr. [Pawlicki?], who pointed to the role of the Polish consul in Jerusalem [Wiszewski?] and to his humanitarian conduct, having protected many Poles and Jews. On behalf of "Mizrachi" spoke Mr. [Piscewski?], who called for a reckoning with the Zionists over their attitude [—]. A strong impression was made by the speech of Mr. [Szpicki?]. The closing word was spoken by Mr. Yehoshiele; with the singing of "Hatikvah" the [rally] was concluded.

Nothing to Be Done — On Unemployment

Nothing to be done.

Zagłębie is "in line" with everywhere else: here too the unemployment problem is worsening, and here too the general crisis shows its force. Nothing to be done.

Gone are the times when the human hand was dear, when a man was paid [good] money, when people were bought for large sums — bought as soldiers, bought as workers; the new times have made the commodity "man" cheap in the market. No one buys a soldier, no one buys a servant. The employer can demand whatever price he sees fit for it — so it is in theory; but in practice it is otherwise: the boss cannot pay for his commodity [labor power] as he pleases, since the [wage] is set by [supply and demand]. When there is much [labor power] and few able to provide work — the price falls; the worker is like any other commodity on the world market and subject to its prices.

The greatest calamity of our age is unemployment. Whoever is left without work, because there is no work, is [cast] to the margins. The worker who has lost his place cannot survive. And as long as this situation continues, unemployment grows year after year — such is the result of the crisis. How are the [factories] to produce goods when there is no one to sell to, when there is no [market], when [promissory notes] are taken that go to protest, and one cannot pay, and the debt goes unpaid — and it goes unpaid also because of the [taxes]? So the factory is shut, though it was still [running] before, [more] by machine power... "Nothing to be done."

In the town it is bad, so bad. When there are unemployed people — everyday life too [deteriorates]. People without work — and society and the government are obliged to help them, so that they can survive. [Charity] is no answer: if they want work — work must be given, and people must not be left without bread and without work. Human beings must not be treated so lightly — when there is no work, it is bad, so bad.

S. Y. M.

Not Only Good Intentions, but Also Deeds

Not only good intentions — but also deeds.

(On the sorrowful events in the Land of Israel.)

The blood-soaked events in the Land of Israel have shaken every stratum of the Jewish population. The savage deeds of the half-savage have roused Jewry the world over; no one can rest, no one can remain indifferent. Everyone in whom a Jewish heart beats was convulsed with anger, dread, hatred, and bitterness. We felt as though we had been humiliated; we could find no place for ourselves, [shame] covered every face, no one could look his fellow in the eye — as though we were the guilty ones. We wept, we mourned, we protested; we were almost senseless, like small innocent children, like people without life and without consciousness. So it was in the first moment. And no wonder — for such unheard-of deeds no one had expected: after all, a Jew in the Land of Israel had set out on his way with a confidence and freedom unmatched in any land.

But now is not the hour to inquire into the causes of all this; on the contrary — we must recover from the terrible despair and become practical. We must begin to render a clear account, and to know where we stand in the world and what we can do for our brethren in the Land of Israel — those who perished for the sanctification of the Name and sacrificed themselves for their homeland like true heroes.

We know that Jewish Zagłębie was shaken by the heartrending savagery that took place on the holy soil of the Land of Israel. We know how much strength and health it cost our brothers and sisters. And yet we must not remain standing in place, mourning and waiting for salvation to come from somewhere. We must take a further step: to examine the situation with full seriousness and composure. We must remember that the beautiful new Land of Israel, built with such great toil, has been destroyed; and those who created all this, who planted the lovely orchards and drained the swamps, are now left plundered and wretched, without a roof over their heads.

And therefore we must comfort those who remain alive, who hope to rebuild the ruins; and therefore we must hasten, above all, to send them material aid. Let Jewish Zagłębie hasten to carry out a great fundraising drive, one that will make it possible to ease the troubles and the [distress] of our wretched brothers and sisters in the Land of Israel.

Let relief committees be established in Zagłębie, with a single aim: to collect money for the wretched in the Land of Israel. Let the committees act jointly in every town; let no party politics rule in this field; let them have one aim — to send bread to the hungry and to save the lives of the sick. Here party politics must vanish; the work of rescue must cut across every direction and every outlook.

Let us therefore set to practical work, let the committees be established now, and let the drive be carried out in an orderly fashion; for with good organization and vigorous collection every Jew will come forward with his donation and will merit to help his wretched brothers and sisters in the Land of Israel. Our editorial office too is ready to receive donations, which we will publish in the columns of our newspaper.

Let Jewish Zagłębie not discharge its duty with tears and protests alone; let it not remain indifferent to the troubles; but let it show deeds, activity, devotion, and love. Let Jewish Zagłębie, together with Upper Silesia, prove that it knows how to come to the aid of the wretched with an open heart and an open hand.

R. Let.
In Moments of Despair and Hope

[Lyrical prose on the events.] Hammers pound... Jewish hammers pound... Here come fresh reports — perhaps [worse] ones, perhaps the murderous hands have already let their work drop, perhaps they have already had their fill of [horrors], for human blood... — the eyes bulge from the head at the sight of a fresh report: an entire Jewish family slaughtered — an orphanage burned down with little innocent tots — a Jewish colony burned, and another colony, and such lines flow one after another, [horrors] like these without end. And a voice such as this asks: perhaps tomorrow it will be [quiet], perhaps... Will tomorrow be quiet?.. But — tomorrow — still...

[A prose-poem of consolation, by "Elgin".] In the hard days the heart yearns for a word — deep, earnest, serene, and full of light let the word be. In the hard days the heart calls for a [prophet].
