Problems of Education

Problems of education.

Subheadings: "The cheder of old and the school of today"; "The teaching staff"; "Safeguarding the children's education." — II.

The question of education has always been a hard one. Jewish fathers and mothers have always placed the education of their children first. And when the "time" came, the father would not haggle over any "business"; the only "business" that occupied him was: how to educate the children so that they would grow up [good] to God and to men. The Jew knew that a man became a melamed only when he was fit for nothing else — the "logic of a jester"; and so the parents of that day knew that they had to keep their children under their own supervision: it was a "duty" to examine ("farheren") the child every Sabbath, and by this measure the melamed's abilities were judged.

From those days to the present we have come a long way. The "cheder" has become a school, and the melamed a qualified teacher; and parents are now confident that they can entrust their children there. But this has led to a stage at which parents no longer concern themselves at all with the question of their children's education: they discharge their duty by choosing a [better] school, and with that the matter ends. They take no interest in how the subjects are taught, neither the religious nor the general; they are content that the child passes to the next grade each year.

In the schools themselves, too, a colossal change has taken place; it is no longer what it once was. The sense of responsibility and the idealistic cast of mind are gone; today a private school is a "business" like any other, in which one looks only at how much profit can be drawn. And of course the institution suffers by this, for in such a case one wants as few expenses and as much income as possible. Therefore the children are not given proper attention; the hour is "taught" formally, to the minute, and then one "finishes" at once. No attention is paid to the psychology of this or that child, to the abilities or capacities of this or that pupil, so as to know how to proceed with his studies. Moreover, complete self-rule prevails in every school: plus-minus, as it happens and as is convenient.

There are indeed parents' committees in many schools, private and public — but the parents take very little interest in them, whether in the school or in their children's education. What is needed, therefore, are committees that exist not only on paper, but are organically bound to the school. This would bring benefit in every respect: many shortcomings that let children deteriorate would be corrected, and the school staff would work more diligently, knowing that a committee exists that watches each week to see that the school maintains a proper standard.

Let us remember at all times that the school is the true house of education, which should be the path along which our children are led — the children in whom we wish to see the humanity of the future. If we remain indifferent to our educational institutions — it means that we are indifferent to our children, who have so great an opportunity to deteriorate, a dangerous thing in our modern age. We must not for a moment lose sight of the fact that the most precious and sacred thing is our future — which we must guard as the apple of our eye.

(The writer adds a warning against the influence of the "cinema", which shows children harmful films that corrupt their soul and spirit, and calls for great care to be taken to guard education from the "demoralization" spreading in every sphere.)

The Polish Press in Zagłębie — On the Events in the Land of Israel

The Polish press in Zagłębie on the events in the Land of Israel.

Besides the telegraphic and telephone reports on the bloody events in the Land of Israel, the Polish press is printing long articles on the conflict between Jews and Arabs around the Western Wall.

"Pogroms against Jews in the Land of Israel" — writes Kurier Zachodni (no. 226): "The attitude of the English government toward the Zionist demands in Palestine has changed utterly in recent years. At the last Zionist Congress in Zurich one of the speakers complained that in the English parliament there is lately a growing tendency to place the interests of the country's long-standing inhabitants above the 'interests of the past' (the historical rights) — that is, to the great sorrow of the Zionists, it is not [acknowledged] that the majority in Palestine is [Arab], and therefore Palestine does not belong to the Jews." The author takes up the [argument] of the Arabs, who in his view do not wish to be slighted and seek to remain masters in their own land.

He then turns to the main cause: "The events by the Western Wall are one of the manifestations of the internal struggle between the Arab population and the Jews in Palestine. On the Arab side the struggle is led by the highly influential [leader] of the entire Muslim world — the Supreme Muslim Council in Jerusalem; with its help the Muslims [come out] against the English administration in Palestine and demand majority rights as the true masters of the land." In conclusion the author sums up that "the bloody events in the Land of Israel are only the beginning of further harmful actions by the Arabs against the Zionists."

It is characteristic — the article concludes — that the Arab conflict sharpened precisely with the close of the 16th Zionist Congress in Zurich and the expansion of the Jewish Agency (which non-Zionists too now joined); this latest move of Jewish policy, it seems, hastened the outbreak.

In the [Endek] Polonia one reads: "Aid in Palestine is a step toward further actions harmful to the Zionists; the Jews' dreams of building a land of their own are but an unattainable illusion — both for reasons of England's own interests and in order to safeguard the route to India. England reckons more with the feelings of the Arabs than with the Jewish demands." It is ironic — the paper writes — that this time the events occurred under the socialist government of MacDonald, who had promised that his government renounces any imperialist policy; the Arab-Jewish conflict thus embarrasses MacDonald's policy. The near future will show whether England will keep its word on the matter of a Jewish national home in the Land of Israel.

The socialist Głos [—] gave a small item on the bloody events — in a [similar] tone to that of the Warsaw "[—]", with much (ironic) "sympathy" toward the Zionists...

The Whole World's Representatives Pay Homage to a Jewish Industrialist (From the Leipzig Fair)

The whole world's representatives pay homage to a Jewish industrialist.

(A joyous occasion at the Leipzig Fair.) By M. Haber. (Special to Zaglembier Tsaytung.)

At the Leipzig Fair, which opened on 25 August, representatives of states and of economic enterprises from all over the world gathered to pay homage to the Jewish industrialist Philipp Rosenthal, who is now celebrating fifty years since he founded his firm.

Few enterprises in the world bear a name as famous as Rosenthal porcelain. There is no "lord" on the face of the earth who does not serve his meal on Rosenthal porcelain; there is not a single magnate in the world, nor even a single king, who does not take pride in owning Rosenthal porcelain. The great steamship companies from every corner of the world write in their prospectuses that food is served aboard them on Rosenthal porcelain. Dr. [—] related that in the last storm at sea a hundred Rosenthal plates were broken aboard the Zeppelin. In a word: Rosenthal porcelain means — the world over — elegance, wealth, and refined taste.

Who is Rosenthal? The answer was given by the great number of eminent personalities from all over the world who gathered at the present Leipzig Fair, where Rosenthal is vice-president. Philipp Rosenthal was born 74 years ago in a small German town, Werl. His parents were petty dealers in glass and porcelain, honest people but not wealthy. At the age of 17 Rosenthal, against his parents' wishes, set out for America, where he suffered greatly: he did every kind of work — apprentice, porter, hotel elevator operator, going from village to village with the post — until he found a salesman's position in a small dry-goods shop. There his sharp business mind was quickly noticed, and he was given charge of the porcelain department. But he held the post only a short time: he saved a few dollars and returned to visit his parents, who would not let him go back to America.

Rosenthal began to manufacture on his own: he bought white porcelain and painted it with various decorations. Here his immense artistic sense revealed itself, the sense that made him famous the world over. He started with a single worker, and after a while he already employed sixty workers, who labored day and night to keep up with the orders. After a few years he began to produce porcelain according to his own ideas and designs, and even traveled from country to country across all five continents, sought out merchants with an artistic sense and entrusted them with the sale of his porcelain — which he knew how to suit to the taste of each land. Gradually he reached the point where there is scarcely a city in the world without his own branches, or at the very least without large firms selling Rosenthal porcelain.

It must be remembered that in almost the whole world there exist state porcelain works, based not only on an ancient tradition but also on state capital, and against these Rosenthal had to wage a struggle. And yet he managed to compete with the state porcelain works and to reach the point where he today has the largest porcelain works in the entire world, and is considered the greatest industrialist in Germany. At the present Leipzig Fair, representatives of governments and of all the great economic enterprises of the world paid homage to the great economic genius of the 20th century — the Jewish industrialist Philipp Rosenthal.

Greater Poland, Lesser Poland, and Upper Silesia (A Historical Study)

Greater Poland, Lesser Poland, and Upper Silesia.

(A little historical research. Special to Zaglembier Tsaytung.)

How did it come about that the Poznań region is called "Greater Poland" and Galicia "Lesser Poland"? Modern Polish scholarship explains it as follows.

As is known, the Poznań region (the basin of the Warta river) was the cradle of the Polish state. The name Polska derives from the fact that the region in question was rich in fields (pola); "Polska" (Poland) designated, until the 13th century, only the Poznań region. The region's inhabitants were called "Polanie". The Poles — like all other peoples — were composed of separate "tribes", which only over time, thanks to proximity, united into one great Polish people. The strongest tribe was the tribe of the "Polanie" (today called "Poznaniacy"), which conquered the other tribes: the "Wiślanie" (inhabitants of Kraków and its environs), the "Ślężanie" (in the ancient historical documents: Ślężanie), the "Mazowszanie" (inhabitants of the environs of Warszawa), the Kujawianie, the Sieradzanie, and others.

The seat of the first Polish kings was Gniezno. In the year 1039 the Czechs broke into Poland and seized Poznań and Silesia; Kazimierz the Restorer moved the seat to Kraków, where it remained until the end of the 16th century. On the medieval maps of Poland the labels were written in Latin: beside the area denoting the Poznań region was written "Polonia Maior" — that is, the [senior]/greater Poland; while beside Galicia was written "Polonia Minor" — that is, the [junior]/lesser Poland. "Maior" means senior/greater ("majorat" — an inheritance passing to the eldest son), and "minor" — junior/lesser. From these, after an imprecise translation into Polish, came "Wielkopolska" (Poznań) and "Małopolska" (Galicia).

The name "Galicia" we already find in medieval documents. To understand it, one must briefly recall a little of Russian-Polish-Ruthenian history: in the 9th–11th centuries the state that stretched from Moscow in the north to Kiev in the south was called "Rus", and was composed of many small principalities (Moscow, Suzdal, Vladimir, Kiev, Łuck, and others). In the 12th century one of the princes broke through and destroyed Kiev, and, taking the title "Grand Prince", transferred it to his seat, Moscow. Thus "Rus" split into two worlds of opposing cultures: the northeast, later called "Rasiya" (Russia), from which developed the powerful Muscovite state that over the course of centuries conquered the neighboring lands in the southwest of Rus (today Ukraine). The latter later concluded, together with Lithuania, an alliance with Poland.

One of the princes of this state tore away from Poland, even before the partition, the region of Lemberg (Lwów), Przemyśl, Czerwień, and others — the region called "Czerwień", in Polish "Ziemia Czerwieńska" — and founded there a separate principality, which was for several centuries under the rule of Ruthenian princes. After its seat, Halicz (a town not far from Stanisławów), the whole principality was called "Halicja". In the Ruthenian and Russian alphabet the "g" and the "h" are marked by the same sign, and it was read by mistake as "Galicja"; afterward the name passed also to the regions southeast of Galicia. When Kazimierz the Great reconquered the region for Poland in the year 1340, it was called "eastern Lesser Poland". After the third partition of Poland (1795) the imperial Austrian government did not wish to recall the historical Polish name "Lesser Poland", and revived in its place the medieval name "Galicia".

Silesia. The main river of Silesia, the Oder (Odra), rises in the Sudetes (which separate Upper Silesia from the Czechs), crosses all of Silesia, and empties near Szczecin (Stettin) into the Baltic Sea. The direction of the current is from south to north: the part lying upstream (not far from the source) is called "Upper Silesia", while the part downstream (around Breslau) — "Lower Silesia".

As for political affiliation: all of Silesia, including Cieszyn Silesia, belonged to Poland at the beginning of the Polish state. When Bolesław Krzywousty, before his death, divided the Polish lands among his sons, he assigned Silesia to his eldest son, Władysław II; the latter, seeking rule over all Poland, waged war on his younger brothers, was driven from the country, and only the intervention of the German emperor restored Silesia to his children. From then on the Silesian Piasts inclined toward Germany.

At the end of the 13th century, when Poland split into principalities ("dzielnice"), there were in Silesia about 12 separate principalities; some of the princes acknowledged themselves as vassals of the king of Bohemia, and some — of the German emperor. Kazimierz the Great, who sought to unite Poland, saw that as long as the Silesian Piasts existed Poland would know no peace, and therefore, in the Treaty of Visegrád (1335), he renounced all of Silesia in favor of the king of Bohemia, Jan (son of the German emperor Henry VI of Luxembourg).

Some of the Silesian principalities that fell away over the course of centuries were also: Oświęcim, Zator, and Siewierz (the historians describe: Siewierz on the Przemsza river, not far from Olkusz — that is, our Siewierz, situated a few kilometers north of Będzin). These last three principalities returned in the 15th century to being Polish provinces: the bishop of Kraków, Zbigniew Oleśnicki, bought the principality of Siewierz for his "biskupstwo" (bishopric), and King Kazimierz Jagiellończyk bought the principality of Oświęcim for his son Jan Olbracht — and the principality of Zator. The remaining Silesian principalities were annexed to Bohemia, and in the year 1620 — after the Czechs suffered a great defeat at the hands of the army of Emperor Ferdinand — they fell for a hundred years under the rule of the Habsburg monarchy, and all of Silesia became an Austrian province.

When Prussia became a Kurfürstentum (an "electorate" — a principality participating in the election of the German emperor) and turned in the year 1701 into a separate kingdom, its disciplined and organized army made conquests in foreign lands, and in the year 1740 it annexed all of Silesia. Maria Theresa, the Austrian empress, declared war on it; but Frederick the Great, king of Prussia, won great battles, and in the Peace of Breslau received all of Silesia. Maria Theresa formed a coalition of states against Prussia and provoked the Seven Years' War (1756–1763); Prussia again won, and in the Peace of Hubertusburg the affiliation of Silesia to Prussia was again recognized. Thus Prussia (today: Germany) held Silesia until the year 1919, when Poland reminded the world of its historical rights to Silesia.

A-T.

Będzin Has Responded — On the Duty to Aid the Victims in the Land of Israel

[Article / appeal.] Będzin has responded: a committee has been set up to aid the victims in the Land of Israel. [Other] towns have already set up committees, have already collected large sums and have already sent them to the Land of Israel. In such a case, in a time of distress, swift help is double help. Late help, after the fact, is worth nothing. One may [assume] that the help will be [generous] — the world will give with an open hand, for within [this] disaster there lies yet another disaster.

As in the moments of disaster and terror, this is a matter for all of Israel. It is not the affair of one place alone, but of the whole community: the entire Jewish settlement in the Land of Israel has been struck. The enemy drew no distinction between the old yishuv and the new; he fell upon Jerusalem as upon the colonies, attacked the yeshiva students as well as the pioneers. All of us — and above all, everyone who carries within him a whole Jew — [must] draw no distinction: we must give our help to everyone who suffered as a Jew. It is a duty to give help in [distress], to stretch out a [saving] hand against [naked] want, to clothe the naked, and not to [spare] our own [very] flesh. This holds for help at home in the first days, when all the roads are [blocked], when one is in danger, when not even with money can anything be [obtained] on the spot and it must be brought from afar, from abroad. But we must give bread to the hungry and clothing to the naked.

This holds too for repairing the [damage] the enemy caused, for rebuilding the [ruin]. Twelve colonies were [laid waste]; how great the [destruction] is in the towns — no one yet knows, and it cannot as yet be [assessed]. Only a poor man knows how [precious a thing is], for only then, when a person has lost all he had, does he [know how to value it]. In times of [tranquility] one does not know how to cherish what one has. The same is true of the Land of Israel: in [ordinary] times one does not know how to appreciate what there is, what it means — a Jewish settlement, a Jewish colony, Jewish [settlement work]. Only after the [destruction] did they [understand] what [there had been and what was lost], and the heart trembled...

[Signed editorial by R. Let — on the kehilla in Będzin and the gymnasium. Note: the subheading extracted from the OCR is garbled ("one must know how to hide the lie... Jews who cannot obtain it"); the body of the text is R. Let's article.]

A few weeks ago the "Agudah" notables in Będzin "reckoned" that the opportune hour had come "to save Judaism" and to install a president of their own at the head of the Jewish kehilla board. To that end they shrank from nothing: they did everything to make the "shtibl" fall apart, so that afterward they would "win" their promised position. Though they are no "geniuses," these political schemers knew how to keep the matter an utter secret, lest, God forbid, anyone find out — and they even brought the rabbi, the visitor in town, secretly from Otwock so that they would have the requisite number of votes.

The affair was planned, the scheme was thought out, and the "route" went off smoothly. And when it was already over and done, and we learned whom we had received as president, we took the floor and said: True, the man is a simple person, an honest householder — but that alone confers no right to become president of the entire Jewish kehilla. For a Jew who cannot utter a word of Polish, who understands nothing of Europeanism, of secular life or of public affairs — and who in fact cannot even express a simple word properly in "mame-loshn" (the mother tongue) — cannot represent Jewish Będzin. This is a Jew who never once poked his nose out of Będzin, and who never dealt with communal affairs even in his own home; and had he not been compelled from the "high windows" to accept the post, he would never have dared to, for he does not feel himself worthy of it.

From this observation we discerned how far our kehillot are sinking. We drew a comparison between the Jewish kehilla of a few years ago and the present leadership, and reached the conclusion that our prestige is declining and sinking ever deeper. We recalled the time when Dr. Weinziher [?] was president and did all he could to raise us higher and higher. Who does not remember with what devotion the man labored so that we should have a gymnasium that would look "laytish-glaykh" (respectable), and how he had to stand up against "sermons" and opposition — precisely from the "Agudah" notables, who would not allow the town to have a gymnasium. He and other noble-minded people stood firm that the gymnasium should be built and completed whatever the cost; and then the [skorniks?] cried that every "brick" in the building was bought with Jewish blood.

And when they drove out Dr. [Weinziher], who saw that the place had become too narrow for him and neither wished nor was able to adapt himself to pettiness — in his place came Mr. Firsztenberg, who likewise has no few merits on behalf of the gymnasium. And in him we then saw the "noble hand" that was so needed.

And now, when contempt is being voiced toward [the respectable people], among the market idlers and professional haters — let the "scribblers" of the "Agudah" bulletin understand: a clique of boors (amei ha'aretz), who monopolize for themselves the title of "privileged householders," must not insult the professional, respectable and honest people of the town — the philanthropists and patrons — who support the institutions without asking whether the matter is "Agudah" or "non-Agudah." We made clear to the [—] organization that we have no wish whatsoever to enter into personal feuds, and certainly not into "politicization"; we sought only to shed light on [the truth]. And the "scribblers" accompanied us with abuse... Nonetheless, all that the [scribblers] write is "vanity and falsehood," and it contains no proof against the Jew as he is.

[The writer closes with a call for the Jews of Będzin to remember that what is done for the community requires good sense, and not merely philanthropy for show; and with a call not to remain indifferent to the fate of the institutions and the future of the generation.]

R. Let.

Problems of Education

Problems of Education. III.

Subheadings: "The sorry state of our hygienic education"; "How ought the question to be solved radically?"

The first two installments of "Problems of Education" drew the attention of an eminent physician from Kraków, who has a large practice among the population of Zagłębie. The present writer received a letter from the doctor, in which he wrote: "I read your 'Problems of Education,' which are most important and timely. But I cannot remain indifferent to the neglect of your sisters and brothers, and your sons and daughters. You absolutely must devote — writes the doctor — a chapter to hygiene within the framework of 'Problems of Education,' for the apathy of your fellow citizens toward hygiene is directly bound up with education."

In this letter of accusation the doctor enumerates a whole series of sins of neglect: he says that children and adults come to him — and precisely not from the poor class — so filthy that he cannot examine them, whereas in other regions even the poorest are clean and well-groomed.

More than once we have dealt with the question of hygiene in the columns of our newspaper; more than once we have said that we do nothing in this field; more than once we have charged our self-government with criminal indifference. But the doctor from Kraków does not know in what conditions we live, does not know that we have no bathing facility at all, does not know how coarse and petty everything among us still is. Let us say it openly: do we even have the means for children and adults to bathe every week? They do not have the means — it is a pity about the money, to say nothing of the lack of money. After all, we have self-governing bodies in Zagłębie with budgets of millions — so why do they not see to it that popular hygiene takes an important place in our lives?

The police see to it that in food shops the sellers wear white smocks — but no one sees to it that, first of all, the seller has clean underwear beneath the smock. Why is the population not given the means to bathe every week, themselves and their children — if not for free, then at least for a few groszy? Is this not no less important than compulsory education, on which in recent years such great emphasis has been placed in Poland?

In his letter the doctor calls for the doctors to speak on the question in the two houses of study (batei midrash). Such a state of lack of culture and backwardness must not be allowed to continue. We already wrote at the time that every Sunday the doctors should hold lectures in the large synagogues, admission to which would be free; and the self-governing bodies should issue free pamphlets in Yiddish and Polish.

But first of all, institutions are needed for the people: where is the population to bathe? For the few baths we possess, admission to which costs a złoty — can a family of several souls afford to spend several złoty a week on bathing? Everyone, adult and child alike, ought to be given the means to bathe once a month for a small sum; and once that is arranged, the population must be prepared and made to understand the necessity of educating the children in hygienic conditions.

When the doctors explain to the children in the schools the necessity of keeping the body clean, the children laugh and say to themselves: it is well for him, he has a bathroom at home and can bathe; but we, how are we to do all this? Such cases are, in truth, a question that will not soon be solved so long as we do not have the necessary bathing facilities; such a family cannot afford it materially.

Therefore let us say, in the doctor's words: hygiene belongs to the "Problems of Education," and we must see to it that the problem is solved; for in times of epidemics and infectious diseases people begin to take fright and wonder whence the calamity came. Is it not better to remove the danger in advance, to accustom ourselves to the thought that we must live under different conditions, and to root out the filth radically — and in its place to plant hygienic education?

The councils and authorities in Zagłębie must see to it that this urgent matter is dealt with soon at one of the coming sessions; and the doctors must work to arouse interest so that the question is finally solved. Hygiene still stands among us at a very low level; and while everywhere it is a self-evident thing and an urgent necessity — among us we are still at the stage of rallying and preparing the population to create the needed institutions.
Moshe Feivkin: Moses Mendelssohn and His Bride (On the 200th Anniversary of the Great Philosopher's Birth)

Moses Mendelssohn and His Bride.

By Moshe Feivkin. (On the 200th anniversary of the great philosopher's birth.)

One of the wonders of the world, they say, was the great Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn. Short of stature, hunchbacked front and back, with a large face — and on his head he was obliged to wear a wig... His thinness and his hunched back came to him from the poverty he endured in the home of his poor father, the scribe Reb Menachem Mendel, while he was studying in Berlin. And when he came of age, he found it hard — for all his learning and greatness — to find a match; the young women shunned him.

It was the "Gespräche" (the "Conversations") that Lessing published anonymously for Mendelssohn — and not the "Phädon" and his other works by which he made a name for himself — that brought him a bride, and only indirectly, by way of the "catalogue" of the house of Damensohn [?]. What Mendelssohn published as a "yomayish" (a diary/catalogue) with the manufacturer Reb Pinchas Berger in Berlin made him famous in the "women's world," and it was thanks to this that the match came to him.

It is told that as he was strolling in the street with his friend Lessing, they overheard the conversation of two ladies walking by, talking about the latest designs of women's dresses put out by the firm Berger. The ladies praised Mendelssohn highly as the author of that catalogue of designs. On hearing this characteristic conversation about the famous Jewish philosopher — who was called "the German Plato" and "the Jewish Socrates" — Lessing envied him for being popular even among the ladies. The "catalogue of designs" on the one hand and his "Conversations" on the other brought it about that Mendelssohn found a bride to his taste.

B. The wealthy banker from Hamburg, Guggenheim, had a very accomplished daughter, an only child, for whom he was seeking a worthy groom. When he learned of Moses Mendelssohn, he traveled specially to Berlin to make his acquaintance. Guggenheim invited Mendelssohn to him, and Mendelssohn indeed did not need to be urged for long and traveled to Hamburg to visit the wealthy prospective in-law. Fromet Guggenheim, the young lady of the house, took advantage of the visit and debated with Mendelssohn about philosophy, metaphysics, and also about the latest fashions. Their conversation ranged far and wide, and Mendelssohn found great favor in the eyes of the banker, the girl's father, and of all the household. Mendelssohn also grasped the mind of the banker from Hamburg, and Fromet pleased him greatly.

But because of his humility he did not have the boldness to speak with him or with her about a match. Nor did the banker manage to draw from his daughter a word as to whether Mendelssohn pleased her, and he already supposed that Mendelssohn would leave with nothing. But as they were parting, Mrs. Fromet stopped him at the last moment and asked him: Is it true, as it is written in the Talmud, that forty days before a child is born it is proclaimed in heaven, "the daughter of so-and-so to so-and-so" — that is, that each person's match is ordained?

Mendelssohn, the great sage of the world, understood the intent of her bashful question and replied: what is written there is the holy truth. And he related: when my match was proclaimed in heaven before my birth — that a hunched back like his was destined for her — he fell at the feet of the Master of the Universe and begged for mercy, that He take pity on so delicate a creature and not cast a hunched back upon her; better that he himself should bear the hump... And so the hump, front and back, was decreed upon him, and his bride was spared it.

On hearing this reasoning from Mendelssohn's lips, and feeling that she was destined for him by Providence as his bride, Fromet Guggenheim clung to him in love and became his bride.

Fromet Guggenheim was already somewhat advanced in years when she married Moses Mendelssohn. She was not beautiful, but she was very educated and wise, and the Jewish philosopher admired her — not only for her education, but also for her gentle character. Nevertheless, Mendelssohn suffered from her not a little, for he desired a religious Jewish home, and that was his warmest heart's wish; but Fromet was not devout, and her children were not raised in a religious upbringing — and this was Mendelssohn's tragedy, that after his death his children abandoned Judaism and converted to Christianity.

The War of Extermination Against the Jewish Teachers — The Teachers Halted Classes in Protest

[Education.] For several years now a systematic war has been waged against the Jewish teachers in the "powszechne" (public elementary) schools. In the schools various supposed "reforms" are being introduced, whose whole aim is to reduce the presence of Jewish teachers in these schools. That same method of extermination was recently applied also against the teachers of the evening courses for Jewish artisans and commercial clerks, who work a full day and in their free evening hours attend the evening courses. The evening courses for Jews had developed very nicely; young Jewish [working] people study in them, and the students had grown attached to the Jewish teachers, who treat the courses with particular love.

The first step of the school [authority], the "dozór szkolny" (school board), was to cast an "eye" on the number of Jewish teachers, and in the evening courses it increased the number by... Christian teachers. But they were not content with that — they went further, in order to [blur] entirely the Jewish [character]... This week a system of [mixing] was introduced in the evening courses; that is, the students from the Christian schools were sent in among the Jewish students, and thus "one big [obstacle]" was made... Understandably, the Jewish teachers, Messrs. Rotenberg, Ajzner, Grosman and Wizenfrajnd, could not tolerate such an act, and in protest they halted classes.

Autumn Maneuvers

Autumn maneuvers.

The military autumn maneuvers are already ending; the soldiers are marching back from the field to the barracks. In their place, however, the political autumn maneuvers are now beginning in earnest: the political 'armies' have already taken to the field. One can already see how the 'army' is mustering: on one side — the government army of the 'Egel' [?] [the Sanacja]. This army is for the time being concealing its plans, and is under the command of experienced military men, equipped with everything needed and with ample ammunition to wage a prolonged struggle. Those in the know say that this army's strategic position is not among the worst.

A second army, under the command of a [Czech? — that is, the Center bloc] field marshal, is maneuvering with much pretension, even brandishing its sword — but no great importance is attached to it; some see in it a 'maneuvering' factor between the government army and a third army — the most important in the present maneuvers: the army of the workers, the peasants, and, aiding them, part of the middle class as well. This army already formulated a joint ultimatum last week:

'We are not coming to consult with the government. We do not believe that consulting with you can bring any positive benefit; besides, we do not trust you either. We demand: lay down your arms — resign.'

It must be admitted that the 'Lewica' (the Left) has never yet confronted the government so sharply. It is now clear that the final moment of decision is approaching in the drawn-out conflict between the government camp and the 'Sejm.'

The 'Robotnik' (the PPS newspaper) openly declares that the PPS, which has placed itself at the head of the Sejm opposition, has now sharpened its tactics. It writes — addressing the Sanacja — that there are attempts 'to split and sharpen the political-social struggle in the country.' In enumerating the government's 'register of sins' against the people, and in threatening to 'break bones,' the paper asks that the Sanacja press not shed a tear of supposed sorrow over the opposition and its methods of struggle:

'We hold that the liquidation of the present regime is a necessity — not only from the standpoint of socialism or democratic doctrine, but also, in all seriousness, for the sake of the interests of Poland as an independent state. We aspire to liquidate the present regime by a legal and peaceful path, and shall therefore rely on parliamentary struggle; we threaten no one with "breaking bones" or with a "monarchist coup." Whether the regime will be liquidated "peacefully" depends not on us alone, but also on the other side.'

The 'Głos Prawdy' [the Sanacja newspaper] too has its say on the new situation. It is no longer the confident and 'aggressive' tone it once was; the 'Głos Prawdy' ascribes the leading role to the PPS alone, and assures that the government does not take the [threat] to heart. The PPS, it writes, 'goes with its left hand together with the socialists of the national minorities, and with its right hand — with the [Piast] and so on.' And as for the fist: 'We want to see these maneuvers not only on paper, but on the battlefield as well.'

Thus the political autumn maneuvers have begun with an interesting exchange of blows between the sides: the 'Robotnik' calling on the adversary to capitulate and raise the white flag, and the 'Głos Prawdy' answering: 'Let us first see it on the battlefield'...
Great Material Losses to the Jews of Zagłębie in the Riots in the Land of Israel — A Letter from Haifa

[Report + letter.] In the Land of Israel blood has been spilled; the mail reaching us from the Land of Israel carries sad greetings from the ruined Jewish community. Among the victims are also [natives] of Zagłębie, who have been utterly impoverished, and formerly well-to-do householders are now forced to turn to relief institutions to receive a little food and a shirt for their backs. Mr. Złotnik of Dąbrowa received a letter from his family and relatives that one of them [who owned property] in a colony extending over more than 1,400 [dunams] — has become a heap of ashes: the Arabs fell upon the colony before the Sabbath and destroyed it utterly, then slaughtered several Jews, wrapped the mutilated bodies in Torah scrolls and set them alight.

A heartrending letter reached us from Mr. Zindel Weisfrak (Weismark), who nine years ago left Będzin for the Land of Israel, where in time he built up a livelihood — a carpentry factory in Haifa — and lived with his family in comfort. But in the recent riots Mr. Weisfrak was left naked and destitute: his property, amounting to about a thousand pounds, went up in smoke, and his household belongings — including a complete dowry for his daughter — were plundered by the Arabs. Mr. Weisfrak, wandering with his family naked, barefoot and without a roof over their heads, sent the following letter (in its Hebrew original) to the representatives of the Będzin community, to his good friends and former comrades in Będzin, asking them to help him out of his critical situation:

'With God's help. To the honor of the great and esteemed rabbi of the holy community of Będzin, may he live long, and to the honor of the town council of Będzin. Esteemed rabbi! In connection with the terrible pogroms — of which you have surely heard — that befell my town and the inhabitants of the Land of Israel most grievously, I was [suddenly] reduced to a poor man lacking everything; from a factory owner I became one lacking bread and a place of refuge. [Wickedness?] and a fire burned down my factory with its machines, and my home and property, my belongings and furniture, and I was left naked and destitute, without food for a single meal. I therefore beg my dear friend the rabbi to call a meeting of the council, and in particular my acquaintances: Messrs. Yeshaya Firsztenberg, Jacob Matman [?], Izydor [Isaac] Grundman [?], Samson Rozenblum [?] and the others [with whom] I worked together in all the town's affairs [and in matters] of various charities — they know of my terrible situation, and let them come to my aid, so that I may rebuild my factory and support myself by the labor of my hands. Needless to add that while I was in Będzin I took an important and active part in all the town's affairs, and never shirked fulfilling my [duty]. [I built] my factory about three years ago... [and since I] think that my share through the Zionist administration will be very small, being among the burned-out ones who were harmed and ruined by the pogroms — I therefore beg the esteemed rabbi and the council that, if it is their wish to raise me up from my degradation and poverty, they remit [to my account] in my name; for if the money reaches [only] the Zionist administration, then my share will be very small and I shall be able to do [nothing] with it. With great and esteemed respect, and in expectation of your swift aid, Zindel Weismark. 25 Av 5689, Haifa, may it be rebuilt.'

The letter is accompanied by the stamp of the 'Rabbinical Office of the Hebrew Community of Haifa,' which writes: 'We the undersigned, the Rabbinical Office in Haifa, confirm that the words of Mr. Zindel Weisfrak are true and correct, namely that on the day of the [recent] pogroms that took place here his factory was burned and all that he had was looted, and he was left destitute. And to this we set our hands. Sunday, Rosh Chodesh Elul 5689, Land of Israel. The Rabbinical Office of the Hebrew Community of Haifa.' The address: Zindel Weismark, Haifa, P.O. Box 253, Palestine, Land of Israel.

'And We Thought...'

And we thought...

Subheads: 'The great relief effort for the Land of Israel — in what manner did the "Agudah" come to help?'

When we read the sad tidings that in the Land of Israel Jewish blood is being spilled and whole families are being destroyed to their foundations — we were all shaken. We felt the grief of our sisters and brothers in the Land of Israel. No one, on hearing of such terrible events, could remain indifferent; I myself wept like a little child and was shaken to the core.

I thought in those sad days: we are a people; I felt that a single Jewish heart beats within us all, that we are all one people — with one pain, one hope, one ideal. And in those moments, in the moments of our brethren's suffering, we felt all the limbs joining together into one body. I dreamed a beautiful dream: that our people had awakened from its 'drunkenness,' from the exile, from unconsciousness and disorientation, and was beginning green labor, understanding only now that it must provide for and sustain with bread and a roof over their heads the widows and orphans.

And precisely then we ran up against the terrible abyss of 'Agudah' 'politicization.' It is truly impossible to grasp so naive a question: how can it be that people cannot come to an understanding in order to gather alms for the wretched sisters and brothers in the Land of Israel? And really — what 'understanding' is needed here at all? What is there to quarrel about?

Ridiculous — and sad at once — is the demand of the 'Agudah' representatives: that the funds be deposited for the time being in [their] bank, and that only when they receive word from the Land of Israel that 'Agudah' representatives too have been included in the [gathering of the victims] — only then will the local representatives agree that the money be sent there.

Do we know these people by their words? Do they really suppose that it is permissible to 'strike at the common treasury' at so grave an hour, when help is needed and urgent? What does it mean that the 'Agudah' must be represented in a 'sufficient number,' and that without this the collection effort will be halted? Are they aware of what they are doing? What does it mean to make a distinction between one Jew and another, between one brother and another? Is one to distinguish between one wretched Jew and the next? Is one to classify the victims of the Land of Israel? Is one to demand to know who among the slain was rich and who was poor, who was a Sephardi Jew and who an Ashkenazi — when all are equally wretched, all perished together as martyrs for their homeland? And with a sick person who must be saved — must one first ascertain his biography, to which party he belonged and what his outlook was? Surely these people ought to be ashamed of making themselves so ridiculous.

When a Jew came to us at the editorial office a week ago to seek advice — he throws up both hands and does not know what to do: for both sides call to give money for the Land of Israel, and he does not know to which party to give, since to give to both is beyond his means. Understand, then: even into this holy work they inject party 'activism'!

Are they already preparing to turn the whole appeal into a party 'collection of penny-alms'? For the 'Agudah' has always sworn to place itself in opposition and to come out against the general [interests]. Pretexts for this will always be found: one time it will not be 'proper,' another time the [effort] will not be 'clean' — they always have something to 'break' and something to 'spoil.' But where the saving of life is concerned, this has no place.

We still remember with anguish how the 'Agudah' people labored during the Sejm elections so that the Jewish mandate would not win [a seat], and that Zagłębie would not receive even a single Jewish deputy — in order to [—]. Now the same deeds again: again they wish only to split, to halt and to shatter. There is no political platform involved here — so why is a divisive 'activism' now needed for the [work] of relief?

These people deliberately set out to disrupt this work; and for this an account must be given openly, so that the people may know with whom they are dealing. Instead of uniting — they seek only to split and to shatter, to harm the people's institutions and to do damage. We thought that if a Jewish heart beats, if the Jewish people is shaken — they would not allow a holy enterprise to be shattered, nor let it be attacked from all sides; we thought that we are a people with decent human beings.

In this difficult hour we must band together as one, mobilize all our forces for the sake of the wretched — and not split apart. Let all these people know: the saving of life overrides everything.

R. Let.

An Interesting Phenomenon

An interesting phenomenon.

Subheads: 'Why do they want to replace the [Jewish] teaching staff in the evening courses with Christian ones? — This must be responded to.'

Pedagogy is one of the most interesting occupations — and at the same time one of the most responsible. To be a pedagogue means to go beyond the accepted notions. A pedagogue, a teacher — from the moment he takes on the role — becomes embodied in that 'world of children,' and binds himself heart and soul to the profession and to the pupils. A pedagogue, from the moment he crosses the school's threshold, must also become a psychologist: he must know the pupil's psychology, penetrate into him, embody himself in the child's soul and the pupil's soul. Understandably, besides the great and difficult effort, this is also responsible work that requires training.

We know, for example, that there are teachers, men and women, who are utterly devoted to their work — not because they have filled all their hours, but simply because the school is their world, and the pupils are their delight. In time the teachers are drawn into that 'world of children,' until they no longer know that beyond this world there is anything else. This devotion we see chiefly among the teachers of the public elementary schools (the 'powszechna'), and thanks to it we meet there children who are attached to their teachers as to their parents.

As is known, in Poland the compulsory-education schools have existed for only a short time, and we therefore have a certain number of adult illiterates. The Będzin magistrat therefore arranged evening courses ('komplety'), in which adults study in their free hours. Several young Jews were found who devoted themselves to organizing the evening courses, so that over the course of a few years a number of several hundred pupils took shape, with whom the young Jews are engaged. It is interesting to note that both the teachers and the pupils bind themselves to the studies with rare devotion and love.

But this harmony has begun to be disturbed: it is being planned that the Jewish pupils will receive — instead of Jewish teachers — Christian teachers. To this end they have begun to mix the small number of Christian pupils with the large number of Jews, so that it will be possible to push out the Jewish teachers and replace them with Christians.

The Jewish teachers, seeing that they are being made a blind instrument in someone's hands, responded to the injustice and stopped the lessons in protest. As these lines are being written the matter has not yet been resolved; it still stands at the same dead point. But be that as it may — it is unheard of to permit this kind of politics. Why the 'big eyes' at the Jewish teachers, and why seek to replace them with Christians? If they are unworthy — this must be argued; but one cannot simply push them out and give their places to others. Let the Christian pupils have their Christian teachers — but the Jewish pupils must be taught precisely by Jewish teachers.

One must not estrange oneself from either the teachers or the pupils — who are, incidentally, already grown young people; and while they study with much love and devotion under the Jewish teachers, they will gain nothing from the Christian teachers. For, as said, the teacher must know the physiognomy of his pupils and penetrate their souls — something made possible thanks to the mutual love between teacher and pupil; and such harmony cannot exist between a Christian teacher and a Jewish pupil, for these are two worlds, two outlooks, two opposing notions.

From a practical standpoint too, the 'dozór szkolny' (the school inspectorate) ought not to permit so strange an outcome; one must not forget that we are dealing here with grown young people, complete illiterates, to whom only a Jewish teacher can speak — for only a Jew knows and senses the soul, the strength and the spirit of these young people. Our self-government authorities must not allow the young Jews to suffer neglect; to such an undesirable and unhealthy phenomenon one must respond at once, as is fitting.

Selekt.

On Order in the Synagogue during the High Holy Days

[Editorial.] As our dear readers know, every year, during the most solemn prayers of Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur at the municipal synagogue, unpleasant incidents occur — quarrels and even brawls. All this stems from the enormous overcrowding, and above all from the chaos and disorder, since no order is kept because of the [sale of] certain seats. On Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur the number of worshippers in the synagogue reaches [thousands]; the crush is great, and the [commotion] among the worshippers of the second half of the synagogue, by the door, is greater still. Instead of reverence for a holy place, [chaos] and confusion prevail. Even among the more [discerning] worshippers of the first half of the synagogue, by the Holy Ark, [shoving] sometimes breaks out, leading to brawls and afterward to lawsuits, as happened this Yom Kippur as well. People off the street, who are not regular worshippers, take the places of the regulars. When someone has paid for a single "seat," he grabs 4 or even 5 seats for his children, his family, and mere acquaintances...

Subheading: "Hebrew has been introduced in the public elementary schools — will the children get anything out of it?"

It is a fine thing that the great majority of school pupils are educated in the public elementary schools; and therefore it would be fitting for us to devote to them — and to the educational institutions — a little more attention. For each of us knows that among the broad strata of the population there are children of various sorts, and not infrequently we meet very simple children; and for this reason alone it is fitting to take a greater interest in this problem. But this is not something anyone particularly cares about; the teachers are subject to their instructions and their officials, and are obliged to teach their material according to the prescribed directives.

From the current year a new thing has been introduced: in all the schools Hebrew is now taught as a subject — in addition to religion, which exists to this day as well. Of course the phenomenon is welcome. But let us examine how this function is fulfilled: if we take a pencil and reckon, we see that in Będzin, for example, we have 40 public elementary schools, in which 2,000 children study; and these 2,000 children study both religion and Hebrew — and it is all "handled" by three people in all. Obviously no more than one hour, and at most two hours a week, comes of it; and the question arises: can three teachers teach 2,000 children? And can a child get anything out of such a kind of instruction?

This is a caricature. We know that from instruction of this kind nothing will come, that the child will get nothing out of it. Of course the parents are not versed in these matters and do not give an account of them; on the contrary — they are confident that their children will learn Hebrew, and many of them are convinced that the Hebrew of the public elementary school will replace even the "cheder." If only the parents knew that this is "nothing with nothing," that it is no more than "medicine on the tip of a spoon"; take whatever kind of instruction you like — it comes out as a sort of toy.

Grinbaum fought in the Sejm for Hebrew to be introduced in the public elementary schools for the Jewish children; but he did not reckon that the thing would simply come out a caricature. It is either-or: either one teaches in such a way that it can be called "they learned" — that the children get something out of the instruction; and if not — it is better not to begin at all, and not to mislead the parents into expenses and order them to buy Hebrew books. And if one nevertheless wants to teach Hebrew — it must be introduced properly: to employ a whole row of teachers who can properly teach all the children studying in the public elementary schools.

There are, after all, parents' committees attached to the schools, whose task it is to consider how the studies are taught; why, then, should they not take an interest in seeing that the instruction is properly conducted and that the children derive benefit from it? There is no point in teaching in such a way — which is nothing but a kind of fiction; it would have been better for it to remain as it was. There is no purpose in "wasting" years on nothing: the children will learn nothing as long as the matter remains as it is today. We do not know how the thing is conducted in the "powszechna" (public) schools generally, whether the authorities have the possibility of increasing the number of hours and employing a sufficient number of teachers.

The staff must also apply to the bureau authorities, so that the matter will not be left pending; the duty of instruction must be fulfilled properly — or it should be introduced correctly and see to it that the children actually learn the language, so that the thing is not done as a kind of useless caricature. The matter must not be left "hanging in the air"; better thus than to leave it "nothing with nothing."

Selekt.
The Economic Situation in Poland

The economic situation in Poland.

According to the report of the [Institute] for the Study of the Economic Situation in Poland, the crisis trend that characterized the Polish economy in the first quarter of 1929 continued in July as well. The political situation [contributed] to the tension too, and the payments situation worsened. The process of economic deterioration gained momentum, and in some regions a [decline] in production was evident.

Work in [industry] fell in recent months, as shown by the indices of industrial production. The situation in the field of raw materials is [difficult]; the textile industry did not [employ] its full workforce this year, and in [Łódź and Białystok] strikes and cutbacks broke out in the textile industry in July, lasting about two months. In the coal industry too there were [reductions]: the number of [workers] and the number of working days fell.

The official statistics show that in the textile industry (chiefly in Łódź) a considerable [decline] occurred; and in the coal industry work was [reduced]. The cost-of-living index fell from 5.81 to 5.37 [points?]; and in total [—] about 115 million złoty. According to the official statistics, in June [—] about 98 million złoty.

[The report concludes] that the crisis in the Polish economy and industry is deepening, that the situation of workers and industrialists alike is worsening, and that the general trend of the economic situation remains negative.

Subheading: "The people's representatives must be on guard and fulfill their mission."

When an evil decree happens to come, when a new and heavy tax arrives that destroys livelihoods — people begin to shout and make noise, as if the heavens were falling; they cast the blame on the representatives, and there — there are no representatives. In short: uproar, spectacle, and agitation arise, as if one were ready to do something; but it lasts no more than a few hours or days, the heat cools, and gradually people begin to grow accustomed to the bad, to the hard. It is of course very bad to grow accustomed to the bad; but the characteristic thing is that one never first tries to put one's hand into the cold water, so as to avoid and guard against the evil at the very outset.

More than once we have seen that various decrees erupted in our civic life and destroyed Jewish livelihoods — and the interesting thing is that only after the fact, when we see that we had not grasped in advance what it was about, does it become clear that had we known in good time what the matter was heading toward and how harmful it might be, we would have fought in advance and every possible measure would have been taken not to let the situation worsen. Therefore "initiative from the start" — that is, examining every project from all its sides from the very beginning — plays a great role in our life, as the past has already taught us.

Even now we must look with open eyes at the project that has now been submitted — that the powiat (district) of Będzin be annexed to Upper Silesia. At this moment we cannot express a firm opinion on the question; it may be to our detriment, and who knows — perhaps actually to our benefit. We have not yet given ourselves a clear account of it, nor examined it from all its sides; but in any case one must not pass over the project lightly, for this is a very complex matter, which must be grasped with full awareness and complete composure.

We know only that the big industrialists are firmly opposed to the proposed project and are fighting with utter devotion so that it will not be realized; and it may be that it could ruin our Jewish merchant as well, who is liable to be swallowed up by the organized and experienced merchant of Upper Silesia.

And see how much frivolity our representatives show toward this important question — the heart truly aches. Here, for example, we know that last week a session of the council of the merchants' associations of Zagłębie was held in Będzin, whose agenda included the question of putting forward candidates to the Chamber of Commerce for the [committee for the] turnover tax for the year 1929. And it would seem that both questions are so important that any explanation is superfluous — and yet Sosnowiec, Jewish Sosnowiec, did not send its representatives to such an important session!

How can such conduct be called? What kind of tactic is this? Is this in the people's interest? Can it be excused only as indifference? And is such indifference not graver than any crime, than any public harm that the individual cannot make good? Do the representatives understand what mission they have taken upon themselves, when they make light of so heavy a responsibility?

It is sad and painful when one has to rouse the representatives on such important matters, so that they will not neglect what has been entrusted to them. Take even the important question of the candidates for the turnover tax: how many victims this tax has claimed among us! How many incorrect assessments were made, until real and large firms were forced to lose all their property! Surely the years that have passed ought to have taught us something — that we should know how far we can preserve the positions to which we are entrusted.

As for the second question — the annexation of our powiat to the województwo of Upper Silesia: we said that we do not know for certain what results it will bring; but one fact is clear — that such a reform could definitely bring about a revolution in our world of commerce and industry, and this we must take seriously into account. In any case the question is important enough for us to devote time to it; and the hour is important enough that all citizens should be aware of it, so that each may have his say in it.

The high time has come not to remain indifferent to the most important interests and the most serious questions. We have already paid dearly for our indifference; let us at least now look with a clear eye at our future. One must not make light of what is so important — of what means human existence, human life. Sosnowiec frightens us: Sosnowiec has already shown, from the outset, a rare indifference toward the two questions — and such indifference can be called nothing but a "crime without equal"; and it must not be allowed to recur again and again.

We must demand of our representatives in Sosnowiec that they not neglect our interests, that they not regard as "pettiness" what has such important significance. Let our representatives remember that, when all is said and done, they are responsible for every mistake they make. True, this is not legal or material responsibility, but only moral — yet moral responsibility is worth far more to a people than legal responsibility; it is the highest expression, which can never be paid for with money.

Let our people's envoys take this to heart, and keep these "Ten Commandments" always before their eyes; for to take upon oneself the mission of a people's representative and not to keep it — this is no pettiness, especially when it concerns questions of the very greatest importance.

Dr. Papori.

The Year 5689 in Jewish Life (A Brief Summary)

[A review of the year.] The year 5689 was not — as we had so hoped — a year of building and [flourishing], but a year of the harshest [trials].

[Soviet Russia:] In the Soviet Union the Jewish population was cruelly [oppressed], both spiritually and economically. The Soviet regime brought down the status of the Jewish shtetl and of the three-million-strong Jewry of Russia, which stands on the brink of [ruin]. The Bolshevik attempt to move Jews to agricultural settlement did not succeed; among the migrants to the Crimea and to Birobidzhan there is great dissatisfaction, and matters often come to bloody clashes between them and the earlier settlers. The wild region of Birobidzhan, which was supposedly to bring "redemption" to the oppressed and declassed Jews of Russia, is turning out to be a failure (bankrupt); and in order to save the failing enterprise, the "Yevsektsiya" is sending special emissaries out into the Jewish world to agitate on behalf of the Russian settlement. The pioneer colonies were disbanded on account of their Zionist views; young Zionist-Socialists are exiled to the icy regions of Siberia and thrown into the prisons of the [G.P.U.]. The spiritual oppression and the persecution of the Jewish religion, of Zionism and of Hebrew grow ever harsher; schools and houses of study are turned into Communist clubs; Jews are forced to work even on the High Holy Days; in the Jewish schools of the Soviet Union a new subject called "anti-religion" has been introduced, whose purpose is to uproot and stifle in Jewish children every religious feeling. The works of the Jewish classic writers — Mendele Mocher Sforim, Sholem Aleichem, Peretz and others — are being withdrawn from the Jewish schools for fear that they are too "nationalist". Jewish teachers are persecuted by their Communist "comrades", who spread the slogan "Russia for the Russians, down with the Jews!" The war of Jewish annihilation is being waged on every front, and there is a danger that our brethren in Russia may, God forbid, be utterly wiped out.

[Antisemitic countries:] Among the antisemitic countries are: Yugoslavia, where a bloody blood-libel agitation broke out in the village of [—]; Bessarabia, where severe antisemitic outbreaks occurred; Hungary, where the "bearers" of culture and enlightenment, the local students, staged demonstrations [against kosher slaughter]; Lithuania too "honored" us with pogroms and with blood-libel incitement, and Jewish property was looted, and there too a 40-year-old man, [—] Shaksel [?], fell victim. In Romania a change for the better has taken place in the government's attitude toward the Jews...

[The Land of Israel:] And first and foremost — the bloody riots of 5689 in the Land of Israel, which claimed many victims and destroyed colonies and property...
The Head Office in Jerusalem Sends a New Year Greeting to the Editorial Staff and Readers

The Head Office in Jerusalem

sends a New Year greeting to the editorial staff and readers of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".

Esteemed Editor of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung",

On the occasion of the New Year we wish you, your esteemed co-workers, your newspaper, and its dear men and women readers — with all our heart — "May you be inscribed and sealed for a good year". At the same time we express to you our sincere thanks — to you and to your esteemed co-workers — for the devotion and sympathy you have shown, in the columns of your esteemed newspaper, toward the [idea] of Keren Kayemet and toward aid for the Land of Israel.

We allow ourselves to hope that your alertness and sympathy will now grow still greater, in view of the recent events in the Land of Israel. For we must know that every Jew, and all that is precious in the Land of Israel — whoever is harmed in his [person] or in his labor — is, according to his fate, nothing less than an expression of the fate of the entire Jewish people, whose sacred duty it is [to stand by him]. And therefore the columns of your newspaper too bear the duty of rousing the public to help the Land of Israel — not only material aid for the victims, but also the [strengthening] of the idea of building up the Land.

The Land of Israel, which was built with the toil of [years] and with sacrifices, now needs the aid of the entire Jewish people. And in this difficult hour, when the world [looks on] at the Jewish fate, the Jewish people must stand as one man with the Land of Israel — for thereby it will be rebuilt.

Nathan Bistritzky, Z. Kotler.

[The writer, a native of Dąbrowa who immigrated to the Land, tells how he was fortunate to receive an invitation to a wedding celebration at the home of Sheikh Abu Husha, head of a [Bedouin/village] tribe known as a friend of the Jews, who invited him specially for the exact date so that there would be no "misunderstanding."]

Abu Husha, the well-known leader of his tribe, invited me; and on the way I passed through the [colonies] of the Sharon, where joy prevails. All the colonies — for example "Mother" Mikveh (Mikveh Israel) and the colonies [—] Ein Chai, Gan Chaim, [—] — gather at one [celebration]; each colony arrives with its gift, and we meet in the [valley]. We go to the appointed [place], and there all the colonies already stand with their gifts. At the head of all the guests was [—] Avraham Shapira (the veteran watchman), with the gift of [Petach Tikva].

From afar we see how Abu Husha's horsemen gallop toward us to receive us. At the head we were received by the Sheikh himself, with the groom and his retinue. The first to offer a greeting was Avraham Shapira, who presented the gift of [Petach Tikva] — comprising 3 fine sheep, [—] rice, a sack of sugar, coffee, tea [—]; then he introduced all the representatives of the colonies, and each representative presented his gift. The Sheikh gives thanks and invites all the guests to the hospitality tent, where Abu Husha's son is already present with his white-robed brothers.

We sit together; we are served lemonade and black coffee to drink in tiny cups, in the manner of the Arabs; and meanwhile the guests strike up a conversation with the groom, who is only about 15 years old. The groom's uncle relates that in their tribe, apart from the women and children who are not counted, the family is very large, and almost the entire branching region belongs to them. It is a fact that to this day agitators and instigators come to them [from time to time], urging them to attack the Jewish settlement — but they reject this: "I gave my word to the Jews in 1921, I will not attack again; the Jews made me a [—], I keep my word."

The bride is not [—]; she [sits] with the women, who adorn her and make her up with a silk kerchief. When Abu Husha's [—] had passed, the celebration began: the Jews [dance] together, others in [circles]; the women [—] with kerchiefs. Finally the Sheikh [asked] that the groom [dance] a few dances; and his tribesmen staged a "fantasia" (an equestrian display). The [gifts] at the "mishan" (the feast) included several sheep, and even 3 [—] roasted [—] meat; and delicacies were not lacking.

Finally the Sheikh [asked] that we taste the most precious dish; and the groom tasted from [—], as is the custom. The Sheikh delivered a short speech about their friendship with the colonies and the guests, and wished that we live in peace. We too wished all the colonies [—]; and with this the letter takes its leave. The dancers [—] with hearts full of joy at having been received with such great hospitality. And this proves that Abu Husha and his tribesmen know how to keep their friendship with the Jews in this difficult hour.

Naftali Rechnitz, Tel Aviv.

The Power of Money, Given with an Open Hand — Do We Know How to Value It?

The power of money — given with an open hand. Do we know how to value it?

[Sub-heading: When public life declines, when the state of public institutions grows more dismal.]

The question arises: what of Sosnowiec? Sosnowiec, which before the war stood higher in civic importance and even surpassed Będzin — now, on all sides, one hears of it neglect and a criminal indifference toward the sharpest and most urgent questions. And when we ask Sosnowiec, "Where are you going, and what will become of you?", its citizens answer: "For you Będziners it is well; you are cultured, you have a mecenas (patron)"... Would that it were so. We are far from flattering anyone; we are not among those who dispense unwarranted praise. But the real truth must be properly valued.

And so the question arises: how do we value the merits of such a patron? With full awareness, a clear conscience and a whole heart we answer: no, we do not value sufficiently the high merits and fine deeds of Mr. Firsztenberg. A man with an open hand — right and left; a man who supports everyone in need of support, so handsomely and with understanding — and the town takes no notice of it. We cannot properly value the [deeds] of this man with a heart of gold.

The man took upon himself the initiative and the idea of building a magnificent edifice for the Jewish gymnasium — not in miniature format, but large and impressive, with a broad [façade], with the most comfortable halls in the latest modern style. One stands and marvels when beholding these buildings. And when representatives of the authorities enter, they will feel respect and reverence before it all.

Moreover, the school has become recognized by the government: it obtained government rights on the basis of the new building — in place of the one it had before, in which it struggled under the harshest conditions. So splendid a building has been erected that not everyone can afford the ready conveniences, the various classrooms, the well-lit halls, and the gymnasium hall with its perfected apparatus. Now the beautiful courtyard is a world unto itself, "spacious".

Mr. Firsztenberg did not content himself with building the beautiful monument and handing it over to the school administration; he continues to give money, has all the furnishings made at his own expense, brings in the furniture, provides the lamps, and does not cease — from the largest thing to the smallest. His unbreakable will and his selfless love for the gymnasium are evident in everything. A whole building, finished and fully built, which seems to say to the passer-by: come and enjoy, behold its beauty and grandeur. In such quiet, modesty and devotion the beautiful building was erected — and almost no one takes notice; not even a house-dedication has yet been held. This must not be allowed: a dedication must be held properly, and the town, the parents and the public must express their appreciation and their sympathy to the patron for the beautiful monument-project given to modern Będzin.

And one more thing: it would be fitting to open the gates of the gymnasium for a time, so that entry be free to all — so that people may behold the beautiful institution. Let people see how great is the power of a generous heart and a good will. We must be fully aware, we must know how to value at its full height what the man has created: the town demanded a proper building in which to educate people, good and national Jews — and to that end the man created a monument that will bear his name for generations.

The Plight of the Middle Class — Can It Be Borne Like This?

[Editorial signed R. Let — note: the OCR title is garbled; from the body of the text this is an article on the plight of the middle class.]

[Sub-heading: The difficult situation of the bourgeois middle class in the country. Can it be borne like this?]

Once again the income-tax assessments (income-Steuer) cast melancholy over people's faces. People tremble at the sight of the assessments: they must bear an unbearable burden. The writer spoke with people who know how much they must pay in income tax; they walk about dejected and cannot understand how they will carry on their weak shoulders the great wave of taxes, which grows ceaselessly.

I happened to speak with a [merchant] who was assessed at [—] thousand złoty — and he laughs. He laughs not because someone is playing a "little game" with him, but because [he has] nowhere to pay it from: "Where," he says, "is a man to take it, when there is no merchandise and no income? I once had a little money, and it is gone; they laugh and laugh, for there is nothing to be done."

In Poland too they "laugh": the government sets heavy taxes, and the small merchant cannot "laugh" — he must hold on. The petty trader, with his tiny means and tiny income, is charged so large a tax that he cannot pay it.

Humanity advances so much nowadays — and yet with us [—] the body of the state [—]. The middle class is the [backbone] of every state; and it would be right to understand, with reason and level-headedness, that the middle class must be helped first of all. It must not be left to fall: whoever wishes to work and earn a piece of bread — he should be given the possibility.

When a man is once charged such heavy taxes, he says to himself: "I will pay, so long as I do not [—]"; and he sells his last little property in order to pay — until nothing is left to him, and his health and his rest are lost. And this must be appreciated. With such an income a man reckons: where is he to take it from, when there is no merchandise? [—] He is forced to sell his last in order to pay the tax — and in the end the government has nothing more to collect from him. A man invests much toil, loses his health and his livelihood — and thus the middle class declines.

These taxes drain the middle class in Poland: a man sells his last, collapses, and it seems there is no longer any remedy. Just as the state [rests] upon the middle class, so must it give it the possibility to survive. The high time has come for the state to take the middle class into account and to help it — before it is too late.

R. Let.
