Sub-headings: "Our poverty, our neglect, and our indifference. Should this be allowed to go on like this?"

As a "journalist," last week I took up a topical question; the author of the article asks why domestic servants (dinst-meydlekh) have become so rare among us — even though this is no longer a bad occupation, since nowadays they are not treated as they once were, and even in the street one cannot tell a servant girl from the daughter of an educated householder. And the same goes for the Jewish "stróże" (janitors/porters). The "journalist" asks: why are there almost no more such "stróże" and craftsmen?

This is indeed a question worth dwelling on, and in earnest. For more than once we hear laments over this or that branch, this or that trade, from which the Jews are being pushed out and losing their place. And what do Jewish families do when they lose their livelihood? From where and how are they to make a living? Once, a family would begin to live off the wind, off the street, off [luck]: the Jew would go out into the street with his stick and look for a "living." Today everything has changed, and the situation has grown more extreme, so that earning a living "off the wind and the street" has become impossible; and the end of it is that such Jews have sunk until they fell to the level of poverty and want, and in time became "professionals" of [begging].

True, it was hard for them at first to hold out their hand; but in time, once they saw that the trade [is not so shameful], they said: "the cap of shame has already been handed in." True, the trade is not a fine one — it degrades a man; but the wretched then grow blind and no longer see anything — they get used to the idea that the town "owes" them, that the town must support them. And then such a family demands a doctor, a [lawyer], a hospital — "for free," since it is "doing the town a favor" by its very existence.

Among us it never occurred to anyone to prevent this element from sinking to a lower and lower level; and we have already grown accustomed to the idea that we must support poor people who turn into professional beggars; and the beggars have children, who likewise grow up neither to work nor to "respectability" — and we support them too. Can it be that we are raising a generation of beggars?

The question of the servant girls is not so grave: these girls will not take service positions in any case — it does not appeal to them; they prefer to loaf about, and "to blacken their faces" they will not. Not seldom we see such girls going out all dressed up, in gloves, collecting "alms" for "others" — and it has already been proved more than once that the money is meant for [amusement] at the theater... And if we still have Jewish servant girls at all, it is thanks to the provinces, where the poverty is so bitter: our region no longer produces such girls — out of sheer poverty and distress.

What else? When Passover and Sukkot come, when people here begin to clean (royshn), you will find Jewish women scrubbing floors; the Christian cleaning-women then are beside themselves and raise their prices as high as they can — yet even so, not one of the poor women will cease to trudge from door to door and earn a living. And so it is in the matzah season too. There — to the matzah-baking — our poor women do not want to go, though they know they would earn well, because there too one must work with a "kosher" (clean) hand.

We let this branch [deteriorate] by giving out the [small] pennies, and so we raise a generation of begging. Not seldom we blush with shame when the new month comes around — at the sight of the [beggars] straggling through the streets, going from house to house and from courtyard to courtyard, calling out: "good morning for four, good morning for five" (that is, how many [pennies] are due them).

Of course we ourselves are to blame for the trouble, for had we not given alms to able-bodied people, they would have been forced to take up some work, and would not have scorned any trade — and all these would have been no less fine and honorable than "going from door to door." We do not see the disgrace and the trouble that "begging" (the roaming "chalyastre") brings upon us, and we remain indifferent to the dangerous plague spreading in our midst. It has already become accepted that "begging is no worse a trade than any other 'black labor'"; and at the first opportunity people hold out their hand — and that must not be permitted.

Had we not been indifferent to everything, "favors" and "pity" would not be handed to just anyone among us; the "mitsesis" (the begging) would not multiply so quickly, and we would not have so many "shameless householders." We know we have enemies who wish to lodge the morsel in our throat; not a few Jews have already lost their livelihood and become "beggars," who themselves now ask [—], for now respectable people are being pushed aside; we are being pushed out of various branches in which we sustained ourselves for many years.

So that we shall not be forced to turn to "begging," we must seek new work and new trades and make our living from them. I do not mean to say that we should be idle and let the town support us; but rather that [we should acquire] the new trades from which the broad strata of the toiling Jewish population once made their living. It would be right, in all honesty, to think about this seriously — and to take a radical step in this field.

R. Let.

Subheadings: "The question of the Old Market. — How did people react to it? — The failure of both sides."

The Old Market tax assessments [were] postponed, since they were forcibly reduced in the "black" days — at the very best time, before the good days (the festival days), when people needed to earn [a living] and to sustain themselves for the holiday. The magistrat further claims that they [the merchants] did not extend the deadline even once, and that the stalls had in time already managed to arrange themselves and settle into the halls (hale).

And the trouble is that we do not know how to examine anything with full awareness and seriousness; we never react in time, even though it is made clear to us that a change is about to occur. They knew well that the stalls would be moved from the market to the halls, and the tax people did not react to it; therefore they ought to have reacted at once and taken an interest, and not waited until they were hauled off with the "little bundle" from the market. Surely people should have known that the moment a decision is made, it is immediately carried out; and the halls will scarcely be erected before the stalls are transferred there. But people did not react to it in time, did not grasp the matter — until they had already been driven out.

When the decision was taken, [it was] too late; feeble and late. Had they reacted in time, they would have achieved much; but they always come after the fact, when there is no longer any power to change anything, and then they feel helpless.

True, the magistrat is also to blame: it did not act honestly when it drove the merchants out of the market without first preparing the halls; therefore it appears that in fact it did nothing for the people's benefit, but only as a "for the time being" (a temporary measure). The halls are small and impractical, and each merchant [gets] barely half a hall; and even that is granted "for the time being", without anyone knowing when a [permanent one] will be erected. And now the question arises: how and by what right can the magistrat drive the merchants out of the market without having prepared proper halls for them? For the stalls stand under the open sky, since the merchants cannot carry them home at night and bring them back again in the morning; and this costs a great deal of money.

The market is neglected and untended, though it is much needed. At the very least the magistrat should have marked out a definite place with fixed stalls; and if it demanded that the merchants come to the market, the stalls ought to have been fixed and orderly. Such a public matter must not be treated lightly — for this is not a thing of anarchy, that one may do with it as one pleases and however one wishes. The self-government ought to have understood this, and to have arranged the merchants' place properly, with care and with sense.

And the merchants, too, have proven more than once that they do not know how to stand up for themselves when necessary. And from this case both sides — both the merchants and the magistrat — must learn a lesson: let them know that from indifference and neglect nothing is gained, but rather one loses at every step. Let all know, once and for all: whoever does not take an interest and react in time — loses; and when they finally open their eyes, they will no longer see what they sought.

R. Let.

The Artificial Antisemitism of Upper Silesia

The artificial antisemitism of Upper Silesia.

Subheading: "One must stand on guard."

For some time now an artificial antisemitic propaganda has been noticeable in Upper Silesia — [spurring on] antisemitic parties and a movement [toward the formation of] antisemitic blocs, a Völkisch-Klub and the like, and it is hard to understand what [feeds] them. But one must understand: this is an artificial antisemitism, [made to order], which does not arise from real [neighborly relations] but from a deliberate creation — one that seeks to [turn a blind eye] to the distress of the times and to divert the anger onto the Jew as a "scapegoat".

One must observe this question with an open eye and an alert heart; not treat it lightly. True, the situation in Upper Silesia is not so terrible as in other places; but at the first opportunity the [antisemites] raise their heads. The incitement is becoming systematic, and its aim is one: to push the Jew out of his livelihood and his positions, on the pretext that he is a "foreigner". One must understand that this propaganda is organized and directed — not a spontaneous phenomenon of neighborly hatred.

Therefore we must stand on guard. Let us not underestimate this danger: it begins "small", but grows quickly. We must track it, expose its sources and its operators, and react to it in time — before it spreads. For whoever remains indifferent to such a danger pays dearly for his indifference.

It must be remembered that antisemitism in Upper Silesia rests on "artificial" foundations — and therefore it can be withstood, if only we are not indifferent. The Jewish organizations in Upper Silesia are still weak and scattered; they must be strengthened and united, so that they can stand up to the incitement. We must be alert — and stand on guard.

Dr. Papori.
International Savings Day

International Savings Day.

All the countries of the world [mark] International Savings Day, for saving is [important] not only for the state but also for society and the individual. There is no [—] greater benefit than saving — whether for the state, for society, or for the individual person.

Saving enables a person to live a more secure life, to accumulate a [reserve] for times of trouble and for old age. A person who saves need not turn to strangers in a time of distress; he has someone to rely on — himself and his [savings]. Saving educates a person to order, diligence and responsibility, and grants him independence and confidence in life.

It is important for the state as well that its citizens save: the citizens' savings are a [source] of national capital, serving the development of the economy, construction and enterprises. The more the state's citizens save, the stronger the state is economically. Therefore states encourage savings institutions — banks, savings funds and the post office — and devote a special day to explaining the value of saving.

It is fitting, then, that everyone — adult and child alike — should acquire the habit of saving, be it but "a single grosz to savings"; for penny by penny adds up to a large account, and today's saving is tomorrow's security.

Al. Berkenheim.

By Leon Speyer.

Subheadings (the structure of the essay): the last destruction of the Land of Israel in the thirteenth century; the era of the Crusades and their persecutions; the destruction of Ashkenazi Jewry and the [decline] wrought by the Crusaders; the Jewish settlement in the Land of Israel at that time; the conquest of Jerusalem by the Crusaders; the destruction of the Jewish settlement in the year 1099; the impoverishment of the land through the frequent wars; the complete destruction of the Land of Israel [in the 13th century]; and the Crusades (1096–1230).

The Crusades, which lasted nearly a century and a half (1096–1230), are among the saddest and most blood-soaked chapters in the Jewish history of the Middle Ages. Already with the First Crusade a [massacre began] of Ashkenazi Jewry and of the [Jewish settlement] in the Land of Israel: when the Crusaders conquered Jerusalem in the year 1099, they destroyed the Jewish settlement in the city, and the land was impoverished by the frequent wars until it was almost entirely laid waste.

Against the background of this destruction, in the 13th century, arises the figure of Nachmanides (Rabbi Moshe ben Nachman) — who came up to the Land of Israel and worked to renew the Jewish settlement in ruined Jerusalem. Nachmanides is regarded as the pioneer of the renewed Jewish settlement in the land, who laid a cornerstone for the Jewish community in Jerusalem after its destruction.

(The essay surveys the historical background of the Crusades, the destruction of the communities, and Nachmanides' work as the renewer of the settlement.)

Subtitles: "Responsibility and abandonment toward the public. — Where does the line between them run?"

It is clear to everyone that when a new and heavy tax is imposed — one that destroys livelihoods and pushes people out of their means of subsistence — the matter is not about this or that tax, this or that class, but about a catastrophe: people descend from "the street of commerce" and cease to exist. These people are forever oppressed, because they could not go with the current and could not bear the great burden of the taxes imposed on them; and instead of money — they took "debts" upon themselves. These are people who fulfilled their duties as citizens and as human beings — and yet no one takes them into account.

When it comes to tax assessment, people are as terrified as on "the Day of Judgment": a person of moderate means, saddled with an excessive assessment, may lose his head — for he does not know where he will get it from. And no wonder: when he must fear that such an assessment may liquidate him entirely, he loses his peace of mind.

It is a disgrace that in the 20th century, in the heart of Europe, and on parliamentary foundations, not every class, every people and every party can obtain fair representation — representation that would know how to protect the individual. It is, after all, self-evident that the people's representatives must be devoted to the [public] in order to protect it; that the representation should stand guard over the interests of the whole. And when a people neglects what is laid upon it from above, what is its "quintessence" (its very essence), what is left abandoned and is everyone's fault — then this is a city laid waste through neglect and indifference.

We must therefore prepare in good time; to seize every opportunity to explain that the existence of the individual and the existence of the public must not be abandoned. We ought to have a worthy public representation, one that would take the population into account and not neglect it. For whoever neglects his duty toward the public is like one who abandons the city to ruin.

R. Let.
The Vilna Tower

The Vilna Tower.

By M. Y. Stupnicki.

At the [opening] of the "Jewish Scientific Institute" (YIVO) in Vilna [—]. The celebration was grandiose: Jewish cultural activists came from Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Germany, and even America was represented... It was a holiday of Jewish culture. The cornerstone was laid for a building for the institute.

But the solemnity was marred by wretched politics, which introduced here too — in the sacred garden of culture — a dissonance, a jarring note that spoiled the mood for a while. What is culture? We all know — or none of us knows. Until now we believed that culture in general, and Jewish culture in particular, is something common to all people and to all Jews: science, history, philosophy, linguistics and folklore, economics and research — all these are universally human and universally Jewish.

But it turns out we were mistaken. At the gathering in Vilna, representatives of the "Bund" and of "Poalei Zion" Left came forward and argued that the institute should be "proletarian", that it must work for a "proletarian" culture, and so on. We say "and so on", because we truly do not know what they argued and what they wanted there. We do not know — not only because we were not present, but because even had we been present we would not have known; for we simply cannot understand what that "proletarian culture" is — the culture that the world [supposes] it can create as a kind of [—].

The ideologues of socialism — Lassalle, Marx and Engels — grew up and created in a "bourgeois" world; Judaism itself is a rich world of [values]. The proletariat has to this day not created any "world-value", nor does it create one, for whoever creates a world-value is already [no longer] merely proletarian. Today, when people speak of "proletarian culture", and understand by it [—]... True, one may speak of a proletarian world, of a world that would be created socially; but proletarian culture — that is a contradiction in itself.

Science, history, language, folklore — are neither "bourgeois" nor "proletarian", but universally human. And why turn the "science of Judaism" (Chochmat Yisrael) into a party? Why bring "class war" into the temple of culture? The Jewish Scientific Institute must be an exemplary tower, standing above every party — "the Vilna Tower", to which the whole Jewish people will look. It must be guarded from every party "dissonance", and allowed to stand in its full cultural height — as a tower of light for the whole of Jewish culture.

[Sosnowiec.]

A father-in-law takes revenge on his son-in-law. All of Upper Silesia is astir over an extraordinary tale involving a merchant from [Kaszowice?] some time ago. A resident of Czeski Cieszyn, Mr. Eli[—] Weksberg [?], fell under the wheels of a moving train and was killed on the spot. The tragic deceased, Weksberg, had a son-in-law who, a month after the wedding, left his young wife and went to live in [Kaszowice?], bearing a grudge against her. When relatives and acquaintances pleaded with him to return to live with his wife, he said: "If I do not receive 1,000 dollars, I do not want her." For a long time the Weksberg family scraped together this heavy sum, and when the appointed day came and they demanded that the "son-in-law" take the 1,000 dollars provided he return to his wife, he answered with still greater insolence: "Now it comes to 3,000 dollars, and if not — nothing at all will come of it!" The bride's parents had to return home to Czeski Cieszyn empty-handed, and their daughter remained a living agunah, for he would not even give her a divorce (get). Last Sunday the son-in-law traveled on business to Oświęcim, and as he slept at night in the hotel his father-in-law, Eli[—] Weksberg, came to him in a dream and said: "If you do not return to my daughter in Czeski Cieszyn — I will strangle you at once." On rising in the morning the dreamer laughed off the whole story and paid it no mind; he only told his friends about it. On the third day the son-in-law died.
